title.raw: How to Add a Job Board or Careers Page to WordPress with WP Job Manager
title.rendered: How to Add a Job Board or Careers Page to WordPress with WP Job Manager

content.raw:
This guide contains affiliate links. If you buy through them, we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. It never changes our recommendations. Learn more.

Quick answer: install the free WP Job Manager plugin, create three pages (Jobs, Post a Job and Job Dashboard), and add a shortcode to each: [jobs], [submit_job_form] and [job_dashboard]. That gives you searchable job listings, front-end job submission and an employer dashboard. Paid add-ons (from $29 a year) add applications, paid listings, job alerts and more.

Key takeaways

  • WP Job Manager is a free plugin made by Automattic and works with most themes.
  • It suits both a simple careers page for your own business and a full job board where employers post jobs.
  • Listings include Google job schema, which helps them appear in job search results.
  • Add-ons cost from $29 to $79 a year each, or all core add-ons in a bundle from $159 a year.
Quick pick

Adding job listings to your site? Get WP Job Manager →

We may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. It never changes our recommendations.

Careers page or job board: which do you need?

WP Job Manager handles both. A careers page is the quickest win: it gives job seekers a page on your own domain instead of only third-party job sites.

What does the free WP Job Manager plugin include?

  • Searchable, filterable listings by keyword, location, category and job type.
  • Front-end forms so employers (or you) can submit and preview jobs without the admin area.
  • A jobs dashboard where logged-in employers manage their listings and see views.
  • Apply options: each job can use an application email address or a link to an external form.
  • Google job schema, so search engines can read your listings.
  • RSS feeds of jobs.

Its WordPress.org page showed 70,000+ active installations and a 4.4 out of 5 rating when we checked, and it was updated in November 2026.

How to set up WP Job Manager: step by step

  1. Install the plugin. Plugins → Add New, search for “WP Job Manager”, install and activate. The setup wizard can create the pages for you.
  2. Create the Jobs page. Add a page called “Jobs” (or “Careers”) and insert a Shortcode block containing [jobs].
  3. Create the Post a Job page (job boards only). Add a page with [submit_job_form] for front-end submissions.
  4. Create the Job Dashboard page (job boards only). Add a page with [job_dashboard] so logged-in employers can manage listings.
  5. Review the settings. Under Job Listings → Settings, choose listings per page, whether categories and job types are on, who can post, whether new jobs need your approval and how long listings last.
  6. Add categories and job types such as Full-time, Part-time and Contract.
  7. Post a test job, check it on desktop and mobile, then publish your real openings.
  8. Add the Jobs page to your menu and link it from your About or Contact page.

The official shortcode reference also says not to wrap shortcodes in other tags. In the block editor, use a Shortcode block.

Useful shortcode options

Which paid add-ons are worth it?

These are the “from” prices on WP Job Manager’s core add-ons page in November 2026 (single-site licenses with a year of updates and support):

Our suggestion: for a careers page, start free and add Applications only if you want applications kept in WordPress instead of email. For a paid job board, start with Simple Paid Listings (or WC Paid Listings if you already run WooCommerce) plus Job Alerts. WP Job Manager offers refunds within 14 days of purchase.

Tips for a job board that works

  • Require approval for new listings so spam does not go live.
  • Set listings to expire (for example after 30 days) so old jobs do not linger.
  • Write clear titles (“Part-time Dental Receptionist, Austin”) and include pay where you can.
  • Applications contain personal data: use HTTPS, keep WordPress updated, and see our secure form guide.
  • Check your listings in Google Search Console after launch; our Search Console guide shows how.

WP Job Manager pros and cons

FAQ

Is WP Job Manager free?

Yes. The core plugin is free on WordPress.org. Paid add-ons extend it.

Will my jobs show up in Google job search?

WP Job Manager adds Google job schema to listings, which makes them eligible. Google decides what it shows, so follow its job posting guidelines and keep listings current.

Can I charge employers to post jobs?

Yes, with the Simple Paid Listings add-on (Stripe or PayPal) or WC Paid Listings (WooCommerce).

Does it work with my theme?

It is shortcode-based and works with most themes, sometimes with small CSS tweaks. Some themes are built specifically for WP Job Manager.

Can candidates upload a resume?

With the Applications add-on candidates can apply on your site, and Resume Manager lets them submit full resumes.

Conclusion

For a careers page, the free WP Job Manager plugin and one Jobs page with [jobs] are all you need. For a full job board, add the submission and dashboard pages, require approval, and add paid listings and job alerts when you are ready to earn from it. Prices and features were checked on the vendors’ official pages in November 2026. They change, so confirm on the vendor’s site before you buy.

title.raw: How to Sell Online Courses on WordPress with Sensei LMS (2026)
title.rendered: How to Sell Online Courses on WordPress with Sensei LMS (2026)

content.raw:
This guide contains affiliate links. If you buy through them, we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. It never changes our recommendations. Learn more.

Quick answer: to sell online courses on WordPress with Sensei LMS you need three things: the free Sensei LMS plugin to build courses, the free WooCommerce plugin to take payments, and Sensei Pro ($179 a year for one site) to connect the two. You then pair each course with a WooCommerce product, and students are enrolled automatically when they pay.

Key takeaways

  • The free Sensei LMS plugin lets you publish unlimited free courses with lessons, basic quizzes and certificates.
  • Selling courses needs both WooCommerce and Sensei Pro. The free plugin alone cannot take payments.
  • You keep your students, content and data on your own site, and choose your own payment provider.
  • Sensei is not a video host: upload videos to VideoPress, YouTube or Vimeo and embed them.
Quick pick

Ready to build a course? Get Sensei LMS →

We may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. It never changes our recommendations.

Why sell courses on your own WordPress site?

Hosted course platforms are quick to start, but you pay monthly fees and sometimes a share of each sale, and your students live on someone else’s platform. Selling from your own WordPress site means you own the student list and content, choose your payment provider and keep course pages on your domain, where they build your search traffic.

The trade-off is setup and upkeep: you are responsible for hosting, updates and backups. If you are new to WordPress, read how to start a WordPress website first.

What is Sensei LMS?

Sensei LMS is a learning management system (LMS) plugin for WordPress made by Automattic, the company behind WooCommerce and WordPress.com. It turns WordPress into a course platform: you build courses from lessons and quizzes in the normal block editor, and students get a distraction-free “learning mode” that works with any theme.

Sensei free vs Sensei Pro

Sensei Pro has a 14-day refund guarantee and no free trial, because the free plugin lets you try most of the course-building features first. An Agency plan ($360 a year) covers up to 20 sites.

What you need before you start

  • WordPress hosting. Courses with many students and video embeds need reliable hosting. A managed host such as Pressable or the options in our hosting comparison will handle it.
  • A video host. Sensei embeds video from VideoPress, YouTube or Vimeo; it does not store videos itself.
  • A payment account. WooPayments, Stripe, PayPal or another gateway WooCommerce supports.
  • Your course outline: modules, lessons, and what each quiz checks.

How to sell a course with Sensei: step by step

  1. Install Sensei LMS. Plugins → Add New, search “Sensei LMS”, install and activate, then run the setup wizard.
  2. Create your course. Go to Sensei LMS → Courses → Add New. Add a title, description and featured image, then use the course outline block to add modules and lessons.
  3. Write your lessons. Each lesson is a normal block editor page: text, images, embedded video and downloads.
  4. Add quizzes. Attach a quiz to a lesson and set a pass mark if students must pass to continue.
  5. Install WooCommerce and Sensei Pro. Add the free WooCommerce plugin and set up your payment gateway, then install Sensei Pro with your license key.
  6. Create a product for the course. In WooCommerce, add a product with the course price (a one-off price, or a subscription if you add WooCommerce Subscriptions).
  7. Pair the course and product. In the course settings, link the WooCommerce product. Buyers are enrolled automatically after checkout.
  8. Test the whole journey. Buy the course yourself (use a test payment mode or a 100% coupon), check the enrollment email, take a lesson and finish a quiz.
  9. Launch. Add the course to your menu, link it from relevant blog posts, and announce it to your email list.

To sell memberships instead of single courses, Sensei works with WooCommerce Memberships; see our WooCommerce extensions guide for what that and Subscriptions cost.

Tips for a course that sells

  • Make lesson one free as a preview, so visitors can see the quality before they buy.
  • Keep lessons short (5 to 15 minutes) with one clear outcome each.
  • Use drip content (Pro) for cohort-style courses so students move through together.
  • Collect testimonials after the first cohort and add them to the sales page.
  • Keep your site secure: courses hold student accounts and payment flows. Follow our WordPress security checklist.

Sensei pros and cons

FAQ

Can I sell courses with the free Sensei LMS plugin?

No. Sensei’s own FAQ says you can create courses without WooCommerce, but to sell them you need WooCommerce and Sensei Pro.

How much does Sensei Pro cost?

When we checked, Sensei Pro was $179 a year for one site, and the Agency plan was $360 a year for up to 20 sites. Prices can change; check the pricing page.

Does Sensei take a cut of my sales?

Sensei’s pages do not mention a revenue share. You pay your payment provider’s transaction fees.

Can I give certificates?

Yes. Sensei offers a free Certificates extension that creates downloadable PDF certificates when students complete a course.

Do I need WooPayments?

No. Sensei says you can use any WooCommerce payment provider, such as Stripe or PayPal.

Conclusion

Sensei LMS is a sensible way to sell courses from a site you own: build with the free plugin, then add WooCommerce and Sensei Pro when you are ready to take payments. Test the full student journey before launch, and keep hosting and security in good shape. Prices and features were checked on the vendors’ official pages in November 2026. They change, so confirm on the vendor’s site before you buy.

Ready to start? See Sensei LMS and Sensei Pro (14-day refund guarantee on Pro). We may earn a fee at no extra cost to you.

title.raw: Essential WooCommerce Extensions for a Small Online Store (2026)
title.rendered: Essential WooCommerce Extensions for a Small Online Store (2026)

content.raw:
This guide contains affiliate links. If you buy through them, we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. It never changes our recommendations. Learn more.

Quick answer: a small WooCommerce store usually needs only three free extensions to start: a payment gateway (WooPayments or Stripe), a shipping tool and automated tax. Add paid extensions only for a specific job: Product Add-Ons for custom options, Subscriptions for recurring billing, Bookings for appointments, and AutomateWoo for marketing emails. Every paid extension on the official WooCommerce Marketplace comes with a 30-day refund window.

Key takeaways

  • WooCommerce itself is free and takes no revenue share. You pay for hosting, payment processing and any paid extensions.
  • Marketplace extensions are annual subscriptions that include updates and support. Budget for renewals.
  • Payments, shipping labels and tax calculation are free extensions; you pay per transaction or per label.
  • Buy a paid extension when a customer need is clear, not “just in case”. Each one adds cost and upkeep.
Quick pick

Building a store? Browse the official WooCommerce Marketplace →

We may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. It never changes our recommendations.

How do WooCommerce extensions work?

WooCommerce is a free plugin that turns a WordPress site into an online store. Extensions are add-on plugins that give it new abilities. The official WooCommerce Marketplace sells them as yearly subscriptions: the pricing page puts most paid extensions between $29 and $299 a year each. Each paid product page says the subscription includes updates, customer support and a 30-day money-back guarantee, and you can choose a 1-year or 2-year plan (the 2-year option showed a 20% saving when we checked).

You do not need everything at launch. The rule we use with clients: install the free essentials, launch, then add a paid extension when real customers ask for something.

The free essentials every store needs

1. A payment gateway: WooPayments or Stripe

WooPayments is WooCommerce’s own payments extension. It is free to install with no setup or monthly fees, and charges per transaction. For US cards, its fees page listed 2.9% + $0.30 per transaction when we checked, with a $15 dispute fee; rates vary by country and card type. The free Stripe extension is the main alternative and supports Apple Pay, Google Pay and buy-now-pay-later options. Pick one, not both, unless you have a reason.

2. WooCommerce Shipping

Free. It lets US-based stores buy and print USPS, UPS, DHL Express and FedEx labels from the WordPress dashboard at discounted rates. You pay only for labels. If you ship from outside the US, use your carrier’s own extension instead.

3. WooCommerce Tax

Free. It calculates sales tax automatically by location for supported countries, including the US, Canada, Australia, the UK and many EU countries. It does not file or pay your tax returns, so keep your accountant in the loop.

Paid extensions worth buying (when you need them)

Prices are the 1-year plan shown on each product page in November 2026.

Product Add-Ons ($79/year)

The most useful first purchase for many shops. If you sell anything personalised (printed names, engraving, custom sizes, gift messages), Product Add-Ons lets customers choose options on the product page and adds the cost to the price.

WooCommerce Subscriptions ($279/year)

For subscription boxes, memberships billed monthly, retainers or replenishment products. It automates renewals through supported payment gateways. It is one of the more expensive extensions, so only buy it if recurring billing is part of your business model.

WooCommerce Bookings ($249/year)

For service businesses that take paid appointments, classes or rentals. Before buying, check whether a simpler scheduling tool would do; our appointment scheduling guide compares standalone options. Bookings’ marketplace reviews are mixed, so test it within the 30-day refund window.

AutomateWoo ($159/year)

Marketing automation inside WooCommerce: abandoned-cart reminders, follow-up emails after purchase, review requests and personalised coupons. For a store with steady traffic, recovering a few abandoned carts a month can cover the cost. SMS needs a separate paid Twilio account.

WooCommerce Memberships ($199/year)

Restricts products or content to members and gives members discounts. Pair it with Subscriptions if you want members to pay monthly. If you sell courses rather than memberships, look at Sensei LMS instead.

Recommended setups by store type

Tips to avoid extension bloat

  • Buy from the official marketplace or a well-reviewed developer, and check the “last updated” date and compatibility.
  • Test new extensions on a staging site before your live store.
  • Keep a list of what each extension does and its renewal date. Cancel what you no longer use.
  • Fast hosting matters more for a store than for a brochure site; see our Pressable review and speed guide.
  • Protect checkout and customer data: follow our WordPress security checklist.

FAQ

Is WooCommerce free?

Yes. The WooCommerce plugin is free and open source with no monthly fee or revenue share. You pay for hosting, payment processing and any paid extensions or themes.

Do WooCommerce extensions stop working if I do not renew?

The marketplace subscription covers updates and support for the plan period. Without renewing you lose access to updates and support, which matters for security and compatibility. Check each product’s terms.

Can I get a refund on a WooCommerce extension?

Quick answer: Pressable is managed WordPress hosting owned by Automattic. Plans start at $250 a year for one site (about $20.83 a month, billed yearly) and every plan includes staging sites, a global CDN, daily file backups with hourly database backups, 24/7 support and a free Jetpack Security license. It is priced above budget hosts, so it suits businesses, online stores and agencies that want WordPress handled for them.

Key takeaways

  • Plans are sized by number of WordPress installs, monthly visits and storage, not by “unlimited” promises.
  • Every Signature plan includes Jetpack Security, which Pressable values at $239 a year.
  • Going over your visits or storage is billed: $1.20 per 1,000 visits and $1.00 per GB, per the pricing page.
  • There is a 30-day money-back guarantee, but no free trial.
Quick pick

Want managed WordPress hosting? See Pressable’s plans →

We may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. It never changes our recommendations.

What is Pressable?

Pressable is a managed WordPress host: it runs only WordPress, and handles server setup, caching, core updates, backups and security for you. It is part of Automattic, the company behind WordPress.com, Jetpack and WooCommerce, and pitches itself mainly at agencies, WooCommerce stores and growing businesses.

Managed hosting costs more than shared hosting. You pay for performance, expert WordPress support and less time spent on maintenance. If you are new to hosting types, start with our guide to starting a WordPress website.

How much does Pressable cost?

These are the Signature plans on Pressable’s pricing page in November 2026, billed yearly (yearly billing shows “2 months free” compared with monthly):

Larger Signature plans (up to 100 installs) and custom Premium plans (from $350 a month, sales-led) are also listed. Monthly billing is available; the homepage showed the one-site plan at $25 a month. Each plan also includes the same number of staging and sandbox sites as installs.

Watch the overage fees. Usage above your plan’s visits and storage is billed at $1.20 per 1,000 visits and $1.00 per GB. Check your current monthly visits in your analytics before choosing a plan, and leave headroom for busy seasons.

What is included on every plan?

The Jetpack Security license is the stand-out value. If you would otherwise buy Jetpack backups and scanning separately, that cost is covered by the hosting plan. Our Jetpack review explains what it includes.

Performance and data centers

Each site runs with dedicated PHP workers (Pressable lists 5 per site on Signature plans) and automatic failover between a primary and secondary server. Its data-center help article lists four primary locations: Amsterdam, Washington DC, Los Angeles and Dallas. You choose one when you create a site and cannot change it later, so pick the one closest to most of your visitors. The global CDN serves cached pages and images from locations nearer your visitors.

Pressable pros and cons

Who is Pressable best for?

  • Agencies and freelancers managing several client sites from one dashboard. The multi-install plans and staging per site fit that workflow.
  • WooCommerce stores that need dependable performance and support. See our WooCommerce extensions guide for the store side.
  • Growing business sites that have outgrown shared hosting and want someone else to handle updates, caching and backups.

Who should skip it: a brand-new blog or hobby site with little traffic. A budget host is cheaper while you find your feet, and you can move later. Compare alternatives in our managed hosting comparison, our SiteGround review and our Hostinger review. If you would rather not manage hosting at all, WordPress.com bundles hosting into its plans.

How to move your site to Pressable

  1. Pick a plan with enough visits for your current traffic and the data center nearest your visitors.
  2. Request a free migration from Pressable’s team, or use its migration plugin.
  3. Test the copied site on its temporary URL: pages, forms, checkout and logins.
  4. Point your domain’s DNS to Pressable and confirm SSL is active.
  5. Connect Jetpack Security and confirm the first backup completes.

Our guide to moving a website to a new host covers each step and the checks that protect your search rankings.

FAQ

Is Pressable owned by Automattic?

Yes. Pressable is an Automattic company, alongside WordPress.com, Jetpack and WooCommerce.

Does Pressable have a free trial?

No standard free trial was listed when we checked. It offers a 30-day money-back guarantee instead.

Does Pressable include email?

No. Like most managed WordPress hosts, Pressable focuses on WordPress. Use a business email service; see our business email guide.

What happens if I go over my monthly visits?

Pressable bills overages: $1.20 per 1,000 visits and $1.00 per GB of storage above your plan, according to its pricing page. You can upgrade at any time.

Can I host WooCommerce on Pressable?

Yes. Pressable specifically markets its hosting to WooCommerce stores.

Verdict: is Pressable worth it?

Pressable is a solid pick if you want managed WordPress hosting from the company that builds WordPress.com, especially if you value having Jetpack Security, staging and expert support included. It costs more than budget hosting, and the visit-based limits mean you should size your plan carefully. For an established business site, store or agency it is worth shortlisting. title.rendered: Jetpack Review (2026): What It Does, Free vs Paid, and Is It Worth It?

content.raw:
This guide contains affiliate links. If you buy through them, we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. It never changes our recommendations. Learn more.

Quick answer: Jetpack is a free WordPress plugin made by Automattic, the company behind WordPress.com. The free version adds site stats, downtime alerts, brute-force login protection, an image CDN, a newsletter and automatic social sharing. The paid plans add real-time backups, malware scanning, a firewall, spam protection and bigger limits. Most small sites should start free and pay only when they need reliable backups.

Key takeaways

  • The free plugin is genuinely useful: stats, downtime monitoring, login protection, an image CDN and social auto-sharing cost nothing.
  • Backups are the main reason to pay. Real-time, off-site backups with one-click restore are not in the free plan.
  • You can install single-purpose plugins instead (Jetpack Boost, Protect, Social, VaultPress Backup) if you only need one feature.
  • Jetpack needs a free WordPress.com account connection, and your site must be publicly reachable.
Quick pick

Want backups and security in one place? Compare Jetpack plans →

We may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. It never changes our recommendations.

Disclosure from our own setup: ProSiteGuide runs Jetpack. We use Jetpack Social to auto-share new guides to our Facebook Page and LinkedIn, so parts of this review come from day-to-day use, not just the sales page.

What is Jetpack?

Jetpack is a plugin that connects your self-hosted WordPress site to Automattic’s cloud services. Some features run on Automattic’s servers (stats, the image CDN, backups, downtime checks), which is why you link the site to a free WordPress.com account during setup. Its WordPress.org listing shows millions of active installs, which makes it one of the most widely used plugins in the directory.

Jetpack is not a page builder or a theme. Think of it as a toolbox for security, performance, growth and site management, where you switch on only the modules you want.

What does the free Jetpack plugin include?

Jetpack’s pricing page lists features that “work the same on every plan,” and its free plan comparison sets the limits. The useful free features are:

Note the stats rule: the free plan covers personal sites. Jetpack’s plan table lists commercial-use stats in the paid plans, so a business site should read the current terms before relying on free stats.

What do the paid plans add?

The paid plans are where Jetpack becomes a security and backup service. On the pricing page in November 2026, the two all-in-one plans were:

Jetpack often runs first-year discounts (a 50% Black Friday offer was running when we checked), and the pricing page says plans renew at the regular price. Budget for the regular rate. Refunds are available within 14 days for yearly plans and 7 days for monthly plans, according to the pricing FAQ.

You can also buy single products. When we checked, VaultPress Backup started at $9.95/month regular (billed yearly), Jetpack Social’s paid tier was $9.95/month billed $119.40 yearly, and Jetpack Boost’s paid tier was $19.95/month billed $239.40 yearly.

Is Jetpack Backup worth paying for?

For most business sites, yes, if your host does not already give you reliable off-site backups. Jetpack’s VaultPress Backup saves changes in real time, stores copies on Jetpack’s servers (not your hosting account), and lets you restore to any point from the activity log with one click, even when the site is offline.

Check your host first. Many managed WordPress hosts include daily backups, and some (Pressable, for example) include Jetpack Security on every plan. Paying twice for backups is a common waste. Our website maintenance guide explains how often to test a restore, whichever tool you use.

Jetpack Boost and the image CDN: do they speed up your site?

They can help. The free Boost plugin optimizes CSS loading, defers non-essential JavaScript, caches pages and gives you performance scores. The paid tier automates critical CSS and adds performance history. The image CDN serves images from Automattic’s servers.

Speed still starts with good hosting and a light theme. Use Boost alongside the fixes in our Core Web Vitals guide, and avoid stacking two caching plugins (for example Boost page caching plus your host’s cache) without testing.

Jetpack Social: how we use it

Jetpack Social’s free tier auto-shares each new post to connected accounts when you publish, with a preview and an optional custom message. It supports Facebook, Instagram, Threads, Bluesky, LinkedIn, Mastodon, Nextdoor and Tumblr. The paid tier adds per-network custom messages and media, templates and a social image generator.

Our honest limitation from using it: an auto-share posts one image per post. If you want carousels or multi-image posts on Facebook, you still need Meta Business Suite.

Jetpack pros and cons

Who should use Jetpack?

  • Bloggers and small business sites on regular hosting: install the free plugin for stats, downtime alerts and social sharing.
  • Sites that take leads or orders: add real-time backups (VaultPress Backup or a plan that includes it) if your host does not back up off-site.
  • Sites already on a managed host with backups and a firewall: you may only need the free features.
  • Developers who prefer separate tools: pick the single-purpose plugins instead of the full plugin.

Spam is the other common reason to upgrade. Paid plans include Akismet, the anti-spam service from the same company; it is also sold on its own. Our essential WordPress plugins list and security plugin comparison show where Jetpack fits next to other options.

How to set up Jetpack in 5 steps

  1. In your dashboard go to Plugins → Add New, search for “Jetpack”, then install and activate it.
  2. Click “Set up Jetpack” and connect (or create) a free WordPress.com account.
  3. Choose the free plan to start. You can upgrade later from the Jetpack dashboard.
  4. Under Jetpack → Settings, switch on what you want: brute-force protection, downtime monitoring, the image CDN, stats.
  5. Under Jetpack → Social, connect your Facebook Page and LinkedIn so new posts share automatically.

FAQ

Is Jetpack free?

Yes, the core plugin is free. Backups, malware scanning, the firewall, Akismet spam protection, commercial stats and higher limits are paid.

Does Jetpack slow down WordPress?

Jetpack loads only the modules you turn on, and several of them (the image CDN, lazy loading, Boost) are meant to speed sites up. Test your pages in PageSpeed Insights before and after enabling features.

Do I need Jetpack if my host has backups?

Not necessarily. If your host keeps daily off-site backups you can restore yourself, Jetpack Backup is optional. It adds real-time backups and a restore that works even if the host has an outage.

Can I use Jetpack on WordPress.com?

WordPress.com sites already include many Jetpack features as part of their plans. The plugin is mainly for self-hosted WordPress.org sites.

Is Jetpack safe?

Jetpack is built by Automattic and is one of the most installed plugins on WordPress.org. As with any plugin, keep it updated.

Verdict: is Jetpack worth it?

Install the free plugin. Its stats, downtime alerts, login protection and social sharing are worth having on almost any WordPress site. Pay for a plan when you need off-site, real-time backups and malware scanning that your host does not already provide, and compare the regular renewal price, not the first-year discount. Prices and features were checked on the vendors’ official pages in November 2026. They change, so confirm on the vendor’s site before you buy.

The paid plans add real-time backups, malware scanning, a firewall, spam protection and bigger limits. Most small sites should start free and pay only when they need reliable backups.

Key takeaways

  • The free plugin is genuinely useful: stats, downtime monitoring, login protection, an image CDN and social auto-sharing cost nothing.
  • Backups are the main reason to pay. Real-time, off-site backups with one-click restore are not in the free plan.
  • You can install single-purpose plugins instead (Jetpack Boost, Protect, Social, VaultPress Backup) if you only need one feature.
  • Jetpack needs a free WordPress.com account connection, and your site must be publicly reachable.

Disclosure from our own setup: ProSiteGuide runs Jetpack. We use Jetpack Social to auto-share new guides to our Facebook Page and LinkedIn, so parts of this review come from day-to-day use, not just the sales page.

What is Jetpack?

Jetpack is a plugin that connects your self-hosted WordPress site to Automattic’s cloud services. Some features run on Automattic’s servers (stats, the image CDN, backups, downtime checks), which is why you link the site to a free WordPress.com account during setup. Its WordPress.org listing shows millions of active installs, which makes it one of the most widely used plugins in the directory.

Jetpack is not a page builder or a theme. Think of it as a toolbox for security, performance, growth and site management, where you switch on only the modules you want.

What does the free Jetpack plugin include?

Jetpack’s pricing page lists features that “work the same on every plan,” and its free plan comparison sets the limits. The useful free features are:

Note the stats rule: the free plan covers personal sites. Jetpack’s plan table lists commercial-use stats in the paid plans, so a business site should read the current terms before relying on free stats.

What do the paid plans add?

The paid plans are where Jetpack becomes a security and backup service. On the pricing page in November 2026, the two all-in-one plans were:

Jetpack often runs first-year discounts (a 50% Black Friday offer was running when we checked), and the pricing page says plans renew at the regular price. Budget for the regular rate. Refunds are available within 14 days for yearly plans and 7 days for monthly plans, according to the pricing FAQ.

You can also buy single products. When we checked, VaultPress Backup started at $9.95/month regular (billed yearly), Jetpack Social’s paid tier was $9.95/month billed $119.40 yearly, and Jetpack Boost’s paid tier was $19.95/month billed $239.40 yearly.

Is Jetpack Backup worth paying for?

For most business sites, yes, if your host does not already give you reliable off-site backups. Jetpack’s VaultPress Backup saves changes in real time, stores copies on Jetpack’s servers (not your hosting account), and lets you restore to any point from the activity log with one click, even when the site is offline.

Check your host first. Many managed WordPress hosts include daily backups, and some (Pressable, for example) include Jetpack Security on every plan. Paying twice for backups is a common waste. Our website maintenance guide explains how often to test a restore, whichever tool you use.

Jetpack Boost and the image CDN: do they speed up your site?

They can help. The free Boost plugin optimizes CSS loading, defers non-essential JavaScript, caches pages and gives you performance scores. The paid tier automates critical CSS and adds performance history. The image CDN serves images from Automattic’s servers.

Speed still starts with good hosting and a light theme. Use Boost alongside the fixes in our Core Web Vitals guide, and avoid stacking two caching plugins (for example Boost page caching plus your host’s cache) without testing.

Jetpack Social: how we use it

Jetpack Social’s free tier auto-shares each new post to connected accounts when you publish, with a preview and an optional custom message. It supports Facebook, Instagram, Threads, Bluesky, LinkedIn, Mastodon, Nextdoor and Tumblr. The paid tier adds per-network custom messages and media, templates and a social image generator.

Our honest limitation from using it: an auto-share posts one image per post. If you want carousels or multi-image posts on Facebook, you still need Meta Business Suite.

Jetpack pros and cons

Who should use Jetpack?

  • Bloggers and small business sites on regular hosting: install the free plugin for stats, downtime alerts and social sharing.
  • Sites that take leads or orders: add real-time backups (VaultPress Backup or a plan that includes it) if your host does not back up off-site.
  • Sites already on a managed host with backups and a firewall: you may only need the free features.
  • Developers who prefer separate tools: pick the single-purpose plugins instead of the full plugin.

Spam is the other common reason to upgrade. Paid plans include Akismet, the anti-spam service from the same company; it is also sold on its own. Our essential WordPress plugins list and security plugin comparison show where Jetpack fits next to other options.

How to set up Jetpack in 5 steps

  1. In your dashboard go to Plugins → Add New, search for “Jetpack”, then install and activate it.
  2. Click “Set up Jetpack” and connect (or create) a free WordPress.com account.
  3. Choose the free plan to start. You can upgrade later from the Jetpack dashboard.
  4. Under Jetpack → Settings, switch on what you want: brute-force protection, downtime monitoring, the image CDN, stats.
  5. Under Jetpack → Social, connect your Facebook Page and LinkedIn so new posts share automatically.

FAQ

Is Jetpack free?

Yes, the core plugin is free. Backups, malware scanning, the firewall, Akismet spam protection, commercial stats and higher limits are paid.

Does Jetpack slow down WordPress?

Jetpack loads only the modules you turn on, and several of them (the image CDN, lazy loading, Boost) are meant to speed sites up. Test your pages in PageSpeed Insights before and after enabling features.

Do I need Jetpack if my host has backups?

Not necessarily. If your host keeps daily off-site backups you can restore yourself, Jetpack Backup is optional. It adds real-time backups and a restore that works even if the host has an outage.

Can I use Jetpack on WordPress.com?

WordPress.com sites already include many Jetpack features as part of their plans. The plugin is mainly for self-hosted WordPress.org sites.

Is Jetpack safe?

Jetpack is built by Automattic and is one of the most installed plugins on WordPress.org. As with any plugin, keep it updated.

Verdict: is Jetpack worth it?

Install the free plugin. Its stats, downtime alerts, login protection and social sharing are worth having on almost any WordPress site. Pay for a plan when you need off-site, real-time backups and malware scanning that your host does not already provide, and compare the regular renewal price, not the first-year discount. Prices and features were checked on the vendors’ official pages in November 2026. They change, so confirm on the vendor’s site before you buy.

title.rendered: How to Start a WordPress Website: A Beginner’s Step-by-Step Guide (2026)

content.raw:
This guide contains affiliate links. If you buy through them, we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. It never changes our recommendations. Learn more.

Quick answer: to start a WordPress website, you need four things: a domain name, web hosting, the free WordPress software installed on that hosting, and a theme. Most hosts install WordPress in one click, so a basic site can be online in an afternoon. Then you add essential pages, a few plugins and run a launch checklist.

Key takeaways

  • WordPress.org (self-hosted) is the free software you install on your own hosting. WordPress.com is a hosted service that bundles hosting into a plan.
  • You pay for two things: a domain (yearly) and hosting. Compare the renewal price, not just the first-year offer.
  • Pick a block theme, keep plugins to a short list of categories, and set permalinks before you publish anything.
  • Backups, security and a tested contact form matter more than fancy features at launch.
Quick pick

Registering a domain? Search your firm’s domain on Namecheap →

We may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. It never changes our recommendations.

What do you need to start a WordPress website?

You need a domain name (your address, like yourbakery.com), hosting (the computer that stores your site and serves it to visitors) and WordPress itself. WordPress is software that lets you create and edit pages without writing code. The picture below shows how the pieces connect.

Official requirements are modest. WordPress.org recommends a host that supports PHP 8.3 or greater, MariaDB 10.11+ or MySQL 8.4+, and HTTPS (WordPress requirements). Any reputable host that advertises WordPress support already meets this, so you rarely need to check it yourself.

WordPress.org vs WordPress.com: which should you use?

Both run on the same WordPress software. The main difference is hosting: WordPress.com includes managed hosting, while WordPress.org is a free download that you upload to a host you choose and pay for yourself (WordPress.com Support). When people say “WordPress for beginners” they usually mean one of these two paths.

This guide follows the self-hosted WordPress.org route, because it is the most common choice for blogs and small businesses and the one with the most room to grow. If you would rather not manage anything, WordPress.com is a legitimate option; compare its current plans on its own pricing page.

Step 1: How do you choose and register a domain name?

Choose a short, easy-to-spell name that matches your business or brand, then register it with a domain registrar. A domain name is your website’s permanent address, and you rent it by the year.

  1. Keep it short and easy to say aloud. Avoid hyphens and numbers.
  2. Prefer .com if it is available; it is the extension people type by default. A local or niche extension can work if it suits your brand.
  3. Check that the matching social handles are free.
  4. Turn on auto-renew and keep your contact details current so you never lose the name.
  5. Check the renewal price. Registrars often advertise a low first-year price that rises later.

You can search for and register a name at Namecheap’s domain search. Our walkthrough on registering a domain on Namecheap covers each screen, and our registrar comparison helps if you want to shop around.

Step 2: How do you choose WordPress hosting?

Compare hosts on renewal price, backups, SSL, support and how easily you can upgrade. Cheap introductory pricing is common, so read what the plan costs when it renews. Hosting is the service that keeps your site online around the clock.

Hosts that offer WordPress plans include Namecheap’s WordPress hosting, among many others. For deeper comparisons, read our review of a popular budget host, our review of a beginner-friendly managed host and our review of a premium managed WordPress host. Weighing two of them head to head? See our two-host comparison. For overall budgeting, what a website costs breaks down the ongoing expenses. We do not quote hosting prices here because they change often; see each provider’s pricing page.

If you bought your domain and hosting separately, you must point the domain to the host. Our guide to connecting a Namecheap domain to hosting shows how.

Step 3: How do you install WordPress?

Most hosts include a one-click installer in their control panel. You choose your domain, create an admin username and a strong password, and the installer does the rest. The exact screens differ by host, so follow your provider’s help page.

  1. Log in to your hosting account and find the WordPress installer (often under “Websites”, “Apps” or “Auto Installer”).
  2. Select your domain and enter a site name, admin username and password. Avoid “admin” as the username.
  3. Confirm HTTPS is enabled, then finish the install.
  4. Log in at yourdomain.com/wp-admin with the details you just created.

Prefer a manual install? WordPress.org provides the download and an installation guide at wordpress.org/download.

Step 4: What basic WordPress settings should you change first?

Set your site title, timezone and permalinks before you publish anything. These take five minutes and are awkward to change later, especially permalinks.

Site title, tagline and timezone

Go to Settings → General. Enter your site title and a short tagline, confirm the administration email, and choose your timezone so scheduled posts go out on time. WordPress documents each field on its Settings General screen page.

Permalinks

Permalinks are the permanent URLs of your pages and posts. In Settings → Permalinks, choose a readable structure such as “Post name” so a page looks like yoursite.com/about/ instead of ?p=123. WordPress notes that links are meant to be permanent, so set this before you publish (Permalinks screen documentation).

Search visibility

Under Settings → Reading, make sure “Discourage search engines from indexing this site” is unchecked when you are ready to launch. Many owners tick it while building and forget to clear it.

Step 5: Should you use a block theme or a page builder?

For most beginners, start with a block theme. A block theme uses WordPress’s built-in blocks for every part of the site, including header, menus and footer, which you edit in the Site Editor (block themes documentation). A page builder is a plugin or theme layer that gives you its own drag-and-drop editor.

Browse free themes in the official theme directory and filter by “Block themes”. Choose one that is regularly updated and fits your content, and keep the design simple. If you want curated picks, see our guide to WordPress themes.

Step 6: Which pages does a new website need?

Start with five pages: Home, About, Services (or Blog), Contact and Privacy Policy. You can add more later; these cover what visitors and search engines expect from a new site.

  • Home: say who you help and what to do next, in the first screen. A bakery might lead with “Fresh sourdough, baked daily” and an order button.
  • About: who you are and why people should trust you. Real details beat vague claims.
  • Services or Blog: what you offer, or your latest posts if you are a blogger. A consultant would list services and how an engagement works.
  • Contact: a form plus any email, phone or address you want public.
  • Privacy Policy: explains what data you collect, such as form entries and analytics. WordPress creates a draft under Settings → Privacy that you must review and edit; have a professional check it if you collect sensitive data.

Then build your menu under Appearance → Editor → Navigation (block themes) and set your Home page under Settings → Reading.

Step 7: What are the essential WordPress plugins?

Install a few plugins by category, and no more. A plugin adds a feature to WordPress, and every extra one adds something to maintain and update. These examples all have free versions in the official WordPress.org plugin directory as of November 2026; pricing for any paid tiers is on each vendor’s site.

Check whether your host already provides backups or caching before adding a plugin for the same job. Some hosts also run their own caching tools. For more detail, see our rundown of essential WordPress plugins, our WordPress security checklist and our tips for speeding up your website.

Step 8: What should you check before launching?

Run through a launch checklist: test every form, confirm HTTPS, check on a phone and make sure search engines are allowed in. Print the graphic below or copy it into your notes.

  1. Browse every page on your phone and on a desktop. Fix broken links and missing images.
  2. Submit a test message through your contact form and confirm it reaches your inbox (also check spam).
  3. Confirm automatic backups are scheduled and you know how to restore one.
  4. Delete unused themes and plugins, and update everything that needs it.
  5. Use a strong, unique password and consider two-factor login for admin accounts.
  6. Add your site to Google Search Console and submit your sitemap.

FAQ

How do I make a WordPress website for free?

You can download WordPress.org software for free, but a live site needs a domain and hosting, which cost money. WordPress.com offers a free plan, though it has limits; check its pricing page for what is included.

How long does it take to start a WordPress website?

A basic site can be installed in under an hour with a one-click installer. Writing your pages, choosing a theme and testing usually takes days, depending on how much content you have ready.

Do I need to know how to code to use WordPress?

No. The block editor and block themes let you build pages visually. Code only becomes useful for custom features.

Is WordPress good for beginners?

Yes, with realistic expectations. Installing and editing content is approachable, but you are also responsible for updates, backups and security when you self-host. A managed host or WordPress.com reduces that upkeep.

How much does it cost to start a WordPress website?

Expect to pay for a domain and hosting each year, plus optional premium themes or plugins. Prices vary and promotional rates rise at renewal; see what a website costs and each provider’s pricing page.

Can I switch from WordPress.com to WordPress.org later?

Yes. WordPress.com states that you own your content and are free to move it. Plan the move carefully so your URLs and search rankings are preserved.

Conclusion: your next steps

Register your domain, choose a host with fair renewal pricing and backups, install WordPress, set permalinks and your site title, then add a block theme and five core pages. Finish with a short plugin list and the launch checklist. For a guided overview of our other beginner resources, visit Start Here or compare options on our tool comparisons page.

title.raw: How to Connect a Namecheap Domain to Kinsta, SiteGround or Hostinger (2026)
title.rendered: How to Connect a Namecheap Domain to Kinsta, SiteGround or Hostinger (2026)

content.raw:
Quick answer: To connect a Namecheap domain to your host, either switch the domain to your host's nameservers (Domain List → Manage → Nameservers → Custom DNS) or keep Namecheap's DNS and add the A and CNAME records your host gives you on the Advanced DNS tab. SiteGround and Hostinger accept either method, and Kinsta usually uses records. Move your email records first if the firm already uses email on the domain, or email can stop.

Key takeaways

  • Your host's dashboard tells you exactly which nameservers or records to use. Copy them from there rather than from any guide, including this one.
  • Changing nameservers moves all DNS to your host, including email records. Keeping Namecheap DNS and adding records changes only the website.

title.rendered: How to Register a Law Firm Domain on Namecheap (2026)

content.raw:
Quick answer: To register a law firm domain on Namecheap, search for your firm name, add the domain to your cart, create the account in the firm's name with a firm-controlled email address, skip the extras you have not chosen, and pay. Then turn on auto-renew, two-factor authentication and the registrar lock before you connect your website and email. The purchase takes about ten minutes; the DNS setup afterwards is where most mistakes happen.

Key takeaways

  • The firm, not the web designer, should own the Namecheap account and be listed as the registrant.
  • Namecheap includes free domain privacy on eligible extensions, so you do not need to pay for it.
  • A .com was $12.08 for the first year on sale (regular $15.98) and renews at $19.98 a year when we checked on November 18, 2026. Budget for the renewal, not the promo.
  • Legal extensions cost more: .law $105.98, .attorney $65.98 and .lawyer $74.48 a year at Namecheap.
  • Turn on auto-renew, two-factor authentication and the registrar lock the same day you buy.
Quick pick

Registering a domain? Search your firm’s domain on Namecheap →

We may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. It never changes our recommendations.

Step 1: Which domain should a law firm register?

Start with the .com version of your firm name if it is available and short. If it is taken, a legal extension such as .law (licensed lawyers only), .attorney or .lawyer is the next choice. Our guide to .law vs .com vs .attorney walks through the trade-offs, eligibility rules and trademark checks. Decide on one primary domain before you start shopping, so the checkout does not talk you into extras.

Step 2: How do you search for and buy a domain on Namecheap?

  1. Go to Namecheap's domain search and type the name you want, for example smithfamilylaw.
  2. Namecheap shows the extension you typed and a list of suggestions with prices. Check the yearly price and look for a "premium" label; premium names cost far more and renew higher.
  3. Click Add to cart next to the name you want, then open the cart.
  4. In the cart, choose the registration length (Step 3) and confirm domain privacy shows as free.
  5. Create your account (Step 4), then pay. Namecheap accepts cards and PayPal.

Namecheap often shows a promo code or a sale price for new customers. These apply to the first year only. The renewal price is what the firm will pay every year after that, so compare that number when you shop.

Prices from Namecheap's own domain search and pricing pages, checked November 18, 2026. Prices and promotions change often; confirm the total at checkout.

Step 3: How long should you register the domain for?

One year is fine if auto-renew is on and the card on file stays current. Registering for several years gives a little protection against a missed renewal, and Namecheap offers a discount on extra years for some extensions (for .com it listed 10% off each additional year for 2–5 years and 15% for 6–10 years). Either way, set a calendar reminder a month before the expiry date so someone checks the card and the account email.

Step 4: Who should own the Namecheap account?

Create the account in the firm's name with an email address the firm controls long-term, such as admin@ or it@ your firm's domain, or a partner's firm address. Do not use a web designer's account or an employee's personal Gmail. If a developer needs to work on DNS, give them access through your account rather than registering the domain in theirs. Whoever controls the registrar account controls the firm's website and email.

Step 5: Which checkout add-ons are worth buying?

  • Domain privacy: keep it. It is free on eligible extensions at Namecheap and hides personal contact details from public WHOIS lookups.
  • Hosting: skip it unless you have already chosen Namecheap hosting. Compare options in our law firm hosting guide first.
  • Business email (Private Email): optional. Namecheap's Private Email starts at $14.88 a year for one mailbox after a 30-day trial. Most firms are better served by Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 for retention and compliance features; see Workspace vs 365.
  • PremiumDNS, SSL and other security extras: skip them at checkout. Most hosts include free SSL, and you can add these later if you need them.

Step 6: How do you turn on auto-renew, 2FA and the registrar lock?

  • Auto-renew: in your Namecheap Dashboard, open Domain List and switch on auto-renew for the domain. Keep a valid card on the account.
  • Two-factor authentication: under your profile's security settings, enable 2FA. Namecheap supports an authenticator app or a U2F security key (one method at a time).
  • Registrar lock: open the domain's Manage page, go to Sharing & Transfer, and make sure the domain lock is on. This blocks unauthorized transfers.

Step 7: How do you point a Namecheap domain to your website host?

You connect the domain to your host with DNS. Your host will tell you which of two methods to use:

  • Change the nameservers. In Domain List, click Manage, find Nameservers, switch the dropdown from Namecheap BasicDNS to Custom DNS, paste the nameservers your host gives you and click the green checkmark. DNS is then managed at your host.
  • Keep Namecheap's nameservers and add records. On the Advanced DNS tab, under Host Records, click Add New Record. Usually that is an A record with host @ pointing to your host's IP address, and a CNAME record with host www.

Changes usually take effect within an hour but can take up to 48 hours. Our step-by-step guide to connecting a Namecheap domain to Kinsta, SiteGround or Hostinger covers each host.

Step 8: How do you set up email records (MX, SPF, DKIM, DMARC)?

Email will not reach your domain until it has the right records. MX records say which servers receive mail, SPF lists who may send as you, DKIM signs outgoing mail, and DMARC tells receivers what to do when the checks fail. In Namecheap, open Advanced DNS, set the Mail Settings section to Custom MX, then add the records your email provider gives you. Follow our Google Workspace setup guide or Microsoft 365 setup guide for the exact values. If you changed nameservers to your host in Step 7, add these records at the host instead.

Namecheap domain mistakes to avoid

  • Registering the domain in a vendor's or employee's personal account.
  • Comparing first-year promo prices instead of renewal prices.
  • Leaving auto-renew off, or letting the card on file expire.
  • Changing nameservers without moving your email records first, which can stop email.
  • Buying a premium name without checking its renewal price.

FAQ

Is Namecheap a good registrar for a law firm?

Yes, for most small firms. It has free domain privacy, security-key 2FA, a clear dashboard and a wide choice of extensions. It is not the cheapest at renewal; Porkbun and Cloudflare charge less for .com and legal extensions. See our registrar comparison.

Do I need to buy hosting or email from Namecheap?

No. You can register only the domain and connect it to any host and any email provider.

Can I register a .law domain on Namecheap?

Yes. Namecheap sells .law ($105.98 a year when we checked), but the registry verifies that the registrant is a licensed lawyer or law firm before the domain goes live.

What happens if my domain expires?

The website and email stop working. There is usually a short grace period to renew at the normal price, followed by a redemption period that costs much more. Auto-renew avoids this.

Conclusion and next steps

  1. Choose the name and extension, then search for it at Namecheap.
  2. Buy it in a firm-owned account and keep free privacy; skip extras you have not chosen.
  3. Turn on auto-renew, 2FA and the registrar lock.
  4. Connect your website, then your email records.
  5. Next, read the Start Here page or our website security checklist.

title.raw: Online Legal Directories: Which Are Worth It for Small Firms? (Avvo, Justia, FindLaw, Martindale, 2026)
title.rendered: Online Legal Directories: Which Are Worth It for Small Firms? (Avvo, Justia, FindLaw, Martindale, 2026)

content.raw:
Quick answer: For most small firms, the best legal directories for lawyers are the ones that are free to claim and that match how clients actually search: your Google Business Profile, your state or local bar directory, and a claimed free profile on Avvo, Justia, FindLaw/Lawyers.com or Martindale-Hubbell. Paid upgrades are optional. Buy one only if you can measure calls and signed matters against the fee, and only after your name, address and phone number match everywhere.

Key takeaways

  • Claim and complete free profiles first. A consistent listing costs time, not money.
  • Most directories do not publish prices for paid tiers (as of November 2026). Expect to talk to sales.
  • Name, address and phone (NAP) must match across your website, Google and every directory.
  • Paying for a directory is advertising or lead generation, so check your state bar rules on both.
  • Judge each paid listing by tracked calls and signed matters, not by impressions.

What are legal directories, and do they still matter?

A legal directory is a website that lists lawyers by location and practice area so the public can compare them. They matter in two ways. Some send people to you directly. Others act as independent mentions of your firm on the web, which help confirm that your details are real and consistent. Google says local results are ranked mainly by relevance, distance and prominence, and that prominence includes signals such as links and reviews (see Google's local ranking explanation). Directories can contribute to that picture, but Google also states there is no way to pay for a better local ranking.

This article covers directories. For the rest of the checklist, see our hub, local SEO for lawyers.

Which legal directories are worth it? A side-by-side look

The table summarizes what each directory says on its own site. We did not test any of these, and we give no traffic or lead figures because none are published. This comparison is based on official pages and may be out of date, so confirm details with each provider. Last checked: 17 November 2026.

Avvo vs Justia: which should a small firm start with?

Start with both free profiles if you can keep them accurate. Avvo describes its profile as free to claim and describes the Avvo Rating as a 1 to 10 rating; its paid products are Authority Suite and sponsored advertising, with no published prices (Avvo for Lawyers). Justia offers free profiles to licensed attorneys that you claim and verify, with paid upgrades sold separately. If budget is tight, spend nothing on either until you have tracking in place. The real "avvo vs justia" decision is about price and terms, and both require a conversation or a current pricing page.

FindLaw and Lawyers.com

FindLaw's lawyer page directs lawyers to a premium profile and lawyer marketing solutions, and does not publish pricing (FindLaw for lawyers). Treat it as a paid product and ask for terms in writing, including contract length and cancellation.

Martindale-Hubbell and Super Lawyers

These are as much about reputation as exposure. Martindale-Hubbell runs peer review ratings, where lawyers rate other lawyers; clients do not take part in that peer process. Super Lawyers describes a "patented multiphase selection process" that is "peer influenced and research driven" and selects the "top 5% of attorneys" (Super Lawyers). Its homepage does not state whether a fee applies to selection and gives no marketing prices. Before you advertise a rating, read Rule 7.1 below.

State and local bar association directories

Your state bar's lawyer search and any county or specialty bar directory are often free with membership. They are also a trusted, official-looking source for your name and contact details, so keep them current. Many bars also run lawyer referral services. Ask your bar how its program works and what it costs.

Google Business Profile

This is the most important free listing for local searches. It has its own guide: Google Business Profile for law firms. If you also want to understand paid placement on Google, see Google Local Services Ads for lawyers.

How do I claim and complete a legal directory listing?

  1. Write one master record: exact firm name, street address with suite, main phone, website, and a one-paragraph firm description.
  2. Search the directory for your name. If a profile exists, use its "claim" option and verify your identity; if not, create one.
  3. Fill every field: practice areas, bar admissions, education, languages, photo, website link and office hours.
  4. Reuse your attorney bio text, shortened, so descriptions stay consistent.
  5. Link back to your own site's contact page, not just the homepage.
  6. Remove or merge duplicate profiles. Directories sometimes hold old firm names or former addresses.
  7. Save the login in a password manager and note the renewal date.

What is NAP consistency, and why does it matter for local SEO and AI answers?

NAP stands for name, address and phone number. Consistency means writing them the same way everywhere. Google's own guidance says to use the name customers know from your signage and stationery, an accurate address, a local number you control, and one profile per location (Google Business Profile content guidelines). When your details differ across sites, search engines and AI answer engines have conflicting data and may show the wrong phone number or skip you. We cannot quantify the effect, and no one outside Google can promise one, but clean, matching data is a low-cost fix.

  • Pick one format for suites and abbreviations ("Suite 200", not sometimes "Ste. 200").
  • Use one main number; if you use tracking numbers, keep the main number as a secondary phone where the directory allows it.
  • If you move or rename, update every listing and your website footer the same week.
  • Add the same details to your site using schema markup for law firms so machines can read them.

How should I handle reviews on directories?

Directories such as Avvo and Lawyers.com show client reviews, and Google shows reviews on your profile. Respond politely and briefly. Do not reveal confidential information, even if the client has already posted details, and do not confirm that the person was a client. Do not offer gifts for reviews or write them yourself. Rules on responding and on client confidentiality come from your state bar, so check them. See the review section of our Google Business Profile guide for a practical workflow.

Is paying for a directory listing allowed? What do the ABA Model Rules say?

This is general information, not legal advice, and your state's rules control. Two ABA Model Rules are the usual starting point. Rule 7.1 prohibits false or misleading communications about a lawyer or the lawyer's services. That covers how you describe ratings, awards and "top" lists. Rule 7.2 permits advertising in any media but, in general, does not allow giving anything of value to someone for recommending your services, with exceptions such as paying the reasonable cost of advertising and certain qualified lawyer referral services. The ABA publishes the text in its Model Rules of Professional Conduct. We could not open those pages automatically for this article, so read them directly.

The practical question is whether a paid listing is advertising (generally fine) or payment for a recommendation or lead (more regulated, and some states restrict fee-sharing and lead generation). Ask the directory how it describes the product, check your state bar's advertising rules and any opinions on lead generators, and keep copies of what you agreed to. Some states also require disclaimers or filing for advertisements.

How do I know if a paid directory listing is worth it?

Treat it like any ad: test it, measure it, and renew only if it pays. GA4 and Search Console will show visits from a directory to your website, and a call tracking number or a "how did you hear about us?" intake field covers the rest.

  • Ask for the contract term, renewal terms and cancellation rights before you sign.
  • Ask what exactly you receive: placement, exclusivity by practice area or county, number of profiles, reporting.
  • Set a review date at the end of the term and write down your decision rule in advance, for example "at least one signed matter".
  • Compare the fee with the average fee for the matters you want, using your own numbers.
  • Do not rely on directory-supplied "visitor" numbers alone. Count your own calls and forms.

Decision guide: what should a small firm do first?

More guides are at Start Here.

FAQ

Are free legal directory listings worth claiming?

Yes, if you keep them accurate. They cost time, give you a consistent public record, and can only be controlled by you once claimed.

What is the best legal directory for lawyers?

There is no single best. For local reach, Google Business Profile plus your bar directory come first; Avvo, Justia, FindLaw/Lawyers.com and Martindale-Hubbell are the main national options to compare.

Do legal directory backlinks help SEO?

A link from a reputable directory is one more mention of your firm, but Google has not published a link value for directories. Do not buy listings only for links.

How much do paid legal directory profiles cost?

Avvo, FindLaw and Super Lawyers do not publish prices on the pages we reviewed. Check any figures you see on blogs against the directory directly.

Can I pay a directory for leads?

Possibly, but lead generation and fee-sharing are regulated differently from ordinary advertising. Check Rules 7.1 and 7.2 as adopted in your state and your bar's ethics opinions.

Conclusion: next steps

  1. Write your master NAP record and audit every listing against it.
  2. Claim free profiles on Google, your bar directory, Avvo, Justia and, if relevant, Martindale-Hubbell.
  3. Set up tracking before spending, then test one paid listing for one term.
  4. Re-check your state bar advertising rules.
