title.raw: Google Local Services Ads for Lawyers: How They Work, Costs and Setup (2026)
title.rendered: Google Local Services Ads for Lawyers: How They Work, Costs and Setup (2026)

content.raw:
Quick answer: Google local services ads for lawyers are pay-per-lead ads that appear above regular search results. You pay when a prospective client contacts you from the ad, not when someone clicks. Google does not publish a fixed price per lead: according to Google's billing help page, prices vary by location, job type, lead type and bidding mode. To run them you complete Google's screening and verification, set a weekly budget and a maximum bid, and answer every contact quickly.

Update you may have missed: many older guides talk about the "Google Screened" badge for lawyers. Google's help page says it is replacing its advertiser badges with a single Google Verified badge (About the Google Verified badge). The screening step still exists for new advertisers. Only the badge name changed.

Key takeaways

  • LSAs bill per valid lead (a call, message or booking request), not per click.
  • Google publishes no fixed lawyer lead price. Cost depends on location, practice area, lead type and your bidding mode.
  • New advertisers must pass Google's screening and verification to earn the Google Verified badge. Ranking is an auction on bid and profile quality.
  • You set an average weekly budget. Google caps spending at a monthly maximum.
  • Advertising rules for lawyers vary by state. Check your state bar before you launch.

How do Google local services ads work for lawyers?

Local Services Ads (LSAs) are a separate Google ad product from the Search ads you manage in a standard Google Ads campaign. Per Google, the Local Services unit appears prominently in Search results, and potential clients can contact you by call, message or by booking directly through the ad (Getting started with Local Services Ads). Google's eligibility list includes many legal categories, such as bankruptcy, personal injury, family, criminal, immigration and real estate. Check the eligibility tool in your area, since availability is limited to certain categories and locations.

Instead of keywords and ad copy, an LSA profile is built from your business details, practice areas, service area, hours, reviews, photos and a bio. A searcher sees a short list of firms, each with a rating and a button to call or message.

How are LSAs different from Google Search ads?

The practical difference: with LSAs your Google Business Profile-style reputation (reviews, responsiveness) matters more than your website, while Search ads depend heavily on your landing pages and keyword work. Many firms run both, but this guide stays on LSAs. For organic visibility see our local SEO checklist for lawyers and Google Business Profile guide.

What is Google Verified (formerly Google Screened) and how do law firms get it?

The Google Verified badge signals that a business has passed Google's screening process. Google's help page says new advertisers must complete the Local Services screening and verification process to earn it, while advertisers who had already completed verification receive it automatically (About the Google Verified badge). The page also says the badge change does not affect ad ranking.

Google says screening varies by category and region and may include license checks, insurance, third-party background checks and, for some categories, advanced verification such as a review of your Google Ads account, public data and video interviews (How providers qualify). Google's pages I reviewed do not list lawyer-specific requirements in detail, so expect to be asked for your bar license information and confirm the exact steps inside your own sign-up flow.

Google also notes that firms can run pre-badge ads before finishing onboarding. These need a license or business registration, billing, a budget and, for professional categories, headshots. Pre-badge listings appear but rank below providers with the badge (Getting started with Local Services Ads).

How does pay-per-lead billing work?

Google bills per lead. According to Google's billing help page:

  • You choose a bidding mode and a maximum amount you will pay per lead.
  • Invalid or low-quality leads are not charged. Valid leads include answered calls, missed calls where the caller stays on for more than 20 seconds during business hours, texts or emails from customers, voicemails and (in the US and Canada) booking requests.
  • A repeat contact from the same phone number or email within 15 days is not charged again. After 15 days of inactivity, a new contact is a new lead.
  • The Leads page shows a charge status: Charged, Not charged, In review or Credited.

How much do LSAs cost for lawyers?

There is no number Google will give you in advance. Google states that prices vary by location, job type, lead type and bidding mode, and that message leads are usually cheaper than phone leads, but not always. Competitive practice areas in big metro areas are generally priced by that auction, so treat any fixed figure in a blog post as an estimate. The honest way to find your cost is to start with a small budget and read the Leads page. For the wider budget picture, see how much a law firm website costs.

How do budgets work?

You set an average weekly budget based on how many leads you want in a typical week. Google says you can exceed it in a given week, but never your monthly maximum (weekly budget times the average number of weeks in a month). When you reach the monthly maximum, your ad stops showing for the rest of the month unless you raise it (Google's billing help page). Billing runs through Google Ads, and if that account is suspended your LSAs are suspended too.

What affects ranking?

Google describes ranking as an auction based on your bid and overall profile quality (About ad rankings). The factors Google lists:

Google adds that higher-quality profiles may rank higher and may pay lower costs per lead. It does not publish weights for each factor, so be wary of anyone who claims to know exact formulas.

How do I dispute a bad lead or get a credit?

On the pages I reviewed, Google describes a reassessment process: it re-evaluates charged leads over 30 days, and leads found to be poor quality, duplicate or invalid receive an automatic credit to your balance (Google's billing help page). You can also submit feedback on individual leads through the survey on the Leads page, and Google may occasionally credit leads reported this way. Credits are not available in every vertical or region, and the page notes some exclusions, so check your account's Leads page for what applies to lawyers. Practical steps:

  1. Open the Leads page and filter by charge status.
  2. Look for leads marked In review before reporting anything.
  3. For a wrong-number, spam or unrelated-case lead, submit the lead feedback survey promptly with a clear reason.
  4. Keep call notes so you can compare Google's status with what actually happened.

Older third-party articles describe a manual dispute form with a deadline. Google's current billing page does not describe one, so rely on the Leads page in your account.

How do I set up Local Services Ads for a law firm?

  1. Check eligibility for your practice area and location on Google's Getting started with Local Services Ads page.
  2. Sign up online or contact Google sales, then enter business details, practice areas, service area and hours.
  3. Submit the license and screening information Google asks for, and add headshots and a short bio.
  4. Set billing, bidding mode and average weekly budget.
  5. Turn on message leads (and booking where offered) and set phone answering hours you can actually staff.
  6. Verify how calls reach you. If nobody can answer, consider a service such as those in Smith.ai vs Ruby virtual receptionists.
  7. Ask satisfied clients for honest reviews, consistent with your state's rules.
  8. Review leads weekly and adjust budget.

What should a firm do after the lead arrives?

A paid lead is only worth it if you convert it. Answer quickly, because Google lists responsiveness as a ranking input. Track which leads become consultations using your own intake notes, and use GA4 and Search Console for the website side. A strong practice area page helps clients who check your site before calling. Our Start Here guide lists the other basics.

Are local services ads allowed for attorneys in my state?

Attorney advertising rules vary by state, and state bars may have rules on advertising claims, reviews and testimonials, specialization wording, required disclaimers and solicitation. A useful starting point is the ABA Model Rules of Professional Conduct (Rules 7.1 to 7.3 cover communications, advertising and solicitation). These are model rules, not binding by themselves; each state adopts its own version. This is general information, not legal advice. Check with your state bar or ethics counsel before you publish a profile, bio or review request.

Pros and cons

FAQ

Quick answer: Google local services ads for lawyers are pay-per-lead ads that appear above regular search results. You pay when a prospective client contacts you from the ad, not when someone clicks. Google does not publish a fixed price per lead: according to Google’s billing help page, prices vary by location, job type, lead type and bidding mode. To run them you complete Google’s screening and verification, set a weekly budget and a maximum bid, and answer every contact quickly.

Google’s help page says it is replacing its advertiser badges with a single Google Verified badge (About the Google Verified badge). The screening step still exists for new advertisers. Only the badge name changed.

Key takeaways

  • LSAs bill per valid lead (a call, message or booking request), not per click.
  • Google publishes no fixed lawyer lead price. Cost depends on location, practice area, lead type and your bidding mode.
  • New advertisers must pass Google’s screening and verification to earn the Google Verified badge. Ranking is an auction on bid and profile quality.
  • You set an average weekly budget. Google caps spending at a monthly maximum.
  • Advertising rules for lawyers vary by state. Check your state bar before you launch.

How do Google local services ads work for lawyers?

Local Services Ads (LSAs) are a separate Google ad product from the Search ads you manage in a standard Google Ads campaign. Per Google, the Local Services unit appears prominently in Search results, and potential clients can contact you by call, message or by booking directly through the ad (Getting started with Local Services Ads). Google’s eligibility list includes many legal categories, such as bankruptcy, personal injury, family, criminal, immigration and real estate. Check the eligibility tool in your area, since availability is limited to certain categories and locations.

Instead of keywords and ad copy, an LSA profile is built from your business details, practice areas, service area, hours, reviews, photos and a bio. A searcher sees a short list of firms, each with a rating and a button to call or message.

How are LSAs different from Google Search ads?

The practical difference: with LSAs your Google Business Profile-style reputation (reviews, responsiveness) matters more than your website, while Search ads depend heavily on your landing pages and keyword work. Many firms run both, but this guide stays on LSAs. For organic visibility see our local SEO checklist for lawyers and Google Business Profile guide.

What is Google Verified (formerly Google Screened) and how do law firms get it?

The Google Verified badge signals that a business has passed Google’s screening process. Google’s help page says new advertisers must complete the Local Services screening and verification process to earn it, while advertisers who had already completed verification receive it automatically (About the Google Verified badge). The page also says the badge change does not affect ad ranking.

Google says screening varies by category and region and may include license checks, insurance, third-party background checks and, for some categories, advanced verification such as a review of your Google Ads account, public data and video interviews (How providers qualify). Google’s pages I reviewed do not list lawyer-specific requirements in detail, so expect to be asked for your bar license information and confirm the exact steps inside your own sign-up flow.

Google also notes that firms can run pre-badge ads before finishing onboarding. These need a license or business registration, billing, a budget and, for professional categories, headshots. Pre-badge listings appear but rank below providers with the badge (Getting started with Local Services Ads).

How does pay-per-lead billing work?

Google bills per lead. According to Google’s billing help page:

  • You choose a bidding mode and a maximum amount you will pay per lead.
  • Invalid or low-quality leads are not charged. Valid leads include answered calls, missed calls where the caller stays on for more than 20 seconds during business hours, texts or emails from customers, voicemails and (in the US and Canada) booking requests.
  • A repeat contact from the same phone number or email within 15 days is not charged again. After 15 days of inactivity, a new contact is a new lead.
  • The Leads page shows a charge status: Charged, Not charged, In review or Credited.

How much do LSAs cost for lawyers?

There is no number Google will give you in advance. Google states that prices vary by location, job type, lead type and bidding mode, and that message leads are usually cheaper than phone leads, but not always. Competitive practice areas in big metro areas are generally priced by that auction, so treat any fixed figure in a blog post as an estimate. The honest way to find your cost is to start with a small budget and read the Leads page. For the wider budget picture, see how much a law firm website costs.

How do budgets work?

You set an average weekly budget based on how many leads you want in a typical week. Google says you can exceed it in a given week, but never your monthly maximum (weekly budget times the average number of weeks in a month). When you reach the monthly maximum, your ad stops showing for the rest of the month unless you raise it (Google’s billing help page). Billing runs through Google Ads, and if that account is suspended your LSAs are suspended too.

What affects ranking?

Google describes ranking as an auction based on your bid and overall profile quality (About ad rankings). The factors Google lists:

Google adds that higher-quality profiles may rank higher and may pay lower costs per lead. It does not publish weights for each factor, so be wary of anyone who claims to know exact formulas.

How do I dispute a bad lead or get a credit?

On the pages I reviewed, Google describes a reassessment process: it re-evaluates charged leads over 30 days, and leads found to be poor quality, duplicate or invalid receive an automatic credit to your balance (Google’s billing help page). You can also submit feedback on individual leads through the survey on the Leads page, and Google may occasionally credit leads reported this way. Credits are not available in every vertical or region, and the page notes some exclusions, so check your account’s Leads page for what applies to lawyers. Practical steps:

  1. Open the Leads page and filter by charge status.
  2. Look for leads marked In review before reporting anything.
  3. For a wrong-number, spam or unrelated-case lead, submit the lead feedback survey promptly with a clear reason.
  4. Keep call notes so you can compare Google’s status with what actually happened.

Older third-party articles describe a manual dispute form with a deadline. Google’s current billing page does not describe one, so rely on the Leads page in your account.

How do I set up Local Services Ads for a law firm?

  1. Check eligibility for your practice area and location on Google’s Getting started with Local Services Ads page.
  2. Sign up online or contact Google sales, then enter business details, practice areas, service area and hours.
  3. Submit the license and screening information Google asks for, and add headshots and a short bio.
  4. Set billing, bidding mode and average weekly budget.
  5. Turn on message leads (and booking where offered) and set phone answering hours you can actually staff.
  6. Verify how calls reach you. If nobody can answer, consider a service such as those in Smith.ai vs Ruby virtual receptionists.
  7. Ask satisfied clients for honest reviews, consistent with your state’s rules.
  8. Review leads weekly and adjust budget.

What should a firm do after the lead arrives?

A paid lead is only worth it if you convert it. Answer quickly, because Google lists responsiveness as a ranking input. Track which leads become consultations using your own intake notes, and use GA4 and Search Console for the website side. A strong practice area page helps clients who check your site before calling. Our Start Here guide lists the other basics.

Attorney advertising rules vary by state, and state bars may have rules on advertising claims, reviews and testimonials, specialization wording, required disclaimers and solicitation. A useful starting point is the ABA Model Rules of Professional Conduct (Rules 7.1 to 7.3 cover communications, advertising and solicitation). These are model rules, not binding by themselves; each state adopts its own version. This is general information, not legal advice. title.rendered: SiteGround Review for Law Firms (2026): Is It the Best Value Managed WordPress Host?

content.raw:
Quick answer: This SiteGround review comes down to one point. SiteGround is a strong, low-hassle choice for a small law firm's WordPress site, as long as you budget for the renewal price and not the sign-up price. GrowBig is the plan most firms should pick: it costs $3.99/mo for the first 12 months, then renews at $29.99/mo on a 12-month term, and it adds staging and on-demand backups that the cheapest plan lacks (prices as of November 2026).

Key takeaways

  • Best plan for most firms: GrowBig. StartUp has no staging and no manual backups. GoGeek mainly makes sense for agencies or busy sites.
  • The renewal jump is large: GrowBig goes from $47.88 for the first year to $359.88 a year at the 12-month regular rate. That's about 7.5 times the first-year price.
  • Backups are good but not complete: you get up to 30 daily copies and 5 manual backup slots on GrowBig. Downloading a backup as a file needs the paid Premium Backup add-on.
  • Email is included but basic: all mailboxes share 10 GB in total. SiteGround itself recommends Google Workspace for heavier business email.
  • Compared with alternatives: it costs far less than Kinsta or WP Engine and more than Hostinger after renewal. Of the four, only SiteGround and Hostinger include email hosting, and SiteGround's doesn't expire after year one.

How we compared

We haven't run speed or uptime tests on SiteGround, and this review has no scores. Everything below comes from SiteGround's official pages, checked in November 2026: the WordPress hosting plans page, the full feature comparison, its knowledge base, and its legal terms. We then looked at what a small firm actually needs: predictable costs, backups, safe updates, email and someone to call when the site breaks. Competitor prices come from each vendor's own pricing page.

Is SiteGround good for law firms? The verdict

Yes, for most solo and small firms that run one brochure-style WordPress site. SiteGround sits in the middle of the market. It's shared hosting, which means your site shares a server with other customers. On top of that it adds managed WordPress features such as automatic updates, daily off-site backups, one-click staging, a web application firewall, free SSL and 24/7 phone, chat and ticket support.

Who SiteGround fits

  • Solo attorneys and firms of 2–10 lawyers with a practice-area site, a blog and a contact form.
  • Firms that want phone support and a simple control panel instead of a developer-only platform.
  • Firms (or their web developer) running a few sites, such as a main site plus a microsite for one practice area. GrowBig allows unlimited websites.
  • Buyers who want US data centers. SiteGround lists Ashburn, Council Bluffs, Dallas and Los Angeles among its 11 locations.

Who should look elsewhere

  • The lowest long-term price matters most: Hostinger renews for much less (see the comparison below).
  • You want premium managed hosting with container isolation and a dashboard built for agencies: look at Kinsta or WP Engine, and expect to pay several times more.
  • Your firm sends a lot of email or needs large mailboxes: keep the website on SiteGround but put email on Google Workspace or Microsoft 365.

SiteGround pricing: intro vs. renewal (November 2026)

SiteGround pricing has two layers. The first is a discounted price for your first invoice. The second is the regular price that applies to every renewal after that. The feature comparison page puts it plainly: advertised prices apply to prepaid 12-month plans, "Special prices are applicable for the first invoice," and regular prices apply to all renewals. Prices exclude sales tax.

Three details matter here. First, the plans page now says "unlimited traffic." The visit numbers above are SiteGround's own suggestions for which plan suits a site, not hard caps. Data transfer is listed as unmetered. Second, when we checked, the page showed an "early Black Friday" banner that offered a free domain and a free site transfer on all plans "for a limited time." Third, the intro prices matched what SiteGround showed earlier in November, but promotions change, so confirm at checkout.

What does SiteGround really cost over 3 years?

Assume you buy the 12-month intro deal and then renew. How much you pay over three years depends on the renewal term you choose. A 24-month renewal has a lower monthly rate than two 12-month renewals.

So a realistic budget for GrowBig is about $215–$255 a year averaged over three years, not $48. That's still cheap for a law firm's main marketing asset. Just put the renewal date in the firm's calendar. To see how hosting fits the full budget, read our guide to the best hosting for law firm websites.

SiteGround GrowBig vs StartUp vs GoGeek: which plan should a firm choose?

Choose GrowBig if you'll ever update plugins or redesign pages on a live site. It's the cheapest plan that includes staging (a private copy of your site where you can test changes before they go live) and on-demand backups (a snapshot you make yourself just before a risky change). Both features are listed under GrowBig's "Exclusive Features" on the plans page.

  • StartUp fits a single, rarely changed site where you accept relying on the automatic daily backups alone.
  • GrowBig fits most firms. It adds staging, 5 manual backup slots, "30% faster PHP" (SiteGround's claim), unlimited sites and 50 GB of storage.
  • GoGeek adds Git with staging, white-label client access, private DNS, priority support and a higher email sending limit. It's aimed at developers and agencies.

What's included with SiteGround hosting?

Every plan includes free SSL, CDN, daily backups, email, a free domain for the first year, managed WordPress autoupdates, and the Speed Optimizer and Security Optimizer plugins. Each also includes WP-CLI and SSH, plus an AI agent for WordPress with free monthly AI tokens (per the plans page). Here is what the main items mean for a firm.

SiteGround pros and cons

Pros

  • Very low first-year price, and published regular rates. You can see the renewal price before you buy.
  • Staging and manual backups on GrowBig, which most firms need for safe updates.
  • Daily off-site backups kept for up to 30 days, with restores of files, databases or email.
  • 24/7 phone support, which many budget and premium hosts don't offer.
  • Email hosting included, plus a free email migrator.
  • Four US data centers, with the option to change location later.

Cons

  • A steep renewal jump: GrowBig goes from $3.99 to $29.99/mo on a 12-month renewal.
  • The intro price only applies to a 12-month prepay. Monthly billing costs $34.99/mo for GrowBig.
  • Downloadable backups cost extra through Premium Backup.
  • Email storage is 10 GB shared across every mailbox, and new mail bounces once you hit the limit.
  • It's still shared hosting. Very busy sites, or firms wanting dedicated resources, should look at cloud or premium managed hosts.

Law-firm considerations before you buy SiteGround

1. Plan for the renewal, not the deal

Put the 12-month renewal date on the firm calendar. A month before, decide whether to renew for 24 months, which lowers GrowBig to $24.99/mo. SiteGround's refund policy allows a full refund of a renewal if you cancel within 30 days of payment and before the new term starts, and a partial refund after the term starts. That gives you a short window if you forget.

2. Email: SiteGround mailboxes vs Google Workspace or Microsoft 365

SiteGround's email is designed for "standard communication needs." Its own email policy recommends Google Workspace for heavier business use. All of a plan's mailboxes share 10 GB, and attachments are capped at 50 MB to send and 80 MB to receive. When the 10 GB is full, incoming mail is rejected, not queued. For a firm that receives scanned documents and long client threads, that limit can arrive quickly. Most firms are better off keeping the website on SiteGround and running email on a dedicated suite. See Google Workspace vs Microsoft 365 for law firms to choose one. Either way, set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC as covered in our law firm business email setup guide. Confidentiality duties around client communications come from your state's rules of professional conduct, so check your state bar's guidance.

3. Backups: keep one copy you control

SiteGround's 30 daily copies live in SiteGround's systems. Per the Backup KB, once you delete a site you lose access to its backups, and downloading backups needs Premium Backup. A sensible setup is SiteGround's daily backups plus either Premium Backup or a reputable WordPress backup plugin that sends copies to cloud storage the firm owns.

4. Use staging for every meaningful update

A broken contact form can cost you leads without anyone noticing. On GrowBig, copy the site to staging, run the plugin and theme updates there, test the intake form, then push the changes live. SiteGround's staging copies have WordPress cron turned off by default, so test emails and scheduled tasks may behave differently on staging than on the live site.

5. Vendor due diligence

SiteGround publishes a Data Processing Agreement alongside its terms. Keep a copy in your vendor file. Remember that a marketing website should never be where you store client files. Use the website for public information and a secure form, and keep matter data in your practice management software.

SiteGround vs Kinsta vs Hostinger vs WP Engine

SiteGround sits between budget and premium hosting. Here is how the entry WordPress plans compared on each vendor's pricing page in November 2026. Several vendors were running Black Friday promotions, so check current prices before you buy.

For the details, read our Kinsta review for law firms, our Hostinger review and our WP Engine review. The head-to-head Kinsta vs WP Engine vs SiteGround comparison runs the 3-year math for the three managed hosts. For other side-by-side guides, browse our tool comparisons hub.

How to sign up for SiteGround and migrate a law firm site

SiteGround offers three ways to move an existing WordPress site: its free Migrator plugin, a manual transfer done by its team, or a do-it-yourself move. According to the SiteGround Academy migration guide, your first "Manual Transfer by our Team" is free with a new plan, for one site. Extra transfers are paid, with the price shown when you order. The transfer KB article notes that the professional transfer doesn't include moving your domain registration.

  1. Pick GrowBig and the closest US data center on the plans page. Choose the 12-month term to get the intro price.
  2. Decide where email will live before you touch DNS. If email stays with Google Workspace or Microsoft 365, write down your current MX, SPF and DKIM records so you don't break mail during the move.
  3. Back up the current site at your old host and keep a copy offline.
  4. Migrate. Either request the free first team transfer from the Client Area, or install the free SiteGround Migrator plugin on the old site and paste in the migration token from Site Tools. SiteGround says the plugin copies the site without taking the live one down (Migrator tutorial).
  5. Check the copy on SiteGround's temporary URL. Look at forms, the attorney bio pages, redirects and tracking codes.
  6. Point DNS to SiteGround. Update the nameservers (or A records), keeping your email records exactly as they were.
  7. After launch: confirm SSL is active, submit a test form, take a manual backup, and add the renewal date to the calendar.

For the full zero-downtime process, including DNS timing, read how to move a law firm website to a new host without downtime.

FAQ

Is SiteGround good for a small law firm?

Yes, for most small firms running a standard WordPress site. GrowBig gives you staging, manual and daily backups, free SSL, a CDN and 24/7 phone support at a mid-range price after renewal. Firms that want the lowest long-term cost, or premium dedicated resources, have better-fitting options.

How much does SiteGround cost after the first year?

On a 12-month renewal, StartUp costs $17.99/mo, GrowBig $29.99/mo and GoGeek $44.99/mo. On 24-month renewals the rates drop to $14.99, $24.99 and $39.99/mo. All are before tax, as of November 2026.

Is SiteGround GrowBig worth it over StartUp?

For a law firm, usually yes. The $12/mo difference at renewal buys staging and 5 on-demand backup slots, the two tools that make plugin and theme updates safe. It also allows unlimited websites and gives you 50 GB of storage instead of 10 GB.

Does SiteGround include email?

Yes. Every plan includes unlimited email accounts, but they share 10 GB of storage and StartUp and GrowBig can send up to 400 emails per hour. SiteGround recommends Google Workspace for heavier business email.

Does SiteGround offer a free migration?

Yes. The SiteGround Migrator plugin is free for WordPress sites, and SiteGround says the first manual transfer by its team is free with a new plan, for one site. Additional team transfers are paid.

Does SiteGround have a money-back guarantee?

Yes. Shared hosting plans come with 30 days from activation, and you request the refund by cancelling in the Client Area. Domain fees aren't refundable and may be charged even if the domain was free as part of a promotion.

Where are SiteGround's US data centers?

Ashburn (Virginia), Council Bluffs (Iowa), Dallas (Texas) and Los Angeles (California), out of 11 locations worldwide.

Conclusion: is SiteGround the best value managed WordPress host?

For a small law firm, SiteGround GrowBig is arguably the best value among hosts that include staging, daily backups and 24/7 phone support. You have to treat the $29.99/mo renewal as the real price, though. Your next steps:

  1. Budget about $650–$770 for three years of GrowBig, depending on your renewal term.
  2. Decide whether email stays on SiteGround or moves to Google Workspace or Microsoft 365.
  3. Plan the migration using the free first transfer or the Migrator plugin, and keep your own backup copy.
  4. If you're still choosing, compare it against Kinsta, WP Engine and Hostinger in the reviews linked above.

Want this handled for you? ProSiteGuide builds and maintains fast, secure WordPress sites for law firms. Book a free consultation.

For a direct look at price, backups and support, read our Hostinger vs SiteGround comparison.

Assume you buy the 12-month intro deal and then renew. How much you pay over three years depends on the renewal term you choose. A 24-month renewal has a lower monthly rate than two 12-month renewals.

So a realistic budget for GrowBig is about $215–$255 a year averaged over three years, not $48. That’s still cheap for a law firm’s main marketing asset. Just put the renewal date in the firm’s calendar. To see how hosting fits the full budget, read our guide to the best hosting for law firm websites.

SiteGround GrowBig vs StartUp vs GoGeek: which plan should a firm choose?

Choose GrowBig if you’ll ever update plugins or redesign pages on a live site. It’s the cheapest plan that includes staging (a private copy of your site where you can test changes before they go live) and on-demand backups (a snapshot you make yourself just before a risky change). Both features are listed under GrowBig’s “Exclusive Features” on the plans page.

  • StartUp fits a single, rarely changed site where you accept relying on the automatic daily backups alone.
  • GrowBig fits most firms. It adds staging, 5 manual backup slots, “30% faster PHP” (SiteGround’s claim), unlimited sites and 50 GB of storage.
  • GoGeek adds Git with staging, white-label client access, private DNS, priority support and a higher email sending limit. It’s aimed at developers and agencies.

What’s included with SiteGround hosting?

Every plan includes free SSL, CDN, daily backups, email, a free domain for the first year, managed WordPress autoupdates, and the Speed Optimizer and Security Optimizer plugins. Each also includes WP-CLI and SSH, plus an AI agent for WordPress with free monthly AI tokens (per the plans page). Here is what the main items mean for a firm.

SiteGround pros and cons

Pros

  • Very low first-year price, and published regular rates. You can see the renewal price before you buy.
  • Staging and manual backups on GrowBig, which most firms need for safe updates.
  • Daily off-site backups kept for up to 30 days, with restores of files, databases or email.
  • 24/7 phone support, which many budget and premium hosts don’t offer.
  • Email hosting included, plus a free email migrator.
  • Four US data centers, with the option to change location later.

Cons

  • A steep renewal jump: GrowBig goes from $3.99 to $29.99/mo on a 12-month renewal.
  • The intro price only applies to a 12-month prepay. Monthly billing costs $34.99/mo for GrowBig.
  • Downloadable backups cost extra through Premium Backup.
  • Email storage is 10 GB shared across every mailbox, and new mail bounces once you hit the limit.
  • It’s still shared hosting. Very busy sites, or firms wanting dedicated resources, should look at cloud or premium managed hosts.

Law-firm considerations before you buy SiteGround

1. Plan for the renewal, not the deal

Put the 12-month renewal date on the firm calendar. A month before, decide whether to renew for 24 months, which lowers GrowBig to $24.99/mo. SiteGround’s refund policy allows a full refund of a renewal if you cancel within 30 days of payment and before the new term starts, and a partial refund after the term starts. That gives you a short window if you forget.

2. Email: SiteGround mailboxes vs Google Workspace or Microsoft 365

SiteGround’s email is designed for “standard communication needs.” Its own email policy recommends Google Workspace for heavier business use. All of a plan’s mailboxes share 10 GB, and attachments are capped at 50 MB to send and 80 MB to receive. When the 10 GB is full, incoming mail is rejected, not queued. For a firm that receives scanned documents and long client threads, that limit can arrive quickly. Most firms are better off keeping the website on SiteGround and running email on a dedicated suite. See Google Workspace vs Microsoft 365 for law firms to choose one. Either way, set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC as covered in our law firm business email setup guide. Confidentiality duties around client communications come from your state’s rules of professional conduct, so check your state bar’s guidance.

3. Backups: keep one copy you control

SiteGround’s 30 daily copies live in SiteGround’s systems. Per the Backup KB, once you delete a site you lose access to its backups, and downloading backups needs Premium Backup. A sensible setup is SiteGround’s daily backups plus either Premium Backup or a reputable WordPress backup plugin that sends copies to cloud storage the firm owns.

4. Use staging for every meaningful update

A broken contact form can cost you leads without anyone noticing. On GrowBig, copy the site to staging, run the plugin and theme updates there, test the intake form, then push the changes live. SiteGround’s staging copies have WordPress cron turned off by default, so test emails and scheduled tasks may behave differently on staging than on the live site.

5. Vendor due diligence

SiteGround publishes a Data Processing Agreement alongside its terms. Keep a copy in your vendor file. Remember that a marketing website should never be where you store client files. Use the website for public information and a secure form, and keep matter data in your practice management software.

SiteGround vs Kinsta vs Hostinger vs WP Engine

SiteGround sits between budget and premium hosting. Here is how the entry WordPress plans compared on each vendor’s pricing page in November 2026. Several vendors were running Black Friday promotions, so check current prices before you buy.

For the details, read our Kinsta review for law firms, our Hostinger review and our WP Engine review. The head-to-head Kinsta vs WP Engine vs SiteGround comparison runs the 3-year math for the three managed hosts. For other side-by-side guides, browse our tool comparisons hub.

How to sign up for SiteGround and migrate a law firm site

SiteGround offers three ways to move an existing WordPress site: its free Migrator plugin, a manual transfer done by its team, or a do-it-yourself move. According to the SiteGround Academy migration guide, your first “Manual Transfer by our Team” is free with a new plan, for one site. Extra transfers are paid, with the price shown when you order. The transfer KB article notes that the professional transfer doesn’t include moving your domain registration.

  1. Pick GrowBig and the closest US data center on the plans page. Choose the 12-month term to get the intro price.
  2. Decide where email will live before you touch DNS. If email stays with Google Workspace or Microsoft 365, write down your current MX, SPF and DKIM records so you don’t break mail during the move.
  3. Back up the current site at your old host and keep a copy offline.
  4. Migrate. Either request the free first team transfer from the Client Area, or install the free SiteGround Migrator plugin on the old site and paste in the migration token from Site Tools. SiteGround says the plugin copies the site without taking the live one down (Migrator tutorial).
  5. Check the copy on SiteGround’s temporary URL. Look at forms, the attorney bio pages, redirects and tracking codes.
  6. Point DNS to SiteGround. Update the nameservers (or A records), keeping your email records exactly as they were.
  7. After launch: confirm SSL is active, submit a test form, take a manual backup, and add the renewal date to the calendar.

For the full zero-downtime process, including DNS timing, read how to move a law firm website to a new host without downtime.

FAQ

Is SiteGround good for a small law firm?

Yes, for most small firms running a standard WordPress site. GrowBig gives you staging, manual and daily backups, free SSL, a CDN and 24/7 phone support at a mid-range price after renewal. Firms that want the lowest long-term cost, or premium dedicated resources, have better-fitting options.

How much does SiteGround cost after the first year?

On a 12-month renewal, StartUp costs $17.99/mo, GrowBig $29.99/mo and GoGeek $44.99/mo. On 24-month renewals the rates drop to $14.99, $24.99 and $39.99/mo. All are before tax, as of November 2026.

Is SiteGround GrowBig worth it over StartUp?

For a law firm, usually yes. The $12/mo difference at renewal buys staging and 5 on-demand backup slots, the two tools that make plugin and theme updates safe. It also allows unlimited websites and gives you 50 GB of storage instead of 10 GB.

Does SiteGround include email?

Yes. Every plan includes unlimited email accounts, but they share 10 GB of storage and StartUp and GrowBig can send up to 400 emails per hour. SiteGround recommends Google Workspace for heavier business email.

Does SiteGround offer a free migration?

Yes. The SiteGround Migrator plugin is free for WordPress sites, and SiteGround says the first manual transfer by its team is free with a new plan, for one site. Additional team transfers are paid.

Does SiteGround have a money-back guarantee?

Yes. Shared hosting plans come with 30 days from activation, and you request the refund by cancelling in the Client Area. Domain fees aren’t refundable and may be charged even if the domain was free as part of a promotion.

Where are SiteGround’s US data centers?

Ashburn (Virginia), Council Bluffs (Iowa), Dallas (Texas) and Los Angeles (California), out of 11 locations worldwide.

Conclusion: is SiteGround the best value managed WordPress host?

For a small law firm, SiteGround GrowBig is arguably the best value among hosts that include staging, daily backups and 24/7 phone support. You have to treat the $29.99/mo renewal as the real price, though. Your next steps:

  1. Budget about $650–$770 for three years of GrowBig, depending on your renewal term.
  2. Decide whether email stays on SiteGround or moves to Google Workspace or Microsoft 365.
  3. Plan the migration using the free first transfer or the Migrator plugin, and keep your own backup copy.
  4. If you’re still choosing, compare it against Kinsta, WP Engine and Hostinger in the reviews linked above.

title.rendered: Google Analytics for Law Firms: GA4 and Search Console Setup and What to Track (2026)

content.raw:
Quick answer: Setting up Google Analytics for law firms takes four jobs. Create a Google Analytics 4 (GA4) property and web data stream, install the tag on your site, mark your real lead actions as key events, and connect Google Search Console. Track form submissions, click-to-call taps, consultation bookings and chat starts. Never send names, emails, phone numbers or form contents to Google Analytics.

This guide walks through each step using Google's own help documentation, as of November 2026. It covers the WordPress setup options, a privacy checklist written for law firms, a KPI table and a 30-minute monthly reporting routine.

Key takeaways

  • GA4 shows what visitors do on your site. Search Console shows how you appear in Google Search. You need both, and you should link them.
  • "Key events" is the new name for what GA4 used to call conversions. Mark only the actions that create a potential client: forms, calls, bookings and chats.
  • Use a Domain property in Search Console. It covers http, https and every subdomain, but it can only be verified through DNS.
  • Keep personal data out. Google's policy bans sending PII to Analytics. For a law firm, that includes the details on an intake form.
  • On WordPress, pick one way to install the tag. Use Site Kit, Tag Manager or Rank Math, never two at once, or every visit gets counted twice.

What is the difference between GA4 and Google Search Console?

Google Analytics 4 measures what people do after they land on your website. Google Search Console measures what happens before the click: the searches you appear for, how often people click, and whether Google can crawl and index your pages. Both are free. Neither one replaces the other.

How do you set up Google Analytics for a law firm?

Create the account and property under a firm-owned Google account, not a personal Gmail and not your agency's account. Then give outside vendors their own access. If a developer leaves, the firm keeps its data. These steps follow Google's Set up Analytics for a website guide.

  1. Create an account. Go to analytics.google.com and click Start measuring. If you already have an account, go to Admin → Create → Account. Name the account after the firm.
  2. Create a property. Enter a property name, your reporting time zone (the firm's local time) and currency. Then choose an industry, a business size and your goals.
  3. Add a web data stream. Go to Admin → Data streams → Add stream → Web. Enter your domain and keep enhanced measurement on. Enhanced measurement records page views, scrolls, outbound clicks, site search, video engagement, file downloads and form interactions without extra code.
  4. Copy your Measurement ID. It starts with G- and appears under the stream details. You'll paste it into a plugin or Tag Manager in the next section.
  5. Install the tag. Choose one of the WordPress options below.
  6. Raise data retention to 14 months. Go to Admin → Data settings → Data retention. Standard properties can choose 2 or 14 months. The setting affects explorations and funnel reports, which you'll want for comparing one year with the next.
  7. Filter out office traffic. Define your office IP address as internal traffic in the stream's tag settings, then create an internal traffic data filter. Leave the filter in Testing first. An active exclude filter permanently discards the data it matches.
  8. Check data redaction. In the web stream, open Redact data. Email redaction is on by default for new properties. You can also add query parameters to strip, such as name, email or phone.
  9. Confirm data is arriving. Open the Realtime report and visit your site from a phone. Google says data can take up to 30 minutes to appear.

How do you install GA4 on a WordPress law firm website?

Most small firms on WordPress use one of three methods: the Site Kit by Google plugin, Google Tag Manager, or the Rank Math SEO plugin's Analytics module. Each one can place the GA4 tag. Pick exactly one. If two plugins, or a plugin and your theme, both print the tag, every page view is counted twice.

A practical combination for many firms: Tag Manager places the tag and handles events, and Site Kit is connected only for its dashboard and Search Console data, with its own Analytics snippet turned off. Whatever you choose, record it in your site documentation so the next developer doesn't add a second tag. For other plugins worth installing (and ones to avoid), see our guide to the best WordPress plugins for law firms.

To add GA4 through Tag Manager, follow Google's Google tag setup steps. Create a new tag of type Google Analytics → Google tag and enter your G- ID. Set the trigger to Initialization – All Pages, test in Preview, then click Submit → Publish.

How do you set up Google Search Console for lawyers?

Add your site as a Domain property, verify it with a DNS record, submit your XML sitemap, and link it to GA4. These steps take about 20 minutes, plus DNS waiting time.

Domain property or URL-prefix property?

Choose a Domain property if you can edit your DNS. Google's verification help explains that a Domain property (example.com) includes all protocols and subdomains. DNS is the only way to verify it. A URL-prefix property (https://www.example.com) covers only that exact prefix. It can be verified with an HTML file, an HTML tag, your Google Analytics tag or your Tag Manager container. That makes it handy if your domain registrar login is hard to find.

  1. Add the property. In Search Console, open the property selector → Add property → Domain, and type your domain without https or www.
  2. Verify with DNS. Copy the TXT record Search Console gives you and add it at your DNS host. That may be your registrar or Cloudflare. If your registrar is listed in Search Console, you can choose it and sign in instead. Google says DNS changes can take up to two or three days. Leave the record in place after verification, or you may lose access.
  3. Submit your sitemap. WordPress SEO plugins usually generate one, for example /sitemap_index.xml in Rank Math or Yoast. In the Sitemaps report, paste the URL and click Submit. You want a status of Success. Couldn't fetch often means robots.txt is blocking it or the URL returns a 404.
  4. Add users, not owners. Give your agency or developer Full or Restricted user access. Keep ownership with the firm.
  5. Link Search Console to GA4. In GA4, go to Admin → Product links → Search Console links → Link. You need the Editor role in GA4 and must be a verified Search Console owner. Then publish the Search Console report collection under Library, because it's unpublished by default (Google's linking guide).

After linking, GA4 shows two extra reports. Google Organic Search Queries lists the searches that brought visitors. Google Organic Search Traffic lists landing pages with both Search Console and GA4 metrics. Search Console data reaches GA4 about 48 hours after Google collects it.

Moving hosts or rebuilding the site? Keep the same GA4 property and Search Console property, and check both reports for a few weeks after launch. Our guide to redesigning a law firm website without losing SEO covers redirects and the post-launch checks.

What should a law firm track in Google Analytics?

Track the four actions that start a client relationship: contact form submissions, phone calls from the site, consultation bookings and chat conversations. Mark each one as a key event. Google defines a key event as an action "particularly important to the success of your business." Google's Events and key events page explains that events previously marked as conversions are now called key events. "Conversion" now refers to the version shared with Google Ads for bidding.

You can mark up to 30 key events on a standard property, which is far more than a law firm needs. Fewer is better. If page views or scrolls count as key events, your "lead" numbers stop meaning anything. To mark an event, go to Admin → Events and click the star next to it (Google's steps). The change applies from that point forward, not to past data.

How do I track form submissions in GA4?

The most reliable way is to send visitors to a dedicated thank-you page after a successful submission, such as /thank-you/, and count views of that page as generate_lead. Enhanced measurement's form_submit event can fire on searches, newsletter boxes and failed submissions. Treat it as a backup, not your lead count. Many form plugins also offer their own GA4 integration. Recent Site Kit versions can detect lead events from several popular form plugins, so check its settings if you use Site Kit.

Two rules matter more than the method. The thank-you URL must not contain form data (no ?name=…&email=…). The event must never carry what the person typed. Our guide to a secure contact form for a law firm website covers the form side: spam protection, notifications and where submissions are stored.

How do I track click-to-call on a law firm website?

Make every phone number a tel: link, then use Tag Manager. Create a Just Links click trigger that fires on Some Link Clicks where Click URL contains tel:. Attach a GA4 Event tag named phone_click (Google's GA4 event tag steps). This counts taps, not completed calls. To measure answered calls by source, you need a call-tracking service or your phone system's reports. Phone numbers that appear only as plain text can't be tracked at all.

How do I track consultation bookings and chat?

Embedded schedulers and chat widgets often run inside an iframe or on the vendor's domain. Your GA4 tag can't see what happens inside them. Use the vendor's own GA4 or Tag Manager integration if it has one, or redirect to a confirmation page on your own site after booking. Then test it with a real booking in Tag Manager's Preview mode or GA4's DebugView. If you're still choosing a scheduler, our comparison of Calendly vs Acuity vs Microsoft Bookings for law firms covers the options.

How do you keep client information out of Google Analytics?

Google prohibits sending personally identifiable information to Analytics. Its PII policy names email addresses, personal mobile numbers, Social Security numbers and names as examples. It warns that PII often leaks through page URLs, page titles, form fields and search terms. For a law firm the risk goes beyond Google's terms. Someone filling in an intake form may describe their legal problem. Your duty to protect that information is set by your state's rules of professional conduct, so check your state bar's guidance on website data.

  • Never send form field values. No names, emails, phone numbers, case descriptions or "type of matter" answers in event parameters or custom dimensions.
  • Check thank-you URLs and page titles. Some form plugins append entries to the redirect URL. Turn that off, and add those parameters to GA4 data redaction as a safety net.
  • Watch site search. People type names and case details into search boxes. If that happens on your site, consider turning off the site search option in enhanced measurement.
  • Don't use User-ID with client identifiers. Small firm websites rarely need it.
  • Limit access. Give each person their own login with the lowest role that works. Remove former staff and vendors.
  • Keep GA out of client portals. Pages behind a login (portals, payment pages) generally shouldn't load marketing tags at all.

Do I need a cookie banner for Google Analytics?

It depends on where your visitors are and which privacy laws apply to the firm. There is no single US rule. Some state privacy laws and non-US laws (if you serve EU or UK visitors) can require notice or consent. Google says site owners are responsible for obtaining any required consent. Its consent mode passes a visitor's choice to Google tags through settings such as analytics_storage and ad_storage. At a minimum, disclose analytics in your privacy policy. If you add a consent banner, choose a consent platform that supports consent mode, and get advice on which laws apply to your firm.

Which Search Console reports should a law firm check?

Three reports cover most of what a small firm needs: Performance, Page indexing and Core Web Vitals.

  • Performance shows clicks, impressions, CTR (clicks ÷ impressions) and average position, broken down by query, page, country and device. Filter queries by your firm name to separate branded searches (people who already know you) from non-branded ones like "divorce lawyer near me." Non-branded growth is the clearest sign that SEO is working. Pages with many impressions but low CTR usually need a better title and description.
  • Page indexing lists which URLs are indexed and why others aren't. Google says not every URL should be indexed. Check that your home page, attorney bios and every practice area page are. Statuses like "Crawled – currently not indexed" on a practice area page usually mean the page is thin or duplicates another. Our guide on how to write practice area pages covers fixing that.
  • Core Web Vitals groups your URLs as Good, Needs improvement or Poor, based on real-visitor data for LCP (good is 2.5 s or less), INP (200 ms or less) and CLS (0.1 or less). Low-traffic sites often show "no data." That's normal. See our guide to law firm website speed and Core Web Vitals for fixes.

Search Console covers your website, not your Maps listing. Calls and direction requests from Google Maps appear in your Google Business Profile performance data. Report both side by side. Many local searches end in a call straight from the profile without a website visit.

Which law firm website analytics KPIs matter most?

Track a short list of numbers tied to new matters, and watch the trend month over month and year over year. A single month on its own tells you little. Practice areas have different seasons and different search volumes, so compare against your own past results rather than "industry averages."

GA4 counts inquiries, not clients. Once a quarter, compare GA4 leads with the intakes your firm actually logged, and how many became signed matters. That's the only way to know which channels bring cases and not just contacts. Keep that comparison in your practice management or intake system, not in GA4.

Monthly reporting checklist for law firm analytics

This 30-minute routine, done on the same day each month, catches broken tracking early and turns the data into decisions.

  1. Test your lead paths. Submit the contact form, tap the phone link on a phone and make a test booking. Confirm each one shows in GA4 Realtime. Exclude or note your test leads.
  2. Record total key events, compared with last month and the same month last year.
  3. Break leads down by channel and by landing page. Note the top three pages and any page whose leads dropped.
  4. In Search Console Performance, compare the last 28 days with the previous period. Record non-branded clicks, and list queries with high impressions but low CTR.
  5. Review Page indexing. Make sure every practice area page and attorney bio is indexed, and inspect anything new.
  6. Check Core Web Vitals and Sitemaps for new Poor URLs or fetch errors.
  7. Pull Google Business Profile calls and website clicks to show Maps performance alongside the website.
  8. Audit access. Remove anyone who no longer needs GA4, Tag Manager or Search Console access.
  9. Write three lines: what changed, the likely reason, and one action for next month.

When the report shows non-branded clicks stalling, the next step is usually local SEO work rather than more tracking. Our local SEO checklist for lawyers picks up where this guide stops. New to all of this? Our Start Here page shows the order to tackle domain, hosting, website and marketing tasks.

FAQ

Is Google Analytics free for law firms?

Yes. The standard version of Google Analytics 4 and Google Search Console are both free. Analytics 360, the paid enterprise tier, adds higher limits that a small firm won't need.

Are key events the same as conversions in GA4?

Yes, for practical purposes. Events that used to be marked as conversions in GA4 are now called key events. In Google's current terms, a "conversion" is a key event that you share with Google Ads for ad measurement and bidding.

Can I verify Search Console with my Google Analytics tag?

Yes, but only for a URL-prefix property. A Domain property can only be verified through DNS. If GA4 is already installed, the Analytics method is the quickest way to get started. Add a Domain property later when you have DNS access.

Why don't my GA4 and Search Console numbers match?

They measure different things. Search Console counts clicks from Google Search results. GA4 counts sessions recorded by your tag, which can be blocked or affected by consent choices, and it counts all channels. Small differences are normal. Use each tool for what it does well.

How long until GA4 shows data?

Realtime data usually appears within 30 minutes. Standard reports can take up to 24 hours. Search Console data linked into GA4 arrives about 48 hours after collection. Plan on a full month of data before you draw conclusions.

Should my marketing agency own our Google Analytics account?

No. The firm should own the Analytics account, the Tag Manager account and the Search Console property, and grant the agency user access. That way your history stays with you if you change vendors.

Can GA4 tell me which visitor became a client?

Not on its own, and you shouldn't try to make it, because that would mean sending identifying data to Google. Compare GA4's lead counts by channel with your intake records instead.

Next steps

Start by creating the GA4 property and Search Console Domain property under a firm-owned account. Install the tag one way only and link the two tools. Then set up form, phone, booking and chat key events. Test each lead path, check that no client details reach Google, and put the monthly checklist on the calendar. After three months you'll know which pages and channels bring in inquiries. Use that to decide where your next marketing dollar goes.

How do you set up Google Analytics for a law firm?

Create the account and property under a firm-owned Google account, not a personal Gmail and not your agency’s account. Then give outside vendors their own access. If a developer leaves, the firm keeps its data. These steps follow Google’s Set up Analytics for a website guide.

  1. Create an account. Go to analytics.google.com and click Start measuring. If you already have an account, go to Admin → Create → Account. Name the account after the firm.
  2. Create a property. Enter a property name, your reporting time zone (the firm’s local time) and currency. Then choose an industry, a business size and your goals.
  3. Add a web data stream. Go to Admin → Data streams → Add stream → Web. Enter your domain and keep enhanced measurement on. Enhanced measurement records page views, scrolls, outbound clicks, site search, video engagement, file downloads and form interactions without extra code.
  4. Copy your Measurement ID. It starts with G- and appears under the stream details. You’ll paste it into a plugin or Tag Manager in the next section.
  5. Install the tag. Choose one of the WordPress options below.
  6. Raise data retention to 14 months. Go to Admin → Data settings → Data retention. Standard properties can choose 2 or 14 months. The setting affects explorations and funnel reports, which you’ll want for comparing one year with the next.
  7. Filter out office traffic. Define your office IP address as internal traffic in the stream’s tag settings, then create an internal traffic data filter. Leave the filter in Testing first. An active exclude filter permanently discards the data it matches.
  8. Check data redaction. In the web stream, open Redact data. Email redaction is on by default for new properties. You can also add query parameters to strip, such as name, email or phone.
  9. Confirm data is arriving. Open the Realtime report and visit your site from a phone. Google says data can take up to 30 minutes to appear.

How do you install GA4 on a WordPress law firm website?

Most small firms on WordPress use one of three methods: the Site Kit by Google plugin, Google Tag Manager, or the Rank Math SEO plugin’s Analytics module. Each one can place the GA4 tag. Pick exactly one. If two plugins, or a plugin and your theme, both print the tag, every page view is counted twice.

A practical combination for many firms: Tag Manager places the tag and handles events, and Site Kit is connected only for its dashboard and Search Console data, with its own Analytics snippet turned off. Whatever you choose, record it in your site documentation so the next developer doesn’t add a second tag. For other plugins worth installing (and ones to avoid), see our guide to the best WordPress plugins for law firms.

To add GA4 through Tag Manager, follow Google’s Google tag setup steps. Create a new tag of type Google Analytics → Google tag and enter your G- ID. Set the trigger to Initialization – All Pages, test in Preview, then click Submit → Publish.

How do you set up Google Search Console for lawyers?

Add your site as a Domain property, verify it with a DNS record, submit your XML sitemap, and link it to GA4. These steps take about 20 minutes, plus DNS waiting time.

Domain property or URL-prefix property?

Choose a Domain property if you can edit your DNS. Google’s verification help explains that a Domain property (example.com) includes all protocols and subdomains. DNS is the only way to verify it. A URL-prefix property (https://www.example.com) covers only that exact prefix. It can be verified with an HTML file, an HTML tag, your Google Analytics tag or your Tag Manager container. That makes it handy if your domain registrar login is hard to find.

  1. Add the property. In Search Console, open the property selector → Add property → Domain, and type your domain without https or www.
  2. Verify with DNS. Copy the TXT record Search Console gives you and add it at your DNS host. That may be your registrar or Cloudflare. If your registrar is listed in Search Console, you can choose it and sign in instead. Google says DNS changes can take up to two or three days. Leave the record in place after verification, or you may lose access.
  3. Submit your sitemap. WordPress SEO plugins usually generate one, for example /sitemap_index.xml in Rank Math or Yoast. In the Sitemaps report, paste the URL and click Submit. You want a status of Success. Couldn’t fetch often means robots.txt is blocking it or the URL returns a 404.
  4. Add users, not owners. Give your agency or developer Full or Restricted user access. Keep ownership with the firm.
  5. Link Search Console to GA4. In GA4, go to Admin → Product links → Search Console links → Link. You need the Editor role in GA4 and must be a verified Search Console owner. Then publish the Search Console report collection under Library, because it’s unpublished by default (Google’s linking guide).

After linking, GA4 shows two extra reports. Google Organic Search Queries lists the searches that brought visitors. Google Organic Search Traffic lists landing pages with both Search Console and GA4 metrics. Search Console data reaches GA4 about 48 hours after Google collects it.

Moving hosts or rebuilding the site? Keep the same GA4 property and Search Console property, and check both reports for a few weeks after launch. Our guide to redesigning a law firm website without losing SEO covers redirects and the post-launch checks.

What should a law firm track in Google Analytics?

Track the four actions that start a client relationship: contact form submissions, phone calls from the site, consultation bookings and chat conversations. Mark each one as a key event. Google defines a key event as an action “particularly important to the success of your business.” Google’s Events and key events page explains that events previously marked as conversions are now called key events. “Conversion” now refers to the version shared with Google Ads for bidding.

You can mark up to 30 key events on a standard property, which is far more than a law firm needs. Fewer is better. If page views or scrolls count as key events, your “lead” numbers stop meaning anything. To mark an event, go to Admin → Events and click the star next to it (Google’s steps). The change applies from that point forward, not to past data.

How do I track form submissions in GA4?

The most reliable way is to send visitors to a dedicated thank-you page after a successful submission, such as /thank-you/, and count views of that page as generate_lead. Enhanced measurement’s form_submit event can fire on searches, newsletter boxes and failed submissions. Treat it as a backup, not your lead count. Many form plugins also offer their own GA4 integration. Recent Site Kit versions can detect lead events from several popular form plugins, so check its settings if you use Site Kit.

Two rules matter more than the method. The thank-you URL must not contain form data (no ?name=…&email=…). The event must never carry what the person typed. Our guide to a secure contact form for a law firm website covers the form side: spam protection, notifications and where submissions are stored.

How do I track click-to-call on a law firm website?

Make every phone number a tel: link, then use Tag Manager. Create a Just Links click trigger that fires on Some Link Clicks where Click URL contains tel:. Attach a GA4 Event tag named phone_click (Google’s GA4 event tag steps). This counts taps, not completed calls. To measure answered calls by source, you need a call-tracking service or your phone system’s reports. Phone numbers that appear only as plain text can’t be tracked at all.

How do I track consultation bookings and chat?

Embedded schedulers and chat widgets often run inside an iframe or on the vendor’s domain. Your GA4 tag can’t see what happens inside them. Use the vendor’s own GA4 or Tag Manager integration if it has one, or redirect to a confirmation page on your own site after booking. Then test it with a real booking in Tag Manager’s Preview mode or GA4’s DebugView. If you’re still choosing a scheduler, our comparison of Calendly vs Acuity vs Microsoft Bookings for law firms covers the options.

How do you keep client information out of Google Analytics?

Google prohibits sending personally identifiable information to Analytics. Its PII policy names email addresses, personal mobile numbers, Social Security numbers and names as examples. It warns that PII often leaks through page URLs, page titles, form fields and search terms. For a law firm the risk goes beyond Google’s terms. Someone filling in an intake form may describe their legal problem. Your duty to protect that information is set by your state’s rules of professional conduct, so check your state bar’s guidance on website data.

  • Never send form field values. No names, emails, phone numbers, case descriptions or “type of matter” answers in event parameters or custom dimensions.
  • Check thank-you URLs and page titles. Some form plugins append entries to the redirect URL. Turn that off, and add those parameters to GA4 data redaction as a safety net.
  • Watch site search. People type names and case details into search boxes. If that happens on your site, consider turning off the site search option in enhanced measurement.
  • Don’t use User-ID with client identifiers. Small firm websites rarely need it.
  • Limit access. Give each person their own login with the lowest role that works. Remove former staff and vendors.
  • Keep GA out of client portals. Pages behind a login (portals, payment pages) generally shouldn’t load marketing tags at all.

Do I need a cookie banner for Google Analytics?

It depends on where your visitors are and which privacy laws apply to the firm. There is no single US rule. Some state privacy laws and non-US laws (if you serve EU or UK visitors) can require notice or consent. Google says site owners are responsible for obtaining any required consent. Its consent mode passes a visitor’s choice to Google tags through settings such as analytics_storage and ad_storage. At a minimum, disclose analytics in your privacy policy. If you add a consent banner, choose a consent platform that supports consent mode, and get advice on which laws apply to your firm.

Which Search Console reports should a law firm check?

Three reports cover most of what a small firm needs: Performance, Page indexing and Core Web Vitals.

  • Performance shows clicks, impressions, CTR (clicks ÷ impressions) and average position, broken down by query, page, country and device. Filter queries by your firm name to separate branded searches (people who already know you) from non-branded ones like “divorce lawyer near me.” Non-branded growth is the clearest sign that SEO is working. Pages with many impressions but low CTR usually need a better title and description.
  • Page indexing lists which URLs are indexed and why others aren’t. Google says not every URL should be indexed. Check that your home page, attorney bios and every practice area page are. Statuses like “Crawled – currently not indexed” on a practice area page usually mean the page is thin or duplicates another. Our guide on how to write practice area pages covers fixing that.
  • Core Web Vitals groups your URLs as Good, Needs improvement or Poor, based on real-visitor data for LCP (good is 2.5 s or less), INP (200 ms or less) and CLS (0.1 or less). Low-traffic sites often show “no data.” That’s normal. See our guide to law firm website speed and Core Web Vitals for fixes.

Search Console covers your website, not your Maps listing. Calls and direction requests from Google Maps appear in your Google Business Profile performance data. Report both side by side. Many local searches end in a call straight from the profile without a website visit.

Which law firm website analytics KPIs matter most?

Track a short list of numbers tied to new matters, and watch the trend month over month and year over year. A single month on its own tells you little. Practice areas have different seasons and different search volumes, so compare against your own past results rather than “industry averages.”

GA4 counts inquiries, not clients. Once a quarter, compare GA4 leads with the intakes your firm actually logged, and how many became signed matters. That’s the only way to know which channels bring cases and not just contacts. Keep that comparison in your practice management or intake system, not in GA4.

Monthly reporting checklist for law firm analytics

This 30-minute routine, done on the same day each month, catches broken tracking early and turns the data into decisions.

  1. Test your lead paths. Submit the contact form, tap the phone link on a phone and make a test booking. Confirm each one shows in GA4 Realtime. Exclude or note your test leads.
  2. Record total key events, compared with last month and the same month last year.
  3. Break leads down by channel and by landing page. Note the top three pages and any page whose leads dropped.
  4. In Search Console Performance, compare the last 28 days with the previous period. Record non-branded clicks, and list queries with high impressions but low CTR.
  5. Review Page indexing. Make sure every practice area page and attorney bio is indexed, and inspect anything new.
  6. Check Core Web Vitals and Sitemaps for new Poor URLs or fetch errors.
  7. Pull Google Business Profile calls and website clicks to show Maps performance alongside the website.
  8. Audit access. Remove anyone who no longer needs GA4, Tag Manager or Search Console access.
  9. Write three lines: what changed, the likely reason, and one action for next month.

When the report shows non-branded clicks stalling, the next step is usually local SEO work rather than more tracking. Our local SEO checklist for lawyers picks up where this guide stops. New to all of this? Our Start Here page shows the order to tackle domain, hosting, website and marketing tasks.

FAQ

Is Google Analytics free for law firms?

Yes. The standard version of Google Analytics 4 and Google Search Console are both free. Analytics 360, the paid enterprise tier, adds higher limits that a small firm won’t need.

Are key events the same as conversions in GA4?

Yes, for practical purposes. Events that used to be marked as conversions in GA4 are now called key events. In Google’s current terms, a “conversion” is a key event that you share with Google Ads for ad measurement and bidding.

Can I verify Search Console with my Google Analytics tag?

Yes, but only for a URL-prefix property. A Domain property can only be verified through DNS. If GA4 is already installed, the Analytics method is the quickest way to get started. Add a Domain property later when you have DNS access.

Why don’t my GA4 and Search Console numbers match?

They measure different things. Search Console counts clicks from Google Search results. GA4 counts sessions recorded by your tag, which can be blocked or affected by consent choices, and it counts all channels. Small differences are normal. Use each tool for what it does well.

How long until GA4 shows data?

Realtime data usually appears within 30 minutes. Standard reports can take up to 24 hours. Search Console data linked into GA4 arrives about 48 hours after collection. Plan on a full month of data before you draw conclusions.

Should my marketing agency own our Google Analytics account?

No. The firm should own the Analytics account, the Tag Manager account and the Search Console property, and grant the agency user access. That way your history stays with you if you change vendors.

Can GA4 tell me which visitor became a client?

Not on its own, and you shouldn’t try to make it, because that would mean sending identifying data to Google. Compare GA4’s lead counts by channel with your intake records instead.

Next steps

Start by creating the GA4 property and Search Console Domain property under a firm-owned account. Install the tag one way only and link the two tools. Then set up form, phone, booking and chat key events. Test each lead path, check that no client details reach Google, and put the monthly checklist on the calendar. After three months you’ll know which pages and channels bring in inquiries. Use that to decide where your next marketing dollar goes.
