title.raw: E-Signature Software for Law Firms: DocuSign vs Adobe Acrobat Sign vs Dropbox Sign (2026)
title.rendered: E-Signature Software for Law Firms: DocuSign vs Adobe Acrobat Sign vs Dropbox Sign (2026)

content.raw:
Quick answer: For most small firms, the best e-signature software for law firms comes down to how many documents you send. Dropbox Sign is the lowest-cost choice for a busy solo or small team, because its pricing page advertises unlimited signature requests. DocuSign Business Pro fits firms that want to collect a retainer payment in the same step as the signature. Adobe Acrobat Pro makes sense when your lawyers already live in Acrobat and Microsoft 365.

Below you will find a verdict by firm type, a side-by-side table of plans and limits (checked on each vendor's official pages in November 2026), what US law says about electronic signatures, and a step-by-step engagement-letter workflow you can copy.

Key takeaways

  • Volume is the deciding factor. DocuSign's Standard and Business Pro plans allow 100 envelopes per user per year on annual billing. Dropbox Sign advertises unlimited signature requests.
  • Bulk send and payments live on upper tiers. DocuSign puts them on Business Pro. Adobe puts them on Acrobat Pro and Acrobat Studio.
  • Compliance claims differ by plan. Adobe says its Acrobat Standard and Pro e-signature features do not offer the same level of compliance as Acrobat Sign Solutions, its enterprise product.
  • US law supports e-signed engagement letters under the federal ESIGN Act and state laws based on UETA. Wills, family law matters and court documents are carved out of ESIGN, so check your state's rules.
  • Using Clio? Check what your practice management software already includes before you buy a separate tool.

Best e-signature software for law firms, by firm type

The right tool depends on your firm's size, sending volume and the software you already pay for. Here is the short version by firm type.

If you mostly need clients to sign one engagement letter per new matter, any of the three will do. The differences show up in volume caps, bulk sending, payments and how each tool fits into your email and document storage.

DocuSign vs Adobe Acrobat Sign vs Dropbox Sign: comparison table

The table compares the self-serve plans a small firm would actually buy. Prices are as of November 2026, in US dollars, and come from DocuSign's eSignature pricing page, Adobe's Acrobat for business pricing page and Dropbox Sign's pricing page. "Envelope" is DocuSign's word for one package of documents sent for signature. It counts as soon as you send it, whether or not anyone signs.

A few notes on the fine print. Dropbox Sign's pricing page also displays promotional offer terms, so first-year prices may differ from renewal prices. Confirm the figure at checkout. Adobe's team plans are annual commitments. Its page says a fee of half the remaining annual commitment applies if you cancel the monthly-billed option after 14 days. DocuSign's page notes that envelopes beyond your allowance are billed pay-as-you-go.

How we compared

This comparison is based only on each vendor's official pricing pages, feature pages, integration pages and trust or compliance pages, read in November 2026. We did not run hands-on tests and we do not score or rate the products. Where a vendor's page did not state something, the table says so instead of guessing. Plans and limits change often, so check the vendor's page before you buy.

DocuSign for lawyers: strengths and trade-offs

DocuSign is the best-known name, and its plans are the most clearly tiered. That clarity also makes the limits easy to see.

  • Pros: a real-time audit trail on every plan. Business Pro adds bulk send, payments, signer attachments and PowerForms. Broad Microsoft coverage (Word, Outlook, Teams, SharePoint). An Identify product family that covers ID document checks with liveness, knowledge-based authentication (US only) and phone or SMS one-time passcodes.
  • Cons: the 100-envelopes-per-user-per-year cap on Standard and Business Pro is tight for a high-volume intake practice. Standard does not include bulk send or payments. ID verification and SMS are paid add-ons.
  • Compliance claims: DocuSign's trust center lists ISO 27001:2022, SOC 1 Type 2, SOC 2 Type 2 and PCI-DSS. It also says DocuSign adheres to HIPAA, among other regulations.

Best for: firms that want payment collection at signing, intake via PowerForms, and an audit trail clients and opposing counsel will recognize.

Adobe Acrobat Sign: strengths and trade-offs

For small firms, "Adobe Sign" now usually means the e-signature features built into Acrobat Standard, Acrobat Pro and Acrobat Studio. Adobe sells its separate enterprise product, Acrobat Sign Solutions, through sales.

  • Pros: one license covers PDF editing and e-signature. Acrobat Pro adds Send in bulk, web forms, reusable signable templates and payments through Braintree. Adobe lists deep Microsoft integrations for Word, Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and Power Automate.
  • Cons: the pricing page does not state transaction limits, so confirm them with Adobe before relying on high volume. Plans are annual commitments with cancellation fees after 14 days. Adobe's own footnote says Acrobat Standard and Pro e-signature capabilities "do not offer the same level of compliance" as Acrobat Sign Solutions.
  • Compliance claims: Adobe's compliance list shows SOC 2 Type 2, ISO 27001:2022 and HIPAA-ready status for Acrobat Sign Solutions (enterprise) and Acrobat Sign for Government. Those listings apply to the enterprise offering, not automatically to an Acrobat Pro license.

Best for: firms that already buy Acrobat Pro for PDF work and want e-signature without another subscription.

Dropbox Sign for law firms: strengths and trade-offs

Dropbox Sign (formerly HelloSign) is the simplest of the three. Its pricing page leads with "unlimited signature requests with no hidden fees."

  • Pros: no envelope counting. Standard includes bulk send, signer attachments, template links, branding, an admin console and SMS authentication. The features page lists tamper-proof documents and a non-editable audit trail.
  • Cons: Essentials is limited to 1 user and 5 templates. Standard allows 15 templates and tops out at 5 users before you need a quote. SSO, data residency and advanced reporting are Premium-only. Payments are not listed on the pricing page. The integrations page names Microsoft Word and OneDrive, but not Outlook or Teams.
  • Compliance claims: Dropbox Sign states SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, GDPR and eIDAS compliance, plus AES 256-bit encryption at rest. HIPAA support requires a signed BAA and a minimum contract value.

Best for: solos and small teams who send many engagement letters, fee agreements and authorizations and do not want to track a quota.

Adobe Sign vs DocuSign: which costs less for a small firm?

On list price, Adobe Acrobat Pro for teams ($23.99 per license per month on an annual plan) costs less than DocuSign Business Pro ($45 per user per month billed annually). Both include bulk send and payments. The trade-off is that DocuSign publishes its envelope limit (100 per user per year) while Adobe's pricing page does not publish one.

A quick worked example for a three-lawyer firm on annual billing, at November 2026 list prices:

  • DocuSign Business Pro: 3 × $540 = $1,620 a year, with up to 300 envelopes in total
  • Adobe Acrobat Pro for teams: 3 × $287.88 = $863.64 a year
  • Dropbox Sign Standard: 3 × $17.50 × 12 = $630 a year at the displayed yearly rate (confirm the renewal price)

All three price by sender (user or license), so if not every lawyer sends documents, you may only need licenses for the people who send.

Is electronic signature legal for law firms?

Yes, for most documents a firm uses day to day. The federal ESIGN Act (15 U.S.C. § 7001) says a signature, contract or record relating to a transaction in or affecting interstate commerce may not be denied legal effect "solely because it is in electronic form." At the state level, most states have adopted the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (UETA) from the Uniform Law Commission. New York uses its own Electronic Signatures and Records Act (ESRA).

Some documents are carved out. ESIGN's exceptions (15 U.S.C. § 7003) include:

  • wills, codicils and testamentary trusts
  • state laws on adoption, divorce and other family law matters
  • court orders, notices and official court documents such as briefs and pleadings
  • certain notices, such as foreclosure or eviction notices for a primary residence and cancellation of health or life insurance

An exception from ESIGN does not mean electronic signing is always banned. It means another law governs, and that law varies by state and by court. Before e-signing estate planning documents, family law agreements, real estate instruments or anything that must be notarized or witnessed, check your state's statutes, your court's e-filing rules and your state bar's guidance.

One more rule matters when your client is a consumer. If a law requires you to give the client certain information in writing, ESIGN's consumer consent provision (§ 7001(c)) requires affirmative consent and specific disclosures before an electronic record can satisfy that requirement. Most e-signature tools show a consent screen, but confirm it fits your situation.

E-signature vs digital signature: what is the difference?

An electronic signature is any electronic mark or process a person adopts to sign a record, such as a typed name or a click. A digital signature is a specific technology that uses certificates and encryption to seal a document so any later change is detectable. Dropbox Sign's "tamper-proof documents" feature, for example, adds a digital seal to each document after signing.

How to send an engagement letter for e-signature: step by step

This workflow works in any of the three tools. Build it once as a template, and every new client gets the same clean process.

  1. Finalize your engagement letter template. Put the scope, fee terms and any required disclosures in one document. Have the responsible attorney approve the master version.
  2. Create a reusable template in the e-signature tool. Add signature, date and initials fields, and text fields for client name and matter. Lock the fields clients should not edit (DocuSign locked templates are on Business Pro).
  3. Set the signing order. Usually the client signs first and the attorney countersigns. Add a CC recipient for your file or practice management inbox.
  4. Choose signer authentication. Email-only is common for routine letters. For higher-risk matters, add an access code, SMS authentication or ID verification, where your plan includes it.
  5. Add the retainer step, if any. DocuSign Business Pro and Acrobat Pro can request a payment during signing. Before you take advance fees this way, check your state's trust accounting rules on where advance fees must be deposited.
  6. Send and set reminders. Turn on automatic reminders so you do not have to chase signatures by hand.
  7. File the completed package. Save the signed PDF and the audit trail (also called a certificate of completion) to the client matter, in your document system or practice management software.
  8. Review access. When staff leave, remove their accounts and transfer their templates and documents to an admin.

Getting clients to the signing step is often the slow part. If you book consultations online, see our guide to appointment scheduling tools for law firms. If calls go to voicemail, compare Smith.ai vs Ruby virtual receptionists, which can handle intake before you send the letter.

Security and confidentiality: what to check before you buy

Engagement letters, retainer agreements and medical authorizations contain confidential client information. Your duty to protect that information applies to the e-signature tool just as it does to email and file storage. Use this checklist when you set up any of the three:

  • Turn on two-factor authentication for every sender account (Dropbox Sign lists 2FA as an account security option).
  • Use your firm's domain email for sender accounts, not personal Gmail. See our Microsoft 365 setup guide for law firms or the Google Workspace setup guide.
  • Read the vendor's compliance page for the exact plan you buy. Adobe's and Dropbox Sign's certifications and HIPAA terms depend on the offering or contract.
  • If you need a HIPAA business associate agreement, get it in writing from sales before you upload health records.
  • Decide who can see completed envelopes. Shared team folders are convenient, but not every staff member needs every client's documents.
  • Do not email signed copies around unencrypted. Our guide to law firm email encryption covers safer options.

If clients reach you through your website first, the same care applies there. Read how to add a secure contact form to a law firm website and work through our law firm website security checklist.

What about Clio and other practice management software?

Check your practice management software first, because it may already include e-signature or a direct connector. Clio, for example, promotes an e-signature feature inside Clio Manage, and its app directory includes a DocuSign app. We could not open Clio's help pages to confirm the current plan requirements and limits, so ask Clio which plans include e-signature and what volume limits apply. If the built-in option covers your engagement letters, you may not need a standalone subscription at all.

Your office suite matters too. DocuSign and Adobe both list Word, Outlook, Teams and SharePoint integrations. Dropbox Sign lists Word, OneDrive and Google Workspace. If you have not picked a suite yet, start with Google Workspace vs Microsoft 365 for law firms.

Alternatives worth a look

Other e-signature tools also market to law firms, including SignNow, PandaDoc, SignWell and OneSpan Sign. We have not compared their official pricing here. Apply the same tests: sending limits, template count, bulk send, audit trail, signer authentication, integrations you actually use, and the compliance terms for the specific plan. For more side-by-side reviews, browse our tool comparisons hub.

FAQ

Is DocuSign legally binding for lawyers and clients?

Generally yes, for ordinary contracts such as engagement letters. Under the ESIGN Act and state UETA laws, a signature cannot be denied legal effect just because it is electronic. Exceptions such as wills, family law matters and court documents are governed by other rules, so check your state.

Which is cheaper, Adobe Sign or DocuSign?

At November 2026 list prices, Adobe Acrobat Pro for teams ($23.99 per license per month, annual) is cheaper than DocuSign Business Pro ($45 per user per month, billed annually) for similar features like bulk send and payments. DocuSign Personal ($11 per month, billed annually) is the cheapest single-user entry point of the two.

Does Dropbox Sign limit how many documents I can send?

Dropbox Sign's pricing page advertises unlimited signature requests. The limits are on users (1 on Essentials, up to 5 on Standard before a quote) and templates (5 on Essentials, 15 on Standard). SMS features carry their own limits.

Can I e-sign a will or a divorce agreement?

Not under ESIGN's general rule. ESIGN excludes wills, codicils, testamentary trusts and state family law matters. Whether those documents can be signed electronically depends on your state's laws and court rules, so check them and your state bar's guidance first.

Is DocuSign HIPAA compliant?

DocuSign's trust center says it adheres to HIPAA. Adobe lists HIPAA-ready status for Acrobat Sign Solutions, its enterprise product. Dropbox Sign requires a signed BAA and a minimum contract value. If your firm handles protected health information, confirm a BAA with the vendor for your exact plan.

Do my clients need an account to sign?

Generally no. All three price their plans per sender (user or license), and clients sign from a link they receive by email, or by SMS where enabled. Confirm the signer experience during your free trial.

What is an audit trail, and why do lawyers need it?

An audit trail is a record of who viewed and signed a document, when, and from what email address or device. It is your evidence if a client later disputes signing. Save it with the signed document in the client file.

Quick answer: For most small firms, the best e-signature software for law firms comes down to how many documents you send. Dropbox Sign is the lowest-cost choice for a busy solo or small team, because its pricing page advertises unlimited signature requests. DocuSign Business Pro fits firms that want to collect a retainer payment in the same step as the signature. Adobe Acrobat Pro makes sense when your lawyers already live in Acrobat and Microsoft 365.

Below you will find a verdict by firm type, a side-by-side table of plans and limits (checked on each vendor’s official pages in November 2026), what US law says about electronic signatures, and a step-by-step engagement-letter workflow you can copy.

Key takeaways

  • Volume is the deciding factor. DocuSign’s Standard and Business Pro plans allow 100 envelopes per user per year on annual billing. Dropbox Sign advertises unlimited signature requests.
  • Bulk send and payments live on upper tiers. DocuSign puts them on Business Pro. Adobe puts them on Acrobat Pro and Acrobat Studio.
  • Compliance claims differ by plan. Adobe says its Acrobat Standard and Pro e-signature features do not offer the same level of compliance as Acrobat Sign Solutions, its enterprise product.
  • US law supports e-signed engagement letters under the federal ESIGN Act and state laws based on UETA. Wills, family law matters and court documents are carved out of ESIGN, so check your state’s rules.
  • Using Clio? Check what your practice management software already includes before you buy a separate tool.

Best e-signature software for law firms, by firm type

The right tool depends on your firm’s size, sending volume and the software you already pay for. Here is the short version by firm type.

If you mostly need clients to sign one engagement letter per new matter, any of the three will do. The differences show up in volume caps, bulk sending, payments and how each tool fits into your email and document storage.

DocuSign vs Adobe Acrobat Sign vs Dropbox Sign: comparison table

The table compares the self-serve plans a small firm would actually buy. Prices are as of November 2026, in US dollars, and come from DocuSign’s eSignature pricing page, Adobe’s Acrobat for business pricing page and Dropbox Sign’s pricing page. “Envelope” is DocuSign’s word for one package of documents sent for signature. It counts as soon as you send it, whether or not anyone signs.

A few notes on the fine print. Dropbox Sign’s pricing page also displays promotional offer terms, so first-year prices may differ from renewal prices. Confirm the figure at checkout. Adobe’s team plans are annual commitments. Its page says a fee of half the remaining annual commitment applies if you cancel the monthly-billed option after 14 days. DocuSign’s page notes that envelopes beyond your allowance are billed pay-as-you-go.

How we compared

This comparison is based only on each vendor’s official pricing pages, feature pages, integration pages and trust or compliance pages, read in November 2026. We did not run hands-on tests and we do not score or rate the products. Where a vendor’s page did not state something, the table says so instead of guessing. Plans and limits change often, so check the vendor’s page before you buy.

DocuSign for lawyers: strengths and trade-offs

DocuSign is the best-known name, and its plans are the most clearly tiered. That clarity also makes the limits easy to see.

  • Pros: a real-time audit trail on every plan. Business Pro adds bulk send, payments, signer attachments and PowerForms. Broad Microsoft coverage (Word, Outlook, Teams, SharePoint). An Identify product family that covers ID document checks with liveness, knowledge-based authentication (US only) and phone or SMS one-time passcodes.
  • Cons: the 100-envelopes-per-user-per-year cap on Standard and Business Pro is tight for a high-volume intake practice. Standard does not include bulk send or payments. ID verification and SMS are paid add-ons.
  • Compliance claims: DocuSign’s trust center lists ISO 27001:2022, SOC 1 Type 2, SOC 2 Type 2 and PCI-DSS. It also says DocuSign adheres to HIPAA, among other regulations.

Best for: firms that want payment collection at signing, intake via PowerForms, and an audit trail clients and opposing counsel will recognize.

Adobe Acrobat Sign: strengths and trade-offs

For small firms, “Adobe Sign” now usually means the e-signature features built into Acrobat Standard, Acrobat Pro and Acrobat Studio. Adobe sells its separate enterprise product, Acrobat Sign Solutions, through sales.

  • Pros: one license covers PDF editing and e-signature. Acrobat Pro adds Send in bulk, web forms, reusable signable templates and payments through Braintree. Adobe lists deep Microsoft integrations for Word, Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and Power Automate.
  • Cons: the pricing page does not state transaction limits, so confirm them with Adobe before relying on high volume. Plans are annual commitments with cancellation fees after 14 days. Adobe’s own footnote says Acrobat Standard and Pro e-signature capabilities “do not offer the same level of compliance” as Acrobat Sign Solutions.
  • Compliance claims: Adobe’s compliance list shows SOC 2 Type 2, ISO 27001:2022 and HIPAA-ready status for Acrobat Sign Solutions (enterprise) and Acrobat Sign for Government. Those listings apply to the enterprise offering, not automatically to an Acrobat Pro license.

Best for: firms that already buy Acrobat Pro for PDF work and want e-signature without another subscription.

Dropbox Sign for law firms: strengths and trade-offs

Dropbox Sign (formerly HelloSign) is the simplest of the three. Its pricing page leads with “unlimited signature requests with no hidden fees.”

  • Pros: no envelope counting. Standard includes bulk send, signer attachments, template links, branding, an admin console and SMS authentication. The features page lists tamper-proof documents and a non-editable audit trail.
  • Cons: Essentials is limited to 1 user and 5 templates. Standard allows 15 templates and tops out at 5 users before you need a quote. SSO, data residency and advanced reporting are Premium-only. Payments are not listed on the pricing page. The integrations page names Microsoft Word and OneDrive, but not Outlook or Teams.
  • Compliance claims: Dropbox Sign states SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, GDPR and eIDAS compliance, plus AES 256-bit encryption at rest. HIPAA support requires a signed BAA and a minimum contract value.

Best for: solos and small teams who send many engagement letters, fee agreements and authorizations and do not want to track a quota.

Adobe Sign vs DocuSign: which costs less for a small firm?

On list price, Adobe Acrobat Pro for teams ($23.99 per license per month on an annual plan) costs less than DocuSign Business Pro ($45 per user per month billed annually). Both include bulk send and payments. The trade-off is that DocuSign publishes its envelope limit (100 per user per year) while Adobe’s pricing page does not publish one.

A quick worked example for a three-lawyer firm on annual billing, at November 2026 list prices:

  • DocuSign Business Pro: 3 × $540 = $1,620 a year, with up to 300 envelopes in total
  • Adobe Acrobat Pro for teams: 3 × $287.88 = $863.64 a year
  • Dropbox Sign Standard: 3 × $17.50 × 12 = $630 a year at the displayed yearly rate (confirm the renewal price)

All three price by sender (user or license), so if not every lawyer sends documents, you may only need licenses for the people who send.

Is electronic signature legal for law firms?

Yes, for most documents a firm uses day to day. The federal ESIGN Act (15 U.S.C. § 7001) says a signature, contract or record relating to a transaction in or affecting interstate commerce may not be denied legal effect “solely because it is in electronic form.” At the state level, most states have adopted the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (UETA) from the Uniform Law Commission. New York uses its own Electronic Signatures and Records Act (ESRA).

Some documents are carved out. ESIGN’s exceptions (15 U.S.C. § 7003) include:

  • wills, codicils and testamentary trusts
  • state laws on adoption, divorce and other family law matters
  • court orders, notices and official court documents such as briefs and pleadings
  • certain notices, such as foreclosure or eviction notices for a primary residence and cancellation of health or life insurance

An exception from ESIGN does not mean electronic signing is always banned. It means another law governs, and that law varies by state and by court. Before e-signing estate planning documents, family law agreements, real estate instruments or anything that must be notarized or witnessed, check your state’s statutes, your court’s e-filing rules and your state bar’s guidance.

One more rule matters when your client is a consumer. If a law requires you to give the client certain information in writing, ESIGN’s consumer consent provision (§ 7001(c)) requires affirmative consent and specific disclosures before an electronic record can satisfy that requirement. Most e-signature tools show a consent screen, but confirm it fits your situation.

E-signature vs digital signature: what is the difference?

An electronic signature is any electronic mark or process a person adopts to sign a record, such as a typed name or a click. A digital signature is a specific technology that uses certificates and encryption to seal a document so any later change is detectable. Dropbox Sign’s “tamper-proof documents” feature, for example, adds a digital seal to each document after signing.

How to send an engagement letter for e-signature: step by step

This workflow works in any of the three tools. Build it once as a template, and every new client gets the same clean process.

  1. Finalize your engagement letter template. Put the scope, fee terms and any required disclosures in one document. Have the responsible attorney approve the master version.
  2. Create a reusable template in the e-signature tool. Add signature, date and initials fields, and text fields for client name and matter. Lock the fields clients should not edit (DocuSign locked templates are on Business Pro).
  3. Set the signing order. Usually the client signs first and the attorney countersigns. Add a CC recipient for your file or practice management inbox.
  4. Choose signer authentication. Email-only is common for routine letters. For higher-risk matters, add an access code, SMS authentication or ID verification, where your plan includes it.
  5. Add the retainer step, if any. DocuSign Business Pro and Acrobat Pro can request a payment during signing. Before you take advance fees this way, check your state’s trust accounting rules on where advance fees must be deposited.
  6. Send and set reminders. Turn on automatic reminders so you do not have to chase signatures by hand.
  7. File the completed package. Save the signed PDF and the audit trail (also called a certificate of completion) to the client matter, in your document system or practice management software.
  8. Review access. When staff leave, remove their accounts and transfer their templates and documents to an admin.

Getting clients to the signing step is often the slow part. If you book consultations online, see our guide to appointment scheduling tools for law firms. If calls go to voicemail, compare Smith.ai vs Ruby virtual receptionists, which can handle intake before you send the letter.

Security and confidentiality: what to check before you buy

Engagement letters, retainer agreements and medical authorizations contain confidential client information. Your duty to protect that information applies to the e-signature tool just as it does to email and file storage. Use this checklist when you set up any of the three:

  • Turn on two-factor authentication for every sender account (Dropbox Sign lists 2FA as an account security option).
  • Use your firm’s domain email for sender accounts, not personal Gmail. See our Microsoft 365 setup guide for law firms or the Google Workspace setup guide.
  • Read the vendor’s compliance page for the exact plan you buy. Adobe’s and Dropbox Sign’s certifications and HIPAA terms depend on the offering or contract.
  • If you need a HIPAA business associate agreement, get it in writing from sales before you upload health records.
  • Decide who can see completed envelopes. Shared team folders are convenient, but not every staff member needs every client’s documents.
  • Do not email signed copies around unencrypted. Our guide to law firm email encryption covers safer options.

If clients reach you through your website first, the same care applies there. Read how to add a secure contact form to a law firm website and work through our law firm website security checklist.

What about Clio and other practice management software?

Check your practice management software first, because it may already include e-signature or a direct connector. Clio, for example, promotes an e-signature feature inside Clio Manage, and its app directory includes a DocuSign app. We could not open Clio’s help pages to confirm the current plan requirements and limits, so ask Clio which plans include e-signature and what volume limits apply. If the built-in option covers your engagement letters, you may not need a standalone subscription at all.

Your office suite matters too. DocuSign and Adobe both list Word, Outlook, Teams and SharePoint integrations. Dropbox Sign lists Word, OneDrive and Google Workspace. If you have not picked a suite yet, start with Google Workspace vs Microsoft 365 for law firms.

Alternatives worth a look

Other e-signature tools also market to law firms, including SignNow, PandaDoc, SignWell and OneSpan Sign. We have not compared their official pricing here. Apply the same tests: sending limits, template count, bulk send, audit trail, signer authentication, integrations you actually use, and the compliance terms for the specific plan. For more side-by-side reviews, browse our tool comparisons hub.

FAQ

Is DocuSign legally binding for lawyers and clients?

Generally yes, for ordinary contracts such as engagement letters. Under the ESIGN Act and state UETA laws, a signature cannot be denied legal effect just because it is electronic. Exceptions such as wills, family law matters and court documents are governed by other rules, so check your state.

Which is cheaper, Adobe Sign or DocuSign?

At November 2026 list prices, Adobe Acrobat Pro for teams ($23.99 per license per month, annual) is cheaper than DocuSign Business Pro ($45 per user per month, billed annually) for similar features like bulk send and payments. DocuSign Personal ($11 per month, billed annually) is the cheapest single-user entry point of the two.

Dropbox Sign’s pricing page advertises unlimited signature requests. The limits are on users (1 on Essentials, up to 5 on Standard before a quote) and templates (5 on Essentials, 15 on Standard). SMS features carry their own limits.

Not under ESIGN’s general rule. ESIGN excludes wills, codicils, testamentary trusts and state family law matters. Whether those documents can be signed electronically depends on your state’s laws and court rules, so check them and your state bar’s guidance first.

Is DocuSign HIPAA compliant?

DocuSign’s trust center says it adheres to HIPAA. Adobe lists HIPAA-ready status for Acrobat Sign Solutions, its enterprise product. Dropbox Sign requires a signed BAA and a minimum contract value. If your firm handles protected health information, confirm a BAA with the vendor for your exact plan.

Do my clients need an account to sign?

Generally no. All three price their plans per sender (user or license), and clients sign from a link they receive by email, or by SMS where enabled. Confirm the signer experience during your free trial.

What is an audit trail, and why do lawyers need it?

An audit trail is a record of who viewed and signed a document, when, and from what email address or device. It is your evidence if a client later disputes signing. Save it with the signed document in the client file.

  2. Check whether your practice management software already includes e-signature.
  3. Shortlist one tool from the verdict table and start a free trial with your real engagement letter template.
  4. Confirm sending limits, HIPAA or BAA terms and cancellation terms for the exact plan before you pay.

title.raw: Law Firm Email Encryption: How to Send Confidential Email Securely (2026)
title.rendered: Law Firm Email Encryption: How to Send Confidential Email Securely (2026)

content.raw:
Quick answer: Law firm email encryption means protecting the message itself, not just the connection it travels over. Most small firms already have what they need: Microsoft 365 Business Premium includes Microsoft Purview Message Encryption, and Google Workspace Enterprise Plus includes Gmail client-side encryption. For other plans, a service such as Virtru or Hushmail for Law, or a secure client portal, fills the gap. Gmail's confidential mode is not encryption, so don't rely on it for sensitive client files.

The ethics rule behind this is flexible. ABA Formal Opinion 477R says ordinary unencrypted email is generally still acceptable for routine messages. Stronger measures, such as encryption, are expected when the information is sensitive enough to call for them. This guide explains the three layers of email encryption, which option fits which firm, how to switch it on in Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace, and when you need it.

Key takeaways

  • TLS is the floor, not the ceiling. It protects mail between servers, but the message sits readable in each mailbox, and TLS can quietly fall back to an unencrypted connection.
  • Check your plan before you buy anything. Purview Message Encryption is included in Microsoft 365 Business Premium and E3/E5. Gmail client-side encryption needs Enterprise Plus, Frontline Plus, or Education Standard or Plus.
  • Confidential mode only restricts what recipients can do. Google's own help page says recipients can still take screenshots, and malicious programs may still copy the message.
  • The ethics test is case by case. Weigh how sensitive the information is, how likely a disclosure is, and what safeguards cost (ABA 477R and Model Rule 1.6 Comment [18]).
  • Portals often beat email for large files, ongoing document exchange, and clients who share a computer or email account.
Quick pick

Choosing Google Workspace? Start through our referral link → and ask us for a 10% first-year promo code.

We may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. It never changes our recommendations.

What does "encrypted email" actually mean?

"Encrypted email" covers three different things that offer very different protection. Vendors use the term loosely, so it helps to know which one you're getting.

1. TLS (encryption in transit)

TLS (Transport Layer Security) encrypts the connection between two mail servers, much as HTTPS protects a website connection. Google says Gmail always tries to send messages over TLS. If the receiving server doesn't support it, though, the message is sent anyway over a connection that isn't secure. TLS also does nothing once the message arrives. It sits readable in the sender's Sent folder and the recipient's inbox, and in any forward, sync, or backup along the way.

2. Message-level encryption (provider-managed keys)

Message-level encryption encrypts the email and supported attachments themselves, so only an authorized recipient can open them, whichever servers the message passes through. Microsoft Purview Message Encryption works this way. Recipients outside Microsoft 365 sign in or use a one-time passcode to read the message. By default Microsoft manages the encryption root key, and "bring your own key" (BYOK) is an option. Message-level encryption can also apply rights such as Do Not Forward.

3. End-to-end / client-side encryption

End-to-end (or client-side) encryption encrypts the message on the sender's device, and the provider can't decrypt it. Google describes Workspace client-side encryption as end-to-end encryption that Google servers and third parties can't decrypt. Proton Mail, and services that let the firm hold its own keys, fall into this group too. The trade-off is more setup and more limits: Gmail CSE, for example, turns off some features while encryption is on.

None of the three hides everything. Gmail's CSE documentation notes that the subject, timestamps and recipients don't get the additional encryption. Keep client names and matter details out of subject lines, whichever tool you use.

Do lawyers have to encrypt email? What ABA Opinion 477R says

No blanket rule requires lawyers to encrypt every email. The duty is to make "reasonable efforts" to protect client information. In ABA Formal Opinion 477R (2017, copy hosted by the Tennessee Board of Professional Responsibility), the ABA's ethics committee concluded:

  • A lawyer generally may send client information over the internet after taking reasonable efforts to prevent unauthorized access. The use of unencrypted routine email "generally remains an acceptable method" of communicating with clients.
  • Special precautions may be required when a client agreement or a law requires them, or when the information calls for a higher degree of security. The opinion says "particularly strong protective measures, like encryption, are warranted in some circumstances."
  • Lawyers must decide case by case, using the Model Rule 1.6 Comment [18] factors: how sensitive the information is, how likely a disclosure is without more safeguards, what those safeguards cost, how hard they are to implement, and whether they make it harder to represent the client.
  • Lawyers should be careful when a client uses a device or account that a third party can access, such as an employer's email system. The lawyer should consider warning the client about the risk.
  • For highly sensitive information, the lawyer should explain the risks to the client and agree on a method, such as "high level encryption or personal delivery."

The opinion also lists practical steps: understand the threat, know where client data is sent and stored, use reasonable security measures, label confidential communications, train staff, and vet technology vendors. Many states have their own ethics opinions on email and cloud services, so check your state bar's guidance as well.

When is encryption warranted? A decision table

This table turns the 477R factors into everyday scenarios. It's a starting point for a written firm policy, not a substitute for your own judgment or your state's rules.

Law firm email encryption options compared

How we compared: this table is based on each vendor's official documentation and pricing pages as of November 2026. We haven't run hands-on tests. Where a vendor didn't publish a price we could verify, the table says so.

Paubox is a different model from the others. Its page says outbound email is encrypted automatically, and recipients normally need no portal or password. If the recipient's mail server doesn't support TLS, the message goes to a secure web app instead. It's easy for clients, but ask the vendor how that compares with message-level encryption for your risk level. The page also says a business associate agreement (BAA) is included with all accounts.

Still choosing between the two big suites? Our Google Workspace vs Microsoft 365 comparison for law firms covers pricing, security and practice management integrations. Built-in encryption is one of the clearest differences between them.

Microsoft 365 message encryption: which plans include it?

Microsoft's Message Encryption FAQ lists Purview Message Encryption as part of Microsoft 365 Business Premium, Office 365 and Microsoft 365 Enterprise E3 and E5, Office 365 A1/A3/A5, and Government G3/G5. On Business Basic, Business Standard, Exchange Online Plan 1 or 2, Office 365 E1 or F3, you can add Azure Information Protection Plan 1 to get it. Each user who sends encrypted mail needs a license.

Other limits worth knowing, all from Microsoft's FAQ:

  • Messages, including attachments, can be up to 25 MB.
  • OneDrive and SharePoint "cloud attachments" aren't encrypted. Attach the file itself, or use a portal.
  • PDF attachments are encrypted only if an admin turns on PDF encryption.
  • Revoking a sent message works from Outlook on the web. Expiration and revocation for external recipients are part of Advanced Message Encryption.
  • The old Office 365 Message Encryption was deprecated on July 1, 2023. Purview Message Encryption replaces it.

How to set up encrypted email in Microsoft 365

Do this after the basics in our Microsoft 365 setup guide for law firms (MFA, admin roles, domain), and test with a non-firm account before you roll it out.

  1. Confirm licensing. In the Microsoft 365 admin center, check that each lawyer and staff member who will send encrypted mail has Business Premium, E3/E5, or the AIP Plan 1 add-on.
  2. Verify the service is on. Microsoft says message encryption activates automatically when Azure Rights Management is active, which is usually the case. To confirm, connect to Exchange Online PowerShell and run Get-IRMConfiguration. AzureRMSLicensingEnabled should be True. Then run Test-IRMConfiguration -Sender you@yourfirm.com -Recipient you@yourfirm.com and look for "OVERALL RESULT: PASS".
  3. Show users the manual button. In new Outlook and classic Outlook, compose a message and choose Options > Encrypt, then pick Encrypt or Do Not Forward (Microsoft's steps). Encrypt suits most client mail. Do Not Forward also blocks forwarding, printing and copying.
  4. Add an automatic rule as a safety net. In the Exchange admin center, go to Mail flow > Rules > Create a new rule. Set The sender is located: Inside the organization, add The recipient is located: Outside the organization, and add a trigger such as the subject containing [secure]. Under Do the following, choose Modify the message security > Apply Office 365 Message Encryption and rights protection and select the Encrypt template (Microsoft's guide).
  5. Optionally protect PDFs. In Exchange Online PowerShell, run Set-IRMConfiguration -EnablePdfEncryption $true so PDF attachments are encrypted too.
  6. Test from outside. Send an encrypted message to a personal Gmail address. Open it, reply, and check that the reply stays encrypted.
  7. Check spam and quarantine. Microsoft notes that one-time passcode emails often land in junk folders or quarantine, especially the first ones. Good SPF, DKIM and DMARC setup helps them get through.

Gmail confidential mode vs encryption: what's the difference?

Gmail confidential mode restricts what a recipient can do with a message, and it isn't presented as encryption. Google's confidential mode help page describes expiration dates, revoking access, an optional SMS passcode, and turning off forward, copy, print and download. It doesn't mention encryption. It also warns that recipients can still take screenshots or photos, and that recipients with malicious programs may still be able to copy or download the message.

Confidential mode is fine for a low-risk note you want to expire. For anything you'd describe as sensitive under 477R, use Gmail client-side encryption, a third-party encryption service, or a portal.

Encrypted email for lawyers on Google Workspace

Gmail client-side encryption is available on Enterprise Plus, Frontline Plus, Education Standard and Education Plus. It isn't included in Business Starter, Standard or Plus. According to Google's Gmail CSE article, it encrypts the body, inline images and attachments. With the Assured Controls add-on, users can send end-to-end encrypted email to anyone without setting up S/MIME. Without it, users exchange S/MIME certificates with recipients.

Limits to plan for: encrypted attachments and inline images are capped at 5 MB. Encrypted messages can't be virus-scanned. Email signatures, delegated access, printing, confidential mode and Google AI features are off while encryption is on.

How to set up encryption in Google Workspace

Finish the core setup in our Google Workspace setup guide for law firms first. Then:

  1. Enforce TLS with regular counterparties. In the Admin console, go to Apps > Google Workspace > Gmail > Compliance > Secure transport (TLS) compliance > Configure. Choose Inbound and/or Outbound, attach an address list of the domains (for example a co-counsel firm or a key client), and keep Require CA signed certificate and Validate certificate hostname checked. Mail to those domains then bounces instead of falling back to an insecure connection (Google's steps). Changes can take up to 24 hours.
  2. If you're on an eligible edition, turn on CSE. Google's simplified setup (Enterprise Plus or Frontline Plus with Assured Controls) works like this: go to Data > Compliance > Client-side encryption > Set up, click Provision (Cloud HSM and Google Identity are preselected), accept the Cloud HSM cost agreement, choose the organizational unit, enable Gmail, and save. It needs a Google Cloud organization, a billing account for Cloud HSM costs, and super admin access. It can be run only once. Other setups use the standard method with an external key service and identity provider.
  3. Train users to encrypt per message. In Gmail, click Compose, click the Message security icon, and under Additional encryption click Turn on. Turn encryption on before writing, because switching it on deletes the current draft.
  4. On Business editions, add a tool. Use a service such as Virtru, or a client portal, for sensitive matters, and write down which matters require it.

Secure client portals: often the better alternative

A secure client portal keeps documents in one encrypted place. Clients log in to view or upload files, and nothing travels as an attachment. ABA 477R itself mentions "a well vetted and secure third-party cloud based file storage system" as an alternative to email attachments. Portals help with large files and long-running matters. They also help when a client's email might be read by someone else, because the portal has its own login. Many practice management tools include one. For new-client intake from your website, see our guide to adding a secure contact form to a law firm website. For signatures, our e-signature comparison for law firms covers secure signing workflows.

Habits that matter as much as encryption

  • Turn on MFA for every mailbox. Encryption doesn't help if an attacker logs in as you.
  • Use neutral subject lines. Subjects usually aren't encrypted.
  • Turn off autocomplete for sensitive sends, or double-check recipients. A misaddressed message is the most common email leak, and encryption won't stop it.

The ethics rule behind this is flexible. ABA Formal Opinion 477R says ordinary unencrypted email is generally still acceptable for routine messages. Stronger measures, such as encryption, are expected when the information is sensitive enough to call for them. This guide explains the three layers of email encryption, which option fits which firm, how to switch it on in Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace, and when you need it.

Key takeaways

  • TLS is the floor, not the ceiling. It protects mail between servers, but the message sits readable in each mailbox, and TLS can quietly fall back to an unencrypted connection.
  • Check your plan before you buy anything. Purview Message Encryption is included in Microsoft 365 Business Premium and E3/E5. Gmail client-side encryption needs Enterprise Plus, Frontline Plus, or Education Standard or Plus.

  • The ethics test is case by case. Weigh how sensitive the information is, how likely a disclosure is, and what safeguards cost (ABA 477R and Model Rule 1.6 Comment [18]).
  • Portals often beat email for large files, ongoing document exchange, and clients who share a computer or email account.
Quick pick

We may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. It never changes our recommendations.

What does “encrypted email” actually mean?

“Encrypted email” covers three different things that offer very different protection. Vendors use the term loosely, so it helps to know which one you’re getting.

1. TLS (encryption in transit)

TLS (Transport Layer Security) encrypts the connection between two mail servers, much as HTTPS protects a website connection. Google says Gmail always tries to send messages over TLS. If the receiving server doesn’t support it, though, the message is sent anyway over a connection that isn’t secure. TLS also does nothing once the message arrives. It sits readable in the sender’s Sent folder and the recipient’s inbox, and in any forward, sync, or backup along the way.

2. Message-level encryption (provider-managed keys)

Message-level encryption encrypts the email and supported attachments themselves, so only an authorized recipient can open them, whichever servers the message passes through. Microsoft Purview Message Encryption works this way. Recipients outside Microsoft 365 sign in or use a one-time passcode to read the message. By default Microsoft manages the encryption root key, and “bring your own key” (BYOK) is an option. Message-level encryption can also apply rights such as Do Not Forward.

3. End-to-end / client-side encryption

End-to-end (or client-side) encryption encrypts the message on the sender’s device, and the provider can’t decrypt it. Google describes Workspace client-side encryption as end-to-end encryption that Google servers and third parties can’t decrypt. Proton Mail, and services that let the firm hold its own keys, fall into this group too. The trade-off is more setup and more limits: Gmail CSE, for example, turns off some features while encryption is on.

None of the three hides everything. Gmail’s CSE documentation notes that the subject, timestamps and recipients don’t get the additional encryption. Keep client names and matter details out of subject lines, whichever tool you use.

Do lawyers have to encrypt email? What ABA Opinion 477R says

No blanket rule requires lawyers to encrypt every email. The duty is to make “reasonable efforts” to protect client information. In ABA Formal Opinion 477R (2017, copy hosted by the Tennessee Board of Professional Responsibility), the ABA’s ethics committee concluded:

  • A lawyer generally may send client information over the internet after taking reasonable efforts to prevent unauthorized access. The use of unencrypted routine email “generally remains an acceptable method” of communicating with clients.
  • Special precautions may be required when a client agreement or a law requires them, or when the information calls for a higher degree of security. The opinion says “particularly strong protective measures, like encryption, are warranted in some circumstances.”
  • Lawyers must decide case by case, using the Model Rule 1.6 Comment [18] factors: how sensitive the information is, how likely a disclosure is without more safeguards, what those safeguards cost, how hard they are to implement, and whether they make it harder to represent the client.
  • Lawyers should be careful when a client uses a device or account that a third party can access, such as an employer’s email system. The lawyer should consider warning the client about the risk.
  • For highly sensitive information, the lawyer should explain the risks to the client and agree on a method, such as “high level encryption or personal delivery.”

The opinion also lists practical steps: understand the threat, know where client data is sent and stored, use reasonable security measures, label confidential communications, train staff, and vet technology vendors. Many states have their own ethics opinions on email and cloud services, so check your state bar’s guidance as well.

Law firm email encryption options compared

Paubox is a different model from the others. Its page says outbound email is encrypted automatically, and recipients normally need no portal or password. If the recipient’s mail server doesn’t support TLS, the message goes to a secure web app instead. It’s easy for clients, but ask the vendor how that compares with message-level encryption for your risk level. The page also says a business associate agreement (BAA) is included with all accounts.

Still choosing between the two big suites? Our Google Workspace vs Microsoft 365 comparison for law firms covers pricing, security and practice management integrations. Built-in encryption is one of the clearest differences between them.

Microsoft 365 message encryption: which plans include it?

Microsoft’s Message Encryption FAQ lists Purview Message Encryption as part of Microsoft 365 Business Premium, Office 365 and Microsoft 365 Enterprise E3 and E5, Office 365 A1/A3/A5, and Government G3/G5. On Business Basic, Business Standard, Exchange Online Plan 1 or 2, Office 365 E1 or F3, you can add Azure Information Protection Plan 1 to get it. Each user who sends encrypted mail needs a license.

Other limits worth knowing, all from Microsoft’s FAQ:

To confirm, connect to Exchange Online PowerShell and run Get-IRMConfiguration. AzureRMSLicensingEnabled should be True. Then run Test-IRMConfiguration -Sender you@yourfirm.com -Recipient you@yourfirm.com and look for “OVERALL RESULT: PASS”.
  3. Show users the manual button. In new Outlook and classic Outlook, compose a message and choose Options > Encrypt, then pick Encrypt or Do Not Forward (Microsoft’s steps). Encrypt suits most client mail. Do Not Forward also blocks forwarding, printing and copying.
  4. Add an automatic rule as a safety net. In the Exchange admin center, go to Mail flow > Rules > Create a new rule. Set The sender is located: Inside the organization, add The recipient is located: Outside the organization, and add a trigger such as the subject containing [secure]. Under Do the following, choose Modify the message security > Apply Office 365 Message Encryption and rights protection and select the Encrypt template (Microsoft’s guide).
  5. Optionally protect PDFs. In Exchange Online PowerShell, run Set-IRMConfiguration -EnablePdfEncryption $true so PDF attachments are encrypted too.
  6. Test from outside. Send an encrypted message to a personal Gmail address. Open it, reply, and check that the reply stays encrypted.

Limits to plan for: encrypted attachments and inline images are capped at 5 MB. Encrypted messages can’t be virus-scanned. Email signatures, delegated access, printing, confidential mode and Google AI features are off while encryption is on.

  1. Enforce TLS with regular counterparties. In the Admin console, go to Apps > Google Workspace > Gmail > Compliance > Secure transport (TLS) compliance > Configure. Choose Inbound and/or Outbound, attach an address list of the domains (for example a co-counsel firm or a key client), and keep Require CA signed certificate and Validate certificate hostname checked. Mail to those domains then bounces instead of falling back to an insecure connection (Google’s steps). Changes can take up to 24 hours.
  2. If you’re on an eligible edition, turn on CSE. Google’s simplified setup (Enterprise Plus or Frontline Plus with Assured Controls) works like this: go to Data > Compliance > Client-side encryption > Set up, click Provision (Cloud HSM and Google Identity are preselected), accept the Cloud HSM cost agreement, choose the organizational unit, enable Gmail, and save. It needs a Google Cloud organization, a billing account for Cloud HSM costs, and super admin access. It can be run only once. Other setups use the standard method with an external key service and identity provider.
  3. Train users to encrypt per message. In Gmail, click Compose, click the Message security icon, and under Additional encryption click Turn on. Turn encryption on before writing, because switching it on deletes the current draft.
  4. On Business editions, add a tool. Use a service such as Virtru, or a client portal, for sensitive matters, and write down which matters require it.

A secure client portal keeps documents in one encrypted place. Clients log in to view or upload files, and nothing travels as an attachment. title.raw: Appointment Scheduling Software for Law Firms: Calendly vs Acuity Scheduling vs Microsoft Bookings (2026)
title.rendered: Appointment Scheduling Software for Law Firms: Calendly vs Acuity Scheduling vs Microsoft Bookings (2026)

content.raw:
Quick answer: The best appointment scheduling software for law firms depends on what you already pay for. If your firm runs on Microsoft 365, Microsoft Bookings is included at no extra cost and is fine for free consultations. Choose Acuity Scheduling if you charge for consultations or want intake forms and deposits on one shared office calendar. Choose Calendly if you are a solo or small team that wants the simplest personal booking links, especially on Google Workspace.

Whichever tool you pick, keep the booking form short. Collect contact details and the names needed for a conflict check, not the facts of the case. This guide compares the three tools on price, intake questions, payments, reminders and WordPress embedding, with prices checked on each vendor's official pages as of November 2026.

Key takeaways

  • Microsoft Bookings comes with Microsoft 365 Business Basic, Standard and Premium. It has no payment support, and SMS reminders need a Teams Premium license.
  • Acuity Scheduling (a Squarespace company) is priced per account, not per user. Its Standard plan covers up to 6 calendars and adds SMS reminders. Every plan supports intake forms, payments and deposits.
  • Calendly is priced per seat. The Free plan gives one event type. Payments, reminder workflows and removing Calendly branding start on Standard.
  • All three can be embedded on a WordPress site. Calendly and Acuity provide embed code. Bookings offers an iframe, and a plain link button is the fallback.
  • A booking form is not a secure intake channel. Ask only for contact details and conflict-check names, and link to your secure contact form for anything sensitive.

Which scheduling tool should your law firm choose?

Start with the platform you already pay for, then ask whether you charge for consultations. Those two questions settle most decisions. Here is the verdict by firm type.

Firms on Microsoft 365 offering free consultations: Microsoft Bookings

If every lawyer already has Microsoft 365 Business Basic or higher, Bookings adds no extra cost. It reads staff free/busy time from Outlook, can create a Teams meeting link for each booking, and stores booking data in your Exchange Online tenant. The trade-offs are no online payments, fewer design options, and SMS that needs an add-on license. If you are still setting up the tenant, see our Microsoft 365 setup guide for law firms first.

Firms that charge for consultations: Acuity Scheduling

Acuity is the strongest fit when a paid consultation, deposit or cancellation policy matters. Every plan includes custom intake forms and payments through Stripe, Square or PayPal. Its features page says it can collect a full prepayment, a partial deposit, or store card details at booking. Because Acuity charges per account rather than per user, a firm with 2 to 6 lawyers can share one Standard plan.

Solos and Google Workspace firms that want simple booking links: Calendly

Calendly is the quickest to set up for one lawyer with one or two meeting types. The Free plan covers a single event type and one calendar connection. Most firms will want Standard, which adds payments, automated reminders and white-labeling (removing the Calendly logo). Calendly fits well alongside Google Workspace. If you are deciding between platforms first, read Google Workspace vs Microsoft 365 for law firms.

How we compared these scheduling tools

ProSiteGuide has not run hands-on tests of these products, and we do not give scores. This comparison is based on each vendor's official pricing pages, help-center articles and documentation, which we read in November 2026. Plans and features change often, so confirm details on the vendor's site before you buy.

Calendly vs Acuity vs Microsoft Bookings: comparison table

The table below summarizes what each official source says. "Not documented" means we could not confirm the feature on the vendor pages we opened.

Sources: Calendly pricing, Acuity Scheduling plans, Acuity features, Microsoft Bookings FAQ and Microsoft 365 pricing updates.

What does each option cost a small law firm?

Cost depends on how each vendor counts users. Calendly charges per seat. Acuity charges per account and caps the number of calendars. Bookings is part of your Microsoft 365 subscription. Here is a worked example for a firm with three lawyers who each take consultations, using yearly-billed list prices as of November 2026:

  • Calendly Standard: 3 seats × $10 = about $30 per month.
  • Acuity Standard: $27 per month for the account, which covers up to 6 calendars.
  • Microsoft Bookings: $0 extra if all three already have Microsoft 365 Business Basic ($7/user), Standard ($14/user) or Premium ($22/user). Add Teams Premium only if you need SMS reminders.

Card-processing fees from Stripe, Square or PayPal come on top of these prices whenever you collect payments.

Calendly for lawyers: strengths and limits

Calendly is a per-seat scheduling tool built around personal booking links and event types. An event type is a bookable meeting, such as "30-minute phone consultation."

  • Pros: a usable Free plan; three embed styles; up to 10 invitee questions per event type on all plans, per Calendly's help center; Stripe and PayPal payments on Standard and up; routing forms on Teams for firms that want to send different practice areas to different lawyers.
  • Cons: costs grow with every lawyer you add. Reminders and payments need a paid plan. Text reminders run through Workflows and are not available during a trial, according to Calendly's text-message article.
  • Confidentiality note: Calendly includes invitee answers in notifications by default. On Standard and up you can remove answers from notifications. Do that if any question could draw out case details.

Acuity Scheduling for law firms: strengths and limits

Acuity Scheduling is an appointment platform owned by Squarespace. It focuses on client-facing services: intake forms, payments, packages and reminders.

  • Pros: intake forms and payments on every plan, including deposits; one account can hold several lawyers' calendars; clients can accept terms and cancellation policies at booking; SMS reminders on Standard and up.
  • Cons: no free plan, only a 7-day trial. The Acuity logo is removed only on Premium. The Starter plan supports a single calendar.
  • Good for: flat-fee practices (estate planning, immigration, family law) that charge for a strategy session and want payment taken before the appointment.

Microsoft Bookings for law firms: strengths and limits

Microsoft Bookings is a Microsoft 365 app with a public booking page tied to Outlook calendars. It offers Personal Bookings for one lawyer's own page and Shared Bookings for a team page with services and staff.

  • Which plans include it: Microsoft lists Bookings in Microsoft 365 Business Basic, Business Standard, Business Premium, E1/E3/E5, F1/F3, A3/A5, Teams Essentials and Teams Premium, plus several Office 365 plans. It is not sold as a standalone app.
  • Pros: no extra subscription; booking data is stored in Exchange Online under your tenant's existing compliance policies; Teams links can be created automatically; you can require clients to tick a custom consent box before booking.
  • Cons: the official FAQ says plainly that "there's no payment support in Bookings." Bookings appointments can only be edited in the Bookings web app, not in Outlook. SMS needs Teams Premium and a US, Canada or UK phone number.
  • Watch out: the same FAQ lists a known issue where one attendee cancelling a group booking can send cancellation emails to all other attendees. Avoid group bookings for anything where attendees should not see each other.

What should a law firm booking form ask, and what should it never ask?

A law firm booking form should collect only what you need to confirm the appointment and run a conflict check. It should not collect the facts of the matter. Anything typed into a booking form lands in a third-party system, in notification emails and often in calendar entries that staff can see.

There is also an ethics angle. The ABA's guidance on lawyer websites, summarized by the ABA Journal, notes that a website inquiry may come from a prospective client. That is someone who consults a lawyer about possibly hiring them. Under ABA Model Rule 1.18, information from a prospective client can create confidentiality duties and even conflicts that limit who the firm can represent later. The same guidance suggests clear warnings that tell visitors not to send confidential information before a relationship exists. Rules vary by state, so check your state bar's guidance.

Safe booking form checklist

  1. Ask for: name, email, phone, preferred contact method, and practice area as a dropdown.
  2. For conflict checks: ask for the names of other people or businesses involved, and nothing else about them.
  3. Do not ask for: a "describe your situation" box, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, health details, immigration status or documents.
  4. Add a short notice above the submit button: booking does not create an attorney-client relationship, and please do not include confidential details.
  5. Link a secure channel for anything sensitive, such as your secure contact form on the firm website, or share details during the consultation itself.
  6. Turn off answer copies in notifications where the tool allows it, and limit who can view the booking calendar.

How do online booking tools fit with conflict checks?

None of the three tools runs a conflict check for you. A practical workflow: the client books a slot, staff check the names against your conflicts database the same day, and the lawyer confirms or cancels before the consultation. Use a minimum lead time so you are not booked too soon to finish the check. Bookings calls this "minimum lead time" in its scheduling policy, and Calendly and Acuity have similar notice settings. title.raw: Schema Markup for Law Firms: LegalService, Attorney and Local Business Explained (2026)
title.rendered: Schema Markup for Law Firms: LegalService, Attorney and Local Business Explained (2026)

content.raw:
Quick answer: Schema markup for law firms is a block of structured data (usually JSON-LD) that tells search engines exactly who your firm is, where it is, which lawyers work there and what each page covers. Most small firms need five pieces: LegalService on the home or contact page, Person on each attorney bio, BreadcrumbList site-wide, Article on blog posts, and a link between them using @id. The old Attorney type is deprecated on schema.org, so don't build new markup around it.

Schema will not push a thin page to the top of Google. What it does is remove guesswork. It confirms your name, address, phone, hours, lawyers and practice areas in a format machines read without ambiguity. That's the foundation local search and AI answers draw on.

Key takeaways

  • Use LegalService as the firm's type. Schema.org says the Attorney type is deprecated because "LegalService is more inclusive and less ambiguous."
  • Describe each lawyer as a Person linked to the firm with worksFor, ideally inside ProfilePage on the bio page.
  • Don't add star ratings to your own site's schema. Google says businesses that control reviews about themselves are ineligible for review stars.
  • FAQ rich results have been limited to well-known government and health sites since August 2023. FAQ markup won't get a law firm's FAQ shown in results.
  • One plugin should own your schema. Duplicate or conflicting blocks from a theme, a plugin and hand-written code give search engines mixed signals about your firm.

What is schema markup, and what does it actually do for a law firm?

Schema markup is code that labels the facts on a page using the shared schema.org vocabulary, which Google, Microsoft, Yahoo and Yandex founded together. Instead of a search engine guessing that "(555) 010-0100" in your footer is the firm's main number, your markup states it outright.

Google supports three formats: JSON-LD, Microdata and RDFa. Its introduction to structured data says all three work equally well when valid, and recommends the one that is easiest to maintain, which is usually JSON-LD. JSON-LD sits in a single <script type="application/ld+json"> tag, separate from your visible HTML, so it's the format this guide uses.

Does schema markup improve rankings?

Not directly, and nobody can guarantee it. Google's documentation describes structured data as a way to help it understand a page and to make the page eligible for rich results. It never presents it as a ranking boost. Its general structured data guidelines also say Google "does not guarantee that your structured data will show up in search results," even when the markup is valid.

Here's what schema can and can't do for a firm:

Does schema help with AI Overviews and AI search?

Google says there is no special markup for its AI features. Its page on AI features and your website states that there is "no special schema.org structured data that you need to add" to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode. The same page lists "making sure your structured data matches the visible text on the page" as a best practice that still applies. So treat schema as accurate, consistent labeling that supports your content. It isn't a separate AI optimization trick. Claims that one schema type "gets you cited by ChatGPT" aren't backed by any official documentation we could find.

Which schema types does a law firm need?

A typical solo or small firm site needs only a handful of types, each on the page it describes. Google's guidelines say to place markup on the page it describes and to mark up only content visitors can see.

LegalService vs Attorney vs LocalBusiness: which type should you use?

Use LegalService. Here's how the three relate:

  • LocalBusiness is the broad parent type for any business with a physical location. It inherits from both Organization and Place.
  • LegalService is the LocalBusiness subtype for "a business that provides legally-oriented services, advice and representation, e.g. law firms," in schema.org's own words. Google's LocalBusiness documentation tells you to "use the most specific LocalBusiness sub-type possible."
  • Attorney is a subtype of LegalService that schema.org now marks as deprecated. It still parses, but there's no reason to choose it for new markup. Rank Math's Local SEO documentation also says Attorney has been replaced by LegalService.

A common mix-up: Attorney was a business type, not a type for a person. For the individual lawyer, use Person. If you see older guides marking up each lawyer as "@type": "Attorney", that was describing the lawyer as a business with an address, which was never quite right.

LegalService schema example (JSON-LD for the firm)

The examples below use a fictional firm, "Harbor & Pine Law, PLLC", with placeholder domains (example.com), a reserved 555 phone number and a made-up address. Replace every value with your own details exactly as they appear on your site and your Google Business Profile.

Put this on the home page, or on the contact page if that's where your address and hours are displayed:

{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "LegalService",
  "@id": "https://www.example.com/#firm",
  "name": "Harbor & Pine Law, PLLC",
  "url": "https://www.example.com/",
  "logo": "https://www.example.com/images/logo-512.png",
  "image": "https://www.example.com/images/office-front.jpg",
  "description": "Estate planning and probate law firm serving Anytown and Example County.",
  "telephone": "+1-555-010-0100",
  "email": "info@example.com",
  "address": {
    "@type": "PostalAddress",
    "streetAddress": "100 Example Avenue, Suite 200",
    "addressLocality": "Anytown",
    "addressRegion": "TX",
    "postalCode": "00000",
    "addressCountry": "US"
  },
  "openingHoursSpecification": [
    {
      "@type": "OpeningHoursSpecification",
      "dayOfWeek": ["Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday"],
      "opens": "08:30",
      "closes": "17:30"
    }
  ],
  "areaServed": [
    { "@type": "City", "name": "Anytown" },
    { "@type": "AdministrativeArea", "name": "Example County" }
  ],
  "knowsAbout": ["Estate planning", "Probate", "Wills and trusts"],
  "knowsLanguage": ["en", "es"],
  "sameAs": [
    "https://www.linkedin.com/company/example-firm",
    "https://www.facebook.com/examplefirm"
  ],
  "employee": [
    { "@id": "https://www.example.com/attorneys/jordan-lee/#person" }
  ]
}

On the page, it goes inside a script tag, either in the <head> or the body:

<script type="application/ld+json">
{ ...the JSON above... }
</script>

Notes on the fields that matter most:

  • name and address are the only properties Google lists as required for LocalBusiness. Use your real-world firm name, with no added keywords. The same naming rule applies on your Google Business Profile.
  • telephone should include the country and area code, per Google's docs.
  • url should be the page for that specific location. Multi-office firms point each office's markup at that office's page.
  • @id is a permanent identifier for the firm (a URL plus #firm). It doesn't need to load as a page. It lets other blocks refer to the firm without repeating every detail.
  • areaServed and knowsAbout are valid schema.org properties for listing your service area and practice areas. Keep them consistent with what your pages say.
  • sameAs lists profiles that clearly belong to the firm, such as LinkedIn or a bar directory listing.
  • Google also recommends geo (latitude and longitude to at least five decimal places) and openingHoursSpecification. Add geo with your real coordinates; we left it out because the firm is fictional.

Skip aggregateRating and review here. Google's LocalBusiness page says those are for sites that capture reviews of other businesses. More on that in the mistakes section below.

Attorney schema example: Person markup for a bio page

Today, "attorney schema" means a Person on the lawyer's bio page. Google's ProfilePage documentation lists "an employee page on a company website" as a valid use, as long as the page focuses on one person affiliated with the site. That describes a well-built attorney bio page exactly.

{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "ProfilePage",
  "@id": "https://www.example.com/attorneys/jordan-lee/",
  "url": "https://www.example.com/attorneys/jordan-lee/",
  "mainEntity": {
    "@type": "Person",
    "@id": "https://www.example.com/attorneys/jordan-lee/#person",
    "name": "Jordan Lee",
    "jobTitle": "Attorney",
    "url": "https://www.example.com/attorneys/jordan-lee/",
    "image": "https://www.example.com/images/jordan-lee.jpg",
    "worksFor": { "@id": "https://www.example.com/#firm" },
    "alumniOf": {
      "@type": "CollegeOrUniversity",
      "name": "Example State University School of Law"
    },
    "hasCredential": {
      "@type": "EducationalOccupationalCredential",
      "credentialCategory": "license",
      "name": "Licensed to practice law in Texas",
      "recognizedBy": {
        "@type": "Organization",
        "name": "State Bar of Texas"
      }
    },
    "knowsAbout": ["Estate planning", "Probate"],
    "knowsLanguage": ["en", "es"],
    "sameAs": ["https://www.linkedin.com/in/example-jordan-lee"]
  }
}
  • worksFor points to the firm's @id, so the lawyer and firm are connected without duplicating the firm's address.
  • hasCredential, alumniOf, knowsAbout and knowsLanguage are all schema.org Person properties. Only include what the visible bio states.
  • Be careful with wording. Structured data is still a communication about your services. Don't describe a lawyer as a "specialist" or "expert" in markup unless the visible page can say so under your state's attorney advertising rules. Check with your state bar if you're unsure.

How do the pieces connect? Law firm structured data with @id

Is the Attorney schema type deprecated?

Does a solo lawyer need LegalService or Person schema?

Usually both. Mark up the practice as a LegalService, even if it carries your own name, so the address, phone and hours are described. Not from markup on your own site. Google's review snippet guidelines make reviews a business controls about itself ineligible for star snippets on LocalBusiness and Organization pages. Reviews on your Google Business Profile still appear in Maps and local results on their own.

It's optional. Since August 2023 Google shows FAQ rich results only for well-known government and health sites, so a law firm won't get the expanded FAQ display. Google says existing FAQPage markup doesn't need to be removed. The visible FAQ content itself is still useful to readers.

There's no fixed time. Google has to recrawl the page first. Requesting indexing in Search Console can speed that up for key pages, and the structured data reports update as pages are recrawled. Even then, rich results are never guaranteed.

No. They do different jobs. Your Google Business Profile drives your Maps listing. Schema describes your website's content. Keep the name, address, phone and hours identical in both.
