Most small firms need five pieces: LegalService on the home or contact page, Person on each attorney bio, BreadcrumbList site-wide, Article on blog posts, and a link between them using @id. The old Attorney type is deprecated on schema.org, so don’t build new markup around it.

Schema will not push a thin page to the top of Google. What it does is remove guesswork. It confirms your name, address, phone, hours, lawyers and practice areas in a format machines read without ambiguity. That’s the foundation local search and AI answers draw on.

Key takeaways

  • Use LegalService as the firm’s type. Schema.org says the Attorney type is deprecated because “LegalService is more inclusive and less ambiguous.”
  • Describe each lawyer as a Person linked to the firm with worksFor, ideally inside ProfilePage on the bio page.
  • Don’t add star ratings to your own site’s schema. Google says businesses that control reviews about themselves are ineligible for review stars.
  • FAQ rich results have been limited to well-known government and health sites since August 2023. FAQ markup won’t get a law firm’s FAQ shown in results.
  • One plugin should own your schema. Duplicate or conflicting blocks from a theme, a plugin and hand-written code give search engines mixed signals about your firm.

What is schema markup, and what does it actually do for a law firm?

Schema markup is code that labels the facts on a page using the shared schema.org vocabulary, which Google, Microsoft, Yahoo and Yandex founded together. Instead of a search engine guessing that “(555) 010-0100” in your footer is the firm’s main number, your markup states it outright.

Google supports three formats: JSON-LD, Microdata and RDFa. Its introduction to structured data says all three work equally well when valid, and recommends the one that is easiest to maintain, which is usually JSON-LD. JSON-LD sits in a single <script type="application/ld+json"> tag, separate from your visible HTML, so it’s the format this guide uses.

Does schema markup improve rankings?

Not directly, and nobody can guarantee it. Google’s documentation describes structured data as a way to help it understand a page and to make the page eligible for rich results. It never presents it as a ranking boost. Its general structured data guidelines also say Google “does not guarantee that your structured data will show up in search results,” even when the markup is valid.

Here’s what schema can and can’t do for a firm:

Does schema help with AI Overviews and AI search?

Google says there is no special markup for its AI features. Its page on AI features and your website states that there is “no special schema.org structured data that you need to add” to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode. The same page lists “making sure your structured data matches the visible text on the page” as a best practice that still applies. So treat schema as accurate, consistent labeling that supports your content. It isn’t a separate AI optimization trick. Claims that one schema type “gets you cited by ChatGPT” aren’t backed by any official documentation we could find.

A typical solo or small firm site needs only a handful of types, each on the page it describes. Google’s guidelines say to place markup on the page it describes and to mark up only content visitors can see.

Use LegalService. Here’s how the three relate:

  • LocalBusiness is the broad parent type for any business with a physical location. It inherits from both Organization and Place.
  • LegalService is the LocalBusiness subtype for “a business that provides legally-oriented services, advice and representation, e.g. law firms,” in schema.org’s own words. Google’s LocalBusiness documentation tells you to “use the most specific LocalBusiness sub-type possible.”
  • Attorney is a subtype of LegalService that schema.org now marks as deprecated. It still parses, but there’s no reason to choose it for new markup. Rank Math’s Local SEO documentation also says Attorney has been replaced by LegalService.

  "@type": "LegalService",
  "@id": "https://www.example.com/#firm",
  "name": "Harbor & Pine Law, PLLC",
  "url": "https://www.example.com/",
  "logo": "https://www.example.com/images/logo-512.png",
  "image": "https://www.example.com/images/office-front.jpg",
  "description": "Estate planning and probate law firm serving Anytown and Example County.",
  "telephone": "+1-555-010-0100",
  "email": "info@example.com",
  "address": {
    "@type": "PostalAddress",
    "streetAddress": "100 Example Avenue, Suite 200",
    "addressLocality": "Anytown",
    "addressRegion": "TX",
    "postalCode": "00000",
    "addressCountry": "US"
  },
  "openingHoursSpecification": [
    {
      "@type": "OpeningHoursSpecification",
      "dayOfWeek": ["Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday"],
      "opens": "08:30",
      "closes": "17:30"
    }
  ],
  "areaServed": [
    { "@type": "City", "name": "Anytown" },
    { "@type": "AdministrativeArea", "name": "Example County" }
  ],
  "knowsAbout": ["Estate planning", "Probate", "Wills and trusts"],
  "knowsLanguage": ["en", "es"],
  "sameAs": [
    "https://www.linkedin.com/company/example-firm",
    "https://www.facebook.com/examplefirm"
  ],
  "employee": [
    { "@id": "https://www.example.com/attorneys/jordan-lee/#person" }
  ]
}

On the page, it goes inside a script tag, either in the <head> or the body:

{ ...the JSON above... }
</script>

  5. Request indexing for key pages using URL Inspection in Search Console.
  6. Monitor monthly. Search Console’s rich result status reports show valid and invalid items over time and let you validate fixes. There’s also an “Unparsable structured data” report for syntax problems. Our GA4 and Search Console setup guide walks through getting access.

Common law firm schema mistakes

  • Self-serving review stars. Marking up testimonials or an embedded Google reviews widget on your own site. Google’s review snippet guidelines say pages using LocalBusiness or Organization markup are ineligible for star reviews when the business controls the reviews about itself. This includes embedded third-party widgets. Attorney advertising rules on testimonials apply separately.
  • Relying on FAQ rich results. Google limited FAQ rich results in August 2023 to “well-known, authoritative government and health websites.” Existing FAQPage markup does no harm and needn’t be removed, but it won’t make a firm’s FAQ appear in results. HowTo rich results were dropped entirely in September 2023.
  • Using the deprecated Attorney type for new markup, or using it for individual lawyers.
  • Marking up invisible content. Hours, areas or credentials that appear only in the code. Google’s guidelines say not to mark up content readers can’t see, and violations can lead to a manual action that removes rich result eligibility.
  • Inconsistent NAP. A different suite number or phone in schema than on your Google Business Profile and directory listings. Consistency is part of local SEO for lawyers, and schema should mirror it.
  • Keyword-stuffed names. Using “Anytown Probate Lawyer | Harbor & Pine” as the name. Use the firm’s actual name.
  • One office’s address on every location page. Each office needs its own LegalService entity with its own URL.
  • Set-and-forget. A lawyer leaves, hours change or the firm moves, and the schema keeps the old details for years.

Law firm schema checklist

  • Firm marked up once as LegalService with name, address, phone, URL, hours, logo and a stable @id
  • Each office has its own LegalService entity and page
  • Each attorney bio has a Person (in ProfilePage) with worksFor pointing at the firm
  • Breadcrumbs on all inner pages
  • Article or BlogPosting on posts, with the author linked to a bio page
  • No review or rating markup about the firm on the firm’s own site
  • One tool owns each entity; theme and widget schema turned off where it overlaps
  • Rich Results Test and Schema Markup Validator both pass on live URLs
  • Search Console structured data reports checked monthly

Schema is one item on a bigger list. Our free law firm website checklist covers the rest, and the Start Here guide shows where to begin if you’re building or rebuilding your site.

FAQ

Is the Attorney schema type deprecated?

Yes. The schema.org Attorney page states that the type is deprecated because LegalService is more inclusive and less ambiguous. Existing Attorney markup still parses because Attorney is a subtype of LegalService, but use LegalService for the firm and Person for individual lawyers.

Does a solo lawyer need LegalService or Person schema?

Usually both. Mark up the practice as a LegalService, even if it carries your own name, so the address, phone and hours are described. Then add a Person on your bio or about page, linked with worksFor. If the site truly represents you rather than a practice, Person-only setups in Rank Math or Yoast are an option, but you lose the business fields.

Can I show review stars for my law firm in Google?

Not from markup on your own site. Google’s review snippet guidelines make reviews a business controls about itself ineligible for star snippets on LocalBusiness and Organization pages. Reviews on your Google Business Profile still appear in Maps and local results on their own.

Should I still use FAQ schema on law firm pages?

It’s optional. Since August 2023 Google shows FAQ rich results only for well-known government and health sites, so a law firm won’t get the expanded FAQ display. Google says existing FAQPage markup doesn’t need to be removed. The visible FAQ content itself is still useful to readers.

Do I need schema on every page?

No. Google’s Organization documentation says you don’t need organization markup on every page. Put firm details on the home or contact page, Person markup on bio pages, Article markup on posts and breadcrumbs on inner pages. Other pages can reference the firm by its @id.

How long does it take for schema changes to show up?

There’s no fixed time. Google has to recrawl the page first. Requesting indexing in Search Console can speed that up for key pages, and the structured data reports update as pages are recrawled. Even then, rich results are never guaranteed.

Does schema replace my Google Business Profile?

No. They do different jobs. Your Google Business Profile drives your Maps listing. Schema describes your website’s content. Keep the name, address, phone and hours identical in both.

Next steps

Start by running your home page through the Schema Markup Validator to see what’s already there. In most WordPress sites, an SEO plugin is already outputting something. Then:

  1. Choose one tool to own your schema and turn off overlapping output.
  2. Set the firm type to LegalService with details that match your Google Business Profile.
  3. Add Person markup to each attorney bio and link it to the firm.
  4. Add breadcrumbs and Article markup if your plugin doesn’t already.
  5. Validate live URLs, then check Search Console monthly.

content.raw:
Quick answer: This WP Engine review comes down to one question: who looks after your firm's website? WP Engine is worth the price for a law firm whose site is run by a developer or agency that will use its staging and development copies, 30-plus days of backups and Cloudflare-powered CDN. Its Essential plan starts at $28/month billed annually ($336 upfront) as of November 2026. That is a first-year price for new customers, and WP Engine does not publish what you pay at renewal. A solo or small firm with no developer will usually get a simpler deal from Kinsta, or a cheaper one from SiteGround.

Key takeaways

  • Price: Essential is $28/month billed annually for the first year. A month-to-month option is listed at $35/month for one site. Renewal pricing is "subject to change."
  • Best for: firms with an agency or in-house developer who will use production, staging and development environments.
  • Not included: email hosting, DNS/nameservers, phone support (Business and up only) and help with custom code.
  • Contract terms: plans auto-renew, cancellation needs 30 days' notice, and visits over your plan limit can trigger overage fees.
  • Law-firm angle: put email on Google Workspace or Microsoft 365, route contact-form email through a proper sending service, and keep your own offline backups.

WP Engine review: the verdict for law firms

WP Engine is a managed WordPress host. "Managed" means the company runs the server, caching, platform security and WordPress core updates, while you or your developer look after the site's content, theme and plugins. It is one of the best-known premium hosts, and its plans lean toward agencies and developers.

For a small law firm, that profile cuts both ways. The tools are strong if someone technical uses them. If nobody does, you pay a premium for features that sit idle, and you take on an annual contract with an unknown renewal price.

  • Good fit: a 3–10 lawyer firm whose marketing agency builds and updates the site, tests changes before they go live, and wants long backup retention.
  • Reasonable fit: a firm running several sites (for example a main site plus practice-area microsites) that one developer manages from a single account.
  • Poor fit: a solo attorney maintaining a simple brochure site alone, who wants a predictable flat price and a host that migrates the site for them.

How we reviewed WP Engine

We have not run our own speed or uptime tests on WP Engine, and we don't give scores or star ratings. This review is based on WP Engine's official plans page (USD), its support documentation, its Terms of Service (last updated January 1, 2026) and its Service Level Agreement, all opened in November 2026. We focused on what a small firm actually pays, what happens at renewal and cancellation, and the limits that matter for a law firm site. Prices and terms change, so confirm them at checkout.

WP Engine pricing in 2026: what does it really cost?

WP Engine pricing starts at $28/month for the Essential plan, billed annually, which means paying $336 on day one. WP Engine now sells three plans (Essential, Business and Enterprise) and sizes Essential by a separate "capacity" selector. Many older reviews still quote the retired Startup, Professional, Growth and Scale names, so check plan names before you compare prices.

The table below shows US prices as of November 2026, before tax, from the WP Engine plans page.

Visit numbers are WP Engine's own estimates. A larger 30-site Essential tier also exists ($330/month or $3,168/year), but few small firms need it.

The renewal caveat

The fine print on the plans page says first-year pricing is "valid for new customers purchasing Essential plans only," is "not valid for upgrades, renewals," and that "product renewal pricing [is] subject to change." The annual price is also tagged as including a promotional discount. In plain terms: you know your year-one cost, but not year two.

The Terms of Service add that plans renew automatically for the same term, and that renewal fees are charged at WP Engine's "then-current rates," provided it tells you about any increase before your opt-out deadline. Ask sales for the renewal price in writing before you pay, and put your renewal date in the firm calendar at least 45 days ahead.

Overages, taxes and add-ons

  • Overages: the Terms say you're responsible for overages, invoiced monthly in arrears. WP Engine's overage pricing page lists $2 per 1,000 extra monthly visitors for its older plan families. It does not name Essential, so ask how overages apply to your plan. Repeat visits from one IP address within 24 hours count as one visit, and bot page views don't count.
  • Taxes: the plans page notes that "taxes and overages may apply during checkout."
  • Add-ons: AI-powered plugin updates, uptime monitoring, NitroPack page-speed optimization, and Advanced DDoS with a managed WAF (web application firewall) are optional add-ons on Essential. The plans page shows no prices for them.

What's included on the WP Engine Essential plan?

Essential includes managed WordPress, PHP and MySQL, daily backups, staging and development environments, a Cloudflare-powered CDN, free SSL and 24/7 chat support. According to the plans page and support docs:

  • Backups: automatic daily backups plus on-demand backups. The plans page says backups are kept "no less than 30 days and no longer than 60 days." The backup and restore guide says you can create a backup before any change, restore from the portal, and download a backup as a ZIP file.
  • Three environments per site: the environments guide describes production, staging and development copies, "a total of three environments per site." Your developer can build a redesign in development while testing a plugin update in staging.
  • CDN and SSL: a global CDN "powered by Cloudflare" and auto-renewing SSL. A CDN (content delivery network) serves your images and files from servers close to each visitor.
  • Security: Layer 3+4 DDoS protection, security patching and plugin risk scans. The fuller Global Edge Security bundle (managed WAF, bot management, advanced DDoS) is extra.
  • Caching: WP Engine's EverCache server caching. That is why it bans some caching plugins (more on that below).
  • Extras: 10 premium themes, Genesis Blocks, SSH access and "transferable sites," which let an agency build a site and hand it over to the firm's own account.

Business adds isolated server resources, 24/7 phone support, managed migrations, premium onboarding, Git-based deployment and a 99.99% uptime SLA (a written uptime promise with service credits). Essential runs on a shared environment and doesn't list that SLA.

WP Engine pros and cons

Pros

  • Developer-friendly workflow. Separate staging and development environments on every plan make it safer to change a live firm site.
  • Longer backup retention than many rivals. 30–60 days of daily backups, versus 14 days on Kinsta's entry plans.
  • Cloudflare-powered CDN included on Essential, with SSL that renews itself.
  • Free self-serve migration. WP Engine's FAQ says "it's free to migrate a site to WP Engine" using its migration plugin.
  • Multi-site tiers. The 3-site capacity tier suits firms running more than one WordPress site.

Cons

  • Unknown renewal price. The $28 entry rate is a first-year promotion.
  • Lock-in terms. Auto-renewal, 30 days' notice to cancel, and early termination makes "all remaining fees payable" due at once, per the Terms.
  • No phone support on Essential. Phone help starts with Business, listed at $400/month.
  • No email hosting and no DNS hosting. You need a separate email provider and must manage DNS at your registrar.
  • Disallowed plugins. Some popular caching and backup plugins are removed automatically.
  • No money-back guarantee stated on the current plans page, FAQ or Terms.

Is WP Engine good for law firms? Six things to check

WP Engine for law firms works well when you plan around its gaps. These are the points that matter more for a firm than for a typical small business.

1. Email lives somewhere else

WP Engine's scope of support says it doesn't provide nameservers or email servers and gives only limited help with outgoing email. That's normal for premium hosts and usually a good thing: a website problem or host move won't take your inbox down. Budget for Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 per user, and follow our law firm email setup guide for SPF, DKIM and DMARC.

2. Contact-form emails need a proper sending service

Intake inquiries are revenue, so form notifications must not land in spam. WP Engine recommends a third-party email service for site email, and it sells WP Offload SES (which sends through Amazon SES) as an ecosystem tool. Any reputable transactional email service works. Our guide to a secure contact form for a law firm website covers the setup and what not to collect.

3. Confidentiality is your job, not the host's

No hosting plan makes a firm website compliant with your professional duties on its own. The bigger risks are forms that collect case details, weak admin passwords and outdated plugins. Keep forms short, limit who has admin access, and check your state bar's guidance on technology and client confidentiality. Our law firm website security checklist lists the site-level steps.

4. Keep your own offline backups

WP Engine's backups are good, but its Terms of Service state that "it is your responsibility to maintain offline backups of your site at all times," and that after termination it can't help with migration. Download a full backup ZIP every month or so and store it in the firm's own cloud storage.

5. Check your plugins against the disallowed list

WP Engine's disallowed plugins list includes some caching plugins (such as W3 Total Cache), several backup plugins and many "related posts" plugins. It removes them automatically. Most duplicate features WP Engine already provides, but ask your developer to check the list before you migrate.

6. Support covers the platform, not your site's code

WP Engine support handles caching, CDN, SSL, backups and platform issues. It "cannot assist with custom code" and doesn't fix design, SEO or third-party plugin bugs. If nobody at your firm can do that work, you still need a developer or a website maintenance plan, which is why WP Engine pays off most for firms that already have one.

WP Engine vs Kinsta vs SiteGround

In the WP Engine vs Kinsta matchup, Kinsta is simpler for firms without a developer, while WP Engine offers more environments and longer backups. SiteGround is the budget choice and the only one of the three that hosts email. Entry plans, US prices as of November 2026:

Sources: Kinsta pricing and SiteGround WordPress hosting, opened November 2026. For the full breakdown, including a 3-year cost example, read our Kinsta vs WP Engine vs SiteGround comparison. If Kinsta looks like the better fit, our Kinsta review for law firms covers its plans and limits in detail.

Is WP Engine worth it? A quick decision guide

WP Engine is worth it if you will actually use what you're paying for. Answer these in order:

  1. Does a developer or agency maintain your site? If no, start with Kinsta (migration done for you, flat renewal) or SiteGround (lowest cost, email included).
  2. Will they use staging and development environments? If they only edit pages, the extra environments add little.
  3. Can you commit to annual billing and an unknown renewal? If you need certainty, get the renewal quote in writing or choose month-to-month at $35.
  4. Do you need phone support or an uptime SLA? Those need Business at $400/month, which is overkill for most small firms.
  5. Do you run more than one site? The 3-site tier ($624/year first year) makes WP Engine better value for multi-site firms.

Still weighing budget options? Our roundup of the best hosting for law firm websites also covers lower-cost shared hosting, and our tool comparisons hub lists the other head-to-heads.

How to move a law firm website to WP Engine

On Essential, migration is self-serve with WP Engine's free Site Migration plugin. Based on WP Engine's migration guide, the process looks like this:

  1. Check requirements and plugins. The plugin needs WordPress 5.0+, PHP 7.4+ and the WP REST API enabled. Remove anything on the disallowed list.
  2. Back up the current site at your old host and keep a copy offline.
  3. Prepare the destination. In the WP Engine portal, open Site migration and copy the connection details.
  4. Install the plugin on your current site, paste the details, and run a full migration.
  5. Test the copy on WP Engine: pages, contact forms, redirects and the attorney bios.
  6. Run a second migration if content changed during testing, so nothing is lost.
  7. Add your domain in the portal and update DNS at your registrar. SSL is set up once DNS points to WP Engine.
  8. Keep the old host active for a week or two before cancelling it.

Our step-by-step guide to moving a law firm website without downtime covers DNS timing and email records in more detail.

How do you cancel WP Engine, and can you get a refund?

You cancel WP Engine from the User Portal, and your account may need 30 days' notice. WP Engine's billing support page says only the account Owner can request cancellation, in the Billing section under Manage Plan. The Terms of Service require notice of non-renewal at least 30 days before the term ends. They say fees are not refundable except as stated, and that ending early (unless WP Engine materially breaches the agreement) makes the remaining fees due at once.

We found no money-back guarantee on the current plans page, FAQ or Terms. Some older reviews mention one, so if a trial period matters to you, ask sales to confirm it in writing before you buy.

FAQ

Is WP Engine worth it for a small law firm?

It is worth it if a developer or agency manages your site and will use staging, development environments and long backup retention. A solo attorney maintaining a simple site alone usually gets better value from Kinsta or SiteGround.

How much does WP Engine cost per month?

As of November 2026, Essential costs $28/month billed annually ($336) for the first year, or $35/month month-to-month for one site. Business starts at $400/month billed annually, and Enterprise is quoted individually.

What does WP Engine cost at renewal?

WP Engine doesn't publish its renewal price. The plans page says renewal pricing is "subject to change," and the Terms say renewals are billed at then-current rates after notice. Get a written quote before you sign.

Does WP Engine include email hosting?

No. WP Engine doesn't host mailboxes and recommends a third-party email provider. Most firms use Google Workspace or Microsoft 365.

Does WP Engine have phone support?

Only on Business and higher plans. Essential includes 24/7 chat support.

Will WP Engine migrate my site for free?

Migration is free on Essential, but you or your developer run it with WP Engine's plugin. Managed migrations done by WP Engine staff are listed on Business and above.

WP Engine vs Kinsta: which is better for a law firm?

Kinsta is easier for firms without a developer: it handles migrations and lists the same price at renewal. WP Engine suits agency-run sites that need development environments and 30+ days of backups.

Can I use any WordPress plugin on WP Engine?

Most plugins work, but WP Engine blocks a list of disallowed plugins, mainly some caching, backup and related-posts plugins, because they duplicate its features or slow the server.

Conclusion and next steps

WP Engine is a solid managed WordPress host for law firms whose sites are run by a developer or agency. Its main drawbacks for small firms are the unpublished renewal price, annual-contract terms and phone support locked to a $400/month plan. Before you buy:

  1. Decide who maintains the site, and ask them whether they'll use staging and development environments.
  2. Get the year-two price in writing, and diary the renewal and 30-day notice dates.
  3. Set up email separately and route form notifications through a sending service.
  4. Compare against Kinsta and SiteGround on 3-year cost, not first-year price.
  5. Plan the migration with a tested copy before you change DNS.

WP Engine’s scope of support says it doesn’t provide nameservers or email servers and gives only limited help with outgoing email. That’s normal for premium hosts and usually a good thing: a website problem or host move won’t take your inbox down. Budget for Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 per user, and follow our law firm email setup guide for SPF, DKIM and DMARC.

2. Contact-form emails need a proper sending service

Intake inquiries are revenue, so form notifications must not land in spam. WP Engine recommends a third-party email service for site email, and it sells WP Offload SES (which sends through Amazon SES) as an ecosystem tool. Any reputable transactional email service works. Our guide to a secure contact form for a law firm website covers the setup and what not to collect.

3. Confidentiality is your job, not the host’s

No hosting plan makes a firm website compliant with your professional duties on its own. The bigger risks are forms that collect case details, weak admin passwords and outdated plugins. Keep forms short, limit who has admin access, and check your state bar’s guidance on technology and client confidentiality. Our law firm website security checklist lists the site-level steps.

4. Keep your own offline backups

WP Engine’s backups are good, but its Terms of Service state that “it is your responsibility to maintain offline backups of your site at all times,” and that after termination it can’t help with migration. Download a full backup ZIP every month or so and store it in the firm’s own cloud storage.

5. Check your plugins against the disallowed list

WP Engine’s disallowed plugins list includes some caching plugins (such as W3 Total Cache), several backup plugins and many “related posts” plugins. It removes them automatically. Most duplicate features WP Engine already provides, but ask your developer to check the list before you migrate.

6. Support covers the platform, not your site’s code

WP Engine support handles caching, CDN, SSL, backups and platform issues. It “cannot assist with custom code” and doesn’t fix design, SEO or third-party plugin bugs. If nobody at your firm can do that work, you still need a developer or a website maintenance plan, which is why WP Engine pays off most for firms that already have one.

WP Engine vs Kinsta vs SiteGround

In the WP Engine vs Kinsta matchup, Kinsta is simpler for firms without a developer, while WP Engine offers more environments and longer backups. SiteGround is the budget choice and the only one of the three that hosts email. Entry plans, US prices as of November 2026:

Sources: Kinsta pricing and SiteGround WordPress hosting, opened November 2026. For the full breakdown, including a 3-year cost example, read our Kinsta vs WP Engine vs SiteGround comparison. If Kinsta looks like the better fit, our Kinsta review for law firms covers its plans and limits in detail.

Is WP Engine worth it? A quick decision guide

WP Engine is worth it if you will actually use what you’re paying for. Answer these in order:

  1. Does a developer or agency maintain your site? If no, start with Kinsta (migration done for you, flat renewal) or SiteGround (lowest cost, email included).
  2. Will they use staging and development environments? If they only edit pages, the extra environments add little.
  3. Can you commit to annual billing and an unknown renewal? If you need certainty, get the renewal quote in writing or choose month-to-month at $35.
  4. Do you need phone support or an uptime SLA? Those need Business at $400/month, which is overkill for most small firms.
  5. Do you run more than one site? The 3-site tier ($624/year first year) makes WP Engine better value for multi-site firms.

Still weighing budget options? Our roundup of the best hosting for law firm websites also covers lower-cost shared hosting, and our tool comparisons hub lists the other head-to-heads.

How to move a law firm website to WP Engine

On Essential, migration is self-serve with WP Engine’s free Site Migration plugin. Based on WP Engine’s migration guide, the process looks like this:

  1. Check requirements and plugins. The plugin needs WordPress 5.0+, PHP 7.4+ and the WP REST API enabled. Remove anything on the disallowed list.
  2. Back up the current site at your old host and keep a copy offline.
  3. Prepare the destination. In the WP Engine portal, open Site migration and copy the connection details.
  4. Install the plugin on your current site, paste the details, and run a full migration.
  5. Test the copy on WP Engine: pages, contact forms, redirects and the attorney bios.
  6. Run a second migration if content changed during testing, so nothing is lost.
  7. Add your domain in the portal and update DNS at your registrar. SSL is set up once DNS points to WP Engine.
  8. Keep the old host active for a week or two before cancelling it.

Our step-by-step guide to moving a law firm website without downtime covers DNS timing and email records in more detail.

How do you cancel WP Engine, and can you get a refund?

You cancel WP Engine from the User Portal, and your account may need 30 days’ notice. WP Engine’s billing support page says only the account Owner can request cancellation, in the Billing section under Manage Plan. The Terms of Service require notice of non-renewal at least 30 days before the term ends. They say fees are not refundable except as stated, and that ending early (unless WP Engine materially breaches the agreement) makes the remaining fees due at once.

We found no money-back guarantee on the current plans page, FAQ or Terms. Some older reviews mention one, so if a trial period matters to you, ask sales to confirm it in writing before you buy.

FAQ

Is WP Engine worth it for a small law firm?

It is worth it if a developer or agency manages your site and will use staging, development environments and long backup retention. A solo attorney maintaining a simple site alone usually gets better value from Kinsta or SiteGround.

How much does WP Engine cost per month?

As of November 2026, Essential costs $28/month billed annually ($336) for the first year, or $35/month month-to-month for one site. Business starts at $400/month billed annually, and Enterprise is quoted individually.

What does WP Engine cost at renewal?

WP Engine doesn’t publish its renewal price. The plans page says renewal pricing is “subject to change,” and the Terms say renewals are billed at then-current rates after notice. Get a written quote before you sign.

Does WP Engine include email hosting?

No. WP Engine doesn’t host mailboxes and recommends a third-party email provider. Most firms use Google Workspace or Microsoft 365.

Does WP Engine have phone support?

Only on Business and higher plans. Essential includes 24/7 chat support.

Will WP Engine migrate my site for free?

Migration is free on Essential, but you or your developer run it with WP Engine’s plugin. Managed migrations done by WP Engine staff are listed on Business and above.

WP Engine vs Kinsta: which is better for a law firm?

Kinsta is easier for firms without a developer: it handles migrations and lists the same price at renewal. WP Engine suits agency-run sites that need development environments and 30+ days of backups.

Can I use any WordPress plugin on WP Engine?

Most plugins work, but WP Engine blocks a list of disallowed plugins, mainly some caching, backup and related-posts plugins, because they duplicate its features or slow the server.

Conclusion and next steps

WP Engine is a solid managed WordPress host for law firms whose sites are run by a developer or agency. Its main drawbacks for small firms are the unpublished renewal price, annual-contract terms and phone support locked to a $400/month plan. Before you buy:

  1. Decide who maintains the site, and ask them whether they’ll use staging and development environments.
  2. Get the year-two price in writing, and diary the renewal and 30-day notice dates.
  3. Set up email separately and route form notifications through a sending service.
  4. Compare against Kinsta and SiteGround on 3-year cost, not first-year price.
  5. Plan the migration with a tested copy before you change DNS.

title.rendered: Local SEO for Lawyers: A Practical Checklist for Small Firms (2026)

content.raw:
Quick answer: Local SEO for lawyers means making your firm the most relevant, credible and easy-to-verify option when someone near your office searches for a lawyer. Google says local results are based mainly on three things: relevance, distance and prominence. You can't pay for a better local ranking, so the work is a verified and accurate Business Profile, a website with real practice-area and location pages, consistent listings, policy-compliant reviews, local links, and tracking the results.

This is the pillar checklist for small firms (solo to about 10 lawyers). It puts every local SEO task in order and links to our deeper guides where one exists, so you can work through it in 90 days without buying anything you don't need.

Key takeaways

  • Three factors decide local results: relevance, distance and prominence. Distance is mostly out of your control. The other two are not.
  • The basics come first: a verified Google Business Profile, matching name, address and phone (NAP) everywhere, and one strong page per practice area.
  • Location pages are fine; doorway pages are spam. Google's spam policies name city pages that funnel visitors to one page as doorway abuse.
  • Reviews must follow Google's policy and your bar's rules: no incentives, no asking only happy clients, and no confidential details in replies.
  • Measure calls and forms, not just rankings. Use the Business Profile performance report and Google Search Console.

What is local SEO for lawyers?

Local SEO (search engine optimization) for lawyers is the work of showing up when people search for legal help in a specific place. That includes searches like "divorce lawyer near me" or "DUI attorney Tacoma", and searches where Google guesses the person wants someone nearby.

For these searches, Google usually shows two kinds of results:

  • The local pack and Google Maps: a map with a short list of Business Profiles. Rankings here come from your Google Business Profile for your law firm, plus signals from around the web.
  • Regular ("organic") results: web pages, including your practice-area pages, directory listings and articles. Rankings here depend mostly on your website.

Paid placements, such as Google Ads and Local Services Ads, can also appear at the top. They are advertising, not local SEO, so this checklist leaves them out. Good local SEO helps both the map and the organic results, because Google uses your website and the rest of the web to judge your Business Profile.

How does Google rank law firms in local results?

Google's own help page, Tips to improve your local ranking on Google, says local results are based mainly on relevance, distance and prominence. It also says plainly: "There's no way to request or pay for a better local ranking on Google." Treat any vendor promising a guaranteed spot in the map pack with suspicion.

What this means in practice: you can't rank in the map pack across a whole metro area just by trying harder, because distance limits how far your profile reaches. You can make sure that, within your natural radius, Google has every reason to trust and show your firm.

Step 1: Get your Google Business Profile right

Your Business Profile is the single most important local asset. We cover setup, verification, categories, firm vs. lawyer profiles and suspensions in our full Google Business Profile guide for law firms, so here are only the rules that most often break local rankings, from Google's guidelines for representing your business:

  • Use your real-world name. Google says your name "should reflect your business's real-world name", and adding unnecessary information to it isn't permitted. "Smith Law" is fine; "Smith Law | Best Car Accident Lawyer Dallas" is not.
  • Use a real, staffed address. Google states that a mailing address where you don't operate, "also known as a virtual office", isn't eligible. P.O. boxes are not acceptable.
  • Use a phone number you control that connects to that specific office.
  • Follow the practitioner rules. Lawyers count as individual practitioners. Support staff should not create their own profiles.

Step 2: Build website foundations that support local rankings

Your website is where Google checks whether your profile is relevant and credible. Most small-firm sites lose local visibility because of a few basic gaps, not because of anything advanced.

One strong page per practice area

If you handle DUI, expungement and domestic violence cases, each needs its own page. A single "Criminal Defense" page listing all three gives Google little to match against specific searches. Our guide to writing practice area pages covers structure, depth and ethics wording, so this article won't repeat it.

Local signals on every key page

  • Your full firm name, address and phone in the footer, written exactly as they appear on your Business Profile.
  • A contact page with an embedded map, directions, parking notes and office hours.
  • Page titles that name the service and the place naturally, for example "DUI Defense Lawyer in Tacoma, WA | Smith Law". Google's SEO Starter Guide says a good title is "unique to the page, clear and concise, and accurately describes the contents of the page."
  • Attorney bio pages that show bar admissions, court experience and local ties. See our guide to writing an attorney bio page.

Location pages vs. doorway pages: where is the line?

A location page is a page about a real office you staff. A doorway page is a page made only to rank for a place-name search, with little that helps the reader. Google's spam policies define doorway abuse as pages "created to rank for specific, similar search queries", and give this example: "Having multiple domain names or pages targeted at specific regions or cities that funnel users to one page."

The classic law-firm mistake is 30 pages titled "Car Accident Lawyer in [Town]" with the same text and a swapped city name. Google's spam policies also name "creating substantially similar pages" as doorway abuse. Use this test instead:

  1. Do you have a staffed office there? Build a real location page: address, hours, directions, the lawyers who work there, photos of the actual office, and the cases handled from it.
  2. No office, but you genuinely serve the area? Only create a page if you can say something specific and true: the local courthouse and how its process works, local procedures, or what clients there should expect. Otherwise, list the areas you serve on your main practice pages.
  3. Is the only difference the city name? Don't publish it. Merge it into one strong page.

Structured data (schema)

Structured data is code that labels your firm's name, address, phone and hours so search engines can read them reliably. Google's LocalBusiness structured data documentation lists name and address as required properties, and says Google "does not guarantee that features that consume structured data will show up in search results." It is a clarity signal, not a ranking switch. Our guide to schema markup for law firms has the details and examples.

Step 3: Make your NAP consistent and build citations

NAP stands for name, address and phone number. A citation is any mention of those details on another website, such as a directory listing. When your details match everywhere, Google and potential clients can be more confident that your firm is real and at the address you claim.

Do this in order:

  1. Pick one exact format for the firm name, address (including suite number style) and main phone number, and write it down.
  2. Fix the sources you control: website footer and contact page, Google Business Profile, social profiles and email signatures.
  3. Claim the other major map platforms. Microsoft describes Bing Places for Business as a free platform for listings that appear in Bing search and Bing Maps, and says it improved importing listings from Google. Apple lets businesses claim their location and control how it appears in Apple Maps through Apple Business.
  4. Update your state bar's lawyer directory record. Most bars have a public member lookup. Make sure your firm address and phone there are current, following your bar's own process.
  5. Add or claim legal directory profiles. Choose the well-known national legal directories and any reputable local ones that people in your area actually use. Free profiles are usually enough to start. Judge paid upgrades on whether they send calls you can track, not on promises of SEO value.
  6. Clean up old addresses and duplicates after any office move, merger or name change. Old listings with the wrong phone number cost you clients directly.

You don't need hundreds of citations. A smaller set of accurate, relevant listings beats a mass submission to low-quality directories.

Step 4: Earn reviews the policy-compliant way

Google confirms that "more reviews and positive ratings can help your business's local ranking." For law firms, reviews also have to satisfy two rulebooks at once: Google's review policy and your state's professional conduct rules.

Google's Maps user-generated content policy does not allow businesses to:

  • "Offer incentives – such as payment, discounts, free goods and/or services – in exchange for posting any review."
  • "Selectively solicit positive reviews from customers." That rules out "review gating", where you only send the review link to clients who said they were happy.
  • "Discourage or prohibit negative reviews."
  • Post reviews based on a conflict of interest, such as current or former employment. Staff and family should not review the firm.

On the ethics side, the ABA Model Rules (which most states follow closely) restrict giving anything of value for recommending a lawyer's services. Minnesota's version of Rule 7.2(b), for example, says a lawyer "shall not compensate, give, or promise anything of value to a person for recommending the lawyer's services", with narrow exceptions. Many states also have rules on testimonials and client confidentiality. Check your own state bar's rules and ethics opinions before you start a review program.

A simple, compliant process:

  1. At the natural end of a matter, ask every client the same way, whatever you think they'll say.
  2. Send a short email or text with your direct Google review link. No gift, discount or fee reduction attached.
  3. Reply to reviews without confirming that the reviewer was a client or revealing any details of the matter. Our Business Profile guide covers safe reply wording for negative reviews.
  4. Flag reviews that break Google's policy through the profile; don't argue publicly.

Step 5: Earn local links from real relationships

Links from other websites are part of prominence; Google's local ranking page mentions "how many websites link to your business." For a local firm, the most natural links come from things lawyers already do:

  • Bar associations: state, county and specialty bar member pages, section pages, and speaker bios for CLE (continuing legal education) talks.
  • Community involvement: nonprofit boards, pro bono partners, local scholarships you actually fund, youth sports or community events you sponsor.
  • Local business groups: chamber of commerce member directories and business association pages.
  • Education and media: law school alumni or adjunct pages, local news quotes, and guest articles for local publications.
  • Professional referral partners: accountants, financial planners or therapists who list you as a resource, where that's honest and allowed by your bar.

Avoid paid link schemes. Google's spam policies list "buying or selling links for ranking purposes" as link spam, including "exchanging goods or services for links." A paid sponsorship is fine as a sponsorship, but don't pay specifically for a link to boost rankings.

Step 6: Publish content local clients actually need

Useful local content helps relevance and gives other sites a reason to link to you. Good examples for a small firm:

  • "What to expect at your first hearing at [County] District Court": parking, security, courtroom etiquette, typical timeline.
  • How a local process works, such as protective orders, small claims limits or probate filing steps in your county, linked to the official court page.
  • Answers to the questions your intake staff hear every week, written in plain English.

Skip generic posts that could be about any state. Google's spam policies also warn against "scaled content abuse": generating many pages mainly to manipulate rankings without adding value, whether a person or AI writes them. Five genuinely useful local pages beat 50 thin ones.

Step 7: Cover the technical basics

Technical SEO for a small law firm is mostly hygiene. Make sure that:

  • The site loads quickly and works well on phones, where many local searches happen. See our guide to law firm website speed and Core Web Vitals.
  • The phone number is a tap-to-call link and the contact form works (test it monthly).
  • The site uses HTTPS and has an XML sitemap submitted in Google Search Console.
  • Important pages aren't blocked from indexing and each has a unique title.
  • Hosting is reliable. A site that's often down or slow undercuts everything else; our best hosting for law firm websites comparison covers options.

How do you measure law firm local SEO?

Measure leads first and rankings second. Two free Google tools cover most of what a small firm needs.

  • Business Profile performance: Google's performance help page lists calls from the call button, direction requests, website clicks, the search terms people used to find you, profile views on Search and Maps, and bookings (if you use a booking provider). Search terms update at the start of each month.
  • Google Search Console: the Performance report shows clicks, impressions, click-through rate and average position, and can be grouped by query, page, country and device. Filter for your practice-area pages to see which local searches find them.

Add UTM tags to your Business Profile website link so that visits from it show up separately in Google Analytics. Our GA4 and Search Console setup guide for law firms walks through setup and conversion tracking. Then, once a month, compare three numbers: profile calls, website form submissions, and new consultations booked. Keep in mind that map rankings vary with where the searcher is standing, so a single "rank check" from your office isn't the full picture.

A 30/60/90-day local SEO plan for a small firm

Google's SEO Starter Guide notes that "every change you make will take some time to be reflected on Google's end." Plan in quarters, not days. This plan assumes a few hours a week from a lawyer or office manager, or help from your web developer.

Days 1–30: Fix the foundations

  1. Claim or verify your Google Business Profile and correct name, address, phone, hours and primary category.
  2. Decide your exact NAP format and update your website footer and contact page to match.
  3. Set up Google Search Console and Google Analytics, and add a UTM-tagged link to your profile.
  4. List every practice area you want clients for and check whether each has its own page.
  5. Record your starting numbers: profile calls, website clicks, form leads, Search Console clicks.

Days 31–60: Build relevance

  1. Write or improve your top two or three practice-area pages.
  2. Update attorney bios and the contact or location page; add structured data.
  3. Claim Bing Places and Apple Maps listings; update your bar directory record and key legal directories.
  4. Find and fix duplicate or outdated listings.
  5. Start a consistent, compliant review request at the close of each matter.

Days 61–90: Grow prominence

  1. Publish one or two genuinely local resource pages.
  2. Make sure your bar association, chamber and community memberships link to your site.
  3. Look for one speaking, writing or community opportunity that could earn a natural mention.
  4. Check speed and mobile usability; fix the worst issues.
  5. Compare day-90 numbers with your baseline and choose next quarter's priorities.

The complete local SEO checklist for attorneys

Use this table as your audit. For a broader site review beyond local search, use our free law firm website checklist.

FAQ

How long does local SEO take for a law firm?

There's no fixed timeline. Google's SEO Starter Guide says changes take time to be reflected and suggests waiting a few weeks before judging an individual change. Profile fixes can show up sooner; reviews, links and content build over months. Anyone quoting a guaranteed date is guessing.

How do I rank in Google Maps as a law firm?

Google says Maps and local results depend mainly on relevance, distance and prominence. Verify a compliant Business Profile, choose the right primary category, link it to a strong website, keep your NAP consistent, and earn genuine reviews and local links. You can't pay Google for a better local ranking.

Can I rank in a city where I don't have an office?

In the map pack, it's hard, because distance from the searcher is one of the three factors and virtual offices aren't eligible for a profile. In regular results, a genuinely useful page about serving that area can rank. Just don't create near-identical city pages, which Google treats as doorway abuse.

Do legal directories still help local SEO?

Accurate listings on reputable directories help confirm your firm's details and can send clients directly. Their value varies by practice area and city, so check which directories appear when you search for your own services, and track calls from any paid listing.

Is local SEO different from regular SEO for lawyers?

Local SEO focuses on searches tied to a place, including the map pack, so it adds your Business Profile, citations and reviews to the usual website work. For most small firms, nearly all valuable searches are local, so the two overlap heavily.

Should each lawyer at the firm have a Business Profile?

Google's guidelines treat lawyers as individual practitioners, and the right setup depends on your firm's size and branding. Our Google Business Profile guide explains the options. Support staff should not have their own profiles.

How much does local SEO cost for a small firm?

The core tools are free: Google Business Profile, Bing Places, Search Console and Google Analytics. Costs come from time, content writing, website work and any paid directory listings or agency help, and those vary widely. Doing the 90-day plan yourself first shows you what's worth paying for.

Next steps

Start with the 30-day foundations: verify your profile, fix your NAP, and set up measurement. Then work through the deeper guides in this cluster as you reach each step. If you're new to the site, our Start Here page shows where local SEO fits alongside your domain, hosting and website decisions. Local SEO for lawyers rewards steady, honest work: accurate information, genuinely useful pages and a reputation you earn.

Want this handled for you? ProSiteGuide builds and maintains fast, secure WordPress sites for law firms. Book a free consultation.

If you also want paid placement above the map results, see how Google Local Services Ads for lawyers work and what they cost.

Directory listings are one source of citations, so see our guide to legal directories for lawyers before you pay for any.

Jayce Tuazon Cabangcala, WordPress developer

Jayce is a WordPress developer, webmaster and SEO specialist with 8+ years of experience and 1,000+ websites delivered, including sites for law firms and mediators. ProSiteGuide's guides are researched from vendors' official documentation and pricing and updated when things change. Jayce also sells website design, hosting setup and maintenance services, which never influence our recommendations.

Local signals on every key page

  • Your full firm name, address and phone in the footer, written exactly as they appear on your Business Profile.
  • A contact page with an embedded map, directions, parking notes and office hours.
  • Page titles that name the service and the place naturally, for example “DUI Defense Lawyer in Tacoma, WA | Smith Law”. Google’s SEO Starter Guide says a good title is “unique to the page, clear and concise, and accurately describes the contents of the page.”
  • Attorney bio pages that show bar admissions, court experience and local ties. See our guide to writing an attorney bio page.

Location pages vs. doorway pages: where is the line?

A location page is a page about a real office you staff. A doorway page is a page made only to rank for a place-name search, with little that helps the reader. Google’s spam policies define doorway abuse as pages “created to rank for specific, similar search queries”, and give this example: “Having multiple domain names or pages targeted at specific regions or cities that funnel users to one page.”

The classic law-firm mistake is 30 pages titled “Car Accident Lawyer in [Town]” with the same text and a swapped city name. Google’s spam policies also name “creating substantially similar pages” as doorway abuse. Use this test instead:

  1. Do you have a staffed office there? Build a real location page: address, hours, directions, the lawyers who work there, photos of the actual office, and the cases handled from it.
  2. No office, but you genuinely serve the area? Only create a page if you can say something specific and true: the local courthouse and how its process works, local procedures, or what clients there should expect. Otherwise, list the areas you serve on your main practice pages.
  3. Is the only difference the city name? Don’t publish it. Merge it into one strong page.

Structured data (schema)

Structured data is code that labels your firm’s name, address, phone and hours so search engines can read them reliably. Google’s LocalBusiness structured data documentation lists name and address as required properties, and says Google “does not guarantee that features that consume structured data will show up in search results.” It is a clarity signal, not a ranking switch. Our guide to schema markup for law firms has the details and examples.

Step 3: Make your NAP consistent and build citations

NAP stands for name, address and phone number. A citation is any mention of those details on another website, such as a directory listing. When your details match everywhere, Google and potential clients can be more confident that your firm is real and at the address you claim.

Do this in order:

  1. Pick one exact format for the firm name, address (including suite number style) and main phone number, and write it down.
  2. Fix the sources you control: website footer and contact page, Google Business Profile, social profiles and email signatures.
  3. Claim the other major map platforms. Microsoft describes Bing Places for Business as a free platform for listings that appear in Bing search and Bing Maps, and says it improved importing listings from Google. Apple lets businesses claim their location and control how it appears in Apple Maps through Apple Business.
  4. Update your state bar’s lawyer directory record. Most bars have a public member lookup. Make sure your firm address and phone there are current, following your bar’s own process.
  5. Add or claim legal directory profiles. Choose the well-known national legal directories and any reputable local ones that people in your area actually use. Free profiles are usually enough to start. Judge paid upgrades on whether they send calls you can track, not on promises of SEO value.
  6. Clean up old addresses and duplicates after any office move, merger or name change. Old listings with the wrong phone number cost you clients directly.

You don’t need hundreds of citations. A smaller set of accurate, relevant listings beats a mass submission to low-quality directories.

Step 4: Earn reviews the policy-compliant way

Google confirms that “more reviews and positive ratings can help your business’s local ranking.” For law firms, reviews also have to satisfy two rulebooks at once: Google’s review policy and your state’s professional conduct rules.

Google’s Maps user-generated content policy does not allow businesses to:

  • “Offer incentives – such as payment, discounts, free goods and/or services – in exchange for posting any review.”
  • “Selectively solicit positive reviews from customers.” That rules out “review gating”, where you only send the review link to clients who said they were happy.
  • “Discourage or prohibit negative reviews.”
  • Post reviews based on a conflict of interest, such as current or former employment. Staff and family should not review the firm.

On the ethics side, the ABA Model Rules (which most states follow closely) restrict giving anything of value for recommending a lawyer’s services. Minnesota’s version of Rule 7.2(b), for example, says a lawyer “shall not compensate, give, or promise anything of value to a person for recommending the lawyer’s services”, with narrow exceptions. Many states also have rules on testimonials and client confidentiality. Check your own state bar’s rules and ethics opinions before you start a review program.

A simple, compliant process:

  1. At the natural end of a matter, ask every client the same way, whatever you think they’ll say.
  2. Send a short email or text with your direct Google review link. No gift, discount or fee reduction attached.
  3. Reply to reviews without confirming that the reviewer was a client or revealing any details of the matter. Our Business Profile guide covers safe reply wording for negative reviews.
  4. Flag reviews that break Google’s policy through the profile; don’t argue publicly.

Step 5: Earn local links from real relationships

Links from other websites are part of prominence; Google’s local ranking page mentions “how many websites link to your business.” For a local firm, the most natural links come from things lawyers already do:

  • Bar associations: state, county and specialty bar member pages, section pages, and speaker bios for CLE (continuing legal education) talks.
  • Community involvement: nonprofit boards, pro bono partners, local scholarships you actually fund, youth sports or community events you sponsor.
  • Local business groups: chamber of commerce member directories and business association pages.
  • Education and media: law school alumni or adjunct pages, local news quotes, and guest articles for local publications.
  • Professional referral partners: accountants, financial planners or therapists who list you as a resource, where that’s honest and allowed by your bar.

Avoid paid link schemes. Google’s spam policies list “buying or selling links for ranking purposes” as link spam, including “exchanging goods or services for links.” A paid sponsorship is fine as a sponsorship, but don’t pay specifically for a link to boost rankings.

Step 6: Publish content local clients actually need

Useful local content helps relevance and gives other sites a reason to link to you. Good examples for a small firm:

  • “What to expect at your first hearing at [County] District Court”: parking, security, courtroom etiquette, typical timeline.
  • How a local process works, such as protective orders, small claims limits or probate filing steps in your county, linked to the official court page.
  • Answers to the questions your intake staff hear every week, written in plain English.

Skip generic posts that could be about any state. Google’s spam policies also warn against “scaled content abuse”: generating many pages mainly to manipulate rankings without adding value, whether a person or AI writes them. Five genuinely useful local pages beat 50 thin ones.

Step 7: Cover the technical basics

Technical SEO for a small law firm is mostly hygiene. Make sure that:

  • The site loads quickly and works well on phones, where many local searches happen. See our guide to law firm website speed and Core Web Vitals.
  • The phone number is a tap-to-call link and the contact form works (test it monthly).
  • The site uses HTTPS and has an XML sitemap submitted in Google Search Console.
  • Important pages aren’t blocked from indexing and each has a unique title.
  • Hosting is reliable. A site that’s often down or slow undercuts everything else; our best hosting for law firm websites comparison covers options.

How do you measure law firm local SEO?

Measure leads first and rankings second. Two free Google tools cover most of what a small firm needs.

  • Business Profile performance: Google’s performance help page lists calls from the call button, direction requests, website clicks, the search terms people used to find you, profile views on Search and Maps, and bookings (if you use a booking provider). Search terms update at the start of each month.
  • Google Search Console: the Performance report shows clicks, impressions, click-through rate and average position, and can be grouped by query, page, country and device. Filter for your practice-area pages to see which local searches find them.

Add UTM tags to your Business Profile website link so that visits from it show up separately in Google Analytics. Our GA4 and Search Console setup guide for law firms walks through setup and conversion tracking. Then, once a month, compare three numbers: profile calls, website form submissions, and new consultations booked. Keep in mind that map rankings vary with where the searcher is standing, so a single “rank check” from your office isn’t the full picture.

A 30/60/90-day local SEO plan for a small firm

Google’s SEO Starter Guide notes that “every change you make will take some time to be reflected on Google’s end.” Plan in quarters, not days. This plan assumes a few hours a week from a lawyer or office manager, or help from your web developer.

Days 1–30: Fix the foundations

  1. Claim or verify your Google Business Profile and correct name, address, phone, hours and primary category.
  2. Decide your exact NAP format and update your website footer and contact page to match.
  3. Set up Google Search Console and Google Analytics, and add a UTM-tagged link to your profile.
  4. List every practice area you want clients for and check whether each has its own page.
  5. Record your starting numbers: profile calls, website clicks, form leads, Search Console clicks.

Days 31–60: Build relevance

  1. Write or improve your top two or three practice-area pages.
  2. Update attorney bios and the contact or location page; add structured data.
  3. Claim Bing Places and Apple Maps listings; update your bar directory record and key legal directories.
  4. Find and fix duplicate or outdated listings.
  5. Start a consistent, compliant review request at the close of each matter.

Days 61–90: Grow prominence

  1. Publish one or two genuinely local resource pages.
  2. Make sure your bar association, chamber and community memberships link to your site.
  3. Look for one speaking, writing or community opportunity that could earn a natural mention.
  4. Check speed and mobile usability; fix the worst issues.
  5. Compare day-90 numbers with your baseline and choose next quarter’s priorities.

The complete local SEO checklist for attorneys

Use this table as your audit. For a broader site review beyond local search, use our free law firm website checklist.

FAQ

How long does local SEO take for a law firm?

There’s no fixed timeline. Google’s SEO Starter Guide says changes take time to be reflected and suggests waiting a few weeks before judging an individual change. Profile fixes can show up sooner; reviews, links and content build over months. Anyone quoting a guaranteed date is guessing.

How do I rank in Google Maps as a law firm?

Google says Maps and local results depend mainly on relevance, distance and prominence. Verify a compliant Business Profile, choose the right primary category, link it to a strong website, keep your NAP consistent, and earn genuine reviews and local links. You can’t pay Google for a better local ranking.

Can I rank in a city where I don’t have an office?

In the map pack, it’s hard, because distance from the searcher is one of the three factors and virtual offices aren’t eligible for a profile. In regular results, a genuinely useful page about serving that area can rank. Just don’t create near-identical city pages, which Google treats as doorway abuse.

Do legal directories still help local SEO?

Accurate listings on reputable directories help confirm your firm’s details and can send clients directly. Their value varies by practice area and city, so check which directories appear when you search for your own services, and track calls from any paid listing.

Is local SEO different from regular SEO for lawyers?

Local SEO focuses on searches tied to a place, including the map pack, so it adds your Business Profile, citations and reviews to the usual website work. For most small firms, nearly all valuable searches are local, so the two overlap heavily.

Should each lawyer at the firm have a Business Profile?

Google’s guidelines treat lawyers as individual practitioners, and the right setup depends on your firm’s size and branding. Our Google Business Profile guide explains the options. Support staff should not have their own profiles.

How much does local SEO cost for a small firm?

The core tools are free: Google Business Profile, Bing Places, Search Console and Google Analytics. Costs come from time, content writing, website work and any paid directory listings or agency help, and those vary widely. Doing the 90-day plan yourself first shows you what’s worth paying for.

Next steps

Start with the 30-day foundations: verify your profile, fix your NAP, and set up measurement. Then work through the deeper guides in this cluster as you reach each step. If you’re new to the site, our Start Here page shows where local SEO fits alongside your domain, hosting and website decisions. Local SEO for lawyers rewards steady, honest work: accurate information, genuinely useful pages and a reputation you earn.
