title.rendered: Law Firm Website Redesign: How to Relaunch Without Losing Rankings (2026 Checklist)

content.raw:
Quick answer: A law firm website redesign won't wreck your rankings if you handle it as a site migration first and a design project second. List every URL that brings in traffic or links, keep the pages that work, and 301-redirect each changed URL to its closest new page. Before launch, test forms, tracking and the noindex and robots.txt settings on staging. After launch, watch Search Console for a few weeks while Google re-crawls. A short ranking wobble is normal. A lasting drop usually comes from a missed redirect, deleted content or a leftover block on search engines.

Key takeaways

  • Most ranking losses after a relaunch come from URLs that changed with no redirect, or from pages that were deleted. The new design itself is rarely the problem.
  • Keep URLs that already rank. If a URL must change, use a server-side 301 (permanent) redirect to the closest new page, not to the home page.
  • Use Search Console's Change of Address tool only when the domain changes. You don't need it for a new design, a new host or HTTP to HTTPS.
  • The most common launch-day mistake is leaving staging's noindex tag or robots.txt block on the live site. Check it within minutes of going live.
  • Google says rankings can fluctuate for a while and most pages on a small site move over in a few weeks. Keep your redirects for at least a year.

Does a law firm website redesign hurt SEO?

Not if your URLs, content and crawl settings carry over. Google ranks pages, not designs. Your practice area pages, attorney bios and the posts that earned links are the reason you rank. A new theme, colors or layout doesn't change that, as long as those pages keep their content and can still be found at the same address, or at a new one through a redirect.

Rankings drop when a redesign quietly removes the signals Google relied on. Common examples:

  • A new URL structure (for example /car-accidents/ becomes /practice-areas/auto/) with no redirects. Old links and old search results now lead to 404 pages.
  • Long practice area pages cut down to a headline and a contact form to "clean up" the design.
  • Blog posts deleted in bulk, including the few that brought in most of your links.
  • Staging settings carried over to the live site: a sitewide noindex tag or a Disallow: / line in robots.txt.
  • Title tags, headings and internal links lost because a page builder rebuilt the pages from scratch.

Everything in the checklist below exists to prevent one of these.

Signs your firm needs a website redesign

Redesign because the site is failing at its job, not because it looks a few years old. Good reasons include:

  • Leads have dropped off. Calls and form submissions from the site are falling while traffic holds steady. That points to the page experience, not visibility.
  • It's hard to use on a phone. Tiny tap targets, no click-to-call button, menus that don't open properly.
  • It's slow. Heavy sliders, page builders stacked on page builders, unoptimized images. Our law firm website speed guide covers how to measure this.
  • Your practice has changed. New practice areas, new attorneys or a new office, and the site's structure can't show them cleanly.
  • You can't edit it. Only the original developer can change a phone number, or the platform is locked to a vendor you're leaving.
  • There are accessibility or security problems. For example, an outdated theme that no longer gets updates, or forms that fail basic keyboard and screen reader checks.

If the only problem is speed or hosting, a full redesign may be overkill. Moving to a better host with the same URLs is a much smaller, lower-risk project. See how to move a law firm website to a new host without downtime.

What kind of change is your redesign? (It decides the SEO steps)

Google treats site changes differently depending on whether visitors see new URLs. Work out which case you're in before planning anything else. Google's own guidance also says to make changes one after the other, not everything at the same time, so avoid combining a new domain, a new host and new URLs in one launch if you can.

If you're tempted to switch domains as part of the redesign, think twice. A domain change adds the most risk of any option in the table above, and it's usually worth doing as a separate project once the new design is stable.

Set goals and record a baseline first

Write down two or three measurable goals, such as "more consultation requests from the family law pages" or "a mobile site that loads fast on a phone connection." Then take a snapshot of how the current site performs. Without that snapshot, you won't be able to tell after launch whether you lost anything.

  • Search Console: clicks, impressions and average position for the last 12 months, grouped by page and by query.
  • GA4: sessions by landing page, plus key events such as form submissions and phone-link clicks.
  • Leads: how many calls and forms per month came from the website, from your intake records or call tracking.
  • Speed: Core Web Vitals for your top templates (home, practice area, bio, blog post).
  • Rankings: positions for 20 to 50 money keywords, such as "[city] divorce lawyer."

If analytics isn't set up properly yet, fix that before the redesign starts. See GA4 and Search Console setup for law firms.

Step 1: Build a complete content and URL inventory

A URL inventory is a spreadsheet with one row for every address on your current site and the data showing what each one is worth. Combine three sources, because each one misses URLs the others catch.

  1. Crawl the live site. A desktop crawler such as Screaming Frog SEO Spider lists every URL it can reach by following links, with the status code, title, H1, canonical and word count for each. The free version crawls up to 500 URLs per crawl, which is enough for most small-firm sites.
  2. Export top pages from Search Console. In the Performance report, open the Pages tab for the last 12 months and export it. Search Console's tables show a maximum of 1,000 rows, so a site with more URLs than that needs the API or a connector to get the full list.
  3. Export landing pages from GA4. This catches pages that get traffic from ads, email or referrals, which Search Console doesn't show.
  4. Add pages with backlinks. Use any backlink tool you have access to, or Search Console's Links report, and flag every URL that other sites link to. Bar association directories, local news and old guest posts often point to pages nobody remembers.
  5. Add the URLs nobody links to. Include PDFs, landing pages from old ad campaigns, and anything listed in your current XML sitemap.

Save a copy of the old site's sitemap and the full crawl before anything changes. You'll use both after launch to check that every old URL now redirects or returns the right status code.

Step 2: Decide what to keep, merge or remove

Give every URL in the inventory one of four labels. The default should be to keep the page. Pages with traffic, links or leads need a reason to change.

Look carefully at practice area pages. They usually bring in the most valuable traffic, and redesigns tend to shorten them. If they need work, our guide on how to write practice area pages explains what to add rather than cut. Old blog posts that discuss superseded law may need an update note or a rewrite. Results pages and testimonials should be reviewed against your state bar's advertising rules before they go on the new site.

Step 3: Create your 301 redirect map

A 301 redirect map is a two-column list that pairs each old URL with the single new URL it should permanently point to. It is the most important document in the whole project. Google's site move guide calls it the URL mapping and recommends starting with your most important URLs.

Example URLs are fictional.

Rules for a clean map, based on Google's site move guidance:

  • One to one where possible. Send each old page to the new page that answers the same question.
  • Don't dump everything on the home page. Google says redirecting many old URLs to one irrelevant destination, such as the home page, may be treated as a soft 404. In practice the redirect then passes little or no value.
  • No chains. Point straight to the final URL. If an old redirect already sends /a/ to /b/, and /b/ now moves to /c/, update the first rule to go directly to /c/.
  • Server-side redirects. Use your server config, your host's redirect tool or a well-maintained WordPress redirect plugin. Avoid JavaScript redirects. Google calls them a last resort because rendering can fail.
  • Cover the variants. HTTP and HTTPS, www and non-www, with and without trailing slashes, and old PDFs.
  • Update internal links on the new site to the final URLs, so visitors and crawlers don't hit redirects at all.

301 vs 302: which redirect should a relaunch use?

Use 301 (or 308) for anything that has moved for good. Google's redirects documentation explains that a permanent redirect is a strong signal that the target should be the canonical URL shown in search. A temporary redirect (302, 303 or 307) is followed, but the original URL can stay in results. That's fine for a maintenance page that's up for one evening, and wrong for a redesign. Google also states that 301 and other permanent redirects don't cause a loss in PageRank.

How long should you keep 301 redirects?

Keep them for at least a year, and ideally indefinitely. Google's site move guide recommends "generally at least 1 year". The Change of Address documentation says at least 180 days, and longer while old URLs still get search traffic. People also keep finding old links in emails, PDFs and directory listings for years, so the safest choice is to leave redirects in place.

Step 4: Build on staging, and keep it out of Google

A staging site is a private copy of your website where the new design is built and tested before the public sees it. Most managed WordPress hosts include one. Two settings need care.

  • Block staging from search. Password protection (HTTP authentication) is the most reliable option. Many teams also turn on WordPress's "Discourage search engines from indexing this site" setting, which adds a noindex, nofollow robots meta tag to every page.
  • Write down every block you add. Each one has to come off at launch. WordPress's own documentation notes the setting is only a request to search engines, and it can follow the site to production if you copy staging to live.

Build the new pages at their final URLs on staging. Then import your redirect map and test it there with a crawler: upload the list of old URLs and confirm each one returns a single 301 to the right destination.

Pre-launch QA: the website relaunch checklist

Run this checklist on staging, then run the starred items again on the live site right after launch.

One detail catches many people out. Google can only see a noindex tag on a page it is allowed to crawl. Google's noindex documentation explains that if robots.txt blocks a page, the crawler never reads the tag. So check both settings, and don't use robots.txt to "fix" indexing.

Launch day: step by step

Launch early in a quiet week, on a weekday morning when your developer is available. Avoid Friday afternoons and the day before a holiday.

  1. Take a final backup of the old site and its database.
  2. Freeze content edits on the old site, so no new posts get lost in the switch.
  3. Deploy the new site to production, or point DNS to it if the host is also changing. If you're moving hosts at the same time, lower your DNS TTL at least a week ahead, as Google's no-URL-change move guide advises.
  4. Remove every staging block: password protection, the "Discourage search engines" setting, any noindex header and any Disallow: /.
  5. Turn on the redirects and crawl the old URL list against the live domain.
  6. Re-run the starred QA items on the live site: forms, phone links, tracking, noindex, robots.txt.
  7. Submit the new XML sitemap in Search Console's Sitemaps report. Google's sitemap documentation notes that submitting is a hint, not a guarantee. If URLs changed, Google's move guide also suggests temporarily submitting the old sitemap so its redirects get crawled.
  8. Inspect your top 10 URLs with Search Console's URL Inspection tool and request indexing for the most important ones.
  9. Domain change only: once the redirects are live, file a Change of Address request from the old domain's Search Console property. You need to be verified as owner of both properties with the same Google account.
  10. Update off-site links you control: Google Business Profile, bar association and directory profiles, social profiles, email signatures and ad campaigns.

After launch: what to monitor, and what's normal

Expect some movement. Google's site move guide says a temporary fluctuation in site ranking is expected during a move and that rankings settle over time. It also says a small to medium-sized site can take a few weeks for most pages to move, because Googlebot has to visit every old and new URL at least once. A redesign with no URL changes usually causes less disruption than that.

  • Days 1 to 3: check forms and calls every day. Watch GA4 Realtime to confirm tracking. Re-crawl the live site for 404s, redirect chains and stray noindex tags.
  • Weeks 1 to 4: check Search Console's Page indexing report for spikes in "Not found (404)," "Excluded by noindex tag" or "Soft 404." Each one usually traces back to a single missing redirect or setting. Compare clicks per page against your baseline.
  • Months 1 to 3: compare rankings, clicks and leads against the same period before launch. Old URLs should drop out of the index as new ones replace them.
  • Ongoing: keep the redirects. Add new ones whenever you rename pages later.

When should you worry? If a specific page loses most of its clicks and doesn't recover within a few weeks, check three things in this order. First, does its old URL redirect to the right place? Second, is the new page indexable? Third, did it lose content, headings or internal links in the rebuild? A sitewide collapse in the first days usually means a crawl block, so check robots.txt and noindex first.

Law firm website redesign timeline

For a typical small-firm site of 30 to 150 pages, plan on about 8 to 12 weeks from audit to launch, plus 90 days of monitoring. Scope, content writing and approvals drive the real timeline more than design does.

Budget depends heavily on scope. Rewriting content and migrating many pages costs more than applying a new theme. Our breakdown of how much a law firm website costs in 2026 covers the ranges and what drives them.

Common redesign mistakes that cost rankings

  • Changing URLs "for neatness" when the old ones were already ranking.
  • Redirecting every removed page to the home page.
  • Launching with the staging noindex or robots.txt block still on.
  • Changing domain, host, platform and URLs in one weekend, so nobody can tell which change caused a drop.
  • Cutting practice area content to fit a minimal design.
  • Forgetting the GA4 tag or the form notification email, so leads go missing without anyone noticing.
  • Removing redirects after a few months to "clean up" the server config.

FAQ

How long does it take to recover rankings after a website redesign?

If the redirects and content are right, most small sites settle within a few weeks. Google says a small to medium-sized site can take a few weeks for most pages to move, and that rankings settle over time. Drops that last beyond that usually point to a specific error worth investigating.

Can I redesign my website without changing URLs?

Yes, and it's the lowest-risk option. WordPress lets you rebuild the theme and page layouts while keeping every permalink. You then only need redirects for pages you merge or remove.

Do I need to use Google's Change of Address tool for a redesign?

Only if you're moving to a new domain or subdomain. Google says the tool isn't for HTTP to HTTPS moves, www changes, moving pages within the same site, or switching hosts. For those, redirects and an updated sitemap are enough.

Should I redesign and change hosting at the same time?

It's better to do them separately. Google recommends making site changes one after the other. Move to the new host first with the same URLs, confirm everything is stable, then launch the redesign. Our host migration guide covers the first step.

Is a 302 redirect ever OK during a relaunch?

Only for a genuinely temporary situation, such as a short maintenance page. Pages that have moved permanently should use 301 or 308, so Google treats the new URL as canonical.

What should happen to pages I delete?

If a closely related page exists, 301 the old URL there. If not, let it return a 404 or 410. Google's move guide says content you aren't moving should return one of those codes, rather than redirecting to an irrelevant page.

Next steps

Start with the inventory, because everything else depends on it. Crawl your current site, export your top pages from Search Console and GA4, and put them in one spreadsheet this week. Label each URL keep, rewrite, merge or remove, then build the redirect map before the designer finalizes the new menu. Keep the QA table above open on launch day. If you're still mapping out the bigger picture for your firm's site, our Start Here guide shows which projects to tackle first.

Quick answer: A law firm website redesign won’t wreck your rankings if you handle it as a site migration first and a design project second. List every URL that brings in traffic or links, keep the pages that work, and 301-redirect each changed URL to its closest new page. Before launch, test forms, tracking and the noindex and robots.txt settings on staging. After launch, watch Search Console for a few weeks while Google re-crawls. A short ranking wobble is normal. A lasting drop usually comes from a missed redirect, deleted content or a leftover block on search engines.

Key takeaways

  • Most ranking losses after a relaunch come from URLs that changed with no redirect, or from pages that were deleted. The new design itself is rarely the problem.
  • Keep URLs that already rank. If a URL must change, use a server-side 301 (permanent) redirect to the closest new page, not to the home page.
  • Use Search Console’s Change of Address tool only when the domain changes. You don’t need it for a new design, a new host or HTTP to HTTPS.
  • The most common launch-day mistake is leaving staging’s noindex tag or robots.txt block on the live site. Check it within minutes of going live.
  • Google says rankings can fluctuate for a while and most pages on a small site move over in a few weeks. Keep your redirects for at least a year.

Does a law firm website redesign hurt SEO?

Not if your URLs, content and crawl settings carry over. Google ranks pages, not designs. Your practice area pages, attorney bios and the posts that earned links are the reason you rank. A new theme, colors or layout doesn’t change that, as long as those pages keep their content and can still be found at the same address, or at a new one through a redirect.

Rankings drop when a redesign quietly removes the signals Google relied on. Common examples:

  • A new URL structure (for example /car-accidents/ becomes /practice-areas/auto/) with no redirects. Old links and old search results now lead to 404 pages.
  • Long practice area pages cut down to a headline and a contact form to “clean up” the design.
  • Blog posts deleted in bulk, including the few that brought in most of your links.
  • Staging settings carried over to the live site: a sitewide noindex tag or a Disallow: / line in robots.txt.
  • Title tags, headings and internal links lost because a page builder rebuilt the pages from scratch.

Everything in the checklist below exists to prevent one of these.

Signs your firm needs a website redesign

Redesign because the site is failing at its job, not because it looks a few years old. Good reasons include:

  • Leads have dropped off. Calls and form submissions from the site are falling while traffic holds steady. That points to the page experience, not visibility.
  • It’s hard to use on a phone. Tiny tap targets, no click-to-call button, menus that don’t open properly.
  • It’s slow. Heavy sliders, page builders stacked on page builders, unoptimized images. Our law firm website speed guide covers how to measure this.
  • Your practice has changed. New practice areas, new attorneys or a new office, and the site’s structure can’t show them cleanly.
  • You can’t edit it. Only the original developer can change a phone number, or the platform is locked to a vendor you’re leaving.
  • There are accessibility or security problems. For example, an outdated theme that no longer gets updates, or forms that fail basic keyboard and screen reader checks.

If the only problem is speed or hosting, a full redesign may be overkill. Moving to a better host with the same URLs is a much smaller, lower-risk project. See how to move a law firm website to a new host without downtime.

What kind of change is your redesign? (It decides the SEO steps)

Google treats site changes differently depending on whether visitors see new URLs. Work out which case you’re in before planning anything else. Google’s own guidance also says to make changes one after the other, not everything at the same time, so avoid combining a new domain, a new host and new URLs in one launch if you can.

If you’re tempted to switch domains as part of the redesign, think twice. A domain change adds the most risk of any option in the table above, and it’s usually worth doing as a separate project once the new design is stable.

Set goals and record a baseline first

Write down two or three measurable goals, such as “more consultation requests from the family law pages” or “a mobile site that loads fast on a phone connection.” Then take a snapshot of how the current site performs. Without that snapshot, you won’t be able to tell after launch whether you lost anything.

  • Search Console: clicks, impressions and average position for the last 12 months, grouped by page and by query.
  • GA4: sessions by landing page, plus key events such as form submissions and phone-link clicks.
  • Leads: how many calls and forms per month came from the website, from your intake records or call tracking.
  • Speed: Core Web Vitals for your top templates (home, practice area, bio, blog post).
  • Rankings: positions for 20 to 50 money keywords, such as “[city] divorce lawyer.”

If analytics isn’t set up properly yet, fix that before the redesign starts. See GA4 and Search Console setup for law firms.

Step 1: Build a complete content and URL inventory

A URL inventory is a spreadsheet with one row for every address on your current site and the data showing what each one is worth. Combine three sources, because each one misses URLs the others catch.

  1. Crawl the live site. A desktop crawler such as Screaming Frog SEO Spider lists every URL it can reach by following links, with the status code, title, H1, canonical and word count for each. The free version crawls up to 500 URLs per crawl, which is enough for most small-firm sites.
  2. Export top pages from Search Console. In the Performance report, open the Pages tab for the last 12 months and export it. Search Console’s tables show a maximum of 1,000 rows, so a site with more URLs than that needs the API or a connector to get the full list.
  3. Export landing pages from GA4. This catches pages that get traffic from ads, email or referrals, which Search Console doesn’t show.
  4. Add pages with backlinks. Use any backlink tool you have access to, or Search Console’s Links report, and flag every URL that other sites link to. Bar association directories, local news and old guest posts often point to pages nobody remembers.
  5. Add the URLs nobody links to. Include PDFs, landing pages from old ad campaigns, and anything listed in your current XML sitemap.

Save a copy of the old site’s sitemap and the full crawl before anything changes. You’ll use both after launch to check that every old URL now redirects or returns the right status code.

Step 2: Decide what to keep, merge or remove

Give every URL in the inventory one of four labels. The default should be to keep the page. Pages with traffic, links or leads need a reason to change.

Look carefully at practice area pages. They usually bring in the most valuable traffic, and redesigns tend to shorten them. If they need work, our guide on how to write practice area pages explains what to add rather than cut. Old blog posts that discuss superseded law may need an update note or a rewrite. Results pages and testimonials should be reviewed against your state bar’s advertising rules before they go on the new site.

Step 3: Create your 301 redirect map

A 301 redirect map is a two-column list that pairs each old URL with the single new URL it should permanently point to. It is the most important document in the whole project. Google’s site move guide calls it the URL mapping and recommends starting with your most important URLs.

Example URLs are fictional.

Rules for a clean map, based on Google’s site move guidance:

  • One to one where possible. Send each old page to the new page that answers the same question.
  • Don’t dump everything on the home page. Google says redirecting many old URLs to one irrelevant destination, such as the home page, may be treated as a soft 404. In practice the redirect then passes little or no value.
  • No chains. Point straight to the final URL. If an old redirect already sends /a/ to /b/, and /b/ now moves to /c/, update the first rule to go directly to /c/.
  • Server-side redirects. Use your server config, your host’s redirect tool or a well-maintained WordPress redirect plugin. Avoid JavaScript redirects. Google calls them a last resort because rendering can fail.
  • Cover the variants. HTTP and HTTPS, www and non-www, with and without trailing slashes, and old PDFs.
  • Update internal links on the new site to the final URLs, so visitors and crawlers don’t hit redirects at all.

301 vs 302: which redirect should a relaunch use?

Use 301 (or 308) for anything that has moved for good. Google’s redirects documentation explains that a permanent redirect is a strong signal that the target should be the canonical URL shown in search. A temporary redirect (302, 303 or 307) is followed, but the original URL can stay in results. That’s fine for a maintenance page that’s up for one evening, and wrong for a redesign. Google also states that 301 and other permanent redirects don’t cause a loss in PageRank.

How long should you keep 301 redirects?

Keep them for at least a year, and ideally indefinitely. Google’s site move guide recommends “generally at least 1 year”. The Change of Address documentation says at least 180 days, and longer while old URLs still get search traffic. People also keep finding old links in emails, PDFs and directory listings for years, so the safest choice is to leave redirects in place.

Step 4: Build on staging, and keep it out of Google

A staging site is a private copy of your website where the new design is built and tested before the public sees it. Most managed WordPress hosts include one. Two settings need care.

  • Block staging from search. Password protection (HTTP authentication) is the most reliable option. Many teams also turn on WordPress’s “Discourage search engines from indexing this site” setting, which adds a noindex, nofollow robots meta tag to every page.
  • Write down every block you add. Each one has to come off at launch. WordPress’s own documentation notes the setting is only a request to search engines, and it can follow the site to production if you copy staging to live.

Build the new pages at their final URLs on staging. Then import your redirect map and test it there with a crawler: upload the list of old URLs and confirm each one returns a single 301 to the right destination.

Pre-launch QA: the website relaunch checklist

Run this checklist on staging, then run the starred items again on the live site right after launch.

One detail catches many people out. Google can only see a noindex tag on a page it is allowed to crawl. Google’s noindex documentation explains that if robots.txt blocks a page, the crawler never reads the tag. So check both settings, and don’t use robots.txt to “fix” indexing.

Launch day: step by step

Launch early in a quiet week, on a weekday morning when your developer is available. Avoid Friday afternoons and the day before a holiday.

  1. Take a final backup of the old site and its database.
  2. Freeze content edits on the old site, so no new posts get lost in the switch.
  3. Deploy the new site to production, or point DNS to it if the host is also changing. If you’re moving hosts at the same time, lower your DNS TTL at least a week ahead, as Google’s no-URL-change move guide advises.
  4. Remove every staging block: password protection, the “Discourage search engines” setting, any noindex header and any Disallow: /.
  5. Turn on the redirects and crawl the old URL list against the live domain.
  6. Re-run the starred QA items on the live site: forms, phone links, tracking, noindex, robots.txt.
  7. Submit the new XML sitemap in Search Console’s Sitemaps report. Google’s sitemap documentation notes that submitting is a hint, not a guarantee. If URLs changed, Google’s move guide also suggests temporarily submitting the old sitemap so its redirects get crawled.
  8. Inspect your top 10 URLs with Search Console’s URL Inspection tool and request indexing for the most important ones.
  9. Domain change only: once the redirects are live, file a Change of Address request from the old domain’s Search Console property. You need to be verified as owner of both properties with the same Google account.
  10. Update off-site links you control: Google Business Profile, bar association and directory profiles, social profiles, email signatures and ad campaigns.

After launch: what to monitor, and what’s normal

Expect some movement. Google’s site move guide says a temporary fluctuation in site ranking is expected during a move and that rankings settle over time. It also says a small to medium-sized site can take a few weeks for most pages to move, because Googlebot has to visit every old and new URL at least once. A redesign with no URL changes usually causes less disruption than that.

  • Days 1 to 3: check forms and calls every day. Watch GA4 Realtime to confirm tracking. Re-crawl the live site for 404s, redirect chains and stray noindex tags.
  • Weeks 1 to 4: check Search Console’s Page indexing report for spikes in “Not found (404),” “Excluded by noindex tag” or “Soft 404.” Each one usually traces back to a single missing redirect or setting. Compare clicks per page against your baseline.
  • Months 1 to 3: compare rankings, clicks and leads against the same period before launch. Old URLs should drop out of the index as new ones replace them.
  • Ongoing: keep the redirects. Add new ones whenever you rename pages later.

When should you worry? If a specific page loses most of its clicks and doesn’t recover within a few weeks, check three things in this order. First, does its old URL redirect to the right place? Second, is the new page indexable? Third, did it lose content, headings or internal links in the rebuild? A sitewide collapse in the first days usually means a crawl block, so check robots.txt and noindex first.

Law firm website redesign timeline

For a typical small-firm site of 30 to 150 pages, plan on about 8 to 12 weeks from audit to launch, plus 90 days of monitoring. Scope, content writing and approvals drive the real timeline more than design does.

Budget depends heavily on scope. Rewriting content and migrating many pages costs more than applying a new theme. Our breakdown of how much a law firm website costs in 2026 covers the ranges and what drives them.

Common redesign mistakes that cost rankings

  • Changing URLs “for neatness” when the old ones were already ranking.
  • Redirecting every removed page to the home page.
  • Launching with the staging noindex or robots.txt block still on.
  • Changing domain, host, platform and URLs in one weekend, so nobody can tell which change caused a drop.
  • Cutting practice area content to fit a minimal design.
  • Forgetting the GA4 tag or the form notification email, so leads go missing without anyone noticing.
  • Removing redirects after a few months to “clean up” the server config.

FAQ

How long does it take to recover rankings after a website redesign?

If the redirects and content are right, most small sites settle within a few weeks. Google says a small to medium-sized site can take a few weeks for most pages to move, and that rankings settle over time. Drops that last beyond that usually point to a specific error worth investigating.

Can I redesign my website without changing URLs?

Yes, and it’s the lowest-risk option. WordPress lets you rebuild the theme and page layouts while keeping every permalink. You then only need redirects for pages you merge or remove.

Do I need to use Google’s Change of Address tool for a redesign?

Only if you’re moving to a new domain or subdomain. Google says the tool isn’t for HTTP to HTTPS moves, www changes, moving pages within the same site, or switching hosts. For those, redirects and an updated sitemap are enough.

Should I redesign and change hosting at the same time?

It’s better to do them separately. Google recommends making site changes one after the other. Move to the new host first with the same URLs, confirm everything is stable, then launch the redesign. Our host migration guide covers the first step.

Is a 302 redirect ever OK during a relaunch?

Only for a genuinely temporary situation, such as a short maintenance page. Pages that have moved permanently should use 301 or 308, so Google treats the new URL as canonical.

What should happen to pages I delete?

If a closely related page exists, 301 the old URL there. If not, let it return a 404 or 410. Google’s move guide says content you aren’t moving should return one of those codes, rather than redirecting to an irrelevant page.

Next steps

Start with the inventory, because everything else depends on it. Crawl your current site, export your top pages from Search Console and GA4, and put them in one spreadsheet this week. Label each URL keep, rewrite, merge or remove, then build the redirect map before the designer finalizes the new menu. Keep the QA table above open on launch day. If you’re still mapping out the bigger picture for your firm’s site, our Start Here guide shows which projects to tackle first.

title.raw: How to Speed Up a Law Firm Website: Core Web Vitals Guide (2026)
title.rendered: How to Speed Up a Law Firm Website: Core Web Vitals Guide (2026)

content.raw:
Quick answer: To improve your law firm website speed, start by measuring real-visitor data in PageSpeed Insights and Google Search Console. Then fix things in this order: server response time (hosting and caching), the main hero image, third-party scripts like chat widgets and trackers, fonts, and plugin bloat. Google's "good" Core Web Vitals targets are LCP of 2.5 seconds or less, INP of 200 milliseconds or less, and CLS of 0.1 or less, measured at the 75th percentile of visits.

This guide is for solo and small firms, most of which run on WordPress. It covers what the three metrics mean, how to read your reports without being misled by a single score, and which fixes are worth doing first.

Key takeaways

  • Field data is what counts. Google's Core Web Vitals assessment uses real-user data from the Chrome UX Report. The 0–100 Lighthouse performance score is a lab test for debugging.
  • Most small-firm WordPress sites slow down for the same reasons: cheap or overloaded hosting, no page caching, oversized hero images, and too many third-party scripts.
  • Fix in priority order. Hosting and caching usually help every page at once. Minifying CSS rarely moves the needle on its own.
  • Speed is one signal, not a shortcut. Google says relevance comes first. Treat speed as a quality floor that helps visitors call or fill in your form.
  • Never lazy-load the hero image. That is one of the most common self-inflicted LCP problems.

What are Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS)?

Core Web Vitals are three metrics Google uses to measure real-world page experience: loading, responsiveness and visual stability. The thresholds below come from web.dev's Core Web Vitals guide and the Search Console Core Web Vitals report documentation.

  • LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) is how long it takes the biggest visible element, usually your hero photo or headline, to appear.
  • INP (Interaction to Next Paint) is how quickly the page visibly responds after someone taps, clicks or types. It replaced First Input Delay (FID) on March 12, 2024, so any guide still quoting a "100 ms FID" target is out of date.
  • CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) measures how much content jumps around while the page loads. Think of a "Call now" button that moves just as someone taps it.

A page passes only when all three metrics are "good" at the 75th percentile of visits, measured separately for mobile and desktop. In plain terms, at least three out of four visits need a good experience. Search Console labels each group of URLs by its worst metric, so one poor metric fails the whole group.

Does law firm website speed affect Google rankings?

Yes, a little, but it is not the deciding factor. Google's page experience documentation says Core Web Vitals are used by its ranking systems, but that "there is no single signal." Google also says it will show the most relevant content even if the page experience is sub-par. A fast site with thin practice area pages will not outrank a slower site with genuinely helpful content.

Speed matters most for the people who land on your site. A prospective client searching on a phone, often stressed, needs your phone number, practice areas and contact form to appear quickly and stay put. Slow loading, late pop-ups and shifting buttons get in the way of that first call. We are not quoting a "conversion lift" figure here, because no reliable study measures this for small law firms. The practical case is simple: make it easy to contact you.

How to measure your law firm website speed

Use two free Google tools. Check both before you change anything, so you have a baseline to compare against.

PageSpeed Insights: field data vs lab data

PageSpeed Insights (PSI) shows two very different things on one screen, as explained in the PSI documentation:

  • Field data ("Discover what your real users are experiencing") comes from the Chrome UX Report (CrUX), covering real Chrome visits over the previous 28 days. The Core Web Vitals pass/fail assessment uses only this data.
  • Lab data ("Diagnose performance issues") is a single Lighthouse test on a simulated device and network. It produces the 0–100 performance score (90–100 good, 50–89 needs improvement, 0–49 poor). It is useful for finding problems, but it is not what Google uses to judge your site.

Many small firm sites see "No data" in the field section. CrUX only includes pages and origins that are publicly indexable and have enough Chrome visitors. Google does not publish the exact traffic minimum. If a page lacks data, PSI falls back to origin-wide data for the whole site. If the whole site lacks data, use the lab results and the mobile tab as your guide.

Search Console Core Web Vitals report

In Google Search Console, open Experience → Core Web Vitals. The report groups similar URLs, for example all practice area pages built on one template, and shows which groups are Good, Need improvement or Poor on mobile and desktop. After you fix an issue, start validation from that issue's page in the report. Google then monitors the affected URLs for 28 days. If Search Console is not set up yet, follow our GA4 and Search Console setup guide for law firms first.

Which pages should a law firm test?

Test the pages that bring in clients, not just the homepage: your homepage, your top two or three practice area pages, an attorney bio, and your contact page. Always check the Mobile tab first, since most local legal searches happen on phones and Google indexes the mobile version of your site.

How to speed up a law firm website: fixes in priority order

The order below is based on how much each fix tends to help and how many pages it affects. Do the first steps before you spend money on optimization plugins.

1. Fix slow server response (hosting and TTFB)

Time to First Byte (TTFB) is how long the browser waits for the first byte of your page from the server. web.dev considers 0.8 seconds or less good and over 1.8 seconds poor. TTFB is the first part of LCP, so a slow server makes every other fix less effective. Google's LCP optimization guide suggests TTFB should take roughly 40% of your LCP time, not most of it.

If your lab TTFB is consistently high, the cause is usually crowded shared hosting, an outdated PHP version, or no caching. The official WordPress optimization guide recommends current PHP versions, an opcode cache such as OPcache, and SSD or NVMe storage. Managed WordPress hosts handle most of this for you. See our comparison of the best hosting for law firm websites. If you switch hosts, plan the move so the site never goes offline.

2. Turn on page caching (and object caching if offered)

Page caching stores a ready-made HTML copy of each page, so WordPress does not rebuild it from the database for every visitor. A brochure-style firm site is a perfect fit for it. Many managed hosts include server-level page caching. On other hosts, use one reputable caching plugin, never two. If your host offers Redis or Memcached, a persistent object cache also reduces database work, as the WordPress docs explain. Exclude any pages that must never be cached, such as client portals or payment pages.

3. Optimize the hero image (and every image after it)

On most firm sites, the LCP element is a large hero photo of the office, skyline or attorneys. Common fixes:

  • Resize before uploading. A 5,000-pixel camera photo shown at 1,400 pixels wastes bandwidth. Export at roughly the size it is displayed.
  • Use modern formats. WordPress supports WebP, and WordPress 6.5 added AVIF support, which the core team says can be "up to 50% smaller than JPEGs" at the same quality. AVIF only works if your server's image library supports it. Check under Tools → Site Health → Info → Media Handling.
  • Let the hero image load first. Since WordPress 6.3, core adds fetchpriority="high" to the image it judges most likely to be the LCP. Page builders and sliders sometimes defeat this by loading the hero as a CSS background. If yours does, use a normal image block instead.
  • Avoid sliders and autoplay video heroes. They add scripts and delay the main content. One strong image plus a clear headline and phone number usually works better.

4. Lazy-load below-the-fold images only

Lazy loading delays offscreen images until a visitor scrolls near them. WordPress has added loading="lazy" by default since version 5.5, for images that have width and height attributes. The mistake to avoid is lazy-loading the image at the top of the page. web.dev advises against lazy-loading images likely to be visible on load, especially the LCP image. If an optimization plugin lazy-loads "all images," exclude the hero.

5. Tame third-party scripts (chat widgets, trackers, embeds)

Third-party scripts are often the biggest cause of poor INP on law firm sites. Live chat widgets, intake bots, call-tracking, review badges, heatmaps, multiple ad pixels and embedded YouTube videos all compete for the browser's main thread. Google's guidance on loading third-party JavaScript is direct: load them with async or defer, and "if the script doesn't add clear value to your site, remove it."

  • Audit tags yearly. Remove pixels for ad campaigns you no longer run and duplicate analytics tags.
  • Use facades for chat and video. A facade is a lightweight static stand-in that loads the real widget only when someone clicks it. Lighthouse specifically lists live chat widgets and video players as candidates.
  • Weigh the widget against the alternative. If you use chat mainly for intake, a staffed answering service may cover the same need with less on-page code. Our Smith.ai vs Ruby comparison covers that option.

6. Simplify fonts

Many law firm themes load three or four font families in multiple weights. Each file delays text and can cause layout shifts when the font swaps in. Per web.dev's font best practices: use WOFF2 files, limit the number of families and weights (or use one variable font), preload only the most important font, and set font-display to swap or optional. Self-hosting is not automatically faster than Google Fonts, so measure both.

7. Cut plugin and theme bloat

The WordPress docs put it plainly: "Deactivate and delete any unnecessary plugins," and choose a lightweight theme. Heavy multipurpose themes and page builders load CSS and JavaScript for features you never use. Before buying a new theme, check its demo in PageSpeed Insights. Our guides to WordPress themes for law firms and the plugins law firms actually need help you keep the stack lean.

8. Add a CDN

A content delivery network (CDN) serves copies of your images, CSS and JavaScript from servers close to each visitor. With the right setup, it can cache whole HTML pages too. The WordPress docs note a CDN works best alongside a caching plugin. Some managed hosts include one. Otherwise, see our guide to setting up Cloudflare for a law firm website. Watch for cache rules that strip query strings or bypass caching on marketing URLs, which Google's LCP guide flags as a common TTFB problem.

How to fix layout shift (CLS) on a WordPress site

Most CLS problems come from content that appears without reserved space. Based on web.dev's CLS guide:

  • Give every image and video embed width and height attributes, or a CSS aspect-ratio. WordPress adds these automatically for Media Library images, but custom HTML and some builders do not.
  • Reserve space for cookie banners, review widgets and "free consultation" bars, or overlay them instead of pushing content down.
  • Avoid pop-ups that inject themselves at the top of the page after load.
  • Use matching fallback fonts so text doesn't reflow when the web font loads.

Shifts that happen within 500 ms of a user's tap, like an accordion opening, don't count against CLS.

How to improve INP (responsiveness)

Poor INP means the page is busy running JavaScript when a visitor taps something. Examples include opening the mobile menu, expanding an FAQ, or typing in your contact form. Google's INP guide points to long main-thread tasks, heavy event handlers and very large page structures (DOM size) as the main causes. On a typical firm site, the practical fixes are: remove or defer third-party scripts (step 5), switch away from bloated page-builder layouts, and replace heavy animation libraries. Form plugins can add a lot of script too. Pick a lightweight one and load its scripts only on pages that show a form.

Core Web Vitals WordPress checklist (prioritized)

Step-by-step: speed up a WordPress law firm site this week

  1. Back up the site and, if your host offers one, make changes on a staging copy.
  2. Record a baseline. Run PSI (mobile) on your homepage, top practice pages and contact page. Screenshot the field data and the lab LCP element. Note the Search Console CWV status.
  3. Check your hosting basics. Confirm your PHP version under Tools → Site Health → Info → Server, and ask your host whether server caching and OPcache are on.
  4. Enable one caching layer and clear it after each change.
  5. Fix the LCP element PSI identifies, usually the hero image. Resize it, convert it, and make sure it isn't lazy-loaded.
  6. List every third-party script (PSI's lab diagnostics list third-party code by provider). Remove what you don't use, and defer or facade the rest.
  7. Deactivate unused plugins one at a time, re-testing as you go, then delete them.
  8. Trim fonts to the families and weights your design really uses.
  9. Re-test the same pages and compare against your baseline. Lab results change right away, while field data takes up to 28 days to reflect changes.
  10. Start validation in Search Console and add a monthly speed check to your website maintenance routine.

What not to do

  • Don't chase a 100 score. The Lighthouse score is a lab diagnostic. Passing field Core Web Vitals and a site that feels fast on a phone matter more.
  • Don't stack optimization plugins. Two caching or minification plugins can conflict, break layouts, or cache pages that shouldn't be cached.
  • Don't lazy-load everything. Lazy-loading the hero image makes LCP worse.
  • Don't remove security or backup tools to save milliseconds. Security plugins, backups and updates are part of the baseline, not bloat.
  • Don't defer scripts blindly. Aggressive "delay all JavaScript" settings can break contact forms, consent banners or call tracking. Test form submissions after every change.
  • Don't judge by one test. Lab results vary from run to run. Look for consistent patterns across several pages.

FAQ

What is a good PageSpeed Insights score for a law firm website?

In Lighthouse, 90–100 is rated good, 50–89 needs improvement and 0–49 poor. But the score that matters for Google is the field "Core Web Vitals Assessment" at the top of PSI. Aim to pass it on mobile, with LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 200 ms and CLS ≤ 0.1.

Your pages don't have enough Chrome visitors to appear in the Chrome UX Report, which is common for small firms. Use the lab data and Search Console instead, and focus on the same fixes.

Why is my mobile score so much worse than desktop?

PSI's mobile lab test simulates a slower device and network, so heavy images and scripts hurt more. Real phones are also less powerful than desktops. Prioritize mobile results.

Lab results change immediately. Field data in PSI covers a rolling 28-day window, and Search Console's validation runs for 28 days, so expect about a month before reports fully reflect your fixes.

Not always. If your host provides server caching and a CDN, you may need only an image optimization tool. If not, one well-maintained caching plugin is usually enough. Avoid overlapping plugins.

content.rendered:
Quick answer: To improve your law firm website speed, start by measuring real-visitor data in PageSpeed Insights and Google Search Console. Then fix things in this order: server response time (hosting and caching), the main hero image, third-party scripts like chat widgets and trackers, fonts, and plugin bloat. Google’s “good” Core Web Vitals targets are LCP of 2.5 seconds or less, INP of 200 milliseconds or less, and CLS of 0.1 or less, measured at the 75th percentile of visits.

This guide is for solo and small firms, most of which run on WordPress. It covers what the three metrics mean, how to read your reports without being misled by a single score, and which fixes are worth doing first.

Key takeaways

  • Field data is what counts. Google’s Core Web Vitals assessment uses real-user data from the Chrome UX Report. The 0–100 Lighthouse performance score is a lab test for debugging.
  • Most small-firm WordPress sites slow down for the same reasons: cheap or overloaded hosting, no page caching, oversized hero images, and too many third-party scripts.
  • Fix in priority order. Hosting and caching usually help every page at once. Minifying CSS rarely moves the needle on its own.
  • Speed is one signal, not a shortcut. Google says relevance comes first. Treat speed as a quality floor that helps visitors call or fill in your form.
  • Never lazy-load the hero image. That is one of the most common self-inflicted LCP problems.

What are Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS)?

Core Web Vitals are three metrics Google uses to measure real-world page experience: loading, responsiveness and visual stability. The thresholds below come from web.dev’s Core Web Vitals guide and the Search Console Core Web Vitals report documentation.

  • LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) is how long it takes the biggest visible element, usually your hero photo or headline, to appear.
  • INP (Interaction to Next Paint) is how quickly the page visibly responds after someone taps, clicks or types. It replaced First Input Delay (FID) on March 12, 2024, so any guide still quoting a “100 ms FID” target is out of date.
  • CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) measures how much content jumps around while the page loads. Think of a “Call now” button that moves just as someone taps it.

A page passes only when all three metrics are “good” at the 75th percentile of visits, measured separately for mobile and desktop. In plain terms, at least three out of four visits need a good experience. Search Console labels each group of URLs by its worst metric, so one poor metric fails the whole group.

Does law firm website speed affect Google rankings?

Yes, a little, but it is not the deciding factor. Google’s page experience documentation says Core Web Vitals are used by its ranking systems, but that “there is no single signal.” Google also says it will show the most relevant content even if the page experience is sub-par. A fast site with thin practice area pages will not outrank a slower site with genuinely helpful content.

Speed matters most for the people who land on your site. A prospective client searching on a phone, often stressed, needs your phone number, practice areas and contact form to appear quickly and stay put. Slow loading, late pop-ups and shifting buttons get in the way of that first call. We are not quoting a “conversion lift” figure here, because no reliable study measures this for small law firms. The practical case is simple: make it easy to contact you.

How to measure your law firm website speed

Use two free Google tools. Check both before you change anything, so you have a baseline to compare against.

PageSpeed Insights: field data vs lab data

PageSpeed Insights (PSI) shows two very different things on one screen, as explained in the PSI documentation:

  • Field data (“Discover what your real users are experiencing”) comes from the Chrome UX Report (CrUX), covering real Chrome visits over the previous 28 days. The Core Web Vitals pass/fail assessment uses only this data.
  • Lab data (“Diagnose performance issues”) is a single Lighthouse test on a simulated device and network. It produces the 0–100 performance score (90–100 good, 50–89 needs improvement, 0–49 poor). It is useful for finding problems, but it is not what Google uses to judge your site.

Many small firm sites see “No data” in the field section. CrUX only includes pages and origins that are publicly indexable and have enough Chrome visitors. Google does not publish the exact traffic minimum. If a page lacks data, PSI falls back to origin-wide data for the whole site. If the whole site lacks data, use the lab results and the mobile tab as your guide.

Search Console Core Web Vitals report

In Google Search Console, open Experience → Core Web Vitals. The report groups similar URLs, for example all practice area pages built on one template, and shows which groups are Good, Need improvement or Poor on mobile and desktop. After you fix an issue, start validation from that issue’s page in the report. Google then monitors the affected URLs for 28 days. If Search Console is not set up yet, follow our GA4 and Search Console setup guide for law firms first.

Which pages should a law firm test?

Test the pages that bring in clients, not just the homepage: your homepage, your top two or three practice area pages, an attorney bio, and your contact page. Always check the Mobile tab first, since most local legal searches happen on phones and Google indexes the mobile version of your site.

How to speed up a law firm website: fixes in priority order

The order below is based on how much each fix tends to help and how many pages it affects. Do the first steps before you spend money on optimization plugins.

1. Fix slow server response (hosting and TTFB)

Time to First Byte (TTFB) is how long the browser waits for the first byte of your page from the server. web.dev considers 0.8 seconds or less good and over 1.8 seconds poor. TTFB is the first part of LCP, so a slow server makes every other fix less effective. Google’s LCP optimization guide suggests TTFB should take roughly 40% of your LCP time, not most of it.

If your lab TTFB is consistently high, the cause is usually crowded shared hosting, an outdated PHP version, or no caching. The official WordPress optimization guide recommends current PHP versions, an opcode cache such as OPcache, and SSD or NVMe storage. Managed WordPress hosts handle most of this for you. See our comparison of the best hosting for law firm websites. If you switch hosts, plan the move so the site never goes offline.

2. Turn on page caching (and object caching if offered)

Page caching stores a ready-made HTML copy of each page, so WordPress does not rebuild it from the database for every visitor. A brochure-style firm site is a perfect fit for it. Many managed hosts include server-level page caching. On other hosts, use one reputable caching plugin, never two. If your host offers Redis or Memcached, a persistent object cache also reduces database work, as the WordPress docs explain. Exclude any pages that must never be cached, such as client portals or payment pages.

3. Optimize the hero image (and every image after it)

On most firm sites, the LCP element is a large hero photo of the office, skyline or attorneys. Common fixes:

  • Resize before uploading. A 5,000-pixel camera photo shown at 1,400 pixels wastes bandwidth. Export at roughly the size it is displayed.
  • Use modern formats. WordPress supports WebP, and WordPress 6.5 added AVIF support, which the core team says can be “up to 50% smaller than JPEGs” at the same quality. AVIF only works if your server’s image library supports it. Check under Tools → Site Health → Info → Media Handling.
  • Let the hero image load first. Since WordPress 6.3, core adds fetchpriority="high" to the image it judges most likely to be the LCP. Page builders and sliders sometimes defeat this by loading the hero as a CSS background. If yours does, use a normal image block instead.
  • Avoid sliders and autoplay video heroes. They add scripts and delay the main content. One strong image plus a clear headline and phone number usually works better.

4. Lazy-load below-the-fold images only

Lazy loading delays offscreen images until a visitor scrolls near them. WordPress has added loading="lazy" by default since version 5.5, for images that have width and height attributes. The mistake to avoid is lazy-loading the image at the top of the page. web.dev advises against lazy-loading images likely to be visible on load, especially the LCP image. If an optimization plugin lazy-loads “all images,” exclude the hero.

5. Tame third-party scripts (chat widgets, trackers, embeds)

Third-party scripts are often the biggest cause of poor INP on law firm sites. Live chat widgets, intake bots, call-tracking, review badges, heatmaps, multiple ad pixels and embedded YouTube videos all compete for the browser’s main thread. Google’s guidance on loading third-party JavaScript is direct: load them with async or defer, and “if the script doesn’t add clear value to your site, remove it.”

  • Audit tags yearly. Remove pixels for ad campaigns you no longer run and duplicate analytics tags.
  • Use facades for chat and video. A facade is a lightweight static stand-in that loads the real widget only when someone clicks it. Lighthouse specifically lists live chat widgets and video players as candidates.
  • Weigh the widget against the alternative. If you use chat mainly for intake, a staffed answering service may cover the same need with less on-page code. Our Smith.ai vs Ruby comparison covers that option.

6. Simplify fonts

Many law firm themes load three or four font families in multiple weights. Each file delays text and can cause layout shifts when the font swaps in. Per web.dev’s font best practices: use WOFF2 files, limit the number of families and weights (or use one variable font), preload only the most important font, and set font-display to swap or optional. Self-hosting is not automatically faster than Google Fonts, so measure both.

7. Cut plugin and theme bloat

The WordPress docs put it plainly: “Deactivate and delete any unnecessary plugins,” and choose a lightweight theme. Heavy multipurpose themes and page builders load CSS and JavaScript for features you never use. Before buying a new theme, check its demo in PageSpeed Insights. Our guides to WordPress themes for law firms and the plugins law firms actually need help you keep the stack lean.

8. Add a CDN

A content delivery network (CDN) serves copies of your images, CSS and JavaScript from servers close to each visitor. With the right setup, it can cache whole HTML pages too. The WordPress docs note a CDN works best alongside a caching plugin. Some managed hosts include one. Otherwise, see our guide to setting up Cloudflare for a law firm website. Watch for cache rules that strip query strings or bypass caching on marketing URLs, which Google’s LCP guide flags as a common TTFB problem.

How to fix layout shift (CLS) on a WordPress site

Most CLS problems come from content that appears without reserved space. Based on web.dev’s CLS guide:

  • Give every image and video embed width and height attributes, or a CSS aspect-ratio. WordPress adds these automatically for Media Library images, but custom HTML and some builders do not.
  • Reserve space for cookie banners, review widgets and “free consultation” bars, or overlay them instead of pushing content down.
  • Avoid pop-ups that inject themselves at the top of the page after load.
  • Use matching fallback fonts so text doesn’t reflow when the web font loads.

Shifts that happen within 500 ms of a user’s tap, like an accordion opening, don’t count against CLS.

How to improve INP (responsiveness)

Poor INP means the page is busy running JavaScript when a visitor taps something. Examples include opening the mobile menu, expanding an FAQ, or typing in your contact form. Google’s INP guide points to long main-thread tasks, heavy event handlers and very large page structures (DOM size) as the main causes. On a typical firm site, the practical fixes are: remove or defer third-party scripts (step 5), switch away from bloated page-builder layouts, and replace heavy animation libraries. Form plugins can add a lot of script too. Pick a lightweight one and load its scripts only on pages that show a form.

Step-by-step: speed up a WordPress law firm site this week

  1. Back up the site and, if your host offers one, make changes on a staging copy.
  2. Record a baseline. Run PSI (mobile) on your homepage, top practice pages and contact page. Screenshot the field data and the lab LCP element. Note the Search Console CWV status.
  3. Check your hosting basics. Confirm your PHP version under Tools → Site Health → Info → Server, and ask your host whether server caching and OPcache are on.
  4. Enable one caching layer and clear it after each change.
  5. Fix the LCP element PSI identifies, usually the hero image. Resize it, convert it, and make sure it isn’t lazy-loaded.
  6. List every third-party script (PSI’s lab diagnostics list third-party code by provider). Remove what you don’t use, and defer or facade the rest.
  7. Deactivate unused plugins one at a time, re-testing as you go, then delete them.
  8. Trim fonts to the families and weights your design really uses.
  9. Re-test the same pages and compare against your baseline. Lab results change right away, while field data takes up to 28 days to reflect changes.
  10. Start validation in Search Console and add a monthly speed check to your website maintenance routine.

What not to do

  • Don’t chase a 100 score. The Lighthouse score is a lab diagnostic. Passing field Core Web Vitals and a site that feels fast on a phone matter more.
  • Don’t stack optimization plugins. Two caching or minification plugins can conflict, break layouts, or cache pages that shouldn’t be cached.
  • Don’t lazy-load everything. Lazy-loading the hero image makes LCP worse.
  • Don’t remove security or backup tools to save milliseconds. Security plugins, backups and updates are part of the baseline, not bloat.
  • Don’t defer scripts blindly. Aggressive “delay all JavaScript” settings can break contact forms, consent banners or call tracking. Test form submissions after every change.
  • Don’t judge by one test. Lab results vary from run to run. Look for consistent patterns across several pages.

title.raw: How to Write an Attorney Bio Page That Builds Trust (With Template, 2026)
title.rendered: How to Write an Attorney Bio Page That Builds Trust (With Template, 2026)

content.raw:
Quick answer: A strong attorney bio page tells a prospective client, within a few seconds, who you help, what kinds of matters you handle, why you are qualified, and how to contact you. Lead with a client-focused intro, back it with verifiable credentials (bar admissions, education, experience), add one human detail, and finish with a clear call to action. Keep every claim truthful and check your state's lawyer advertising rules before you publish.

Below you'll find the structure, a fill-in template, a checklist, schema markup tips and the ethics points to watch.

Key takeaways

  • Write the first two sentences for the client: who you help and with what. Move the résumé details lower on the page.
  • Every bio needs the same core blocks: photo, name and title, intro, practice focus, bar admissions and education, experience, a personal touch and a contact CTA.
  • Clear authorship and real credentials are what Google's helpful content guidance calls the "Who" of a page. Legal topics are held to a higher accuracy bar.
  • Add schema.org Person markup with sameAs links to profiles that confirm your identity, such as your state bar listing.
  • Avoid "expert" or "specialist" wording and unqualified case results unless your state's rules allow them. Rules vary, so check with your state bar.

What do clients look for on an attorney bio page?

Clients look for reassurance that you handle their kind of problem, that you are properly licensed, and that you are someone they could talk to. Most people reach a bio after reading a practice area page or seeing your name in Google, so they are already partway through deciding. The bio page has to answer a few unspoken questions:

  1. Do you handle my kind of matter? Name your practice focus in plain words: "I represent employees in wage and overtime disputes," not "litigation."
  2. Are you qualified and licensed where I am? List bar admissions by state and court, plus your education.
  3. Have you done this before? Give years in practice and the types of matters you handle. Past results need care (see the ethics section).
  4. Will I be comfortable working with you? A current, approachable photo and one or two human details help.
  5. How do I reach you, and what happens next? Show a direct phone number, an email or form, and what the first consultation looks like.

Referral sources and other lawyers also read bios, and they tend to care more about credentials and experience. A good structure serves both groups: client-focused language at the top, detailed credentials below.

How to write an attorney bio: the structure

Here is the order that works for most small-firm sites. Each block has one job, and the sequence follows the client questions above.

1. Professional photo

Use a recent, well-lit headshot that looks like you do when you walk into a meeting. Photo tips are covered in their own section below.

2. Name, title and firm

Use your name exactly as it appears on your bar record and your Google Business Profile, for example "Jordan A. Reyes, Partner." Mark the name up as the page's main heading. If you have a nickname clients use, add it once in the intro.

3. Short intro (two to four sentences)

This is the most-read part of the page. Say who you help, with what problem, and where. Leave out your law school here. A formula that works: [Who you help] + [the problem you solve] + [where] + [how you work].

4. Practice focus

List three to six practice areas or matter types, each linked to its own page. Your practice area pages carry the detailed explanation of each service. The bio only needs to show that you are the person who does that work. This avoids two pages competing for the same search.

5. Bar admissions and education

List each state bar and the federal courts you're admitted to, with the year if you like. Then your J.D. and undergraduate degree. Readers check this section to confirm you can take their case, so make it easy to scan as a list.

6. Experience

Describe the kinds of matters you handle and the clients you serve. Include prior roles that matter to clients, such as a former prosecutor in a criminal defense bio or in-house counsel in a business bio. Keep it short and concrete. "Represented landlords in eviction and lease disputes since 2015" says more than "extensive experience."

7. Professional associations

List bar sections, practice-specific associations and committee roles. If you list a directory honor or rating, add one line of plain English on what it is. Many clients won't know what it means, and some states have rules about how ratings are presented.

8. Publications and speaking

CLE presentations, bar journal articles and community talks show expertise without you having to call yourself an expert. Link to each one where you can. That gives readers and search engines something to verify.

9. Personal touch

One or two sentences about why you practice this kind of law, your community involvement, or a life outside work. Keep it relevant and brief. It should make you approachable, not take over the page.

10. Contact call to action

End with a direct next step: phone, email, or a link to book a consultation. Repeat a compact contact button near the top on mobile. If the CTA links to a form, use a secure contact form with a clear note not to send confidential details before you've agreed to represent them.

Attorney bio template (fill-in, with a fictional example)

Copy this template and replace the bracketed text. The example below it uses a fictional attorney and a fictional firm, invented only to show the format. It is not a real lawyer or a real result.

[PHOTO: recent headshot, alt text "[Full name], [title] at [Firm]"]

[Full name as on bar record], [Title]
[Firm name] | [City, State]

INTRO
[I help / Full name helps] [who] with [problem] in [location].
[One sentence on how you work or what clients can expect.]
[Call or book a consultation: phone | link]

PRACTICE FOCUS
- [Practice area 1] (link to practice area page)
- [Practice area 2] (link)
- [Practice area 3] (link)

BAR ADMISSIONS
- [State] State Bar, [year]
- U.S. District Court, [District], [year]

EDUCATION
- J.D., [Law school], [year]
- [Degree], [University], [year]

EXPERIENCE
[2-4 sentences: matter types, client types, relevant prior roles.]

PROFESSIONAL ASSOCIATIONS
- [Association / bar section], [role if any]

PUBLICATIONS & SPEAKING
- "[Title]," [Publication or event], [year] (link)

OUTSIDE THE OFFICE
[1-2 sentences: why you do this work, community, interests.]

CONTACT
[Phone] | [Email or secure form link] | [Office address]
[Book a consultation button]

[Disclaimer if any results or testimonials appear, per your state's rules]

Filled-in example (fictional attorney)

FICTIONAL EXAMPLE. "Jordan A. Reyes" and "Riverbend Family Law" are invented for illustration.

Jordan A. Reyes, Partner
Riverbend Family Law | Springfield, [State]

Jordan Reyes helps parents in [County] County work through divorce,
custody and child support, ideally without a courtroom fight. Clients
get a plan in plain English at the first meeting and a direct line to
Jordan, not a call center.
Call (555) 010-0000 or book a consultation online.

PRACTICE FOCUS
- Divorce and legal separation
- Child custody and parenting plans
- Child support modification
- Mediation

BAR ADMISSIONS
- [State] State Bar, 2014
- U.S. District Court, [District], 2016

EDUCATION
- J.D., [Law school], 2014
- B.A., Psychology, [University], 2011

EXPERIENCE
Jordan has focused on family law since 2014 and handles negotiated
settlements, mediation and contested custody hearings. Before joining
Riverbend, Jordan clerked for a family court judge.

PROFESSIONAL ASSOCIATIONS
- [State] State Bar, Family Law Section, member
- [County] Bar Association

PUBLICATIONS & SPEAKING
- "Parenting Plans for School-Age Children," [County] Bar CLE, 2025

OUTSIDE THE OFFICE
Jordan coaches youth soccer and volunteers at a legal aid clinic
one evening a month.

Notice what the example leaves out: no "best," no "expert," no dollar figures, and no promises about outcomes. It still gives clients what they need to decide.

Should an attorney bio be in first person or third person?

Either works. Pick one and use it consistently on the page. Third person ("Jordan helps…") is the traditional firm style. It is easy to reuse in court filings, conference programs and directories, and it reads well when the firm has several lawyers. First person ("I help…") feels warmer and more direct, and it suits solos and consumer practices such as family law, criminal defense and personal injury.

A common hybrid: write the bio in third person and add a short first-person quote or video intro ("Why I practice family law"). Multi-lawyer firms should choose one voice for every bio so the team pages look consistent.

How long should a lawyer bio be?

Most attorney bio pages land between 300 and 700 words. FindLaw's own bio-writing guide suggests 300 to 500. There's no ideal word count. Length should follow content: a lawyer with publications, speaking and two decades of experience needs more room than a new associate.

What matters more is that the intro is short (under about 80 words) and the rest is scannable with subheadings and lists. Also keep a 50 to 100 word "short bio" for directories, event programs and the team grid on your About page.

E-E-A-T: why your bio matters for SEO and trust

Your bio page is the clearest way to show Google and readers who stands behind your site's legal content. Google's guidance on creating helpful, reliable, people-first content describes E-E-A-T (experience, expertise, authoritativeness and trustworthiness) and says "trust is most important." It is not a single ranking factor. Google says its systems use a mix of signals that line up with it.

The same page explains that topics affecting people's health, finances or safety, called "Your Money or Your Life" (YMYL) topics, get extra weight on E-E-A-T. Most legal questions qualify. Three points from the guidance apply directly to attorney bios:

  • Who: Google recommends bylines where readers expect them, linked to background on the author. Link your blog posts and practice area pages to the bio of the attorney who wrote or reviewed them.
  • Honesty: The guidance says fabricated creator profiles, such as made-up names, AI-generated headshots or false credentials, are deceptive. Use real photos and real, verifiable credentials.

  4. Will I be comfortable working with you? A current, approachable photo and one or two human details help.
  5. How do I reach you, and what happens next? Show a direct phone number, an email or form, and what the first consultation looks like.

Referral sources and other lawyers also read bios, and they tend to care more about credentials and experience. A good structure serves both groups: client-focused language at the top, detailed credentials below.

This is the most-read part of the page. Say who you help, with what problem, and where. Leave out your law school here. A formula that works: [Who you help] + [the problem you solve] + [where] + [how you work].

List three to six practice areas or matter types, each linked to its own page. Your practice area pages carry the detailed explanation of each service. The bio only needs to show that you are the person who does that work. This avoids two pages competing for the same search.

5. Bar admissions and education

List each state bar and the federal courts you’re admitted to, with the year if you like. Then your J.D. and undergraduate degree. Readers check this section to confirm you can take their case, so make it easy to scan as a list.

6. Experience

Describe the kinds of matters you handle and the clients you serve. Include prior roles that matter to clients, such as a former prosecutor in a criminal defense bio or in-house counsel in a business bio. Keep it short and concrete. “Represented landlords in eviction and lease disputes since 2015” says more than “extensive experience.”

7. Professional associations

List bar sections, practice-specific associations and committee roles. If you list a directory honor or rating, add one line of plain English on what it is. Many clients won’t know what it means, and some states have rules about how ratings are presented.

8. Publications and speaking

CLE presentations, bar journal articles and community talks show expertise without you having to call yourself an expert. Link to each one where you can. That gives readers and search engines something to verify.

9. Personal touch

One or two sentences about why you practice this kind of law, your community involvement, or a life outside work. Keep it relevant and brief. It should make you approachable, not take over the page.
