Quick answer: To set up Microsoft 365 for a law firm, pick a plan (Business Premium for most firms that handle confidential client files), buy it from Microsoft or a partner, add your domain, and create users and shared mailboxes. Then turn on MFA, lock down external sharing, set retention policies, and migrate old email last, before you switch your MX record. Allow one focused day for a solo or small firm, plus migration time.

Key takeaways

  • Plan: Microsoft 365 Business Premium costs $22 per user per month (paid yearly, as of November 2026). It is the only Business plan that includes Conditional Access, Intune, Defender for Office 365 Plan 1, message encryption and org-wide retention policies.
  • Security first: security defaults (free MFA for everyone) are fine on Basic and Standard. On Premium you can swap them for Conditional Access policies.
  • Sharing: change SharePoint/OneDrive external sharing away from "Anyone" links. Make "Specific people" the default link type.
  • Order matters: create every mailbox before you point your MX record at Microsoft 365, so no client email goes missing.
  • Ethics: ABA Formal Opinion 477R asks for "reasonable efforts" to protect client information. These settings support that, but check your state bar's guidance.

This guide covers setting up the Microsoft 365 account itself: licenses, admin accounts, security, retention, sharing and migration. Email authentication records (SPF, DKIM and DMARC) have their own guide, our law firm email setup guide covering SPF, DKIM and DMARC. If you haven't decided between Google and Microsoft yet, read Google Workspace vs Microsoft 365 for law firms first.

What do you need before you start?

You need four things: access to your domain registrar, a list of everyone who needs a mailbox, a list of shared addresses (like intake@ or billing@), and admin access to your current email provider. Gather them first so the setup runs in one session.

  • Registrar login for the domain your firm uses for email (where you bought it, or wherever its DNS is hosted, for example Cloudflare). Not sure which registrar fits? See our guide to the best domain registrars for law firms.
  • User list: full names, the email address each person should have, and whether each needs desktop Office apps.
  • Shared addresses: intake, reception, billing, and any old addresses that must keep receiving mail.
  • Old system access: admin rights to Google Workspace, or the IMAP server details for your current host.
  • Software that plugs into email: your practice management tool, scanner/copier, and any client portal. Some of them limit how you can buy or set up Microsoft 365 (see Step 2).

Step 1: Which Microsoft 365 plan should a law firm choose?

Most small firms should choose Microsoft 365 Business Premium, because it is the only Business plan with device management, Conditional Access, built-in email encryption and org-wide retention policies. Business Standard works for a very small firm that will rely on security defaults and doesn't need those controls. Business Basic gives you web and mobile apps only, with no desktop Word or Outlook.

All three plans cover 1 to 300 users. Prices below are from Microsoft's business plan comparison page and the individual plan pages, as of November 2026 (US, per user per month).

Microsoft also sells "with Copilot" bundles of Business Standard ($23.50) and Business Premium ($32.00), both paid yearly as of November 2026, and both note usage-based billing for some advanced AI features. Copilot is optional. You can buy the plain plans and add AI later after you've settled your firm's AI-use policy. The security split in the table follows Microsoft Learn's Microsoft 365 for business security best practices page, which shows feature by feature which plan includes what.

Step 2: Should you buy direct from Microsoft or through a reseller?

Buy direct from Microsoft unless an IT partner will actively manage your tenant. A tenant is your firm's private Microsoft 365 environment: its users, settings and data. Buying direct keeps billing and the Global Administrator account under the firm's control.

  • Direct: you sign up on microsoft.com, pay Microsoft, and get support from Microsoft. This works well for solos and firms with a tech-comfortable partner or office manager.
  • Through a Microsoft partner (Cloud Solution Provider): the partner bills you and usually handles setup and support. This is worth it if they'll actually configure the security settings below and not just sell licenses. Make sure a firm-owned account keeps Global Administrator rights.
  • Bundled with a web host or registrar: be careful. Some legal software treats these accounts differently. MyCase's Outlook add-in guide says the add-in is not compatible with third-party Microsoft 365 accounts. It says firms with Microsoft 365 "from another provider like GoDaddy" must migrate directly to Microsoft. The same guide says the add-in is available on MyCase's Pro and Advanced tiers and doesn't currently work with shared mailboxes.

If you use a different practice management system, check its Outlook integration requirements before you buy.

Step 3: How do you set up admin accounts safely?

Keep admin rights to as few accounts as possible, and keep them separate from everyday mailboxes. The account that creates the tenant automatically becomes Global Administrator, the role that can change everything.

  1. Sign up and create the tenant with a firm-owned admin identity, not a lawyer's personal address.
  2. Create two emergency access ("break glass") accounts with the Global Administrator role. Microsoft's security defaults documentation recommends two cloud-only emergency accounts for when other admins are locked out. Store their credentials securely offline.
  3. Give the attorney or office manager who manages the tenant a separate admin account for admin work only. Microsoft recommends separate accounts for administration and everyday productivity.
  4. Don't assign admin roles to staff who only need a mailbox.

Step 4: How do you add your law firm's domain to Microsoft 365?

Add the domain in the Microsoft 365 admin center under Settings > Domains > + Add domain, verify you own it, then let Microsoft add the DNS records or add them yourself. Microsoft's add a custom domain guide describes two routes:

  • Domain Connect (automatic): if your DNS is at a supported provider (Microsoft lists GoDaddy, IONOS, Cloudflare, WordPress.com and others), you sign in to the registrar in a pop-up and approve the records.
  • Manual: add a TXT record to prove ownership. Microsoft says verification can take up to 10 minutes, or up to 48 hours at some registrars. Then add the service records the wizard shows you.

Important: Microsoft says to add users and set up mailboxes after adding the domain but before adding the MX record. The MX record controls where email is delivered. Switch it too early and messages land in Microsoft 365 before anyone has a mailbox. If your current email still needs to work during setup, use the manual route and hold back the MX change until Step 11 is done. Your website is not affected by these changes. For SPF, DKIM and DMARC, follow our domain email authentication guide.

Step 5: How should you set up users and shared mailboxes?

Give each person their own licensed user account, and use shared mailboxes for role addresses like intake@ and billing@. Never share one login among staff. Shared logins break MFA and make audit logs useless.

  1. In the admin center, go to Users > Active users > Add a user for each person and assign a license.
  2. Create shared mailboxes under Teams & groups > Shared mailboxes and add members.
  3. Leave sign-in blocked on each shared mailbox's account. Microsoft says to "always block sign-in for the shared mailbox account and keep it blocked."

Shared mailbox facts from Microsoft's shared mailbox documentation that matter to law firms:

  • A shared mailbox holds up to 50 GB without a license. Members need their own licensed mailbox to open it.
  • Putting a shared mailbox on litigation hold needs an Exchange Online Plan 2 license, or Plan 1 plus Exchange Online Archiving. Plan for this if intake@ ever holds evidence-relevant mail.
  • Only people inside your organization can be members. Outside co-counsel can't be added.
  • Email sent from a shared mailbox can't be encrypted, so send sensitive documents from a personal mailbox.
  • Up to 25 users is the supported maximum per shared mailbox.

Step 6: How do you turn on MFA with security defaults?

Security defaults are Microsoft's free, one-switch baseline. It makes every user register for multifactor authentication (MFA) and blocks legacy sign-in methods. Microsoft says it may already be on in tenants created on or after October 22, 2019. Check anyway.

  1. Sign in to the Microsoft Entra admin center (entra.microsoft.com) as an admin.
  2. Go to Entra ID > Overview > Properties.
  3. Select Manage security defaults, set it to Enabled, and save.
  4. Ask every user to install Microsoft Authenticator and register at myprofile.microsoft.com (Security info).

According to Microsoft's security defaults page, this setting requires all users to register for MFA and requires admins to use MFA. It also blocks legacy authentication (older IMAP, SMTP and POP3 clients) and blocks device code flow. Since July 2024, users no longer get a 14-day grace period to register.

Watch out for scanners and copiers. Older multifunction devices that "scan to email" with a username and password often use legacy SMTP, which security defaults block. Test scan-to-email right after you enable it. Microsoft documents alternatives in how to set up a multifunction device to send email.

Step 7: How do Conditional Access and Intune work on Business Premium?

Conditional Access is a set of if-then sign-in rules, for example "require MFA and a compliant device to open SharePoint." It requires Microsoft Entra ID P1, which Business Premium includes. Microsoft says organizations with P1 licenses probably shouldn't stay on security defaults, but you must disable security defaults before your Conditional Access policies can replace them.

  1. Review the Microsoft-managed Conditional Access policies. Microsoft says these keep the same protections as security defaults: block legacy authentication, require MFA for admins, MFA for all users, and MFA for Azure management.
  2. Turn those on (start in report-only mode if available), and exclude your two break-glass accounts.
  3. Only then switch security defaults off. Microsoft's guidance is to enable Conditional Access policies immediately after disabling defaults, so there's no unprotected gap.
  4. Add stricter rules only when you need them, such as requiring a compliant device for document access.

Microsoft Intune Plan 1 (also in Business Premium) covers mobile device management (MDM) and mobile app management (MAM). MDM manages a whole firm-owned laptop or phone. MAM protects just the work apps on a personal phone. For a lawyer reading client email on a personal iPhone, an app protection policy can, for example, stop copying firm data into personal apps without taking over the phone. Business Premium also includes Microsoft Defender for Business for endpoint protection on Windows and Mac. Microsoft's Business Premium setup hub walks through these in order.

Step 8: How do you protect email and send encrypted messages?

Every Business plan includes anti-spam, anti-malware and anti-spoofing protection. Business Premium adds Defender for Office 365 Plan 1: impersonation protection, Safe Links and Safe Attachments, which matter for a profession targeted by wire-fraud phishing.

  • Turn on the preset security policies (Standard or Strict) in the Microsoft Defender portal and don't hand-build every rule. Microsoft's best-practice table recommends them for all business plans.
  • Use Microsoft Purview Message Encryption for sensitive email. It's included in Business Premium. Microsoft's Purview service description says Basic and Standard need an Azure Information Protection Plan 1 add-on for it. Recipients don't need a Microsoft subscription to read encrypted mail.
  • Optionally, create a mail flow rule that encrypts messages automatically, for example when the subject contains a keyword your staff agree on.

Step 9: Which licenses include retention policies and Purview features?

Org-wide retention policies for email, SharePoint and OneDrive are licensed in Business Premium, not in Basic or Standard. A retention policy keeps (or deletes) content for a set period, even if a user deletes it. You configure it in the Microsoft Purview portal under Data Lifecycle Management. Licensing per Microsoft's Purview service description:

*Exchange Online Plan 2 or Exchange Online Archiving add-ons also grant rights for mailbox retention policies, and SharePoint Plan 2 grants them for SharePoint/OneDrive.

A practical starting point is one retention policy that keeps email and documents for the period your state's file-retention rules and your engagement letters require. Set it to "retain only" at first, not "retain then delete," until you've decided on deletion. Retention is not a backup and is not a substitute for a records policy, so write down what you chose and why. Microsoft's overview, Learn about retention policies and retention labels, explains how the two work together.

Step 10: What sharing settings should a law firm use in Teams, SharePoint and OneDrive?

Allow sharing only with people who sign in or verify their identity, and make "Specific people" the default link type. Change this in the SharePoint admin center > Policies > Sharing. Microsoft's SharePoint and OneDrive sharing settings guide lists four external sharing levels:

  • Anyone: links work with no sign-in at all. Avoid this for client files.
  • New and existing guests: recipients sign in or enter a verification code. This is a sensible default for firms that share with clients and co-counsel.
  • Existing guests: only guests already in your directory. Stricter, but more admin work.
  • Only people in your organization: external sharing is off.

Then, under More external sharing settings and File and folder links:

  • Set the default link type to Specific people, the most restrictive option.
  • Turn on guest access expiration (for example, guests lose access after a set number of days).
  • Consider limiting external sharing by domain if you mainly work with a few known organizations.
  • If you do allow Anyone links on some sites, make them expire and restrict them to view-only.

OneDrive can be more restrictive than SharePoint but never more permissive. Teams files live in SharePoint, so these settings also govern files shared in Teams. Review guest access in Teams admin settings to match.

Step 11: How do you migrate email from Google Workspace or another host?

Use Microsoft's Google Workspace batch migration if you're leaving Google, and IMAP migration for most other hosts. Both run in the Exchange admin center. Change your MX record only once the copy is complete.

  • From Google Workspace: Microsoft's automated Google Workspace migration moves mail, rules, calendars and contacts. It doesn't move vacation/auto-reply settings, room bookings, shared calendars, event colors or Gmail tags, and contacts carry at most three email addresses. Prerequisites include two routing subdomains and provisioning mail users first.
  • From other hosts (IMAP): per Microsoft's migration options overview, IMAP migration moves email only. Contacts, calendars and tasks must be moved by hand. It also doesn't create mailboxes, so you must create users first (Step 5).
  • PST files: archived mail stored as PST files can be brought in with Microsoft's PST Import service.

Microsoft strongly recommends disabling retention and archival policies during a data migration, so apply Step 9's policies after the migration completes. If you're moving to Google instead, see our Google Workspace setup guide for law firms.

Step 12: How do you train staff and keep the tenant secure?

Show every user how to approve MFA prompts, spot phishing, send an encrypted message and share a file with "Specific people." Then put a recurring task on the calendar to review the tenant: new users, departed staff, guest accounts, and alerts in the Defender portal. When someone leaves, block their sign-in right away. Convert their mailbox to a shared mailbox so client correspondence stays with the firm.

Microsoft 365 law firm settings checklist

Use this table to confirm each setting before you call the setup finished.

What does ABA Formal Opinion 477R mean for your Microsoft 365 setup?

ABA Formal Opinion 477R (2017) says a lawyer generally may send client information over the internet if the lawyer has made reasonable efforts to prevent unauthorized access. Special precautions may be needed when the client agreement, the law, or the sensitivity of the information requires it. You can read the text in the copy of ABA Formal Opinion 477 hosted by the Tennessee Board of Professional Responsibility.

In practice, MFA, restricted sharing, encryption for sensitive messages, managed devices and vetting your vendors are the kinds of measures that show "reasonable efforts." The opinion doesn't name products or required settings, and it's a model opinion, not your state's rule. Check your state bar's ethics opinions on cloud computing and email, and talk with clients about how they want sensitive matters communicated. The same thinking applies to your website. See our law firm website security checklist.

FAQ

Is Microsoft 365 Business Standard enough for a law firm?

Business Standard can work for a very small firm, as long as security defaults stay on and the firm doesn't need encryption or retention policies (both possible only with add-ons). It lacks Conditional Access, Intune, Defender for Office 365 and built-in message encryption, which is why most firms handling confidential files choose Business Premium.

How much does Microsoft 365 Business Premium cost for a law firm?

Business Premium is $22.00 per user per month with an annual commitment, or $26.40 per user per month on a monthly subscription (US pricing, as of November 2026). The bundle with Copilot is $32.00 per user per month, paid yearly. Confirm current pricing on Microsoft's site before you buy.

Are Microsoft 365 security defaults enough?

Security defaults are a strong free baseline: MFA for everyone and legacy sign-in blocked. They're all-or-nothing, though. If you need device requirements, location rules or exceptions, you need Conditional Access, which requires Entra ID P1 (included in Business Premium).

Can I use Microsoft 365 bought through GoDaddy or my web host?

Usually the email itself works, but some integrations don't. For example, MyCase states its Outlook add-in isn't compatible with third-party Microsoft 365 accounts such as GoDaddy's. Check your practice management software's requirements first, and buy directly from Microsoft if in doubt.

Do shared mailboxes like intake@ need a license?

No. A shared mailbox stores up to 50 GB without a license, but every member needs their own licensed mailbox. You'll need an extra license for more storage, an archive, or litigation hold on that mailbox.

Do I need Copilot to set up Microsoft 365?

No. Microsoft still sells Business Basic, Standard and Premium without Copilot. Set up the core tenant first, adopt an AI-use policy, and add Copilot later if the firm decides it's appropriate.

Will setting up Microsoft 365 affect my law firm website?

No. Microsoft says adding a domain and its email records doesn't affect your website. Only edit the email-related DNS records, and leave your site's A/CNAME records alone.

Next steps

Start with the plan decision (Business Premium for most firms), then work through the twelve steps in order: admin accounts, domain, users, MFA, Premium controls, email protection, retention, sharing, migration, and training. Finish with the checklist table above. Next, set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC with our law firm email setup guide, and confirm your state bar's technology guidance.

Allow sharing only with people who sign in or verify their identity, and make “Specific people” the default link type. Change this in the SharePoint admin center > Policies > Sharing. Microsoft’s SharePoint and OneDrive sharing settings guide lists four external sharing levels:

  • Anyone: links work with no sign-in at all. Avoid this for client files.
  • New and existing guests: recipients sign in or enter a verification code. This is a sensible default for firms that share with clients and co-counsel.
  • Existing guests: only guests already in your directory. Stricter, but more admin work.
  • Only people in your organization: external sharing is off.

Then, under More external sharing settings and File and folder links:

  • Set the default link type to Specific people, the most restrictive option.
  • Turn on guest access expiration (for example, guests lose access after a set number of days).
  • Consider limiting external sharing by domain if you mainly work with a few known organizations.
  • If you do allow Anyone links on some sites, make them expire and restrict them to view-only.

OneDrive can be more restrictive than SharePoint but never more permissive. Teams files live in SharePoint, so these settings also govern files shared in Teams. Review guest access in Teams admin settings to match.

Step 11: How do you migrate email from Google Workspace or another host?

Use Microsoft’s Google Workspace batch migration if you’re leaving Google, and IMAP migration for most other hosts. Both run in the Exchange admin center. Change your MX record only once the copy is complete.

  • From Google Workspace: Microsoft’s automated Google Workspace migration moves mail, rules, calendars and contacts. It doesn’t move vacation/auto-reply settings, room bookings, shared calendars, event colors or Gmail tags, and contacts carry at most three email addresses. Prerequisites include two routing subdomains and provisioning mail users first.
  • From other hosts (IMAP): per Microsoft’s migration options overview, IMAP migration moves email only. Contacts, calendars and tasks must be moved by hand. It also doesn’t create mailboxes, so you must create users first (Step 5).
  • PST files: archived mail stored as PST files can be brought in with Microsoft’s PST Import service.

Microsoft strongly recommends disabling retention and archival policies during a data migration, so apply Step 9’s policies after the migration completes. If you’re moving to Google instead, see our Google Workspace setup guide for law firms.

Step 12: How do you train staff and keep the tenant secure?

Show every user how to approve MFA prompts, spot phishing, send an encrypted message and share a file with “Specific people.” Then put a recurring task on the calendar to review the tenant: new users, departed staff, guest accounts, and alerts in the Defender portal. When someone leaves, block their sign-in right away. Convert their mailbox to a shared mailbox so client correspondence stays with the firm.

Microsoft 365 law firm settings checklist

Use this table to confirm each setting before you call the setup finished.

What does ABA Formal Opinion 477R mean for your Microsoft 365 setup?

ABA Formal Opinion 477R (2017) says a lawyer generally may send client information over the internet if the lawyer has made reasonable efforts to prevent unauthorized access. Special precautions may be needed when the client agreement, the law, or the sensitivity of the information requires it. You can read the text in the copy of ABA Formal Opinion 477 hosted by the Tennessee Board of Professional Responsibility.

In practice, MFA, restricted sharing, encryption for sensitive messages, managed devices and vetting your vendors are the kinds of measures that show “reasonable efforts.” The opinion doesn’t name products or required settings, and it’s a model opinion, not your state’s rule. Check your state bar’s ethics opinions on cloud computing and email, and talk with clients about how they want sensitive matters communicated. The same thinking applies to your website. See our law firm website security checklist.

FAQ

Is Microsoft 365 Business Standard enough for a law firm?

Business Standard can work for a very small firm, as long as security defaults stay on and the firm doesn’t need encryption or retention policies (both possible only with add-ons). It lacks Conditional Access, Intune, Defender for Office 365 and built-in message encryption, which is why most firms handling confidential files choose Business Premium.

How much does Microsoft 365 Business Premium cost for a law firm?

Business Premium is $22.00 per user per month with an annual commitment, or $26.40 per user per month on a monthly subscription (US pricing, as of November 2026). The bundle with Copilot is $32.00 per user per month, paid yearly. Confirm current pricing on Microsoft’s site before you buy.

Are Microsoft 365 security defaults enough?

Security defaults are a strong free baseline: MFA for everyone and legacy sign-in blocked. They’re all-or-nothing, though. If you need device requirements, location rules or exceptions, you need Conditional Access, which requires Entra ID P1 (included in Business Premium).

Can I use Microsoft 365 bought through GoDaddy or my web host?

Usually the email itself works, but some integrations don’t. For example, MyCase states its Outlook add-in isn’t compatible with third-party Microsoft 365 accounts such as GoDaddy’s. Check your practice management software’s requirements first, and buy directly from Microsoft if in doubt.

Do shared mailboxes like intake@ need a license?

No. A shared mailbox stores up to 50 GB without a license, but every member needs their own licensed mailbox. You’ll need an extra license for more storage, an archive, or litigation hold on that mailbox.

Do I need Copilot to set up Microsoft 365?

No. Microsoft still sells Business Basic, Standard and Premium without Copilot. Set up the core tenant first, adopt an AI-use policy, and add Copilot later if the firm decides it’s appropriate.

Will setting up Microsoft 365 affect my law firm website?

No. Microsoft says adding a domain and its email records doesn’t affect your website. Only edit the email-related DNS records, and leave your site’s A/CNAME records alone.

Next steps

Start with the plan decision (Business Premium for most firms), then work through the twelve steps in order: admin accounts, domain, users, MFA, Premium controls, email protection, retention, sharing, migration, and training. Finish with the checklist table above. Next, set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC with our law firm email setup guide, and confirm your state bar’s technology guidance.

content.raw:
Quick answer: To set up Google Workspace for a law firm, pick an edition (Business Plus if you want Google Vault for retention and legal holds), verify your domain, create users and a shared intake@ group, then lock down the Admin console: enforce 2-Step Verification, require strong passwords, restrict external Drive sharing, turn on mobile management, and set Vault retention rules before you migrate old email. Most of the work is in the security settings, not the sign-up.

This guide walks through each step in order, with the exact Admin console menu paths from Google's own documentation, a settings checklist you can work through, and the ethics context lawyers should keep in mind. Email DNS records (MX, SPF, DKIM and DMARC) are covered separately in our law firm email setup guide, so this article does not repeat them.

Key takeaways

  • Edition matters: Google Vault and advanced endpoint (mobile) management are included in Business Plus, not Business Starter or Business Standard, according to Google's Business edition comparison.
  • Security is not on by default: 2-Step Verification enforcement, password strength and external sharing limits are settings you have to choose.
  • Vault is not a backup: Google says Vault "isn't a data archive" and retains nothing until you create retention rules.
  • Migrate last: set retention and security first, then copy old mail in with Google's data migration service.
  • Ethics: ABA Formal Opinion 477R asks for "reasonable efforts" to protect client information, which includes vetting vendors and training staff.
Quick pick

Choosing Google Workspace? Start through our referral link → and ask us for a 10% first-year promo code.

We may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. It never changes our recommendations.

What do you need before you start?

  • Your domain and its login. You will add a verification record at your domain registrar or DNS host. If you have not chosen a domain yet, see .law vs .com vs .attorney domains and our best domain registrars for law firms.
  • A list of people and roles. Lawyers, paralegals, staff, and any shared addresses such as intake@ or billing@.
  • An inventory of current data. Where email, calendars and files live today (personal Gmail, Microsoft 365, an IMAP host), and roughly how much there is.
  • Any active litigation holds or retention duties. These shape your Vault rules and should be settled before migration.

Which Google Workspace edition should a law firm choose?

For most small firms that want built-in retention and legal holds, Business Plus is the edition to choose, because it is the lowest Business tier that includes Google Vault. All three Business editions support 1 to 300 users. Prices below are Google's published US list prices per user as of November 2026, from Google's payment plan comparison.

Feature rows come from Google's Compare Business editions page. The annual plan locks in your license count until renewal; the flexible plan lets you add or remove users month to month. Prices exclude tax and can change, so confirm on Google's pricing page before you buy.

How to decide: Business Standard can work for a firm that keeps its system of record in a practice management platform and adds a third-party backup. Business Plus makes more sense if you want retention rules, litigation holds and search across mail and Drive inside Google itself, or advanced control over phones. If you are still choosing between ecosystems, read Google Workspace vs Microsoft 365 for law firms first, and see our Microsoft 365 setup guide if you go the other way.

How do you set up Google Workspace for a law firm? (12 steps)

Work through these steps in order. Doing security and retention before migration means old client data lands in an account that is already protected.

Step 1: Sign up and verify your domain

Sign up at workspace.google.com using your firm's domain, then prove you own it. Google prefers a DNS TXT record added at your registrar or DNS host. According to Google's domain verification guide, you must verify within the first 9 days of a free trial or when you start a paid contract, and an unverified account is deleted within 21 days of sign-up unless billing is active. Google says confirmation can take up to an hour.

Once verified, set up mail routing and email authentication using our MX, SPF, DKIM and DMARC walkthrough. If you are moving from another mail provider, you can hold the MX change until Step 11.

Step 2: Protect the super admin account

The first account you create is a super administrator, meaning it can change every setting and read or delete any user's data. Treat it like the keys to the office. Google now enforces 2-Step Verification for administrator accounts, per its 2SV overview, and recommends security keys as the strongest method. A common practice is to keep a separate admin login that is not used for day-to-day email, and to have a second trusted person (a partner or your IT provider) with admin access so one lost phone does not lock the firm out.

Step 3: Create organizational units, users and groups

An organizational unit (OU) is a folder of users that can get different settings. Small firms often need only two or three: Attorneys, Staff, and perhaps Contractors with tighter sharing. Then add each user under Directory > Users.

For shared addresses such as intake@, use a Google Group rather than paying for a separate user license. Turning the group into a Collaborative Inbox lets members take, assign and close conversations. Google's Collaborative Inbox guide lists the steps:

  1. Create the group (for example, intake@yourfirm.com) and add the people who answer new inquiries.
  2. Turn on conversation history for the group (Collaborative Inbox requires it).
  3. In Google Groups, open Group settings and, under Enable additional Google Groups features, select Collaborative Inbox.
  4. Give members the permissions to take and assign conversations.

Point your website's contact form at this group so new leads are not stuck in one person's inbox. Our guide to a secure contact form for a law firm website covers the form side.

Step 4: Enforce 2-Step Verification for everyone

2-Step Verification (2SV) means signing in needs a second proof, such as a phone prompt or security key, in addition to the password. Google's Deploy 2-Step Verification page recommends telling users first and letting them enroll before you enforce. The setting lives at Security > Authentication > 2-step verification (super admin only):

  1. Check Allow users to turn on 2-Step Verification and ask everyone to enroll.
  2. Under Enforcement, choose On or Turn on enforcement from date. Google notes date-based enforcement can take 24 to 48 hours to start.
  3. Set a short New user enrollment period (Google allows 1 day to 6 months). During it, new accounts can sign in with only a password.
  4. Under Methods, prefer Any except verification codes via text, phone call or Only security key. Google discourages text messages because they can be intercepted.
  5. Leave Frequency (trusted devices) off unless people often switch devices, as Google advises.

Step 5: Set a password policy

Go to Security > Authentication > Password management. Google's password requirements page lets you check Enforce strong password, set a minimum length between 8 and 100 characters, and tick Enforce password policy at next sign-in so existing weak passwords must change. Many firms choose a longer minimum (for example 12 or more) and pair it with a password manager. With 2SV enforced, forced periodic expiration is usually less important than length.

Step 6: Deal with "less secure apps" and old devices

You no longer have a "less secure apps" switch to turn off. Google's transition page says less secure app access was turned off for all accounts, so IMAP, SMTP, POP, CalDAV and CardDAV no longer work with plain passwords. Apps must use OAuth (a sign-in method that grants access without sharing your password). The practical task for a firm is the office scanner or copier that emails PDFs: Google's options are to switch the device to OAuth, use another way to scan, or create an app password for it.

Step 7: Restrict external Drive sharing

Drive sharing is where client files most often leak, usually through an "anyone with the link" setting. Go to Apps > Google Workspace > Drive and Docs > Sharing settings > Sharing options. Google's external sharing guide describes these controls:

  • External sharing On or Off: turn it off entirely, or leave it on with limits.
  • Allowlisted domains: limit sharing to trusted domains, such as co-counsel or a key client.
  • Highlight external files: shows users a warning marker on files from outside the firm.
  • Different rules per OU or group: for example, attorneys can share externally but contractors cannot. Group settings override OU settings.
  • Visitor sharing (people without Google accounts) is a separate setting.

Google notes changes can take up to 24 hours to apply. Also consider shared drives for matter files, so documents belong to the firm instead of an individual who might leave.

Step 8: Turn on mobile device management

Phones are where most lawyers read client email, so manage them. Basic mobile management is on by default in every Business edition, according to Google's basic mobile management page. It works on Android, iPhone and iPad, lets you set password requirements for devices, and lets you wipe a user's work account from a lost or stolen phone. Find it at Devices > Mobile & endpoints > Settings > Universal > General > Mobile management.

Advanced mobile management (Business Plus) adds device approvals, broader app control on Android and iOS, and full-device wipe. Google's endpoint feature comparison lists what each level covers.

Step 9: Configure Vault retention and holds (Business Plus)

Google Vault is Google's tool to retain, hold, search and export Workspace data. Per Google's Vault overview, retention rules decide how long data is kept, holds preserve a user's data for a legal matter even if they delete it, and exports stay available for 15 days. Two points trip up firms:

  • Nothing is retained until you create a rule. Set a default retention rule for Gmail and Drive before migrating data.
  • Retention rules can also delete. A rule that expires data after a set period will remove it. Match periods to your file-retention policy and any state bar rules on client files, and check with your state bar if unsure.

On Business Starter or Standard, Vault is not included. Google's Vault licensing page directs other editions to Google Sales for add-on options, so the practical path for most small firms is upgrading to Business Plus.

Step 10: Set up security alerts

The alert center (Security > Alert center) shows notifications about possible problems, such as suspicious sign-ins or phishing. Google's alert center page explains you can add email notifications by configuring a rule. Send them to an address someone actually reads, such as your IT provider plus the managing partner.

Step 11: Migrate email from Gmail or Microsoft 365

Google's data migration service copies email into Workspace from Microsoft Exchange Online, IMAP providers, another Workspace account, or a personal Gmail account. It runs from Data > Data import & export and needs a super admin. Key limits from Google's documentation:

  • Exchange Online: up to 1,000 users per import; you connect by signing in as a Microsoft 365 Global Administrator, and Google's Exchange Online guide says it copies rather than deletes the source data. Users must already exist in both systems.
  • IMAP: up to 100 users per import.
  • Personal Gmail: useful for a solo who started on a free account. If you do not set a start date, it imports from January 1, 2000.
  • Stopping does not roll back: items already copied stay.

A sensible order: migrate a pilot user, check message counts, migrate everyone, switch MX records, then run a final pass to catch mail that arrived during the cutover. Keep the old system read-only for a while rather than cancelling it the same day.

Step 12: Decide how you will back up

Google keeps your data available, but recovery from mistakes is limited. Admins can restore Drive files for 25 days after a user empties their trash, according to Google's Drive recovery page. Vault holds help preserve data but Google says Vault is not an archive. If you need point-in-time restores beyond those windows, or protection if an account is compromised and data is deleted, consider a third-party Workspace backup service and vet it like any vendor that touches client data.

Google Workspace security settings checklist for law firms

Use this table as a one-page audit after setup and once a year after that. Menu paths are from Google's Admin Help pages linked above and can be renamed over time.

What do legal ethics rules say about cloud email and files?

The ABA's Formal Opinion 477R, "Securing Communication of Protected Client Information" (2017), interprets Model Rule 1.6(c) as requiring reasonable efforts to prevent unauthorized access to client information, judged case by case. A U.S. Court of International Trade article on the opinion notes that unencrypted email remains acceptable for routine, low-sensitivity matters, while more sensitive messages warrant more security. Summaries of the opinion, such as LawPay's, list steps including understanding how client information is transmitted and stored, using reasonable electronic security measures, training lawyers and staff, and doing due diligence on technology vendors.

The settings above map onto those steps: 2SV and password rules are security measures, sharing limits control where data goes, and Vault and backups address storage. ABA opinions are guidance, not binding rules in every state, so check your own state bar's ethics opinions on cloud computing. For your website side, see our law firm website security checklist.

FAQ

Is Google Workspace secure enough for lawyers?

It can be, if it is configured well. The platform provides 2-Step Verification, sharing controls, mobile management and (in Business Plus) Vault, but most of those protections depend on admin settings. Ethics guidance such as ABA Formal Opinion 477R focuses on whether your efforts are reasonable, so document what you set up.

Does Google Workspace Business Standard include Vault?

No. Google's Business edition comparison shows Vault only in Business Plus among the Business editions. Enterprise editions also include it.

Can a lawyer use a free Gmail account for client work?

It is generally a poor fit. A free account has no Admin console, so you cannot enforce 2SV across staff, control sharing, wipe a lost phone's work data, or apply retention rules, and your address will not use your firm's domain. If you started on Gmail, the data migration service can copy that mail into Workspace.

Is Google Vault a backup?

No. Google states Vault "isn't a data archive." It preserves data under retention rules and holds and lets you search and export it, but it does not give you point-in-time restores of a whole account. Use a separate backup service if you need that.

Can I move my firm from Microsoft 365 to Google Workspace?

Yes. Google's data migration service copies email, and optionally calendar and contacts, from Exchange Online for up to 1,000 users per import. You need Microsoft 365 Global Administrator access and matching user accounts in Workspace first.

How long does Google Workspace setup take for a small firm?

It varies with the number of users and the amount of data to migrate. Domain verification is usually quick (Google says up to an hour once the record is in place), and the security settings take an afternoon if you know where they are. Migration of large mailboxes is usually the longest part.

Next steps

Pick your edition, verify the domain, and finish the security baseline (2SV, passwords, sharing, mobile, alerts) before anyone starts sending client email. If you chose Business Plus, create Vault retention rules next, then migrate. Finally, complete your DNS records with the law firm email setup guide and revisit the checklist table once a year.

Google’s password requirements page lets you check Enforce strong password, set a minimum length between 8 and 100 characters, and tick Enforce password policy at next sign-in so existing weak passwords must change. Many firms choose a longer minimum (for example 12 or more) and pair it with a password manager. With 2SV enforced, forced periodic expiration is usually less important than length.

Step 6: Deal with “less secure apps” and old devices

You no longer have a “less secure apps” switch to turn off. Google’s transition page says less secure app access was turned off for all accounts, so IMAP, SMTP, POP, CalDAV and CardDAV no longer work with plain passwords. Apps must use OAuth (a sign-in method that grants access without sharing your password). The practical task for a firm is the office scanner or copier that emails PDFs: Google’s options are to switch the device to OAuth, use another way to scan, or create an app password for it.

Step 7: Restrict external Drive sharing

Drive sharing is where client files most often leak, usually through an “anyone with the link” setting. Go to Apps > Google Workspace > Drive and Docs > Sharing settings > Sharing options. Google’s external sharing guide describes these controls:

  • External sharing On or Off: turn it off entirely, or leave it on with limits.
  • Allowlisted domains: limit sharing to trusted domains, such as co-counsel or a key client.
  • Highlight external files: shows users a warning marker on files from outside the firm.
  • Different rules per OU or group: for example, attorneys can share externally but contractors cannot. Group settings override OU settings.
  • Visitor sharing (people without Google accounts) is a separate setting.

Google notes changes can take up to 24 hours to apply. Also consider shared drives for matter files, so documents belong to the firm instead of an individual who might leave.

Step 8: Turn on mobile device management

Phones are where most lawyers read client email, so manage them. Basic mobile management is on by default in every Business edition, according to Google’s basic mobile management page. It works on Android, iPhone and iPad, lets you set password requirements for devices, and lets you wipe a user’s work account from a lost or stolen phone. Find it at Devices > Mobile & endpoints > Settings > Universal > General > Mobile management.

Advanced mobile management (Business Plus) adds device approvals, broader app control on Android and iOS, and full-device wipe. Google’s endpoint feature comparison lists what each level covers.

Step 9: Configure Vault retention and holds (Business Plus)

Google Vault is Google’s tool to retain, hold, search and export Workspace data. Per Google’s Vault overview, retention rules decide how long data is kept, holds preserve a user’s data for a legal matter even if they delete it, and exports stay available for 15 days. Two points trip up firms:

  • Nothing is retained until you create a rule. Set a default retention rule for Gmail and Drive before migrating data.
  • Retention rules can also delete. A rule that expires data after a set period will remove it. Match periods to your file-retention policy and any state bar rules on client files, and check with your state bar if unsure.

On Business Starter or Standard, Vault is not included. Google’s Vault licensing page directs other editions to Google Sales for add-on options, so the practical path for most small firms is upgrading to Business Plus.

Step 10: Set up security alerts

The alert center (Security > Alert center) shows notifications about possible problems, such as suspicious sign-ins or phishing. Google’s alert center page explains you can add email notifications by configuring a rule. Send them to an address someone actually reads, such as your IT provider plus the managing partner.

Step 11: Migrate email from Gmail or Microsoft 365

Google’s data migration service copies email into Workspace from Microsoft Exchange Online, IMAP providers, another Workspace account, or a personal Gmail account. It runs from Data > Data import & export and needs a super admin. Key limits from Google’s documentation:

  • Exchange Online: up to 1,000 users per import; you connect by signing in as a Microsoft 365 Global Administrator, and Google’s Exchange Online guide says it copies rather than deletes the source data. Users must already exist in both systems.
  • IMAP: up to 100 users per import.
  • Personal Gmail: useful for a solo who started on a free account. If you do not set a start date, it imports from January 1, 2000.
  • Stopping does not roll back: items already copied stay.

A sensible order: migrate a pilot user, check message counts, migrate everyone, switch MX records, then run a final pass to catch mail that arrived during the cutover. Keep the old system read-only for a while rather than cancelling it the same day.

Step 12: Decide how you will back up

Google keeps your data available, but recovery from mistakes is limited. Admins can restore Drive files for 25 days after a user empties their trash, according to Google’s Drive recovery page. Vault holds help preserve data but Google says Vault is not an archive. If you need point-in-time restores beyond those windows, or protection if an account is compromised and data is deleted, consider a third-party Workspace backup service and vet it like any vendor that touches client data.

Google Workspace security settings checklist for law firms

Use this table as a one-page audit after setup and once a year after that. Menu paths are from Google’s Admin Help pages linked above and can be renamed over time.

What do legal ethics rules say about cloud email and files?

The ABA’s Formal Opinion 477R, “Securing Communication of Protected Client Information” (2017), interprets Model Rule 1.6(c) as requiring reasonable efforts to prevent unauthorized access to client information, judged case by case. A U.S. Court of International Trade article on the opinion notes that unencrypted email remains acceptable for routine, low-sensitivity matters, while more sensitive messages warrant more security. Summaries of the opinion, such as LawPay’s, list steps including understanding how client information is transmitted and stored, using reasonable electronic security measures, training lawyers and staff, and doing due diligence on technology vendors.

The settings above map onto those steps: 2SV and password rules are security measures, sharing limits control where data goes, and Vault and backups address storage. ABA opinions are guidance, not binding rules in every state, so check your own state bar’s ethics opinions on cloud computing. For your website side, see our law firm website security checklist.

FAQ

Is Google Workspace secure enough for lawyers?

It can be, if it is configured well. The platform provides 2-Step Verification, sharing controls, mobile management and (in Business Plus) Vault, but most of those protections depend on admin settings. Ethics guidance such as ABA Formal Opinion 477R focuses on whether your efforts are reasonable, so document what you set up.

Does Google Workspace Business Standard include Vault?

No. Google’s Business edition comparison shows Vault only in Business Plus among the Business editions. Enterprise editions also include it.

Can a lawyer use a free Gmail account for client work?

It is generally a poor fit. A free account has no Admin console, so you cannot enforce 2SV across staff, control sharing, wipe a lost phone’s work data, or apply retention rules, and your address will not use your firm’s domain. If you started on Gmail, the data migration service can copy that mail into Workspace.

Is Google Vault a backup?

No. Google states Vault “isn’t a data archive.” It preserves data under retention rules and holds and lets you search and export it, but it does not give you point-in-time restores of a whole account. Use a separate backup service if you need that.

Can I move my firm from Microsoft 365 to Google Workspace?

Yes. Google’s data migration service copies email, and optionally calendar and contacts, from Exchange Online for up to 1,000 users per import. You need Microsoft 365 Global Administrator access and matching user accounts in Workspace first.

How long does Google Workspace setup take for a small firm?

It varies with the number of users and the amount of data to migrate. Domain verification is usually quick (Google says up to an hour once the record is in place), and the security settings take an afternoon if you know where they are. Migration of large mailboxes is usually the longest part.

Next steps

Pick your edition, verify the domain, and finish the security baseline (2SV, passwords, sharing, mobile, alerts) before anyone starts sending client email. If you chose Business Plus, create Vault retention rules next, then migrate. Finally, complete your DNS records with the law firm email setup guide and revisit the checklist table once a year.

title.rendered: Best Domain Registrars for Law Firms (2026)

content.raw:
Quick answer: For most small law firms, the best domain registrar is Cloudflare Registrar if your DNS will live at Cloudflare, or Porkbun if you want flat, low pricing with no strings attached. Both sell a .com for roughly $11–$12 a year with the same price at renewal, include free WHOIS privacy, and support security-key two-factor login. Whichever you pick, the account must be in the firm's name, with auto-renew and registrar lock switched on.

Key takeaways

  • Renewal price matters more than the first-year price. You will renew the firm's domain for decades, so a $0.01 promo followed by a $19.99 renewal costs more than a flat $11.81.
  • Cloudflare and Porkbun price .com at or near cost, with renewal equal to registration. Hostinger and others lead with promos that renew higher.
  • .law is not sold everywhere. Porkbun, Hostinger, Namecheap and GoDaddy offer it; it did not appear on Cloudflare's published TLD list when we checked.
  • The firm, not the web developer, should own the registrar account. Give vendors delegated access or DNS records, never the domain itself.
  • Turn on auto-renew, registrar lock and app- or key-based 2FA the day you register.
Quick pick

Registering a domain? Search your firm’s domain on Namecheap →

We may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. It never changes our recommendations.

How we compared these registrars

We have not run hands-on tests of these registrars, and there are no scores in this article. The comparison is based on each vendor's official pricing pages, help documentation and terms, opened in November 2026. Where a vendor's site blocked automated access and we could not confirm a figure, we say so instead of guessing. Domain prices change often (and the wholesale .com price itself rose from $10.26 to $10.97 on November 1, 2026), so confirm the price at checkout.

Two terms come up repeatedly. A registrar is the company you pay to hold your domain on record. A registrar lock (also called transfer lock) is a setting that blocks the domain from being moved to another registrar until you switch it off.

Best domain registrars for law firms at a glance

Prices below are US dollars for a one-year, non-premium registration, as of November 2026.

Which domain registrar is best for each type of law firm?

Cloudflare Registrar: best if your DNS is (or will be) on Cloudflare

Cloudflare is the cheapest place to keep a .com long term because it does not mark up prices. Its Registrar page says registration, transfer and renewal prices are "always at or below what registries and ICANN charge us." With the new $10.97 wholesale .com fee plus the $0.20 ICANN fee, that works out to roughly $11.17 a year, though Cloudflare shows the exact figure in its dashboard. Domains are locked by default, WHOIS redaction is free and DNSSEC is one click.

The catch is important. Cloudflare's Registrar FAQ states that "all domains on Cloudflare Registrar use Cloudflare nameservers." If your developer or host needs different nameservers, you would have to move the domain elsewhere. You also cannot buy a domain here and park it with outside DNS. And when we checked Cloudflare's TLD policies list, .attorney and .lawyer were listed but .law was not.

  • Pros: at-cost pricing with no renewal jump; lock on by default; security-key 2FA and the option to require 2FA for every account member.
  • Cons: you must use Cloudflare DNS; no .law on its published list; non-refundable registrations.

If you are weighing Cloudflare's wider services (CDN, firewall), see our guide to using Cloudflare for a law firm website.

Porkbun: best overall for flat pricing and .law

Porkbun's domain price list shows .com at $11.81 for registration, renewal and transfer, with no first-year teaser. It also lists .law at $82.90, .attorney at $49.95 and .lawyer at $56.13, each the same price at renewal. Its .com page lists free WHOIS privacy, free Let's Encrypt SSL, DNS powered by Cloudflare, email forwarding and URL forwarding.

Unlike Cloudflare, Porkbun lets you point nameservers anywhere. For security, it supports app-based 2FA and physical security keys (WebAuthn), plus passkeys.

  • Pros: same price every year; sells .law with no renewal jump; free privacy and SSL; use any DNS host.
  • Cons: a few cents above Cloudflare for .com; no hosting or email bundle (which can also be a plus).

Namecheap: a solid, familiar alternative

On Namecheap's own pricing page (checked November 18, 2026), a .com costs $12.08 for the first year on sale (regular $15.98) and renews at $19.98 a year, plus ICANN's $0.20 fee. Legal extensions cost more than at Porkbun: .law is $105.98, .attorney $65.98 and .lawyer $74.48 a year. Namecheap runs frequent promotions, so check the cart total and the renewal price before paying. Its help center does confirm the essentials. A free Domain Privacy subscription is added to every registration, renewal and transfer for eligible extensions and is on by default. 2FA comes as an authenticator app or U2F security key, one method at a time. You can set or release registrar lock under Sharing & Transfer. Namecheap also sells .law under the registry's eligibility rules.

  • Pros: free privacy on by default; security-key 2FA; wide extension choice including .law.
  • Cons: .com renews at $19.98, well above Porkbun or Cloudflare; .law, .attorney and .lawyer cost more than at Porkbun; expect add-on offers at checkout, so read the cart before paying.

Choosing Namecheap? Search for your firm's domain at Namecheap (affiliate link: we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you). Our step-by-step Namecheap registration guide shows which checkout extras to skip and how to lock down the account.

Squarespace Domains: best if your website is on Squarespace

Squarespace took over the former Google Domains customers. Its domain page advertises domains "for only $10" and says WHOIS privacy, SSL, DNSSEC, email forwarding and two-factor authentication are included. It also keeps a domain activity log showing changes by "domain owners and managers," which is useful when a vendor has access. The page did not list an exact .com renewal price or .law availability, so confirm both at checkout.

  • Pros: all-in pricing with privacy and security included; activity log; easy if the site is on Squarespace.
  • Cons: renewal price and .law support not published on the pages we opened.

Hostinger: fine if you host there, but watch the renewal

Hostinger's domain search page showed a .com at $0.01 for the first year, but only "when you choose a 3-year term," with renewal at $19.99 a year and transfers at $9.99. Its .law page lists $80.99 for the first year, then $113.39 a year at renewal. Privacy protection is free "for supported extensions," and account 2FA uses an authenticator app or email codes.

  • Pros: one dashboard for hosting and domain; low promo price.
  • Cons: renewals are much higher than Cloudflare or Porkbun; .law renews about $30 more per year than at Porkbun; no security-key 2FA listed.

For the hosting side, see our best hosting for law firm websites comparison.

GoDaddy: workable, but the upsells add up

GoDaddy's pricing pages blocked our automated requests, so we cannot quote its current .com price. Confirm it, and especially the renewal price, before buying. Its help center confirms that you can lock or unlock a domain from Domain Settings and that two-step verification works by SMS or authenticator app. GoDaddy also sells a separate Domain Protection feature that adds identity checks. Before you can transfer away, you must turn off Domain Privacy and set Domain Protection to none. Its help page also notes that domains bought in a bundle are locked for 120 days after registration. GoDaddy sells .law to eligible legal professionals.

  • Pros: large company, phone support, offers .law.
  • Cons: pricing not verified here; paid protection tiers and add-ons; extra steps and a 120-day lock on bundled domains.

Can a law firm register a .law domain anywhere?

No. Only certain registrars sell .law, and the registry checks eligibility after purchase. Per GoDaddy's .law help page and Namecheap's requirements page, eligible registrants are licensed lawyers, law firms, courts, law schools and legal regulators. Inactive or non-practicing lawyers do not qualify. A domain that fails verification can be suspended or deleted without a refund, so register it in the exact legal name of the lawyer or firm.

Whether .law is worth it compared with a .com is a separate question. We cover that in .law vs .com vs .attorney domains for law firms.

Who should own a law firm's domain account?

The firm should. The domain is the address for your website and, more importantly, your email. Whoever controls the registrar account controls both. Under ICANN's Transfer Policy, the authorization code needed to move a domain goes to the "Registered Name Holder." If that holder is a former developer, a marketing agency or a departed associate, getting your domain back can take weeks, and in the meantime you have no access.

  • Registrant name: the firm's legal entity name, not the developer's company or a personal name.
  • Account email: a role address on the firm's own domain (for example, admin@yourfirm.com) that more than one person can reach, ideally on properly configured firm email.
  • Payment card: a firm card, with a backup card on file so auto-renew does not fail.
  • Vendor access: invite developers as members with limited roles where the registrar supports it (Cloudflare and Squarespace both document multi-user access), or just give them the DNS records they need to add.
  • Recovery: store the login, 2FA backup codes and security key details in the firm's password manager, not in one person's phone.

What security settings should a law firm turn on at its registrar?

Turn on four settings the day you register: auto-renew, registrar lock, strong 2FA and WHOIS privacy. Together they stop the two most common ways firms lose a domain: an expired card, and an account takeover followed by a transfer.

  1. Auto-renew on, with a backup card. Cloudflare, for example, attempts auto-renew about 30 days before expiry and retries if it fails. Consider registering for several years.
  2. Registrar lock on. Leave it on except during a planned transfer.
  3. 2FA with an authenticator app or security key. Avoid SMS where you can. Cloudflare, Porkbun and Namecheap all support hardware keys.
  4. WHOIS privacy on. It keeps personal phone numbers and addresses out of public lookups. It is free at every registrar in this list for eligible extensions.
  5. DNSSEC on, where your DNS host supports it. It helps prevent forged DNS answers. Turn it off before a transfer and back on afterward.

These settings are one part of a broader routine. Our law firm website security checklist covers the rest.

How do you register a domain for a law firm?

  1. Pick the name and extension. Check your state bar's rules on firm names and trade names before you commit.
  2. Create the registrar account in the firm's name, using a shared role email and a firm card.
  3. Turn on 2FA (app or security key) before buying anything, and save the backup codes in the firm password manager.
  4. Search and add the domain to the cart. Remove add-ons you do not need. Hosting, email and "protection" bundles are separate decisions.
  5. Enter the firm's legal name as registrant. For .law, this must match the name the registry can verify.
  6. Check out, then confirm the settings: auto-renew on, lock on, privacy on.
  7. Verify the registrant email. Registrars send a contact verification email. Squarespace, for instance, suspends domains that are not verified within 15 days.
  8. Point DNS to your website host and email provider, or send the records to your developer to add.

How do you transfer a law firm domain to a better registrar?

A transfer moves the domain's registration without touching your website, as long as DNS records are copied first. Most transfers add one year to the registration, and the transfer fee covers it.

  1. Check eligibility. ICANN lets registrars refuse transfers within 60 days of registration, a prior transfer or a registrant change.
  2. Export every DNS record (website, MX, SPF, DKIM, DMARC, verification TXT records) and recreate them at the new DNS host. Missing email records is the most common way a transfer breaks firm email.
  3. Unlock the domain and disable privacy or protection add-ons at the current registrar if they block transfers, as GoDaddy requires.
  4. Turn off DNSSEC if you are also changing DNS hosts. Cloudflare asks you to wait at least 24 hours before changing nameservers.
  5. Get the authorization (EPP) code and start the transfer at the new registrar. For Cloudflare, the domain must first be active on Cloudflare DNS.
  6. Approve the transfer email. Transfers can take up to 5–10 days depending on the losing registrar.
  7. Re-enable lock, auto-renew, 2FA and DNSSEC at the new registrar.

If you are moving hosting at the same time, follow our guide to moving a law firm website to a new host without downtime and change one thing at a time.

FAQ

What is the cheapest domain registrar for a .com?

Over several years, Cloudflare Registrar is usually the cheapest because it charges the registry and ICANN cost with no markup. Porkbun is close at $11.81 a year (as of November 2026). Promo prices like Hostinger's $0.01 first year can look cheaper, but its $19.99 renewal makes it more expensive after year one.

Cloudflare Registrar vs Namecheap vs Porkbun: which should a law firm choose?

Choose Cloudflare if you want the lowest long-term .com cost and will run DNS on Cloudflare. Choose Porkbun if you want flat pricing, freedom to use any DNS host, or a .law domain. Namecheap is a reasonable alternative with free privacy and security-key 2FA, but confirm its renewal price first.

Should my web developer register the domain for us?

No. The developer can do the setup, but the domain should be registered in the firm's name, in an account the firm controls. Give the developer delegated access or the DNS records to add.

Is it better to buy the domain from my web host?

Usually not. Keeping the domain at a separate registrar means you can change hosts without touching your domain or email. Bundled domains also tend to renew at higher prices, and some carry longer transfer locks.

What happens if the firm's domain expires?

Your website and email stop working once the registrar suspends the domain. After the grace and redemption periods, someone else can register it. Auto-renew, a backup card and a multi-year registration prevent this.

Do I need WHOIS privacy if the firm's address is public anyway?

It is still worth turning on. It is free at every registrar here, it cuts spam to the registrant email, and it keeps a personal phone number or home address out of public lookups if one was ever used.

Conclusion: pick a registrar, then lock it down

For most small firms, the short list is Cloudflare Registrar (lowest long-term .com cost, Cloudflare DNS required) or Porkbun (flat pricing, any DNS, .law available). Next steps:

  • Check who your domain is registered to today with a WHOIS lookup, and fix the owner if it is not the firm.
  • Turn on auto-renew, registrar lock, 2FA and privacy.
  • If you are paying high renewals, plan a transfer outside your busy season.
  • Confirm your email authentication records survive any DNS change.

Porkbun: best overall for flat pricing and .law

Porkbun’s domain price list shows .com at $11.81 for registration, renewal and transfer, with no first-year teaser. It also lists .law at $82.90, .attorney at $49.95 and .lawyer at $56.13, each the same price at renewal. Its .com page lists free WHOIS privacy, free Let’s Encrypt SSL, DNS powered by Cloudflare, email forwarding and URL forwarding.

Unlike Cloudflare, Porkbun lets you point nameservers anywhere. For security, it supports app-based 2FA and physical security keys (WebAuthn), plus passkeys.

  • Pros: same price every year; sells .law with no renewal jump; free privacy and SSL; use any DNS host.
  • Cons: a few cents above Cloudflare for .com; no hosting or email bundle (which can also be a plus).

Namecheap: a solid, familiar alternative

On Namecheap‘s own pricing page (checked November 18, 2026), a .com costs $12.08 for the first year on sale (regular $15.98) and renews at $19.98 a year, plus ICANN’s $0.20 fee. Legal extensions cost more than at Porkbun: .law is $105.98, .attorney $65.98 and .lawyer $74.48 a year. Namecheap runs frequent promotions, so check the cart total and the renewal price before paying. Its help center does confirm the essentials. A free Domain Privacy subscription is added to every registration, renewal and transfer for eligible extensions and is on by default. 2FA comes as an authenticator app or U2F security key, one method at a time. You can set or release registrar lock under Sharing & Transfer. Namecheap also sells .law under the registry’s eligibility rules.

  • Pros: free privacy on by default; security-key 2FA; wide extension choice including .law.
  • Cons: .com renews at $19.98, well above Porkbun or Cloudflare; .law, .attorney and .lawyer cost more than at Porkbun; expect add-on offers at checkout, so read the cart before paying.

Choosing Namecheap? Search for your firm’s domain at Namecheap (affiliate link: we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you). Our step-by-step Namecheap registration guide shows which checkout extras to skip and how to lock down the account.

Squarespace Domains: best if your website is on Squarespace

Squarespace took over the former Google Domains customers. Its domain page advertises domains “for only $10” and says WHOIS privacy, SSL, DNSSEC, email forwarding and two-factor authentication are included. It also keeps a domain activity log showing changes by “domain owners and managers,” which is useful when a vendor has access. The page did not list an exact .com renewal price or .law availability, so confirm both at checkout.

  • Pros: all-in pricing with privacy and security included; activity log; easy if the site is on Squarespace.
  • Cons: renewal price and .law support not published on the pages we opened.

Hostinger: fine if you host there, but watch the renewal

Hostinger’s domain search page showed a .com at $0.01 for the first year, but only “when you choose a 3-year term,” with renewal at $19.99 a year and transfers at $9.99. Its .law page lists $80.99 for the first year, then $113.39 a year at renewal. Privacy protection is free “for supported extensions,” and account 2FA uses an authenticator app or email codes.

  • Pros: one dashboard for hosting and domain; low promo price.
  • Cons: renewals are much higher than Cloudflare or Porkbun; .law renews about $30 more per year than at Porkbun; no security-key 2FA listed.

For the hosting side, see our best hosting for law firm websites comparison.

GoDaddy: workable, but the upsells add up

GoDaddy’s pricing pages blocked our automated requests, so we cannot quote its current .com price. Confirm it, and especially the renewal price, before buying. Its help center confirms that you can lock or unlock a domain from Domain Settings and that two-step verification works by SMS or authenticator app. GoDaddy also sells a separate Domain Protection feature that adds identity checks. Before you can transfer away, you must turn off Domain Privacy and set Domain Protection to none. Its help page also notes that domains bought in a bundle are locked for 120 days after registration. GoDaddy sells .law to eligible legal professionals.

  • Pros: large company, phone support, offers .law.
  • Cons: pricing not verified here; paid protection tiers and add-ons; extra steps and a 120-day lock on bundled domains.

Can a law firm register a .law domain anywhere?

No. Only certain registrars sell .law, and the registry checks eligibility after purchase. Per GoDaddy’s .law help page and Namecheap’s requirements page, eligible registrants are licensed lawyers, law firms, courts, law schools and legal regulators. Inactive or non-practicing lawyers do not qualify. A domain that fails verification can be suspended or deleted without a refund, so register it in the exact legal name of the lawyer or firm.

Whether .law is worth it compared with a .com is a separate question. We cover that in .law vs .com vs .attorney domains for law firms.

Who should own a law firm’s domain account?

The firm should. The domain is the address for your website and, more importantly, your email. Whoever controls the registrar account controls both. Under ICANN’s Transfer Policy, the authorization code needed to move a domain goes to the “Registered Name Holder.” If that holder is a former developer, a marketing agency or a departed associate, getting your domain back can take weeks, and in the meantime you have no access.

  • Registrant name: the firm’s legal entity name, not the developer’s company or a personal name.
  • Account email: a role address on the firm’s own domain (for example, admin@yourfirm.com) that more than one person can reach, ideally on properly configured firm email.
  • Payment card: a firm card, with a backup card on file so auto-renew does not fail.
  • Vendor access: invite developers as members with limited roles where the registrar supports it (Cloudflare and Squarespace both document multi-user access), or just give them the DNS records they need to add.
  • Recovery: store the login, 2FA backup codes and security key details in the firm’s password manager, not in one person’s phone.

What security settings should a law firm turn on at its registrar?

Turn on four settings the day you register: auto-renew, registrar lock, strong 2FA and WHOIS privacy. Together they stop the two most common ways firms lose a domain: an expired card, and an account takeover followed by a transfer.

  1. Auto-renew on, with a backup card. Cloudflare, for example, attempts auto-renew about 30 days before expiry and retries if it fails. Consider registering for several years.
  2. Registrar lock on. Leave it on except during a planned transfer.
  3. 2FA with an authenticator app or security key. Avoid SMS where you can. Cloudflare, Porkbun and Namecheap all support hardware keys.
  4. WHOIS privacy on. It keeps personal phone numbers and addresses out of public lookups. It is free at every registrar in this list for eligible extensions.
  5. DNSSEC on, where your DNS host supports it. It helps prevent forged DNS answers. Turn it off before a transfer and back on afterward.

These settings are one part of a broader routine. Our law firm website security checklist covers the rest.

How do you register a domain for a law firm?

  1. Pick the name and extension. Check your state bar’s rules on firm names and trade names before you commit.
  2. Create the registrar account in the firm’s name, using a shared role email and a firm card.
  3. Turn on 2FA (app or security key) before buying anything, and save the backup codes in the firm password manager.
  4. Search and add the domain to the cart. Remove add-ons you do not need. Hosting, email and “protection” bundles are separate decisions.
  5. Enter the firm’s legal name as registrant. For .law, this must match the name the registry can verify.
  6. Check out, then confirm the settings: auto-renew on, lock on, privacy on.
  7. Verify the registrant email. Registrars send a contact verification email. Squarespace, for instance, suspends domains that are not verified within 15 days.
  8. Point DNS to your website host and email provider, or send the records to your developer to add.

How do you transfer a law firm domain to a better registrar?

A transfer moves the domain’s registration without touching your website, as long as DNS records are copied first. Most transfers add one year to the registration, and the transfer fee covers it.

  1. Check eligibility. ICANN lets registrars refuse transfers within 60 days of registration, a prior transfer or a registrant change.
  2. Export every DNS record (website, MX, SPF, DKIM, DMARC, verification TXT records) and recreate them at the new DNS host. Missing email records is the most common way a transfer breaks firm email.
  3. Unlock the domain and disable privacy or protection add-ons at the current registrar if they block transfers, as GoDaddy requires.
  4. Turn off DNSSEC if you are also changing DNS hosts. Cloudflare asks you to wait at least 24 hours before changing nameservers.
  5. Get the authorization (EPP) code and start the transfer at the new registrar. For Cloudflare, the domain must first be active on Cloudflare DNS.
  6. Approve the transfer email. Transfers can take up to 5–10 days depending on the losing registrar.
  7. Re-enable lock, auto-renew, 2FA and DNSSEC at the new registrar.

If you are moving hosting at the same time, follow our guide to moving a law firm website to a new host without downtime and change one thing at a time.

FAQ

What is the cheapest domain registrar for a .com?

Over several years, Cloudflare Registrar is usually the cheapest because it charges the registry and ICANN cost with no markup. Porkbun is close at $11.81 a year (as of November 2026). Promo prices like Hostinger’s $0.01 first year can look cheaper, but its $19.99 renewal makes it more expensive after year one.

Cloudflare Registrar vs Namecheap vs Porkbun: which should a law firm choose?

Choose Cloudflare if you want the lowest long-term .com cost and will run DNS on Cloudflare. Choose Porkbun if you want flat pricing, freedom to use any DNS host, or a .law domain. Namecheap is a reasonable alternative with free privacy and security-key 2FA, but confirm its renewal price first.

Should my web developer register the domain for us?

No. The developer can do the setup, but the domain should be registered in the firm’s name, in an account the firm controls. Give the developer delegated access or the DNS records to add.

Is it better to buy the domain from my web host?

Usually not. Keeping the domain at a separate registrar means you can change hosts without touching your domain or email. Bundled domains also tend to renew at higher prices, and some carry longer transfer locks.

What happens if the firm’s domain expires?

Your website and email stop working once the registrar suspends the domain. After the grace and redemption periods, someone else can register it. Auto-renew, a backup card and a multi-year registration prevent this.

Do I need WHOIS privacy if the firm’s address is public anyway?

It is still worth turning on. It is free at every registrar here, it cuts spam to the registrant email, and it keeps a personal phone number or home address out of public lookups if one was ever used.

Conclusion: pick a registrar, then lock it down

For most small firms, the short list is Cloudflare Registrar (lowest long-term .com cost, Cloudflare DNS required) or Porkbun (flat pricing, any DNS, .law available). Next steps:

  • Check who your domain is registered to today with a WHOIS lookup, and fix the owner if it is not the firm.
  • Turn on auto-renew, registrar lock, 2FA and privacy.
  • If you are paying high renewals, plan a transfer outside your busy season.
  • Confirm your email authentication records survive any DNS change.
