title.raw: Best WordPress Plugins for Law Firms (2026): The Essential Stack
title.rendered: Best WordPress Plugins for Law Firms (2026): The Essential Stack

content.raw:
This guide contains affiliate links. If you buy through them, we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. It never changes our recommendations. Learn more.

Quick answer: Most law firm websites need only one plugin for each of eight jobs: forms, SEO, security, backups, email delivery (SMTP), spam protection, consent (only if you track visitors) and, sometimes, scheduling. A strong default stack is WPForms or Gravity Forms, Rank Math or Yoast SEO, Wordfence, UpdraftPlus, WP Mail SMTP or FluentSMTP and Cloudflare Turnstile. Add caching only if your host doesn't already provide it. Fewer plugins that are well maintained beat a long list every time.

Key takeaways

  • Pick plugins by job, not by popularity. One tool per job. Two SEO plugins or two caching plugins cause conflicts.
  • Every plugin is code you have to keep updated. Check the "Last updated" date, the active installs and the "Tested up to" version on WordPress.org before you install anything.
  • Check your host before you buy a caching or backup plugin. Managed WordPress hosts often include both.
  • Don't use accessibility overlay widgets as a shortcut. In 2025 the FTC fined one overlay vendor $1 million over claims that its tool made sites WCAG compliant.
  • Install in a set order: backups first, then security, then email delivery, then everything else. Test after each step.

How we compared these plugins

This roundup is based on official documentation, WordPress.org plugin listings and vendor pricing pages, all checked in November 2026. We have not run hands-on benchmarks, and we don't give scores. For each plugin we looked at four things: what the free version actually covers, the published price of the paid tier, how many sites use it (as shown on WordPress.org) and how recently it was updated. Prices change often and many vendors show first-year discounts, so always confirm the renewal price before you buy.

Why fewer plugins is the better strategy

A plugin is an add-on that gives WordPress a feature it doesn't have out of the box. Each one is third-party code running on the site that holds your firm's name and your clients' first messages. Every plugin you add is another thing to update, another possible conflict and another place a vulnerability could show up.

So the goal isn't the "best" plugin in every category. It's the smallest set that covers the jobs your site really has. Before you install anything, run this quick check:

  • Last updated: within the past few months. A plugin that hasn't been touched in a year or more is a warning sign. Several law-specific plugins listed in plugin directories have been flagged as possibly abandoned.
  • Tested up to: the current major WordPress release (7.1.x as of November 2026).
  • Active installs: a large user base doesn't make a plugin safe, but it does mean problems get reported and fixed faster.
  • Overlap: does your theme, host or an existing plugin already do this job?
  • Exit plan: can you remove it later without breaking pages? This matters most with shortcodes and page builders.

The essential law firm plugin stack at a glance

Active installs and update dates below are as shown on WordPress.org on November 8, 2026. Paid prices are list or renewal prices from each vendor's pricing page as of November 2026 (first-year promotions are noted in the sections below).

Which form plugin is best for a law firm?

For most small firms, WPForms is the easiest choice and Gravity Forms is the most flexible. Fluent Forms is the value pick. All three can build a consultation request form with conditional fields, such as asking different questions for family law and personal injury inquiries. How you handle confidential details in those forms is a bigger question than which plugin you choose, so read our guide to setting up a secure contact form for a law firm website before you go live.

WPForms

The WPForms pricing page lists Basic (1 site) at $49.50 for the first year, renewing at $99/yr. Plus (3 sites) renews at $199/yr, Pro (5 sites) at $399/yr and Elite (unlimited sites) at $599/yr. Renewals are at full price, and there's a 14-day money-back guarantee. The free WPForms Lite works fine for a simple contact form. Best for: non-technical firms that want a drag-and-drop builder.

Gravity Forms

Gravity Forms has no free version or trial. Basic costs $59/yr for 1 site, Pro $159/yr for 3 sites and Elite $259/yr for unlimited sites. Elite adds add-ons such as Signature, Partial Entries and Webhooks. Best for: firms with a developer who need complex intake logic or CRM integrations.

Fluent Forms

The Fluent Forms Pro single-site license lists at $79/yr, with a lifetime option. At the time of writing a discounted first year was shown. Pro includes conditional logic, multi-step and conversational forms, and conditional email routing on every plan. Best for: budget-conscious firms that still want advanced features.

Rank Math or Yoast: which SEO plugin should lawyers use?

Either is fine. Pick one and never run both. The free versions of both handle the basics: title tags, meta descriptions, XML sitemaps and basic schema markup (code that helps search engines understand your pages).

  • Rank Math: The Rank Math pricing page lists PRO (unlimited personal sites) at $8.99/month billed annually, with a lower first-year promotion at the time of writing. The free version already includes more schema options than most firms need.
  • Yoast SEO: Yoast SEO Premium costs $118.80/yr per site. The page says Premium includes redirect management, internal linking suggestions and the Local SEO, Video and News add-ons.

Our take: if a developer already set one up, keep it. Switching gains you little. A free version plus well-written practice area pages will do more for your rankings than any premium SEO feature.

What security plugin does a law firm website need?

You need one security plugin, plus a host that does its own server-level protection. The plugin's job is login protection (two-factor authentication), a firewall and malware scanning. For the full hardening list (user roles, updates, file permissions), use our law firm website security checklist. We won't repeat it here.

Wordfence

The free Wordfence plugin includes a web application firewall, a malware scanner, two-factor authentication and passkeys. Its listing notes that firewall rules and malware signatures reach free users 30 days later than Premium users. Premium adds real-time updates, an IP blocklist, country blocking and paid support. Premium is billed per site per year. A price change was reported for December 2026, so confirm the current price on Wordfence\'s site before you buy.

Kadence Security (formerly Solid Security / iThemes Security)

The same plugin has carried three names. Its WordPress.org listing shows the free version includes two-factor authentication, brute-force protection, file change detection and scheduled scans. Pro adds passwordless logins, trusted devices and Patchstack virtual patching. We couldn't find a published Pro price after the rebrand, so confirm it with the vendor. Best for: firms that want a lighter plugin focused on logins and hardening.

Sucuri

Sucuri's main product is a cloud firewall that filters traffic before it reaches your server. The free plugin is mostly an auditing and scanning tool. On Sucuri's pricing page, the Basic Firewall costs $9.99/month, and the Basic Platform (firewall plus unlimited malware cleanups) costs $229/yr per site. If you already use Cloudflare's firewall, you may not need it. Check what your existing firewall already covers before adding another.

Do you need a backup plugin if your host backs up your site?

Usually yes, for a second copy stored somewhere else. Host backups are often kept on the host's own infrastructure, and you can't count on them if the account itself has a problem. An off-site copy in Google Drive, Dropbox or Amazon S3 is cheap insurance.

  • UpdraftPlus: The free version handles scheduled backups to remote storage. UpdraftPlus Premium starts at $70/yr for up to 2 sites. It adds incremental backups, automatic backups before updates, one-click migration and database encryption.
  • Duplicator: Best known for migrations, with 1+ million active installs on WordPress.org. It's useful when you move to a new host.

Whichever you pick, test a restore on a staging site at least once. A backup you have never restored is a guess.

Why your law firm site needs an SMTP plugin

SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) is the standard way email is sent between servers. By default, WordPress sends form notifications through your web server, and those messages often land in spam or never arrive. An SMTP plugin sends them through a real email service instead, such as Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Amazon SES or Brevo. For a law firm, a lost consultation request means a lost client.

  • FluentSMTP: The FluentSMTP site says it is "free and will always be free." That includes email logs, multiple connections and a fallback connection if your main service fails. This is the best value in the whole stack.
  • WP Mail SMTP: The free version covers the connection. WP Mail SMTP Pro (1 site) costs $49 for the first year and renews at $99/yr. It adds email logs, failure alerts and backup connections.

SMTP only works well if your domain's SPF, DKIM and DMARC records are correct. Our law firm email setup guide covers that.

Do you need a caching plugin?

Only if your host doesn't already cache pages. Caching means saving a ready-made copy of each page so the server doesn't rebuild it for every visitor. Many managed WordPress hosts do this at the server level, and adding a second caching layer can cause stale pages or broken forms. Check your host's documentation first. Our best hosting for law firm websites comparison notes which hosts include it.

  • Host caching: If it's included, use it and skip the plugin.
  • LiteSpeed Cache: Free, and the right choice if your host runs a LiteSpeed web server. It has 7+ million active installs on WordPress.org.
  • WP Rocket: A paid plugin for Apache or NGINX hosts without built-in caching. The WP Rocket pricing page lists the Single plan (1 site) at $5/month billed yearly, discounted during a promotion at the time of writing. There's no free version, only a 14-day trial.

How to stop contact form spam without annoying clients

Use Cloudflare Turnstile, a CAPTCHA replacement that usually doesn't ask visitors to solve a puzzle. Cloudflare's Turnstile documentation says it can be embedded on any website without routing traffic through Cloudflare. The free plan includes unlimited challenges. Check your form plugin's spam settings for a built-in Turnstile option first. If there isn't one, the free Simple CAPTCHA with Cloudflare Turnstile plugin adds it.

Akismet is a popular alternative, but read the terms. The Akismet pricing page limits the pay-what-you-can plan to personal sites. Commercial sites, which includes a law firm, need Pro from $9.95/month billed yearly.

What's the best scheduling option for consultations?

Often it's no plugin at all. If you already use a scheduling service such as Calendly, or the booking tool in your practice management software, embed its widget on a page. That adds no plugin to update. Choose a WordPress booking plugin only if you want bookings stored on your own site.

  • Simply Schedule Appointments: The free Basic tier includes Google Calendar sync. Paid plans start with Plus at $99 for the first year ($129/yr renewal), which adds Zoom and Google Meet. SMS reminders and Stripe/PayPal payments come with Professional ($249/yr renewal).
  • Amelia: A more feature-heavy booking system with two-way Google Calendar and Outlook sync, Zoom and payments. The free version has 90,000+ active installs on WordPress.org. Its pricing page showed promotional prices we couldn't read reliably, so confirm current pricing with the vendor.

Keep booking forms short. Ask for name, contact details and matter type, not the facts of the case. Those can wait until you've run a conflict check.

Do law firm websites need a cookie consent plugin?

Only if the site uses cookies or scripts that track visitors, such as Google Analytics, ad pixels or embedded videos. Several US states now have privacy laws with opt-out rights, and the rules differ by state. Check with a privacy professional if you're unsure which apply to you. If you do need a banner:

  • Complianz: The free plugin includes a cookie scan, script blocking and a cookie policy generator. Detailed US state law support, Google Consent Mode and records of consent are listed as premium features. Premium Personal costs $59/yr for 1 site.
  • CookieYes: The free plan covers up to 5,000 pageviews a month and includes a US State Laws (opt-out) template and Google Consent Mode v2. Basic costs $100/yr per domain.

Should you use an accessibility overlay plugin?

No, not as a substitute for real accessibility work. An overlay is a widget that adds a toolbar to your site and promises automatic fixes. In January 2025 the Federal Trade Commission announced a $1 million order against accessiBe. The FTC alleged that the company's claims that its AI tool could make any website compliant with the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) were false, misleading or unsubstantiated.

Accessibility comes from the theme, the content and how forms are built: real headings, alt text, color contrast, labeled form fields and keyboard navigation. Plugins can help you find problems, but they don't fix them for you. Our guide to law firm website accessibility and WCAG explains what to check.

Plugins most small firms can skip

  • A second plugin for the same job: two SEO plugins, two caching plugins or two security plugins.
  • Social auto-posters and share-count widgets: they add scripts and rarely bring clients.
  • Old "lawyer directory" or "case manager" plugins: check the update date. Your practice management software should hold client data, not your website.
  • Separate plugins for every tiny feature (a "scroll to top" button, a custom login logo). A developer can add these with a few lines of code.
  • Accessibility overlays, for the reasons above.

Our recommended minimal stack

Here are two versions. Both assume a good host that handles server-side caching and daily backups.

That comes to six to eight plugins in total, not counting your theme. Your monthly website maintenance routine should include updating each one and checking that forms still deliver.

In what order should you set up plugins?

Set up protection first and features second, so that if something breaks you can roll back. Ideally do this on a staging copy of the site.

  1. Back up the site. Install UpdraftPlus (or confirm your host's backups), connect cloud storage and run a first full backup.
  2. Lock down logins. Install one security plugin, turn on two-factor authentication for every admin and run a first scan.
  3. Fix email delivery. Install an SMTP plugin, connect it to your email provider and send a test email to an outside address.
  4. Build or connect forms. Set up the consultation form, add Turnstile and send a test submission. Confirm that it arrives.
  5. Configure SEO. Run the setup wizard, submit the sitemap in Google Search Console and add your firm's details for local schema.
  6. Check performance. Turn on host caching (or one caching plugin). Exclude form and booking pages if the plugin recommends it, then retest the forms.
  7. Add optional plugins. Add scheduling and, if you use tracking scripts, the consent banner. Test the banner in a private browser window.
  8. Remove leftovers. Delete inactive plugins and themes. Deactivated code still sits on the server.

FAQ

How many plugins should a law firm website have?

There's no magic number. A typical small-firm site can cover every essential job with six to eight well-maintained plugins. Quality and update history matter more than the count.

Are free WordPress plugins safe for lawyers to use?

Free plugins from established vendors with recent updates and large user bases are widely used. Paid tiers mostly add support and extra features, not basic safety. What matters most is keeping every plugin updated and removing the ones you don't use.

Are there WordPress plugins made specifically for law firms?

A few exist, such as integrations from practice management vendors. Many generic "lawyer" plugins are rarely updated, though. If your practice management software offers an official form or intake integration, use that. Otherwise stick with mainstream plugins.

Should client information be stored in WordPress form entries?

Keep as little as you can. Many firms turn off entry storage or delete entries on a schedule, and route inquiries to email or their intake software. Our secure contact form guide covers the options. Check your state bar's guidance on confidentiality and technology.

Do I need both a security plugin and Cloudflare?

They do different jobs. Cloudflare filters traffic before it reaches your server. A security plugin protects logins and scans files on the server. Many firms use both, but turn off overlapping features (such as two firewalls set to block the same traffic) to avoid conflicts.

Can I use these plugins on Squarespace or Wix?

No. Plugins are a WordPress feature. Hosted builders use their own built-in tools and app marketplaces. The trade-offs between WordPress and hosted builders are a separate decision.

Conclusion: build a small, maintained stack

The best WordPress plugins for law firms are the ones you'll actually keep updated. Start with a backup, a security plugin with two-factor authentication, an SMTP plugin and a reliable form with Turnstile. Then add SEO, and add caching, scheduling and consent only when your site needs them. Your next steps:

  • List the plugins on your site today and match each one to a job. Remove duplicates and anything that hasn't been updated in a year.
  • Send a test through every form and confirm it reaches the inbox.
  • Work through the security checklist and put plugin updates on a monthly calendar.

Want this handled for you? ProSiteGuide builds and maintains fast, secure WordPress sites for law firms. Book a free consultation.

Before adding a caching plugin, work through our guide to speeding up a law firm website.

SEO plugins can output structured data for you; our guide to schema markup for law firms explains what to check.

If security is your next step, read our comparison of the best WordPress security plugins for law firms.

Quick answer: Most law firm websites need only one plugin for each of eight jobs: forms, SEO, security, backups, email delivery (SMTP), spam protection, consent (only if you track visitors) and, sometimes, scheduling. A strong default stack is WPForms or Gravity Forms, Rank Math or Yoast SEO, Wordfence, UpdraftPlus, WP Mail SMTP or FluentSMTP and Cloudflare Turnstile. Add caching only if your host doesn’t already provide it. Fewer plugins that are well maintained beat a long list every time.

Key takeaways

  • Pick plugins by job, not by popularity. One tool per job. Two SEO plugins or two caching plugins cause conflicts.
  • Every plugin is code you have to keep updated. Check the “Last updated” date, the active installs and the “Tested up to” version on WordPress.org before you install anything.
  • Check your host before you buy a caching or backup plugin. Managed WordPress hosts often include both.
  • Don’t use accessibility overlay widgets as a shortcut. In 2025 the FTC fined one overlay vendor $1 million over claims that its tool made sites WCAG compliant.
  • Install in a set order: backups first, then security, then email delivery, then everything else. Test after each step.

How we compared these plugins

This roundup is based on official documentation, WordPress.org plugin listings and vendor pricing pages, all checked in November 2026. We have not run hands-on benchmarks, and we don’t give scores. For each plugin we looked at four things: what the free version actually covers, the published price of the paid tier, how many sites use it (as shown on WordPress.org) and how recently it was updated. Prices change often and many vendors show first-year discounts, so always confirm the renewal price before you buy.

Why fewer plugins is the better strategy

A plugin is an add-on that gives WordPress a feature it doesn’t have out of the box. Each one is third-party code running on the site that holds your firm’s name and your clients’ first messages. Every plugin you add is another thing to update, another possible conflict and another place a vulnerability could show up.

So the goal isn’t the “best” plugin in every category. It’s the smallest set that covers the jobs your site really has. Before you install anything, run this quick check:

  • Last updated: within the past few months. A plugin that hasn’t been touched in a year or more is a warning sign. Several law-specific plugins listed in plugin directories have been flagged as possibly abandoned.
  • Tested up to: the current major WordPress release (7.1.x as of November 2026).
  • Active installs: a large user base doesn’t make a plugin safe, but it does mean problems get reported and fixed faster.
  • Overlap: does your theme, host or an existing plugin already do this job?
  • Exit plan: can you remove it later without breaking pages? This matters most with shortcodes and page builders.

The essential law firm plugin stack at a glance

Active installs and update dates below are as shown on WordPress.org on November 8, 2026. Paid prices are list or renewal prices from each vendor’s pricing page as of November 2026 (first-year promotions are noted in the sections below).

Which form plugin is best for a law firm?

For most small firms, WPForms is the easiest choice and Gravity Forms is the most flexible. Fluent Forms is the value pick. All three can build a consultation request form with conditional fields, such as asking different questions for family law and personal injury inquiries. How you handle confidential details in those forms is a bigger question than which plugin you choose, so read our guide to setting up a secure contact form for a law firm website before you go live.

WPForms

The WPForms pricing page lists Basic (1 site) at $49.50 for the first year, renewing at $99/yr. Plus (3 sites) renews at $199/yr, Pro (5 sites) at $399/yr and Elite (unlimited sites) at $599/yr. Renewals are at full price, and there’s a 14-day money-back guarantee. The free WPForms Lite works fine for a simple contact form. Best for: non-technical firms that want a drag-and-drop builder.

Gravity Forms

Gravity Forms has no free version or trial. Basic costs $59/yr for 1 site, Pro $159/yr for 3 sites and Elite $259/yr for unlimited sites. Elite adds add-ons such as Signature, Partial Entries and Webhooks. Best for: firms with a developer who need complex intake logic or CRM integrations.

Fluent Forms

The Fluent Forms Pro single-site license lists at $79/yr, with a lifetime option. At the time of writing a discounted first year was shown. Pro includes conditional logic, multi-step and conversational forms, and conditional email routing on every plan. Best for: budget-conscious firms that still want advanced features.

Rank Math or Yoast: which SEO plugin should lawyers use?

Either is fine. Pick one and never run both. The free versions of both handle the basics: title tags, meta descriptions, XML sitemaps and basic schema markup (code that helps search engines understand your pages).

  • Rank Math: The Rank Math pricing page lists PRO (unlimited personal sites) at $8.99/month billed annually, with a lower first-year promotion at the time of writing. The free version already includes more schema options than most firms need.
  • Yoast SEO: Yoast SEO Premium costs $118.80/yr per site. The page says Premium includes redirect management, internal linking suggestions and the Local SEO, Video and News add-ons.

Our take: if a developer already set one up, keep it. Switching gains you little. A free version plus well-written practice area pages will do more for your rankings than any premium SEO feature.

What security plugin does a law firm website need?

You need one security plugin, plus a host that does its own server-level protection. The plugin’s job is login protection (two-factor authentication), a firewall and malware scanning. For the full hardening list (user roles, updates, file permissions), use our law firm website security checklist. We won’t repeat it here.

Wordfence

The free Wordfence plugin includes a web application firewall, a malware scanner, two-factor authentication and passkeys. Its listing notes that firewall rules and malware signatures reach free users 30 days later than Premium users. Premium adds real-time updates, an IP blocklist, country blocking and paid support. Premium is billed per site per year. A price change was reported for December 2026, so confirm the current price on Wordfence\’s site before you buy.

Kadence Security (formerly Solid Security / iThemes Security)

The same plugin has carried three names. Its WordPress.org listing shows the free version includes two-factor authentication, brute-force protection, file change detection and scheduled scans. Pro adds passwordless logins, trusted devices and Patchstack virtual patching. We couldn’t find a published Pro price after the rebrand, so confirm it with the vendor. Best for: firms that want a lighter plugin focused on logins and hardening.

Sucuri

Sucuri’s main product is a cloud firewall that filters traffic before it reaches your server. The free plugin is mostly an auditing and scanning tool. On Sucuri’s pricing page, the Basic Firewall costs $9.99/month, and the Basic Platform (firewall plus unlimited malware cleanups) costs $229/yr per site. If you already use Cloudflare’s firewall, you may not need it. Check what your existing firewall already covers before adding another.

Do you need a backup plugin if your host backs up your site?

Usually yes, for a second copy stored somewhere else. Host backups are often kept on the host’s own infrastructure, and you can’t count on them if the account itself has a problem. An off-site copy in Google Drive, Dropbox or Amazon S3 is cheap insurance.

  • UpdraftPlus: The free version handles scheduled backups to remote storage. UpdraftPlus Premium starts at $70/yr for up to 2 sites. It adds incremental backups, automatic backups before updates, one-click migration and database encryption.
  • Duplicator: Best known for migrations, with 1+ million active installs on WordPress.org. It’s useful when you move to a new host.

Whichever you pick, test a restore on a staging site at least once. A backup you have never restored is a guess.

Why your law firm site needs an SMTP plugin

SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) is the standard way email is sent between servers. By default, WordPress sends form notifications through your web server, and those messages often land in spam or never arrive. An SMTP plugin sends them through a real email service instead, such as Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Amazon SES or Brevo. For a law firm, a lost consultation request means a lost client.

  • FluentSMTP: The FluentSMTP site says it is “free and will always be free.” That includes email logs, multiple connections and a fallback connection if your main service fails. This is the best value in the whole stack.
  • WP Mail SMTP: The free version covers the connection. WP Mail SMTP Pro (1 site) costs $49 for the first year and renews at $99/yr. It adds email logs, failure alerts and backup connections.

SMTP only works well if your domain’s SPF, DKIM and DMARC records are correct. Our law firm email setup guide covers that.

Do you need a caching plugin?

Only if your host doesn’t already cache pages. Caching means saving a ready-made copy of each page so the server doesn’t rebuild it for every visitor. Many managed WordPress hosts do this at the server level, and adding a second caching layer can cause stale pages or broken forms. Check your host’s documentation first. Our best hosting for law firm websites comparison notes which hosts include it.

  • Host caching: If it’s included, use it and skip the plugin.
  • LiteSpeed Cache: Free, and the right choice if your host runs a LiteSpeed web server. It has 7+ million active installs on WordPress.org.
  • WP Rocket: A paid plugin for Apache or NGINX hosts without built-in caching. The WP Rocket pricing page lists the Single plan (1 site) at $5/month billed yearly, discounted during a promotion at the time of writing. There’s no free version, only a 14-day trial.

How to stop contact form spam without annoying clients

Use Cloudflare Turnstile, a CAPTCHA replacement that usually doesn’t ask visitors to solve a puzzle. Cloudflare’s Turnstile documentation says it can be embedded on any website without routing traffic through Cloudflare. The free plan includes unlimited challenges. Check your form plugin’s spam settings for a built-in Turnstile option first. If there isn’t one, the free Simple CAPTCHA with Cloudflare Turnstile plugin adds it.

Akismet is a popular alternative, but read the terms. The Akismet pricing page limits the pay-what-you-can plan to personal sites. Commercial sites, which includes a law firm, need Pro from $9.95/month billed yearly.

What’s the best scheduling option for consultations?

Often it’s no plugin at all. If you already use a scheduling service such as Calendly, or the booking tool in your practice management software, embed its widget on a page. That adds no plugin to update. Choose a WordPress booking plugin only if you want bookings stored on your own site.

  • Simply Schedule Appointments: The free Basic tier includes Google Calendar sync. Paid plans start with Plus at $99 for the first year ($129/yr renewal), which adds Zoom and Google Meet. SMS reminders and Stripe/PayPal payments come with Professional ($249/yr renewal).
  • Amelia: A more feature-heavy booking system with two-way Google Calendar and Outlook sync, Zoom and payments. The free version has 90,000+ active installs on WordPress.org. Its pricing page showed promotional prices we couldn’t read reliably, so confirm current pricing with the vendor.

Keep booking forms short. Ask for name, contact details and matter type, not the facts of the case. Those can wait until you’ve run a conflict check.

Do law firm websites need a cookie consent plugin?

Only if the site uses cookies or scripts that track visitors, such as Google Analytics, ad pixels or embedded videos. Several US states now have privacy laws with opt-out rights, and the rules differ by state. Check with a privacy professional if you’re unsure which apply to you. If you do need a banner:

  • Complianz: The free plugin includes a cookie scan, script blocking and a cookie policy generator. Detailed US state law support, Google Consent Mode and records of consent are listed as premium features. Premium Personal costs $59/yr for 1 site.
  • CookieYes: The free plan covers up to 5,000 pageviews a month and includes a US State Laws (opt-out) template and Google Consent Mode v2. Basic costs $100/yr per domain.

Should you use an accessibility overlay plugin?

No, not as a substitute for real accessibility work. An overlay is a widget that adds a toolbar to your site and promises automatic fixes. In January 2025 the Federal Trade Commission announced a $1 million order against accessiBe. The FTC alleged that the company’s claims that its AI tool could make any website compliant with the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) were false, misleading or unsubstantiated.

Accessibility comes from the theme, the content and how forms are built: real headings, alt text, color contrast, labeled form fields and keyboard navigation. Plugins can help you find problems, but they don’t fix them for you. Our guide to law firm website accessibility and WCAG explains what to check.

Plugins most small firms can skip

  • A second plugin for the same job: two SEO plugins, two caching plugins or two security plugins.
  • Social auto-posters and share-count widgets: they add scripts and rarely bring clients.
  • Old “lawyer directory” or “case manager” plugins: check the update date. Your practice management software should hold client data, not your website.
  • Separate plugins for every tiny feature (a “scroll to top” button, a custom login logo). A developer can add these with a few lines of code.
  • Accessibility overlays, for the reasons above.

Our recommended minimal stack

Here are two versions. Both assume a good host that handles server-side caching and daily backups.

That comes to six to eight plugins in total, not counting your theme. Your monthly website maintenance routine should include updating each one and checking that forms still deliver.

In what order should you set up plugins?

Set up protection first and features second, so that if something breaks you can roll back. Ideally do this on a staging copy of the site.

  1. Back up the site. Install UpdraftPlus (or confirm your host’s backups), connect cloud storage and run a first full backup.
  2. Lock down logins. Install one security plugin, turn on two-factor authentication for every admin and run a first scan.
  3. Fix email delivery. Install an SMTP plugin, connect it to your email provider and send a test email to an outside address.
  4. Build or connect forms. Set up the consultation form, add Turnstile and send a test submission. Confirm that it arrives.
  5. Configure SEO. Run the setup wizard, submit the sitemap in Google Search Console and add your firm’s details for local schema.
  6. Check performance. Turn on host caching (or one caching plugin). Exclude form and booking pages if the plugin recommends it, then retest the forms.
  7. Add optional plugins. Add scheduling and, if you use tracking scripts, the consent banner. Test the banner in a private browser window.
  8. Remove leftovers. Delete inactive plugins and themes. Deactivated code still sits on the server.

FAQ

How many plugins should a law firm website have?

There’s no magic number. A typical small-firm site can cover every essential job with six to eight well-maintained plugins. Quality and update history matter more than the count.

Are free WordPress plugins safe for lawyers to use?

Free plugins from established vendors with recent updates and large user bases are widely used. Paid tiers mostly add support and extra features, not basic safety. What matters most is keeping every plugin updated and removing the ones you don’t use.

Are there WordPress plugins made specifically for law firms?

A few exist, such as integrations from practice management vendors. Many generic “lawyer” plugins are rarely updated, though. If your practice management software offers an official form or intake integration, use that. Otherwise stick with mainstream plugins.

Should client information be stored in WordPress form entries?

Keep as little as you can. Many firms turn off entry storage or delete entries on a schedule, and route inquiries to email or their intake software. Our secure contact form guide covers the options. Check your state bar’s guidance on confidentiality and technology.

Do I need both a security plugin and Cloudflare?

They do different jobs. Cloudflare filters traffic before it reaches your server. A security plugin protects logins and scans files on the server. Many firms use both, but turn off overlapping features (such as two firewalls set to block the same traffic) to avoid conflicts.

Can I use these plugins on Squarespace or Wix?

No. Plugins are a WordPress feature. Hosted builders use their own built-in tools and app marketplaces. The trade-offs between WordPress and hosted builders are a separate decision.

Conclusion: build a small, maintained stack

The best WordPress plugins for law firms are the ones you’ll actually keep updated. Start with a backup, a security plugin with two-factor authentication, an SMTP plugin and a reliable form with Turnstile. Then add SEO, and add caching, scheduling and consent only when your site needs them. Your next steps:

  • List the plugins on your site today and match each one to a job. Remove duplicates and anything that hasn’t been updated in a year.
  • Send a test through every form and confirm it reaches the inbox.
  • Work through the security checklist and put plugin updates on a monthly calendar.

Before adding a caching plugin, work through our guide to speeding up a law firm website.

SEO plugins can output structured data for you; our guide to schema markup for law firms explains what to check.

title.raw: Best WordPress Themes for Law Firms (2026)
title.rendered: Best WordPress Themes for Law Firms (2026)

content.raw:
Quick answer: The best WordPress themes for law firms in 2026 are fast, well-maintained general themes, not "lawyer themes" from template marketplaces. For most small firms, Kadence or Blocksy (both tagged accessibility-ready on WordPress.org) are the strongest starting points, GeneratePress suits developers who want the leanest base, Astra has the most ready-made lawyer templates, and Twenty Twenty-Five is the free, no-add-on choice. If your firm already uses Elementor, pair it with the Hello Elementor theme.

Key takeaways

  • A theme controls your site's layout, typography and header/footer. A good one is lightweight, updated often and works with the WordPress block editor.
  • Every theme below has a free version on WordPress.org with hundreds of thousands to over a million active installations, and all were updated within the last year (as of November 8, 2026).
  • The "accessibility-ready" tag is a useful minimum, not a guarantee of ADA or WCAG compliance. Your content and plugins matter as much as the theme.
  • Never install a "nulled" (pirated) premium theme. Security researchers routinely find backdoors and hidden admin accounts in them.
  • Pro upgrades are optional. Most firm sites (home, attorneys, practice areas, contact) can be built with a free theme plus the block editor.

Best WordPress themes for law firms at a glance

  • Kadence: best all-round choice for a block-editor law firm site.
  • Blocksy: best for firms that want modern design controls and a fair lifetime license.
  • GeneratePress: best lean base for developers who care about every kilobyte.
  • Astra: best if you want to start from a ready-made lawyer template.
  • Twenty Twenty-Five: best free option with zero paid add-ons.
  • Hello Elementor + Elementor Pro: best for firms committed to the Elementor visual builder.

Not sure WordPress is the right platform at all? Read our Squarespace vs WordPress vs Wix comparison for law firms first.

How we compared these themes

We have not run our own speed tests or scored these products. This comparison is based on each theme's official WordPress.org listing (active installations, last update date, feature tags and requirements) and the vendors' own pricing and documentation pages, all checked on November 8, 2026. Prices change often, so confirm them at checkout.

What makes a good law firm WordPress theme?

A good law firm WordPress theme loads quickly, stays updated, is usable with a keyboard and screen reader, and lets you build practice area and attorney pages without heavy add-ons. These are the criteria we used:

  1. Maintenance. Frequent updates and support for the current WordPress version. An abandoned theme is a security and compatibility risk.
  2. Speed. A light theme with few scripts gives your site a head start on Core Web Vitals (Google's page-experience metrics). Hosting and images matter even more.
  3. Accessibility. We noted which themes carry WordPress.org's accessibility-ready tag.
  4. Editor support. Good support for the native block editor (Gutenberg), or a clear builder path such as Elementor.
  5. Schema-friendliness. Clean HTML that does not fight your SEO plugin. Structured data such as LegalService or Attorney markup normally comes from an SEO plugin, not the theme.
  6. Support and price. A usable free version, a clear pro price and an official support channel.

Law firm WordPress theme comparison table

Install counts are the ranges WordPress.org displays. "Last updated" is the free theme's last release on WordPress.org. Pro prices are the lowest listed tier, as of November 2026.

The best WordPress themes for law firms, reviewed

1. Kadence: best all-round law firm WordPress theme

Kadence is a free, block-editor-first theme with a visual header and footer builder, global colors and fonts, and a companion Kadence Blocks plugin for layouts such as tabs, accordions and info boxes (handy for practice area FAQs). Its WordPress.org listing shows 500,000+ active installations, version 1.6.0 released November 6, 2026, and the accessibility-ready tag. It requires WordPress 6.6 and PHP 7.4 or later.

Pricing: Kadence is now sold through Liquid Web. When we checked, the official Kadence pricing page showed an all-in-one software bundle (Kadence plus LearnDash, The Events Calendar and Give) starting at $350/year for one site, and its FAQ refers to separate Kadence Pro and Elite tiers without listing their prices. Confirm current Kadence-only pricing with the vendor before you buy. The free theme and free Kadence Blocks plugin are enough for many small firm sites.

  • Pros: accessibility-ready tag; strong block editor tools; very recent updates; generous free version.
  • Cons: pricing structure has changed and is currently bundle-oriented; extra blocks plugin adds weight if you use every feature.
  • Best for: solo and small firms that want to build in the native editor and keep the option to grow.

2. Blocksy: best for modern design controls

Blocksy is a free theme with a flexible header builder, block patterns and block styles, and support for both the block editor and popular builders. WordPress.org lists 300,000+ active installations, version 2.1.61 updated October 30, 2026, and the accessibility-ready tag. It requires WordPress 6.7 and PHP 7.0 or later.

Pricing: According to Blocksy's pricing page, Blocksy Pro costs $69/year or $199 lifetime for one site (Personal), $99/year or $299 lifetime for 10 sites (Business), and $149/year or $499 lifetime for unlimited sites (Agency), as of November 2026.

  • Pros: accessibility-ready tag; lifetime license option; clean visual customizer.
  • Cons: smaller ecosystem of law-specific starter sites than Astra.
  • Best for: firms (or their developer) that want polished design control without a page builder.

3. GeneratePress: best lean base for developers

GeneratePress is known for being lightweight, and its official site positions it as "a lightweight WordPress theme." WordPress.org shows 500,000+ active installations and version 3.6.1, last updated December 1, 2025. It does not carry the accessibility-ready tag, and it requires WordPress 6.5 and PHP 7.4 or later. Premium features live in the separate GP Premium plugin, so the free theme's update date does not tell the whole story, but it is worth checking the changelog before you commit.

Pricing: Per GeneratePress pricing, GeneratePress One (GP Premium, GenerateBlocks Pro, the site library and priority support) costs $99/year for one site, $149/year for 10 sites, $199/year for 100 sites, or $596 once for a 100-site lifetime plan, as of November 2026. The site library lists 80+ starter sites, none of them law-specific.

  • Pros: minimal footprint; mature, stable codebase; clear pricing with a 30-day refund window.
  • Cons: no accessibility-ready tag; no lawyer templates; best results need some design skill.
  • Best for: developers building a custom firm site who want full control.

4. Astra: best for ready-made lawyer templates

Astra is one of the most widely used WordPress themes: WordPress.org shows 1+ million active installations and version 4.14.2 updated October 29, 2026. It does not carry the accessibility-ready tag. Its Starter Templates library advertises 300+ templates and includes several legal designs, such as Family Lawyer; some lawyer templates require a paid plan, so check the label before importing.

Pricing: The Astra pricing page lists the Astra Pro add-on alone at $69/year or $249 lifetime (discounted from $349). Bundles start with Astra Pro + AI at $99 for the first year (renews at $149/year), then Essential Toolkit + AI at $199 (renews at $299) and Business Toolkit + AI at $279 (renews at $429). Astra states these are introductory prices and renewals are at full price, as of November 2026.

  • Pros: largest template library, including lawyer layouts; works with the block editor and Elementor.
  • Cons: no accessibility-ready tag; bundles push extras you may not need; renewal prices are higher than first-year prices.
  • Best for: firms that want to import a lawyer design and edit the text, rather than design from scratch.

5. Twenty Twenty-Five: best free option with no add-ons

Twenty Twenty-Five is the default block theme made by the WordPress project. A block theme is one where headers, footers and templates are all edited visually in the Site Editor, with no separate customizer. It has 1+ million active installations, version 1.5 updated May 20, 2026, and the accessibility-ready, full-site-editing and style-variations tags. It requires WordPress 6.7 and PHP 7.2 or later.

  • Pros: completely free; maintained by the WordPress project; no third-party upsells; accessibility-ready.
  • Cons: fewer business-focused design controls; updates are less frequent than commercial themes.
  • Best for: a simple solo-attorney site, or a firm that wants zero plugin or license dependencies.

6. Hello Elementor + Elementor Pro: best for Elementor users

Hello Elementor is a minimal theme "built specifically to work seamlessly with the Elementor site builder plugin." WordPress.org shows 1+ million active installations, version 3.5.2 updated November 3, 2026, and the accessibility-ready tag. On its own it does very little; the design work happens in Elementor.

Pricing: The Elementor pricing page lists Essential at $60/year (1 site, includes Theme Builder and Form Builder), Advanced Solo at $84/year (1 site, adds Popup Builder and custom code) and Advanced at $108/year (3 sites), as of November 2026. Elementor notes plans renew at the regular rate, so confirm the renewal price at checkout.

  • Pros: drag-and-drop editing that non-technical staff often find easiest; large template ecosystem.
  • Cons: pages built in Elementor are tied to Elementor; builder output is usually heavier than native blocks, so hosting and caching matter more.
  • Best for: firms whose existing site or developer already works in Elementor.

Also worth a look: Neve

Neve (200,000+ active installations, updated November 6, 2026, accessibility-ready tag) is another solid general theme. Neve Pro starts at $69/year for the first year, with renewals at full price, as of November 2026.

Which law firm WordPress theme should you choose?

Choose based on who will edit the site and how much design work you want to do. The decision chart below sums it up.

  • You (or staff) will edit pages yourselves and want the native editor: Kadence or Blocksy.
  • You want a finished lawyer layout to fill in: Astra with a lawyer starter template.
  • A developer is building a custom site: GeneratePress or Kadence.
  • You want no paid licenses at all: Twenty Twenty-Five.
  • Your team already knows Elementor: Hello Elementor + Elementor Pro.

Why not a "lawyer theme" from a template marketplace?

Niche "attorney WordPress themes" can look impressive in demos, but many bundle sliders, builders and demo plugins you will never use, and some are updated rarely. When a niche theme is abandoned, you are stuck with a redesign. A general theme with a lawyer starter template gives you the same look with a far larger user base and a longer track record. If you still prefer a niche theme, check its changelog, last update date, required plugins and support policy before buying.

Are nulled WordPress themes safe?

No. A nulled theme is a pirated copy of a paid theme with the license check removed. title.rendered: Google Business Profile for Law Firms: Setup and Optimization Guide (2026)

content.raw:
Quick answer: A Google Business Profile for a law firm is the free listing that shows your firm on Google Search and Maps. To set it up, sign in at business.google.com/create with a firm-controlled Google account, enter your firm's real-world name, pick one specific primary category, add a staffed office address (or a service area), verify, then keep hours, photos and reviews current. Google's rules for "individual practitioners" also decide whether each lawyer gets a separate profile, and your ethics duties shape how you reply to reviews.

Key takeaways

  • Use your firm's real name exactly as it appears on your sign and letterhead. Adding practice areas or cities to the name breaks Google's guidelines and can get the profile suspended.
  • Google treats lawyers as individual practitioners. A firm with several public-facing lawyers can have one firm profile plus one profile per lawyer, named only with the lawyer's name.
  • Virtual offices and P.O. boxes are not eligible. If clients don't visit your office, hide the address and set a service area instead.
  • You may ask every client for a review, but never offer anything in return and never ask only happy clients.
  • Never confirm someone was your client, or discuss their matter, in a public review reply. ABA Formal Opinion 496 covers this.

What is a Google Business Profile, and why does it matter for a law firm?

A Google Business Profile (formerly Google My Business) is the free listing that appears in the map results and the knowledge panel when someone searches for your firm or a "lawyer near me" type query. It shows your name, address, phone, hours, website link, photos and reviews, and it lets people call you or get directions in one tap.

Google explains that local results are based on three things: relevance (how well your profile matches the search), distance (how far you are from the searcher) and prominence (how well known you are, including links and reviews). It also says plainly: "There's no way to request or pay for a better local ranking on Google" (Google: How to improve your local ranking). So nobody can promise you a top-three map spot. What you control is accuracy, completeness and staying inside the rules.

Firm profile or lawyer profile? Google's practitioner rules

Google's Guidelines for representing your business on Google name lawyers as "individual practitioners," alongside doctors and financial planners. An individual practitioner is a public-facing professional who has their own clients. The rules that follow decide how many profiles your firm should have.

  • Who qualifies: a lawyer who deals with the public and can be contacted directly at the verified location during stated hours. Paralegals, assistants and other support staff should not have their own profiles.
  • One profile per lawyer: a lawyer may not create separate profiles for each specialty (for example, one for DUI and one for traffic tickets).
  • Several lawyers at one office: the firm gets a profile for the location, and each lawyer's profile uses only the lawyer's name, not the firm name. Credentials such as "Esq." or "J.D." are allowed.
  • A solo lawyer practicing under a firm brand: Google says a sole practitioner at a branded organization should share one profile named "[brand]: [practitioner name]." Google's example is from insurance ("Allstate: Joe Miller"). Applying it to a solo firm is our reading of the rule, so a branded solo practice would follow a pattern like "Rivera Law: Ana Rivera."

Do lawyer profiles help? Sometimes, but they also split your reviews across several listings. They can also become a problem when a lawyer leaves the firm. Many small firms keep only the firm profile. If you do create lawyer profiles, add them as users on accounts the firm controls, and agree in writing what happens to the profile if the lawyer leaves.

What you need before you start

  • A firm-owned Google account. Google suggests using an email on your business domain. Don't let an agency or a departing associate become the only owner. If your firm email isn't set up yet, see our guide to law firm email on your own domain.
  • Your exact legal or trade name as it appears on signage, letterhead and your website.
  • An eligible address. Google says P.O. boxes, remote mailboxes and virtual offices are not eligible. A co-working space qualifies only if it has your signage and staff present who receive clients during your stated hours. Your state bar may have its own office or advertising rules, so check those separately.
  • A local phone number the firm controls, plus the specific page on your website you want to link to.
  • A few real photos: your logo, the building entrance, the office interior and your lawyers.

How to set up a Google Business Profile for a law firm (step by step)

These steps follow Google's create a Business Profile help page as of November 2026. Menu labels change from time to time, but the order stays roughly the same.

  1. Check for an existing listing. Search your firm name on Google Maps. Google often creates listings on its own, and former staff or old agencies may have claimed one. If someone else has already verified it, request ownership rather than creating a duplicate. Google allows only one profile per business location.
  2. Sign in and start. Go to business.google.com/create while signed in to the firm-owned Google account.
  3. Enter the real-world firm name. No taglines, practice areas, city names or phone numbers. "Smith & Lee, PLLC" is fine if that's your actual name. "Smith & Lee Car Accident Lawyers Dallas" is not, unless that is genuinely your registered and signed name. Google allows legal suffixes such as PLLC only if you can show them in real-world use.
  4. Choose your primary category. Pick the most specific category that finishes the sentence "This business is a…". If you only do family law, a family-law attorney category is a better fit than a generic one. Type a few words into the field and choose from Google's list.
  5. Storefront or service area. Google asks whether customers can visit a staffed location during business hours. If clients meet you at your office, answer yes and enter the address. If you only meet clients at their homes, in court or online, answer no and add a service area.
  6. Add the service area if relevant. List cities, ZIP codes or counties, up to 20 areas. Google says the area should usually stay within about two hours' drive of your base. You can't use a radius.
  7. Add the phone number and website. Use the local number that rings at the firm and the page that best matches this listing (see the website section below).
  8. Verify. Google decides which methods you're offered: phone or text, email, postcard, a recorded video, a live video call, or instant verification in some cases (Google: Verify your business). Postcards usually arrive within 14 days and the code expires after 30 days. After you submit, Google may take up to 5 business days to review it. While a postcard is pending, don't edit the name, address or category, and don't request a new code.
  9. Complete the profile. Add hours, a description, extra categories if they truly apply, attributes, photos and an opening date.
  10. Add people with the right roles. Keep the firm as primary owner. Give your marketing person or agency the Manager role. Managers can do almost everything except add or remove users or delete the profile (Google: Manage owners and managers).

How to optimize each section of the profile

Name: what's allowed?

Only your real-world name. Google lists the extras it doesn't allow: marketing taglines, hours, phone numbers, URLs, service descriptions and location details, plus ® or ™ symbols and all caps. Adding keywords to the name is one of the most common reasons local listings get reported and suspended. If you rename the firm, update your sign, website and letterhead first, then the profile.

Categories: how many should a law firm use?

Google lets you pick one primary category and up to 9 more (Google: Edit your Business Profile). Its guidelines also say to "use as few categories as possible." Choose your main practice as the primary category. Add secondary categories only for practice areas you actively handle at that office. Categories describe what the firm is, so leave out services you only "offer" now and then. Put the detail on your website instead. Our guide to writing practice area pages shows how.

Address and service area

A storefront profile shows your address because clients come to you. A service-area profile hides the address and shows the region you serve. A hybrid shows both. Many solo lawyers who work from home but meet clients elsewhere fall into the service-area group. Don't list a virtual office address to look local in another city. It isn't eligible, and it puts the whole profile at risk.

Hours

List the hours when someone answers the phone or receives clients. Add special hours for holidays so people don't call into a closed office. Google's guidelines say businesses that operate only by appointment shouldn't list hours. If your office is staffed on a normal schedule, list those staffed hours.

Description

You get up to 750 characters, with no links, HTML, prices or promotions. Say who you help, which practice areas you handle, where, and in what languages. Plain facts age better than adjectives. Also keep your state's lawyer-advertising rules in mind: words like "expert" or "specialist" are restricted in many states unless you hold a recognized certification.

Photos

Yes. Creating and managing a Business Profile costs nothing. Google Ads and Local Services Ads are separate, paid products, and paying for them doesn't change your free map ranking.

content.raw:
Quick answer: Hostinger is a good fit for a solo attorney or a small firm that needs a simple WordPress brochure site on a tight budget. It is not the right home for a firm that wants daily off-site backups kept for weeks, phone support, or a host that handles day-to-day site care for you. Pick the Unlimited plan rather than Premium, buy the longest term you are comfortable with, and plan for the renewal price, not the sale price.

This Hostinger review looks at the managed WordPress plans from a law firm's point of view: what you get, what it really costs over four years, where the limits are, and when Kinsta or SiteGround is worth the extra money.

Key takeaways

  • The $1.99/mo headline price needs a 48-month prepayment ($95.52). After that, Premium renews at $10.99/mo, as of November 2026.
  • Premium includes weekly backups only. Unlimited ($2.79/mo on a 48-month term) adds daily backups, which most firms should want.
  • The domain and mailboxes are free for the first year only. Budget for both from year two.
  • Hostinger Mail stores mailbox data in Europe (France and Germany). That matters if you plan to use it for client email.
  • Good for: budget-conscious solo and small firms with a simple site. Look elsewhere if you want hands-off management or longer backup history.

How we compared

We have not run hands-on tests of Hostinger for this article, and we do not give scores. This review is based on Hostinger's official pricing pages, help center articles and legal terms, all checked in November 2026. Prices change often, especially around sales, so confirm the figures on the checkout page before you pay.

title.rendered: How to Write Practice Area Pages That Rank and Convert (Law Firm Guide, 2026)

content.raw:
Quick answer: Practice area pages rank and convert when each page covers one service in one place, answers the questions a prospective client has before calling, and makes the next step obvious. Use a consistent structure: a clear H1 with the service and city, an intro that says who you help and where, your process, how fees work, attorney credentials, FAQs and a contact form. Then keep every claim within your state's attorney advertising rules.

This guide covers that structure section by section. It also covers when to split a page into sub-pages, local signals, schema markup, the ethics rules that apply to marketing copy, and how to track results in Google Search Console.

Key takeaways

  • One page per practice area you actively handle. Add sub-pages only where clients search for a distinct problem.
  • The first screen should say what you handle, for whom, and where, and it should show a phone number or form.
  • Google has no preferred word count. Answer real client questions instead of padding to a target length.
  • FAQ rich results have been limited to well-known government and health sites since August 2023. Write FAQs for readers, not for search snippets.
  • "Specialist", "expert", results and testimonials are regulated in many states. Check your state bar's rules before you publish.

What is a practice area page?

A practice area page is a page on a law firm website that describes one type of legal work the firm handles, such as DUI defense, probate or workers' compensation. It is usually the page that matches a prospective client's search ("probate lawyer in Dayton"), so it often decides whether that person calls you or goes back to the results.

A good practice area page has three jobs:

  1. Answer. Confirm that you handle this kind of matter, in this location, and explain in plain words what usually happens next.
  2. Reassure. Show who the lawyer is, how you work and what the client can expect, without hype or promises.
  3. Convert. Make contact easy: a visible phone number, a short form and a clear note on what happens after they reach out.

Most weak practice pages fail at job one. They describe the area of law in general terms ("Family law covers many issues…") and never say who the firm helps or where. Searchers and search engines both need that information near the top.

What should a law firm practice area page include?

A law firm practice area page should include eight building blocks, in roughly this order. The wireframe below shows how they fit on the page.

1. H1 with the service and location

Name the service the way clients search for it, plus the city or region you serve. "Estate Planning Lawyer in Columbus, Ohio" beats "Wills & Trusts Solutions". Your SEO title (the title tag) can be close to the H1 but shorter, roughly 50–60 characters, so it is less likely to be cut off in results.

2. An intro that answers who, where and what

The first two or three sentences should say who you represent, where, and what kinds of matters. If you only represent one side (employees, not employers; defendants, not plaintiffs), say so. This filters out poor-fit calls and helps the right people stay. Put a phone number or a "Request a consultation" button in or right next to this block.

3. Matters you handle (and don't)

List the specific situations covered, such as "contested and uncontested divorce, custody modifications, relocation disputes". Add a line on what you don't take. Specific lists also give you natural wording for the variations people search for, without stuffing keywords.

4. How the process works

Prospective clients worry about the unknown. A numbered list of typical steps (first consultation, documents to gather, filing, negotiation, hearing) is one of the most reassuring things you can add. Use "typically" and "often" and note that timelines depend on the facts and the court.

5. How fees work

You don't have to publish prices, but you should explain how billing works for this service: flat fee, hourly, contingency, or a mix. Say whether the first consultation is free or paid, and what affects cost. If you work on contingency, check your state's rules on how you describe fees and costs in advertising.

6. Attorney credentials

Show the lawyer who handles these matters: name, photo, bar admissions, years in practice, relevant memberships and a link to the full bio. Google's guidance on creating helpful content asks "who created this?" and recommends bylines that link to the author's background. For legal topics, which Google treats as "Your Money or Your Life" subjects, that trust signal matters even more. A "Written by" or "Reviewed by [attorney name]" line with a date works well.

7. FAQs

Add 4–8 questions that callers actually ask, written the way they ask them. Start each answer with a direct one-sentence response, then add detail. Your intake staff or receptionist are the best source of questions.

8. Call to action and contact form

End with a clear next step and a short form (name, phone, email, a brief description). Say what happens after they submit, such as "We reply within one business day", but only if that's true. Warn people not to send confidential details through the form. Our guide to a secure contact form for law firm websites covers encryption, spam filtering and disclaimer wording.

Example outline: a fictional estate planning page

Illustrative only. "Harbor & Pine Law" is a made-up firm and does not refer to any real practice.

  • SEO title: Estate Planning Lawyer in Columbus, OH | Harbor & Pine Law
  • H1: Estate Planning Lawyer in Columbus, Ohio
  • Intro: We help individuals and families in Franklin County prepare wills, trusts and powers of attorney. Flat-fee packages. Call (555) 010-0000 or request a consultation.
  • H2: Estate planning matters we handle: wills, revocable living trusts, powers of attorney, health care directives, plan updates after marriage or divorce. (We do not handle tax litigation.)
  • H2: How the process works: 1) 30-minute consultation, 2) questionnaire and documents, 3) draft review, 4) signing meeting, 5) periodic reviews.
  • H2: What does estate planning cost? Flat fees by package; what changes the price; what the consultation costs.
  • H2: Your attorney: photo, bar admission, years in practice, link to bio.

content.raw:
Quick answer: Law firm website accessibility means building your site so people with disabilities can use it. That includes people who use screen readers, navigate by keyboard only, have low vision or are deaf or hard of hearing. The U.S. Department of Justice says the ADA covers the goods and services businesses offer online, and points to the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) as helpful guidance. For a small firm, the practical target is WCAG 2.2 Level AA, reached through real fixes to your theme, content and forms, not a one-click widget.

Key takeaways

  • The DOJ's web accessibility guidance says ADA Title III applies to what businesses open to the public offer online. It sets no detailed technical rule for private businesses.
  • The DOJ's 2024 Title II web rule (WCAG 2.1 AA) covers state and local governments. It does not directly regulate private law firms.
  • WCAG 2.2 Level AA is the current W3C benchmark. Most problems on firm sites are basic: contrast, alt text, keyboard access, form labels, headings, captions and PDFs.
  • Overlay widgets don't replace fixing the site itself. In 2025 the FTC ordered one overlay vendor to pay $1 million over its compliance claims.
  • Start with the 30-minute self-check below, then have a developer fix what you find. Publish an accessibility statement with a working contact method.

Does the ADA apply to law firm websites?

The DOJ's position is that it does. The ADA itself lists the "office of an accountant or lawyer" among public accommodations covered by Title III (42 U.S.C. § 12181(7)(F)). In its guidance on web accessibility (March 2022), the DOJ says it "has consistently taken the position that the ADA's requirements apply to all the goods, services, privileges, or activities offered by public accommodations, including those offered on the web."

Two points from that guidance matter for small firms:

  • No detailed federal web standard exists for private businesses. The DOJ has no regulation setting technical web rules for Title III businesses. It names WCAG and the federal Section 508 standards as helpful guidance.
  • Businesses have flexibility in how they comply. Flexibility still means the online content has to be accessible.

Courts have not agreed on every question about websites and Title III. State laws can add their own requirements too. This article doesn't assess your firm's legal exposure. If you've received a demand letter, or you want a view on your risk, talk to a lawyer who handles ADA matters in your state.

What about the DOJ's 2024 Title II rule?

The 2024 rule covers governments, not private firms. The DOJ's fact sheet on the Title II web rule says it applies to state and local governments, their agencies, special districts and certain transit authorities. It adopts WCAG 2.1 Level AA as the technical standard. An interim final rule published April 20, 2026 moved the compliance dates. Governments serving 50,000 or more people now have until April 26, 2027. Smaller governments and special districts have until April 26, 2028.

A private law firm isn't directly covered by that rule. It still matters to you in two ways. First, it's the clearest signal yet of the technical standard regulators consider reasonable. Second, a firm that builds websites, apps or online tools for a government client may be asked to meet it under contract.

Why accessibility matters for a small firm

Legal risk is only one reason. Your website is often a prospective client's first contact with your firm. If someone using a screen reader can't fill in your intake form, they'll call the next firm on the list. Accessibility problems also tend to hurt everyone else. Low-contrast grey text is hard to read on a phone in sunlight. Tiny tap targets frustrate older clients. A video without captions gets skipped in a waiting room with the sound off.

Many accessibility fixes overlap with good SEO and usability work: clear headings, descriptive page titles, meaningful link text and fast, simple forms. If you're planning a rebuild, put accessibility in the brief from day one. It's cheaper than retrofitting. (See our guide to what a law firm website costs in 2026 for budgeting.)

What does WCAG 2.2 Level AA mean in practice?

WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) is the W3C's international standard for accessible web content. WCAG 2.2 became a W3C Recommendation on October 5, 2023, with an update in December 2024. It's also published as ISO/IEC 40500:2025. Its success criteria come in three levels. Level A is the minimum, Level AA is the usual target, and Level AAA is the strictest. The 2.x versions are backwards compatible, so a site that meets 2.2 AA also meets 2.1 AA, the standard used in the Title II rule.

The W3C's WCAG at a Glance organizes everything under four principles, often shortened to POUR:

  • Perceivable: text alternatives for images, captions for video, enough contrast to see content.
  • Operable: everything works from a keyboard, users get enough time, navigation is easy.
  • Understandable: readable text, predictable behaviour, help avoiding and fixing form errors.
  • Robust: clean code that works with browsers and assistive technology.

What's new in WCAG 2.2 for a law firm site?

According to the W3C's What's New in WCAG 2.2, version 2.2 adds nine success criteria. Six are at Level A or AA. These are the ones most likely to affect a typical firm site:

  • Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), AA: a sticky header, cookie banner or chat bubble mustn't completely hide the element a keyboard user has tabbed to.
  • Target Size (Minimum), AA: buttons and links should be at least 24×24 CSS pixels or spaced well apart. "Call now" buttons and social icons are frequent offenders. Links inside sentences are exempt.
  • Consistent Help, A: if your phone number, chat or contact link repeats across pages, keep it in the same relative place.
  • Redundant Entry, A: a multi-step intake form shouldn't make people type the same information twice.
  • Accessible Authentication (Minimum), AA: a client portal login shouldn't depend on a memory or puzzle test without an alternative, such as allowing password managers and paste.
  • Dragging Movements, AA: anything that needs dragging, like a slider, needs a click or tap alternative.

Version 2.2 also removed one older criterion, 4.1.1 Parsing, as obsolete.

The most common accessibility issues on law firm websites

The DOJ's guidance lists the same barriers that show up on many small-business sites: poor contrast, information conveyed by color alone, missing alt text, videos without captions, inaccessible forms and mouse-only navigation. Here's how each one tends to appear on a firm site and what fixing it involves.

The contrast thresholds come from the W3C's Understanding Contrast (Minimum) page. It also notes these are hard cut-offs: a ratio of 4.499:1 fails the 4.5:1 requirement.

Why are contact and intake forms the highest priority?

Forms are where a visitor becomes a lead, and they're where accessibility most often breaks. Check labels, error messages, required-field markers and any CAPTCHA. Some CAPTCHA puzzles can't be solved without sight or fine motor control. A quieter spam filter or honeypot field is often a better choice. For the security side of forms, see how to add a secure contact form to a law firm website.

A 30-minute accessibility self-check for your firm's site

The steps below are adapted from the W3C's Easy Checks. You need a browser and no special software. Test your homepage, one practice area page, your attorney bio page and your contact page. The W3C itself warns that a page "could seem to pass these checks, yet still have significant accessibility barriers," so treat this as triage, not an audit.

  1. Page titles (2 min). Look at the browser tab on each page. Every page should have a distinct, descriptive title, such as "Estate Planning Lawyer in Austin | Doe Law". Screen readers announce the title first.
  2. Keyboard only (8 min). Put the mouse away. Press Tab from the top of the page. Can you see where focus is at all times? Is the first stop a "Skip to main content" link? Can you open the menu, reach every link, fill in and submit the contact form, and close any pop-up or chat window with Esc? Does a sticky header ever cover the focused item?
  3. Zoom (3 min). Zoom the browser to 200%. Text should still be readable, with nothing overlapping or cut off. Navigation should still work.
  4. Contrast (4 min). Look for light grey text, text over photos and pale buttons. Check the doubtful ones with a contrast checker. The W3C keeps a list of evaluation tools, though it doesn't endorse specific products. Also look for anything conveyed by color alone, like "fields in red are required".
  5. Images (4 min). Run a free accessibility checker, or inspect your images in WordPress's media library. Headshots, logos that link home and informative graphics need meaningful alt text. Decorative flourishes should have empty alt.
  6. Headings (3 min). Use a heading-outline browser extension or checker. You should see one H1 and a logical H2/H3 outline that reads like a table of contents.
  7. Forms (3 min). Every field needs a visible label that stays put when you start typing. Submit the form empty. Are the errors described in text, and can you tell which field to fix?
  8. Media and documents (3 min). Play each video. Are there accurate captions? Open your most-downloaded PDF and try to select the text. If you can't, it's probably a scanned image that screen readers can't read.

Write down every failure along with the page URL. That list becomes the brief for your developer.

Automated checkers are useful but limited. They can't tell whether alt text is accurate, whether the reading order makes sense or whether a form error is understandable. Only a person can judge those, ideally including someone who uses assistive technology every day.

Are accessibility overlays a shortcut to ADA compliance?

No. An accessibility overlay is a third-party script that adds a toolbar or tries to repair a page automatically in the visitor's browser. It doesn't change your theme, your content or your PDFs. Your underlying problems stay in place. Overlays are often marketed as instant compliance, and that marketing has drawn federal attention.

On April 22, 2025, the FTC approved a final order requiring accessiBe to pay $1 million. The FTC alleged that the company's claims that its accessWidget plug-in could make any website WCAG-compliant were "false, misleading, or unsubstantiated." The order bars the company from making such claims without evidence. It also addresses reviews that were presented as independent. The order binds that one company. It isn't a ruling on every overlay product, but it's a good reason to be skeptical of any "one line of code" compliance promise.

Real fixes happen in the source: an accessible theme, correct markup, edited alt text and captions, labeled forms and remediated documents. For WordPress sites, start with a theme built with accessibility in mind and plugins that don't break keyboard access. Our roundups of the best WordPress themes for law firms and the best WordPress plugins for law firms cover what to look for.

How to work with a developer on accessibility

Most small firms don't need an enterprise audit. They do need a clear target and a clear scope. When you hire or brief a developer:

  1. Name the standard in writing. "Conform to WCAG 2.2 Level AA" is specific. "Make it ADA compliant" isn't.
  2. Hand over your self-check notes and list your key pages: home, practice areas, attorney bios, contact and intake, client portal login.
  3. Ask how they test. A good answer combines automated scans, manual keyboard testing and screen-reader spot checks. Be wary of anyone who only runs a scanner, or who proposes an overlay as the fix.
  4. Fix the template before the content. Theme-level problems like menus, focus styles, colors and headers repeat on every page. Fixing them once pays off fastest.
  5. Plan the content work. Alt text, captions and PDF remediation are often done by your team or a vendor, not the developer. Agree on who owns what.
  6. Re-test after changes. New plugins, page-builder edits and redesigns can quietly break accessibility. Add a quarterly check to your website maintenance routine.

Be cautious with any vendor that "guarantees" ADA compliance or lawsuit protection. No technical vendor can promise how a court or claimant will view your site.

Should your firm publish an accessibility statement?

It's good practice. A statement tells visitors you take accessibility seriously and, more importantly, how to reach you if something doesn't work. The W3C's guidance on accessibility statements recommends at least:

  • A commitment to accessibility for people with disabilities
  • The standard you aim for (for example, WCAG 2.2 Level AA)
  • Contact details for reporting problems: a phone number and email that someone actually monitors

The W3C also suggests listing known limitations, the steps you take and when the site was last reviewed. It offers a free statement generator. Keep the statement honest. Don't claim full conformance you haven't verified, and offer an alternative way to get the same information or service, such as a phone consultation. Link the statement from your site footer.
