FAQ

Is there an official "ADA compliant" certification for websites?

No. The DOJ has not set a detailed technical standard for private businesses' websites, and there's no government certification. Vendors that sell "ADA certified" badges are making their own claims. WCAG conformance is the closest thing to a measurable benchmark.

Should a law firm aim for WCAG 2.1 or WCAG 2.2?

Aim for WCAG 2.2 Level AA. It's the current W3C Recommendation, and because it's backwards compatible, meeting it also covers WCAG 2.1 AA, the version named in the DOJ's Title II rule for governments.

Not directly. The rule covers state and local governments and the services contractors provide on their behalf. A private firm's own website falls under Title III, where DOJ guidance remains flexible. Firms doing government contract work should check their contracts and ask counsel.

A widget alone won't. Overlays don't fix your underlying code, content or documents. The FTC's 2025 order against accessiBe shows regulators take "instant compliance" claims seriously. Some WordPress plugins do help, for example by adding skip links or flagging missing alt text, but they support real fixes rather than replacing them.

If a PDF delivers information or a service clients need, like an intake form, fee information or a guide, it should be usable with assistive technology. The simplest route is often to turn the content into a normal web page. Where a PDF is necessary, use a tagged PDF with real text, not a scan.

What should I do if I receive an ADA website demand letter?

Don't ignore it, and don't rush to install an overlay. Contact a lawyer experienced in ADA matters in your jurisdiction for advice. Separately, document your site's current state and start a real remediation plan with your developer.

Next steps

Accessibility for a small firm is mostly about doing ordinary things well: readable colors, real labels, keyboard-friendly menus, captioned videos and documents people can actually open. Here's where to start:

  1. Run the 30-minute self-check on your four most important pages this week.
  2. Fix theme-level issues first: contrast, focus, menus and forms.
  3. Work through content: alt text, headings, captions and PDFs.
  4. Publish an accessibility statement with a monitored contact method.
  5. Re-check every quarter and after any redesign. For legal questions, consult counsel and your state's guidance.

title.rendered: Cloudflare for Law Firm Websites: Free Security and Speed, Set Up Right (2026)

content.raw:
Quick answer: For most small law firm websites, Cloudflare's Free plan is worth setting up. It adds DNS, a global CDN, unmetered DDoS protection, a free SSL certificate and a basic web application firewall at no cost. Getting it right comes down to a few settings: SSL/TLS mode Full (strict), Always Use HTTPS, email records left DNS-only, and caching rules that never cache the WordPress admin or logged-in pages.

This guide explains what Cloudflare actually does and what the Free plan includes compared with Pro. It then walks through setup step by step, covers the settings that matter for a WordPress law firm site, and shows how to fix the two most common problems: redirect loops and mixed content.

Key takeaways

  • The Cloudflare Free plan ($0) includes unmetered DDoS protection, Universal SSL, a CDN and the Free Managed Ruleset. Pro costs $20/month billed annually or $25 billed monthly (as of November 2026).
  • Use Full (strict) SSL, not Flexible. Flexible leaves traffic between Cloudflare and your server unencrypted, and it is the most common cause of redirect loops.
  • Before you switch nameservers, check that your MX, SPF, DKIM and DMARC records were imported. Mail records are never proxied.
  • Cloudflare does not cache HTML by default. If you add a "cache everything" rule, make sure it skips /wp-admin, the login page and logged-in visitors.
  • If your host already runs Cloudflare for you (Kinsta does, for example), you may not need your own account at all.

What does Cloudflare do for a law firm website?

Cloudflare is a network that sits between your visitors and your web host. Visitors connect to Cloudflare, and Cloudflare then fetches the page from your server, filtering and caching along the way. You set this up by pointing your domain's nameservers to Cloudflare. Your site stays where it is.

The five services that matter for a firm site:

  • DNS: the address book for your domain. It tells the internet where your website and email live, and Cloudflare's DNS is fast and free.
  • CDN (content delivery network): copies of your images, CSS and JavaScript stored on servers around the world, so pages load faster for visitors who are far from your host.
  • WAF (web application firewall): rules that block known attack patterns, such as attempts to exploit vulnerable plugins, before they reach WordPress.
  • DDoS protection: absorbs floods of junk traffic meant to knock your site offline.
  • SSL/TLS: the certificate that puts the padlock in the browser and encrypts form submissions, including your contact or intake form.

Cloudflare is one layer of protection, not a full security program. You still need updates, backups, strong logins and a secure form. Our law firm website security checklist covers the rest.

Cloudflare Free vs Pro: what's included?

For a typical solo or small-firm brochure site, the Free plan covers what matters. The table below is based on Cloudflare's plans page and its developer docs, as of November 2026.

Sources: WAF managed rules, custom rules, rate limiting rules, Cache Rules.

When is Pro worth $20 a month?

Pro makes sense if your host offers no firewall of its own and you want the broader Cloudflare Managed Ruleset. It also helps if you need more than one rate limiting rule, or want image optimization and APO bundled together. The Free Managed Ruleset protects against "high-impact and widely exploited vulnerabilities". The Pro rulesets go further. If you're on a managed WordPress host with its own firewall, Free is usually enough.

Does your host already include Cloudflare?

Check this before you create a Cloudflare account. Some managed WordPress hosts run your site through Cloudflare automatically.

Kinsta is the clearest example. Its documentation describes a free Cloudflare integration. It includes Kinsta's own firewall rules, caching rules and a wildcard SSL certificate installed by default. You can still put your own Cloudflare account in front, on any plan including Free, but there are trade-offs:

  • Your nameservers move to Cloudflare, so you can no longer use Kinsta's DNS.
  • Kinsta says to point the root domain and www at your sitename.hosting.kinsta.cloud address with CNAME records, with the proxy left on.
  • Your firewall rules run first, and you can make them stricter. You can't unblock IPs that Kinsta has blocked.
  • Kinsta says Cloudflare APO and Kinsta Edge Caching are incompatible, so use one or the other.
  • For redirect loops, Kinsta's docs say to use Full, not Flexible.

Cloudflare calls this layered setup "Orange-to-Orange" and documents it in its Kinsta provider guide. If you're comparing hosts, our best hosting for law firm websites guide notes which ones bundle a CDN and firewall. For other hosts, look for "Cloudflare" in their docs or ask support before you add your own account.

How to set up Cloudflare on a WordPress law firm site

Plan for about an hour of work, plus up to 24 hours for nameserver activation. Do it at a quiet time and take a full backup first. Here is the order that avoids downtime, based on Cloudflare's full setup guide.

  1. Write down your current DNS records. Export or screenshot every record at your current DNS provider, especially MX, SPF, DKIM and DMARC. That gives you something to compare against later.
  2. Create a Cloudflare account and add your domain. In the dashboard, onboard the domain (the root, such as smithlaw.com) and choose the Free plan.
  3. Review the imported DNS records. Cloudflare scans your existing records, but its docs warn that the scan may miss some. Check the root domain, www, and every email record against your list from step 1. Add anything that's missing.
  4. Set proxy status correctly. Set your website's A/AAAA/CNAME records (root and www) to Proxied (orange cloud). Set mail hostnames, verification records and non-web services to DNS only (grey cloud). See the email section below.
  5. Turn off DNSSEC at your registrar, if it's on. Cloudflare warns that changing nameservers while DNSSEC is active "can cause your domain to become unreachable." You can turn it back on through Cloudflare after activation.
  6. Change your nameservers at the registrar. Replace the existing nameservers with the two Cloudflare gives you, copying them exactly. Domain registrars handle this in different places; our domain registrar guide covers the main ones.
  7. Wait for activation. Cloudflare emails you when the domain is active, which can take up to 24 hours. Don't edit DNS at the old provider during this time.
  8. Configure SSL/TLS, HTTPS and security settings. Use the settings table below.
  9. Test everything. Load the site over HTTPS, log in to WordPress, submit your contact form, and send and receive a test email.

If you're moving hosts at the same time, change one thing at a time. Our guide to moving a law firm website without downtime explains how to sequence it.

Recommended Cloudflare settings for a law firm WordPress site

These settings are a reasonable starting point for a typical brochure-style firm site on the Free plan. Make one change at a time and test after each.

Why "Full (strict)" and not Flexible?

Full (strict) encrypts traffic between Cloudflare and your host and checks that your host's certificate is valid. Per Cloudflare's docs, the certificate must be unexpired, match your hostname, and come from a public certificate authority (such as Let's Encrypt) or Cloudflare's free Origin CA. Most hosts install a Let's Encrypt certificate automatically, so this usually just works.

Flexible encrypts only the visitor-to-Cloudflare leg. Data from your intake form then travels to your server unencrypted, even though the browser shows a padlock. For a law firm handling prospective-client information, that's a poor trade. Full (without "strict") encrypts both legs but doesn't validate the origin certificate. Some zones now show an Automatic SSL/TLS option that picks the most secure mode your server supports.

Bot Fight Mode: on or off?

Bot Fight Mode is a free, one-switch setting that challenges traffic matching known bot patterns. According to Cloudflare, it applies to the whole domain, can't be bypassed with WAF custom rules, and "may challenge API or mobile app traffic". Turn it on, then test your contact form and any outside integrations, such as a chat widget, scheduling tool or uptime monitor. If something breaks and you can't exempt it, turn Bot Fight Mode off and rely on the WAF and Turnstile.

Use Turnstile to stop contact form spam

Turnstile is Cloudflare's CAPTCHA replacement. It checks whether a visitor is human, usually without asking them to solve a puzzle. The Free plan allows up to 20 widgets with unlimited challenges. It works on any website, even one not proxied through Cloudflare. Major WordPress form plugins offer Turnstile as a spam-protection option. Check yours, then add it to your intake form. Our guide to adding a secure contact form covers the rest of form security.

Caching rules for WordPress: what not to cache

By default, Cloudflare caches static files (images, CSS, JS, PDFs, fonts) but does not cache HTML. That default is safe for WordPress. Problems start when someone adds a "cache everything" rule to speed up pages. A logged-in page can then get cached and served to the public, admin bar and all.

If you cache HTML, add a bypass Cache Rule that matches any of:

  • URI path starts with /wp-admin
  • URI path contains /wp-login.php
  • A cookie containing wordpress_logged_in (the cookie WordPress sets for logged-in users)
  • A cookie containing wp-postpass (password-protected pages), and any client-portal or form-preview paths your site uses

Order matters. Cache Rules stack, and Cloudflare's docs say "the value in the last matching rule wins". Put your bypass rule after any cache-everything rule. The simpler alternative is APO ($5/month on Free, included on Pro), which is built specifically for WordPress and requires the official Cloudflare plugin. If your host already does page caching, as Kinsta's Edge Caching does, don't stack another HTML cache on top.

Don't break your email: DNS records to check

Broken email is the costliest mistake in a Cloudflare move, because missed client email is a real problem for a law firm. The rules are simple:

  • MX and TXT records can't be proxied. Cloudflare's proxy docs say only A, AAAA and CNAME records can be proxied, and MX and TXT records are "always DNS-only."
  • Mail hostnames must be DNS only. If your MX points to something like mail.smithlaw.com, that A record must be grey-clouded. Cloudflare's email records guide shows exactly this.
  • Keep SPF, DKIM and DMARC exactly as they were. These TXT (and sometimes CNAME) records prove your email is genuine. Verification CNAMEs, such as DKIM keys published as CNAMEs, should also be DNS only.

Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 publish the exact records you need. See our law firm email setup guide (SPF, DKIM and DMARC) to confirm every record before you change nameservers.

Troubleshooting: redirect loops and mixed content

How do I fix ERR_TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS after enabling Cloudflare?

Switch your SSL/TLS mode from Flexible to Full (strict). This is the most common cause. In Flexible mode, Cloudflare requests your site over plain HTTP. Your host redirects that to HTTPS, and Cloudflare sends the visitor back to HTTP, which creates a loop. If the loop continues, check for conflicting redirects. These can come from a Cloudflare Redirect Rule or Page Rule, a WordPress redirect plugin, or HSTS combined with an origin that redirects HTTPS back to HTTP.

How do I fix mixed content warnings?

Mixed content means an HTTPS page loads some files, usually images or scripts, over plain HTTP. Browsers then drop the padlock or block those files. Turn on Automatic HTTPS Rewrites first. Cloudflare notes that it can't fix everything, especially URLs added by JavaScript or CSS at runtime, and that "forcing HTTPS does not resolve issues with mixed content". For a permanent fix, make sure WordPress's Site Address and WordPress Address both use https://. Then update old http:// links in your content with a search-and-replace tool after taking a backup.

Error 526 or 525 after switching to Full (strict)

A 526 error means Cloudflare couldn't validate your host's certificate. It may be expired, self-signed, or issued for the wrong hostname, or the host may not accept HTTPS on port 443. Ask your host to issue or renew a certificate that covers both the root domain and www, or install a Cloudflare Origin CA certificate. Don't fall back to Flexible to make the error go away.

FAQ

Is Cloudflare's free plan enough for a law firm website?

For most solo and small-firm websites, yes. The Free plan includes unmetered DDoS protection, Universal SSL, a CDN, the Free Managed Ruleset, five WAF custom rules, one rate limiting rule and Bot Fight Mode. Consider Pro ($20/month billed annually as of November 2026) if you want the broader managed rulesets and your host has no firewall of its own.

Will Cloudflare affect my firm's email?

Not if your DNS records are imported correctly. MX and TXT records are always DNS-only, and any mail hostname's A record must stay grey-clouded. Compare every MX, SPF, DKIM and DMARC record with your old DNS before switching nameservers.

Do I need the Cloudflare WordPress plugin?

No. Cloudflare works at the DNS level without a plugin. You need the official plugin only for APO. It is also handy for purging the cache from WordPress after you update pages.

Does Cloudflare replace a WordPress security plugin?

Partly. Cloudflare blocks many attacks before they reach your server. It doesn't update plugins, scan files for malware or enforce two-factor login. Keep those covered by your host, a maintenance plan or a security plugin.

Can I use Cloudflare with Squarespace or Wix?

You can use Cloudflare for DNS, but hosted builders generally handle their own SSL and CDN, and Cloudflare's docs note that some SaaS-hosted sites aren't compatible with its proxy. Follow your builder's instructions for DNS records. Our Squarespace vs WordPress vs Wix comparison covers how each platform handles hosting.

Does Cloudflare make my website ethics-compliant or confidential?

No. Encryption and a firewall are reasonable safeguards, but your duties around client information come from your state's rules of professional conduct. Check with your state bar for guidance on technology and confidentiality.

Next steps

First, check whether your host already provides Cloudflare. If it doesn't, back up the site and record your DNS, then add the domain on the Free plan. Confirm the email records, switch nameservers, and set Full (strict) with Always Use HTTPS. Add Turnstile to your forms and leave HTML caching alone unless you also set bypass rules. Then work through the rest of our security checklist.

Want this handled for you? ProSiteGuide builds and maintains fast, secure WordPress sites for law firms. Book a free consultation.

Cloudflare is one part of performance; our guide to speeding up a law firm website covers the rest, from images to scripts.

Cloud firewalls like Sucuri work similarly, as covered in the best WordPress security plugins for law firms.

If you are weighing a paid firewall and cleanup service instead, see our Sucuri review for law firms.

The Free plan includes unmetered DDoS protection, Universal SSL, a CDN, the Free Managed Ruleset, five WAF custom rules, one rate limiting rule and Bot Fight Mode. Consider Pro ($20/month billed annually as of November 2026) if you want the broader managed rulesets and your host has no firewall of its own.

Will Cloudflare affect my firm’s email?

Not if your DNS records are imported correctly. MX and TXT records are always DNS-only, and any mail hostname’s A record must stay grey-clouded. Compare every MX, SPF, DKIM and DMARC record with your old DNS before switching nameservers.

Do I need the Cloudflare WordPress plugin?

No. Cloudflare works at the DNS level without a plugin. You need the official plugin only for APO. It is also handy for purging the cache from WordPress after you update pages.

Does Cloudflare replace a WordPress security plugin?

Partly. Cloudflare blocks many attacks before they reach your server. It doesn’t update plugins, scan files for malware or enforce two-factor login. Keep those covered by your host, a maintenance plan or a security plugin.

Can I use Cloudflare with Squarespace or Wix?

You can use Cloudflare for DNS, but hosted builders generally handle their own SSL and CDN, and Cloudflare’s docs note that some SaaS-hosted sites aren’t compatible with its proxy. Follow your builder’s instructions for DNS records. Our Squarespace vs WordPress vs Wix comparison covers how each platform handles hosting.

Does Cloudflare make my website ethics-compliant or confidential?

No. Encryption and a firewall are reasonable safeguards, but your duties around client information come from your state’s rules of professional conduct. Check with your state bar for guidance on technology and confidentiality.

Next steps

First, check whether your host already provides Cloudflare. If it doesn’t, back up the site and record your DNS, then add the domain on the Free plan. Confirm the email records, switch nameservers, and set Full (strict) with Always Use HTTPS. Add Turnstile to your forms and leave HTML caching alone unless you also set bypass rules. Then work through the rest of our security checklist.

title.raw: Smith.ai vs Ruby (2026): Which Virtual Receptionist Is Right for Your Law Firm?
title.rendered: Smith.ai vs Ruby (2026): Which Virtual Receptionist Is Right for Your Law Firm?

content.raw:
Quick answer: Choose Smith.ai if your firm takes a lot of new-client calls that run long (intake, qualification, conflict questions) or you want a cheap AI option. Its plans bill per call and list legal extras like conflict checks and Clio, MyCase and Lawmatics integrations. Choose Ruby if you want a live person to answer every call and most of your calls are short (messages, transfers, "is my attorney in?"). Ruby bills per receptionist minute, so short calls cost less.

Below: a verdict by firm type, a side-by-side table, worked billing examples using each vendor's published prices (as of November 2026), and the confidentiality questions to ask before anyone outside your firm answers your phone.

Smith.ai vs Ruby: the verdict by firm type

How we compared

We have not used either service. This comparison is based only on each vendor's official pricing pages, feature pages, integration pages and billing documents, opened in November 2026. Where the vendors don't publish something (for example, Ruby's overage rate), we say so instead of guessing. Prices change often, so confirm with the vendor before you sign up.

Smith.ai vs Ruby comparison table

Sources: Smith.ai receptionist pricing, Smith.ai AI Receptionist pricing, Smith.ai chat pricing, Smith.ai legal page, Ruby pricing, Ruby integrations. All prices as of November 2026.

Smith.ai pricing explained

Smith.ai sells three things that are easy to mix up: an AI Receptionist, human Virtual Receptionists, and website chat. All of them bill by the call or chat, not by the minute.

Human Virtual Receptionist plans

On the receptionist pricing page (as of November 2026), plans start at $300/month for 30 calls ($11.50 per extra call), then $810 for 90 calls ($10.50 extra) and $2,100 for 300 calls ($8.50 extra). The page says live agents staff the service 24/7 at no extra charge, and that wrong numbers and spam don't count toward your quota as long as forwarded calls pass Caller ID.

The base price includes lead qualification, intake (five short-answer questions), a dedicated number or porting of your existing one, and one CRM integration. Most extras cost a small amount per call. These are the ones most relevant to law firms:

  • Appointment booking: $1.50 per call
  • Extended intake (six more questions): $1.50 per call
  • Conflict checks: $0.50 per call
  • Text and email follow-up: $0.50 per call
  • Call recording and transcription: $0.25 per call
  • Accept payments (including LawPay): $1.00 per call
  • Dedicated Spanish line: $1.00 per call
  • Extra CRM integrations: $0.50 per call each

Add-ons apply to the calls that use them, so a firm that adds booking, conflict checks and recording can pay more per call than the plan price suggests.

AI Receptionist plans

The AI Receptionist is much cheaper. As of November 2026 it has a Free plan with 25 real calls a month ($3.00 per extra call), Pro from $150/month for 75 calls (higher tiers at 150 and 300 calls), and Enterprise from $500/month for 300 calls. Every tier lists 24/7 answering, recording, transcripts and summaries, lead qualification, AI scheduling, and native integrations including Clio. Smith.ai says callers can be transferred to a live, North America-based receptionist. Cancellation needs 30 days' notice.

Before you put an AI on your firm's main line, think about it carefully. Callers to a law firm are often stressed and describe sensitive facts. Decide in advance which calls should go straight to a person.

Ruby receptionist pricing explained

The Ruby pricing page (as of November 2026) lists four receptionist plans. The plans differ only in how many minutes they include:

*Our math: plan price divided by included minutes.

Ruby says there are no extra fees for activation, onboarding, setup or customization, and that optional AI enhancements come with every plan at no extra cost. Its homepage says "No long-term contracts." Ruby doesn't publish its overage rate. Its billing FAQ says extra minutes are billed "at your plan's predetermined rate", that you aren't moved to a bigger plan automatically, and that unused minutes don't roll over. Ask for the overage rate in writing.

What counts as a Ruby "receptionist minute"?

Ruby's billing FAQ says it bills receptionist time, not total call time:

  • The clock starts when a receptionist picks up and stops when they transfer the call (to you or voicemail) or hang up.
  • Hold time counts. Your talk time after a transfer does not.
  • Calls round up to the next 30-second mark, so a 10-second call is billed as half a minute.
  • Outbound call assists count the specialist's call time plus the time spent emailing you the result.
  • Ruby says it doesn't bill for calls outside your live answering hours.

One inconsistency: Ruby's per-minute vs per-call article describes rounding in 60-second increments, but the billing FAQ says 30 seconds. Ask Ruby which one applies to your contract.

Per call vs per minute: what a month might cost

Billing model matters more than headline price. Here's the key comparison at included rates, as of November 2026:

  • A Smith.ai Starter call costs $10.00 ($300 ÷ 30 calls), however long it lasts.
  • A Ruby 200-minute plan minute costs $3.60 ($720 ÷ 200).
  • So at those rates, calls that average less than about 2.8 billable minutes ($10.00 ÷ $3.60) tend to favor Ruby, and longer calls tend to favor Smith.ai.

The scenarios below are illustrations, not quotes. They assume no add-ons, no spam, and that your calls fit the plan described. Ruby overage can't be priced because the rate isn't published.

Example 1: Small intake practice, 60 calls averaging 3 minutes

  • Smith.ai (human): Starter $300 + 30 extra calls × $11.50 = $645. That's cheaper than moving up to Basic at $810. Starter plus overage stays cheaper than Basic up to about 74 calls a month.
  • Ruby: 60 × 3 = 180 receptionist minutes, which fits the 200-minute plan at $720. Hold time and rounding up could push you closer to 200.
  • Smith.ai AI Receptionist: Pro at 75 calls is $150, if you're comfortable with AI answering first.

Example 2: Same 60 calls, but long intake calls averaging 6 minutes

  • Smith.ai (human): still $645, because call length doesn't change the price. Add $90 if every call uses extended intake ($1.50 × 60).
  • Ruby: 360 minutes. That's the 500-minute plan at $1,725, or the 200-minute plan ($720) plus 160 overage minutes at a rate Ruby didn't publish.

Example 3: Busy existing-client line, 150 calls averaging 1.5 minutes

  • Ruby: 225 minutes, so the 200-minute plan at $720 plus 25 overage minutes. With 30-second rounding, a 1-minute-10-second call is billed as 1.5 minutes.
  • Smith.ai (human): Basic $810 + 60 × $10.50 = $1,440. Pro at $2,100 would be worse at this volume.

To use this for your own firm, pull last month's call count and total minutes from your phone system. Divide minutes by calls to get your average call length, then run both models.

AI vs human: how each service answers the phone

Ruby is human-first. Its homepage says, "An AI virtual receptionist that independently picks up and conducts the call isn't how Ruby works." AI is used for transcripts, sentiment analysis and call flows that help its receptionists.

Smith.ai gives you a choice. Its legal page says all calls on Virtual Receptionist plans are answered by a real person 24/7, by agents working from home offices across North America. Its AI Receptionist answers first and can hand callers to a person. Its chat plans are described as "live-staffed web chats — powered by AI."

Integrations: Clio, MyCase and CRMs

Both connect to the big legal practice-management tools. Smith.ai names Clio, MyCase and Lawmatics, plus Zapier. Its first CRM integration is free and each extra one costs $0.50 per call. Ruby's integrations page lists Clio, MyCase, Rocket Matter, Lawmatics, Filevine and Law Ruler, plus HubSpot, Salesforce, Zoho, Keap and Zapier. Neither page we reviewed names PracticePanther or Smokeball, so if you use one of those, ask whether Zapier is the route. If you haven't chosen practice software yet, see our Clio vs MyCase vs PracticePanther comparison.

Confidentiality and intake: what law firms should check

A receptionist service talks to people who may become your clients. Under ABA Model Rule 1.18 (duties to prospective clients), information a prospective client shares can create confidentiality duties. In some situations it can also create conflicts that limit who the firm can represent later, even if you never take the case. Ethics rules also generally make lawyers responsible for supervising non-lawyer help, including outside vendors. Your state's version of these rules may differ, so check your state bar's guidance and ethics opinions.

Practical steps, whichever service you pick:

  1. Limit early intake. Script the receptionist to collect names, contact details, opposing parties and a one-line matter type, not the full story, until conflicts are cleared.
  2. Run conflicts early. Smith.ai offers a conflict-check add-on. With Ruby, ask how opposing-party names can be passed to your conflict process.
  3. No legal advice. Write the script so receptionists (and any AI) never assess a case, quote fees you haven't approved, or promise representation.
  4. Know where data goes. Find out where recordings, transcripts and intake notes are stored, who can access them, and how long they're kept. Ask for the vendor's security documentation.
  5. Health information. If callers may share medical details, note that Smith.ai says it isn't HIPAA-compliant, while Ruby lists HIPAA-compliant services.
  6. Match your website. Your web forms are the other front door. Use the same rules there; see how to add a secure contact form to a law firm website.

Pros and cons

Smith.ai

  • Pro: Per-call billing keeps long intake calls predictable.
  • Pro: Legal extras (conflict checks, LawPay payments, Clio/MyCase/Lawmatics) are priced openly.
  • Pro: AI tier from $0 to $150/month for very small firms.
  • Pro: 30-day money-back guarantee for new clients, and published overage rates.
  • Con: Per-call add-ons add up quickly.
  • Con: Expensive for lots of short calls.
  • Con: Not HIPAA-compliant.

Ruby

  • Pro: Live humans answer every call, with no AI on the line.
  • Pro: Cheaper for short calls and transfers.
  • Pro: Broad legal integration list. No setup fees.
  • Pro: HIPAA-compliant services listed.
  • Con: Overage rate not published.
  • Con: Hold time is billable, and calls round up.
  • Con: Long intake calls get expensive. No guarantee or trial listed.

Alternatives to consider

  • Other legal answering services. Several services focus on law firms. Compare them on the same points: billing unit, overage, intake depth and integrations.
  • A part-time in-house receptionist. Usually costs more, but gives you full control over confidentiality and training.
  • Better self-service intake. A secure web form that feeds your practice-management software can take pressure off the phone. Pair it with voicemail-to-email on your firm's domain email.
  • Chat only. If most leads come from your website, a chat plan from either vendor may cost less than full phone coverage.

FAQ

Is Smith.ai or Ruby cheaper for a law firm?

It depends on call length. At included rates (as of November 2026), a Smith.ai Starter call costs $10.00 and a minute on Ruby's 200-minute plan costs $3.60. Calls averaging under about 2.8 billable minutes tend to favor Ruby, and longer calls tend to favor Smith.ai. Smith.ai's AI Receptionist ($150/month for 75 calls on Pro) is cheaper than either human service.

Does Ruby use AI to answer calls?

No. Ruby says live receptionists answer calls, and AI only helps behind the scenes with transcripts and call flows.

Do both offer 24/7 answering?

Yes. Smith.ai lists 24/7 live staffing at no extra charge, and Ruby lists 24/7 coverage including weekends and holidays. Both let you limit answering to the hours you choose.

Can they schedule consultations and take payments?

Yes. Smith.ai charges $1.50 per call for booking and $1.00 per call for payments (LawPay is supported) on human plans. Ruby lists scheduling and payment collection as features but doesn't show separate prices on its pricing page.

Are there long-term contracts?

Neither requires one. Smith.ai is month-to-month (10% off for 12 months) and offers a 30-day money-back guarantee to new clients. Ruby says "No long-term contracts" but doesn't publish cancellation terms, so ask before signing.

Is it ethical to use a virtual receptionist for legal intake?

Many firms do, but the lawyer stays responsible for supervising the vendor and protecting what prospective clients share. Keep early intake short, run conflicts before collecting details, and check your state bar's guidance.

Bottom line and next steps

Pick Smith.ai for intake-heavy practices, legal add-ons and the low-cost AI option. Pick Ruby for a human-only front desk and lots of short calls. Before you decide:

  1. Pull last month's call count and total minutes, and run the per-call vs per-minute math above.
  2. Ask Ruby for its overage rate and rounding increment in writing. Ask Smith.ai which add-ons your script would trigger.
  3. Write your intake script with conflict checks and a "no legal advice" rule.
  4. Make sure your website's forms and overall site follow the same intake rules as the phone.

Want this handled for you? ProSiteGuide builds and maintains fast, secure WordPress sites for law firms. Book a free consultation.

Want clients to book consultations online instead? See our comparison of scheduling tools for law firms.

If you also want a hosted office phone system behind your receptionist, compare VoIP phone systems for law firms.

Jayce also sells website design, hosting setup and maintenance services, which never influence our recommendations.

title.rendered: Kinsta vs WP Engine vs SiteGround for Law Firm Websites (2026)

content.raw:
Quick answer: For most small law firms that want hosting they never have to think about, Kinsta is the simplest pick. It costs $35/month or $350/year, and that is the same price at renewal. It also includes free migrations done by its own team. WP Engine suits firms that work with an agency or developer and want separate staging and development copies of the site plus 30 days of backups. Its $28/month entry price is a first-year offer billed annually, and it does not publish the renewal price. SiteGround is the lowest-cost option and the only one of the three that hosts your email, but its $3.99 intro price renews at $29.99/month.

This comparison covers the managed tier: hosts that look after WordPress for you. For a broader comparison that includes budget shared hosting such as Hostinger, see our guide to the best hosting for law firm websites.

Verdict by firm type

  • Solo or 2–3 lawyer firm, no developer on call: Kinsta. The price stays flat, its staff migrate the site for free, every site gets one-click staging, and support runs 24/7 by chat.
  • Firm with a marketing agency or in-house developer: WP Engine. Each site gets production, staging and development environments, backups kept at least 30 days, and a Cloudflare-powered CDN. Phone support and an uptime SLA (a written uptime promise) come only with the much pricier Business plan.
  • Budget-first firm that wants website and email with one company: SiteGround GrowBig. Email accounts, daily backups and staging are included. Budget for the renewal price, not the intro price.
  • Firm that has outgrown basic shared hosting: pick Kinsta or WP Engine. Then follow our guide to moving a law firm website without downtime.

Kinsta vs WP Engine vs SiteGround: side-by-side

The table compares each host's entry plan for a single WordPress site. Prices are in USD as of November 2026 and exclude tax.

How we compared

We have not run our own tests of these three hosts, and we don't give scores. This comparison is based on each company's official pricing pages, plan details, documentation and terms, checked in November 2026. We looked at what matters to a small firm's website: what you pay now and at renewal, backups and restores, staging, migration help, email and support.

One limitation: SiteGround's website blocked our automated checks while we wrote this. Its figures come from our November 2026 check of SiteGround's WordPress hosting page, done for our other hosting guides. Confirm them on SiteGround's checkout page before you buy.

What does each host really cost?

Kinsta pricing

Kinsta's pricing page lists its entry single-site plan at $35/month on monthly billing. Paying annually costs $350/year, which works out to about $30/month. Kinsta says the plan renews at the same price, and it is currently running a "first month free" offer. Adding a second site costs $30/month.

WP Engine pricing

WP Engine's plans page shows the Essential plan at $28/month, billed annually, which means paying $336 upfront. The fine print says this is first-year pricing for new customers on Essential plans only, and that "product renewal pricing [is] subject to change." The page shows no monthly-billed Essential price. The next tier, Business, is listed at $400/month billed annually. Two more terms are worth knowing. WP Engine's FAQ says it charges overage fees when visits exceed your plan limit ($2 per 1,000 extra visits on several plan families). It also says cancellations require 30 days' notice.

SiteGround pricing

SiteGround's GrowBig plan is $3.99/month for the first 12 months when you prepay a year. After that it renews at $29.99/month. That makes the first year cheap and the later years comparable to Kinsta.

Total cost over 3 years: an example

Intro prices make hosting look cheaper than it is, so here is the cost of one firm website over three years. Assumptions: one site, entry plan, annual billing, no add-ons or overages, and US prices as of November 2026 before tax. Domain and email costs are not included.

Two things change the picture. First, Kinsta and WP Engine don't host email. If your firm doesn't already pay for Google Workspace or Microsoft 365, add that per-user cost; our law firm business email guide covers setup. Most firms should use one of those anyway, for reasons explained below. Second, ask WP Engine for the renewal price in writing before you sign, because its year-two cost is the one number we could not pin down.

Kinsta: pros and cons for law firms

Kinsta is a managed WordPress host. Its staff handle the server, caching and backups, so your firm only looks after the site itself.

Pros

  • Flat pricing. The renewal price matches the first-year price, so the budget is predictable.
  • Hands-off migration. Kinsta's migrations page says migrations are "free and unlimited." Its team does the work, usually within one business day.
  • Strong backup tooling. According to Kinsta's backup docs, it takes a daily backup and also backs up automatically before restores, staging pushes and plugin updates. You can keep up to 5 manual backups and download one backup per week. For more frequent backups, Kinsta sells a 6-hourly add-on ($20/site per month) and an hourly add-on ($100/site per month).
  • Free staging on every plan. Kinsta's staging docs describe a free staging copy for each site. You can push only files or only selected database tables to the live site, which helps avoid overwriting new contact-form entries.

Cons

  • No phone support. Kinsta's support docs say support is 24/7 by chat inside the MyKinsta dashboard, and they explain why there is no phone line.
  • No email hosting. Kinsta's email docs say it doesn't provide email on its plans. It sends only site emails, such as form notifications, with a cap of 150 per day on entry plans.
  • Shorter backup retention on entry plans (14 days) than WP Engine.

For a deeper look at Kinsta alone, see our Kinsta review for law firms.

WP Engine: pros and cons for law firms

WP Engine is a managed WordPress host whose plans lean toward agencies and developers, with multiple environments per site and Git-based deployment on higher tiers.

Pros

  • Three environments per site. WP Engine's environment docs describe separate production, staging and development copies. Your developer can build a redesign in development while a plugin update is tested in staging.
  • Longer backup retention. The backup and restore guide says daily backups are made automatically and kept for 30 days. You can create a manual backup before any change and restore from the dashboard. The plans page states retention of 30 to 60 days.
  • Cloudflare-powered CDN and auto-renewing SSL on Essential.
  • Free self-serve migration. The FAQ says "it's free to migrate a site to WP Engine" using its migration plugin. You can test the copied site before switching your domain.

Cons

  • Renewal price is unknown at signup. The $28 entry price is a first-year offer, and it must be paid annually.
  • Phone support, an uptime SLA and managed migrations sit on Business, which is listed at $400/month. Essential gets 24/7 chat.
  • No email hosting, and limited email support. WP Engine's scope of support says it does not provide nameservers or email servers. It offers only "limited support on outgoing email" and recommends a third-party email service.
  • Overage fees and a 30-day cancellation notice, per its FAQ.

SiteGround: pros and cons for law firms

SiteGround's GrowBig is shared hosting with WordPress tools built in. It is cheaper than the other two but less hands-off.

Pros

  • Lowest cost over three years in our example, even after the renewal increase.
  • Email included. It is the only one of the three that hosts mailboxes on your domain.
  • Daily backups (up to 30 copies), plus on-demand backups and staging on GrowBig and up.

Cons

  • Big renewal jump, from $3.99 to $29.99/month.
  • Do-it-yourself migration. SiteGround's free WordPress Automatic Migrator plugin does the copying. Having SiteGround staff transfer the site is a paid service.
  • Shared hosting: your site shares a server with other customers' sites. It is fine for a typical brochure site, but it gives less headroom than a managed plan.

Does having email with your web host matter for a law firm?

Usually it doesn't. Neither Kinsta nor WP Engine hosts mailboxes, and WP Engine's support docs recommend third-party email hosting. Keeping email separate also means a website problem or host move does not take your inbox down with it. Most firms put mailboxes on Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 and keep the website wherever it runs best.

The detail that matters more is how your contact form emails get delivered. Kinsta caps site emails on entry plans, and WP Engine recommends a third-party sending service. On any of the three hosts, route form notifications through a proper email service with SPF, DKIM and DMARC set up, so intake messages don't land in spam. Our guide to a secure contact form for a law firm website covers this step by step.

Who should choose which?

Choose Kinsta if…

  • You want someone else to move the site and look after the server.
  • You prefer a flat price over a teaser rate.
  • Chat support is fine for you.

Choose WP Engine if…

  • An agency or developer manages your site and wants staging plus development environments.
  • You value 30+ days of backups.
  • You are comfortable with annual billing and will get the renewal quote in writing.

Choose SiteGround if…

  • Cost is the deciding factor.
  • You want website and email under one bill.
  • You or your developer can handle the migration with a plugin.

Alternatives

If even GrowBig is more than a one-page solo site needs, budget hosts such as Hostinger are covered in our law firm hosting roundup. Whichever host you pick, the host only handles part of security. Plugin updates, user accounts and form handling are still your job, so work through our law firm website security checklist.

FAQ

Kinsta vs WP Engine: which is better for a small law firm?

For a firm without a developer, Kinsta is easier: flat pricing, migration done for you and staging on every plan. WP Engine fits better when an agency runs the site and wants separate staging and development environments and longer backup retention.

WP Engine vs SiteGround: is the extra cost worth it?

In year one WP Engine costs far more. From year two, SiteGround's $29.99/month renewal is in the same range as WP Engine's first-year rate. You'd pay WP Engine's premium for its development environment, longer backup retention and Cloudflare CDN. SiteGround's edge is included email.

Do any of these hosts offer phone support?

Kinsta does not; its support is 24/7 chat. WP Engine offers phone support on Business and higher plans, not on Essential. We could not verify SiteGround's current support channels for this article, so check its site.

Can I move my existing firm website to these hosts for free?

Yes, with differences. Kinsta's team migrates sites for free. WP Engine and SiteGround provide free plugins that you or your developer run, and SiteGround charges for a staff-run transfer. Keep the old host active until the new site is tested.

Is managed WordPress hosting required for confidentiality?

No hosting plan by itself makes a site compliant with your professional duties. What matters more is not collecting sensitive case details through website forms, keeping WordPress updated and limiting who has admin access. Check your state bar's guidance on technology and client confidentiality.

Conclusion and next steps

Kinsta is the low-maintenance default for small firms, WP Engine is the developer-friendly option with a renewal price you'll need to confirm, and SiteGround is the budget choice with email included. To decide:

  1. Decide who maintains the site: you, a staff member, or a developer or agency.
  2. Compare three-year costs, not first-month prices, and add email if your host doesn't include it.
  3. Confirm renewal prices and support channels on the checkout page.
  4. Plan the move with a tested copy before you switch DNS.

Leaning toward the budget option? Read our full SiteGround review for law firms.

content.raw:
Quick answer: Kinsta is worth it for a law firm that runs its site on WordPress, wants the host to handle security, backups and speed, and would rather pay more than babysit a server. Its entry WordPress plans cost $35 a month, or $30 a month on annual billing (as of November 2026). That is several times what budget shared hosting costs. Below is a plain-English review for solo and small firms: what you get, what it really costs, where the extra charges hide, and when a cheaper host makes more sense.

Kinsta verdict: who it's best for (and who should skip it)

Kinsta is a managed WordPress host. "Managed" means the host looks after the server, caching, backups, firewall and updates to the hosting stack. You or your web developer look after the website itself.

Kinsta is a good fit if your firm…

  • Gets most new clients through its website and can't afford downtime or a hacked homepage.
  • Has a developer or agency making changes and wants a safe staging copy to test them first.

title.raw: Google Workspace vs Microsoft 365 for Law Firms (2026): Prices, eDiscovery and Which to Choose
title.rendered: Google Workspace vs Microsoft 365 for Law Firms (2026): Prices, eDiscovery and Which to Choose

content.raw:
Quick answer: Most small law firms that draft in Word every day should choose Microsoft 365 Business Standard. It costs $14 per user per month on an annual plan and includes the desktop Office apps. Choose Google Workspace if your firm works mostly in the browser, values simple sharing, and doesn't depend on complex Word templates. If you want built-in retention and legal holds, the plans to compare are Google Workspace Business Plus (which includes Vault) and Microsoft 365 Business Premium, both $22 per user per month on annual billing as of November 2026.

Most comparisons of these two suites for lawyers were written between 2016 and 2022. Since then both vendors have changed plan names, prices and AI bundles. This guide uses the current US pricing pages and admin documentation, then gives you a decision framework for your type of firm.

How much do Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 cost per user?

At the entry and middle tiers the prices are now identical. Below are the published US list prices per user per month with a one-year commitment, as of November 2026. Sources: the Google Workspace pricing page and Microsoft's Microsoft 365 business plan comparison.

Some details are easy to miss on those pages:

  • Month-to-month costs more. Google's pricing toggle says a one-year commitment saves 16%. Microsoft's plan pages list the monthly price separately. For Business Standard it's $16.80 instead of $14.
  • Microsoft now leads with "with Copilot" bundles. Its comparison page puts Business Standard with Copilot ($23.50) and Business Premium with Copilot ($32) first. If you don't want Microsoft's AI add-on yet, choose the plain plan.
  • Microsoft also sells "no Teams" versions. Business Standard (no Teams), for example, is listed at $10.79. That can suit a firm that already uses Zoom.
  • Both suites cap their business plans at 300 users. That limit won't affect a small firm.
Quick pick

Choosing Google Workspace? Start through our referral link → and ask us for a 10% first-year promo code.

We may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. It never changes our recommendations.

Side-by-side: what each suite gives a small law firm

Does your firm need desktop Word and Excel?

Answer this first, because it settles the choice for many firms. Legal work tends to run on Word: tracked changes passed back and forth with opposing counsel, pleading and caption templates, numbered paragraphs, tables of authorities and court-specific formatting. Courts, clients and other firms will keep sending you .docx files.

Google Docs can open and edit Office files, and it's very good for live co-editing. The friction comes from complex formatting going back and forth. A heavily styled brief or a template full of macros is where browser editors tend to struggle. If your lawyers or staff spend hours in Word each day, the desktop app matters.

You can also combine the two. A firm can keep Google Workspace for email and files, then buy Microsoft 365 Apps for business ($10 per user per month on annual billing as of November 2026) for the people who need desktop Word. Microsoft's page lists desktop Word, Excel, PowerPoint and Outlook plus 1 TB of storage, but not business email hosting. Run the numbers, though. Google Business Standard plus Apps for business costs more per person than Microsoft 365 Business Standard on its own.

Retention, legal holds and eDiscovery: Google Vault vs Microsoft Purview

Retention means keeping email and files for a set period, even if a user deletes them. A legal hold preserves data indefinitely for a matter. eDiscovery means searching and exporting that data. Google's pricing page confirms this: Business Plus adds "eDiscovery" and "Vault to retain, archive, and search data."

  • Organization-wide retention policies are licensed with Business Premium (and enterprise E3/E5). Business Basic and Standard are only listed for Teams chat retention.
  • The archive mailbox is 50 GB on Basic and Standard. Business Premium is listed among the licenses that allow a 1.5 TB archive.
  • Purview Audit (Standard) is listed for Business Basic, Standard and Premium.

Bar guidance doesn't prefer either vendor. It asks lawyers to make reasonable efforts to protect client information. North Carolina's 2011 Formal Ethics Opinion 6 allows cloud software "provided the lawyer uses reasonable care to safeguard confidential client information."   • Clio: the Clio for Gmail add-on, published by Clio on the Google Workspace Marketplace, logs emails and attachments to matters and adds contacts and time entries from your inbox. Clio also markets an Outlook add-in. Check Clio's integrations directory for its current requirements.

  2. Litigation or transactional firm that lives in Word: Microsoft 365 Business Standard ($14). You get desktop Office, Outlook and 1 TB per user at the same price.
  3. Firm that wants retention and holds without enterprise licensing: Google Workspace Business Plus ($22) with Vault.
  4. Firm with an IT provider managing Windows laptops and phones: Microsoft 365 Business Premium ($22). It adds Intune, Defender, retention policies and the larger archive. Confirm eDiscovery licensing if you need case searches.
  5. Firm already on Google that has a few Word power users: keep Workspace and add Microsoft 365 Apps for business ($10) for those users.
  6. Firm with a client or co-counsel who requires a specific platform: follow that requirement. Being compatible with your main referral sources is worth more than small feature differences.

title.raw: How Much Does a Law Firm Website Cost in 2026?
title.rendered: How Much Does a Law Firm Website Cost in 2026?

content.raw:
Quick answer: using current vendor price pages, a solo attorney can build a do-it-yourself site for under $1,000 in year one and about $450 a year after that. A small firm paying a freelancer should budget roughly $10,000–$15,000 for year one and $2,000–$2,500 a year after. A growing firm hiring an agency, with ongoing local SEO, can reach $50,000+ in year one and $15,000–$20,000 a year after. The software is cheap. Most of the money goes on labour: design, writing, photos and ongoing SEO.

Most "law firm website cost" pages are written by agencies and give wide ranges with no breakdown. This guide does it the other way round. It prices each component from the vendor's own pricing page (as of November 2026). Labour figures come from named third-party estimates and are labelled as such. Then it adds the line items up into three example budgets you can adapt.

What drives the cost of a law firm website?

Every law firm website is built from the same parts. What changes between a $800 site and a $50,000 site is who does the work and how much of it there is.

  • Fixed software costs: domain, hosting or a website builder subscription, theme and plugin licences, and business email. These are small and predictable.
  • One-time labour: design and development, copywriting, photography and an accessibility review. This is usually the largest part of year one.
  • Ongoing labour: maintenance (updates, backups, security) and, if you pay for it, SEO. This is what makes year two cost more than you expect.

Line-item prices from official sources (November 2026)

Domain name

A .com domain is a small cost. Hostinger's domain price list shows .com at $19.99 for the first year and $19.99 a year to renew, as of November 2026. Squarespace and Wix annual plans include a free domain for the first year. You then pay the renewal fee from year two. Specialty extensions such as .law or .attorney often cost much more. Our guide to .law vs .com vs .attorney domains compares them.

Website builder or hosting

With a website builder, hosting is included in the subscription. With WordPress, the software is free but you pay a host. Look at the renewal price, not only the sign-up price.

Sources: Squarespace pricing, Wix plans, Hostinger WordPress hosting, SiteGround WordPress hosting, Kinsta pricing. Notice the gap between SiteGround's first-year price ($47.88) and its renewal ($359.88 a year). For a fuller comparison, see our guide to the best hosting for law firm websites. If you are still choosing a platform, read Squarespace vs WordPress vs Wix for law firms.

Premium theme and plugin licences (WordPress)

WordPress sites often need a few paid licences. Each one renews every year. Some common examples:

  • Theme: GeneratePress One costs $99/year for 1 site.
  • Forms: Gravity Forms Basic costs $59/year for 1 site.
  • SEO plugin: Yoast SEO Premium costs $118.80/year per site.

Free versions of many plugins work fine for small sites. Budget $150–$300 a year if your developer uses premium tools, and ask who owns each licence. Contact forms on a law firm site need extra care, so budget for a reliable form plugin.

Business email

Email on your own domain is billed per user. It grows with headcount.

Sources: Google Workspace billing help page and Microsoft 365 Business plans, US prices as of November 2026. To pick between them, see Google Workspace vs Microsoft 365 for law firms.

Design and development labour

Labour has no official price list, so treat every figure here as an estimate. As a reference point, the US Bureau of Labor Statistics reports a median wage of $92,650 a year for web developers (May 2025). That works out to roughly $45 an hour on a 2,080-hour year (our calculation). Freelancers and agencies charge more than an employee's wage because they pay their own overhead, software, insurance and unbilled time.

Published third-party estimates for a small law firm site (not vendor quotes):

Sources: Project Cost Estimator law firm guide (states that it is based on project quotes and rate benchmarks) and Webtonic. Project Cost Estimator's small law firm page gives a median freelancer build of $6,500.

Copywriting, photography and accessibility

These three costs are often left out of quotes. The same third-party guide estimates:

  • Practice area pages: $200–$1,200 per page (copy plus design).
  • Attorney bios: $150–$400 per attorney.
  • Headshots: $200–$600 each.
  • Accessibility audit and fixes: $600–$3,500 for small firms, or $2,500–$8,000 for mid-size firms.

On accessibility, the Department of Justice's web accessibility guidance says businesses open to the public must make their online offerings accessible. It points to WCAG as helpful guidance but does not require a specific technical standard for private businesses. Ask your state bar or counsel about your own obligations. From a budgeting view, building accessibility in from the start costs less than fixing it later.

Your state's lawyer advertising rules also apply to website copy, including claims about results and expertise. Whoever writes the copy, an attorney should review it before it goes live. Check your state bar's advertising guidance.

Maintenance and SEO

Webtonic estimates maintenance at $500–$6,000 a year, depending on the site. It puts basic SEO at $500–$1,000 a month and full-service SEO at $1,000–$5,000 a month. Project Cost Estimator puts ongoing local SEO at $300–$1,500 a month. We break maintenance down in law firm website maintenance: what it involves and costs.

Three example budgets, added up

These budgets use the prices above. Where a cost has no official price (labour, copy, photos), we picked a figure inside the cited third-party range and say so. Your quotes will differ. Swap in your own numbers.

Budget 1: Solo attorney, DIY on Squarespace

Assumptions: one lawyer, 5–8 pages written yourself, one professional headshot, no paid SEO or maintenance.

The hidden cost here is your time, which is billable time you are not billing. A Wix Core plan would land in a similar range, depending on your region's pricing.

Budget 2: Small firm (3 lawyers), freelancer-built WordPress site

Assumptions: about 12 pages, including 6 practice area pages and 3 bios. Hosted on SiteGround GrowBig. Copy at $400 per practice page and $250 per bio. Three headshots. A mid-range accessibility audit. A $100/month care plan.

Want to cut year one? Writing your own first drafts and having a freelancer edit them is the easiest saving. Paid SEO is not included. A modest local SEO retainer of $500/month would add $6,000 a year.

Budget 3: Growing firm (8 lawyers), agency build with local SEO

title.raw: Law Firm Email Setup: How to Get Professional Domain Email (SPF, DKIM and DMARC Included)
title.rendered: Law Firm Email Setup: How to Get Professional Domain Email (SPF, DKIM and DMARC Included)

content.raw:
Quick answer: To set up law firm email, sign up for a business email provider (usually Google Workspace or Microsoft 365), verify that you own your domain, create your mailboxes, and point your domain's MX records to the provider. Then add three DNS records that prove your mail is genuine: SPF, DKIM and DMARC. Start DMARC in monitoring mode (p=none), confirm that every service that sends mail as your firm passes, and only then tighten it to quarantine and reject.

This guide walks through each step in order, with example DNS records you can adapt. It assumes you already own a domain. If you're still choosing one, read our guide to .law vs .com vs .attorney domains for law firms first.

Why should a law firm use domain email instead of Gmail or Yahoo?

An address like jane@smithlaw.com does more than look professional. It gives the firm control that a free personal account doesn't:

  • The firm owns the mailbox. When someone leaves, an admin can suspend the account, forward it, or keep the mail. A personal Gmail account belongs to the person.
  • You can enforce security. Business plans let an admin require two-factor authentication for every user, which matters when the inbox holds client information.
  • You can authenticate your mail. SPF, DKIM and DMARC only work on a domain you control. That is what stops someone else sending fake invoices "from" your firm.
  • Clients can tell real messages from fakes. If every firm message comes from one domain, an email from smithlaw.attorney.mail@gmail.com stands out as suspicious.
Quick pick

Budget mailbox option: Namecheap Private Email →

Choosing Google Workspace? Start through our referral link → and ask us for a 10% first-year promo code.

We may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. It never changes our recommendations.

What law firm email address format should you use?

Pick one format and use it for everyone, so clients and opposing counsel can guess an address correctly. Common options:

Then add a few shared, role-based addresses so client communication doesn't depend on one person's inbox:

  • intake@ or info@ for new inquiries and your website contact form.
  • billing@ for invoices and payment questions.
  • dmarc@ (or similar) to receive DMARC reports. Google and Microsoft both suggest a dedicated mailbox or group for these, because report volume can be high.

Role addresses usually don't need their own paid license. Most providers let you set them up as aliases, groups or shared mailboxes. If your website form sends to intake@, pair this with our guide to adding a secure contact form to a law firm website.

Which email provider should you choose?

Most small US firms choose between Google Workspace and Microsoft 365. Both handle everything in this guide. The choice usually comes down to whether your team lives in Word and Outlook or in Google Docs, and what your practice management software integrates with. We compare them in detail in Google Workspace vs Microsoft 365 for law firms, so this guide covers setup for both.

One thing to avoid: the free mailboxes bundled with some web hosting plans. Running email and your website on the same server means one problem can take down both. Moving hosts also gets riskier. If you're planning a move, see how to move a law firm website to a new host without downtime, which covers keeping MX records intact.

How do SPF, DKIM and DMARC work together?

Each record does a different job. Together they let a receiving server decide whether a message claiming to be from your domain is real:

  • SPF (Sender Policy Framework) is a list of servers allowed to send mail for your domain. It's published as a TXT record.
  • DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) adds a digital signature to each message. Receivers check it against a public key in your DNS, which shows the message came from an authorized sender and wasn't altered.
  • DMARC ties the two together. It checks that the domain that passed SPF or DKIM matches the domain in the visible "From" address (called alignment). It tells receivers what to do when a message fails, and it sends you reports.

Alignment is the part most guides skip. As Microsoft's DMARC documentation explains, a message passes DMARC if SPF or DKIM passes and aligns with the From domain. A newsletter tool can pass SPF for its own domain and still fail DMARC for yours.

Before you start: what you need

  • Login to wherever your DNS is managed. That's usually your domain registrar, but it might be your web host or a service like Cloudflare. Check where your domain's nameservers point.
  • An admin account with your chosen email provider.
  • A list of every service that sends email as your domain. Think practice management and billing software, e-signature tools, newsletter platforms, your website's contact form, scheduling tools and payment processors. You'll need this list before you enforce DMARC.
  • If you're switching providers: a plan to migrate old mail, and a quiet time (a Friday evening, say) to change MX records.

Step-by-step law firm email setup

Step 1: Sign up and verify your domain

During signup, your provider gives you a verification code to add to your DNS, usually as a TXT record. This proves you own the domain.

  • Google Workspace: Google says to verify within the first 9 days of a free trial. Once the record is live, confirmation can take up to an hour.
  • Microsoft 365: You add the domain in the admin center under Settings > Domains. If your registrar supports Domain Connect, Microsoft can add the records for you. Otherwise you add them by hand, as Microsoft's DNS guide explains.

Step 2: Create users and shared addresses

Create a mailbox for each lawyer and staff member in your chosen format, then add your role addresses. Do this before changing MX records. Microsoft specifically advises adding users first so mail keeps flowing during the switch.

Step 3: Point your MX records to the provider

MX records tell the internet where to deliver mail for your domain. Delete any old MX records first. Leftover records from a previous host are a common cause of lost mail.

  • Google Workspace: add one MX record with priority 1 pointing to smtp.google.com, then click Activate Gmail in the Admin console. Google notes that new MX records can take up to 72 hours to be recognized. Older "aspmx" records are still supported if your mail already works.
  • Microsoft 365: copy the MX value shown in the admin center (it's unique to your domain). Set priority to the highest available, typically 0. Microsoft also recommends an autodiscover CNAME so Outlook configures itself.

Step 4: Publish one SPF record

Add a TXT record at the root of your domain (host @):

  • Google Workspace: v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com ~all. Google recommends ~all (soft fail) and says SPF can take up to 48 hours to start working.
  • Microsoft 365: v=spf1 include:spf.protection.outlook.com -all. Microsoft recommends -all (hard fail) when DKIM and DMARC are also in place.

Two rules trip people up. First, a domain can have only one SPF record. A second one causes a permanent error, so add each new sender as another include: in the same record. Second, SPF fails if checking it takes more than 10 DNS lookups. Every include: uses at least one lookup, so don't keep adding vendors without checking.

Step 5: Turn on DKIM signing

Google Workspace: In the Admin console, go to Apps > Google Workspace > Gmail > Authenticate email. Google says to wait 24–72 hours after turning on Gmail before generating a key. Choose 2048-bit if your DNS host supports it. Add the TXT record (host google._domainkey), then return and click Start authentication. Test by emailing a different Gmail or Workspace user, not yourself, and look for dkim=pass in the message headers.

Microsoft 365: DKIM uses two CNAME records, selector1._domainkey and selector2._domainkey. Their values are unique to your tenant. Get them from the Microsoft Defender portal under Email authentication settings > DKIM, add both at your DNS host, then switch signing on. The Microsoft DKIM guide has the full procedure.

Step 6: Authenticate every third-party sender

This is the step that decides whether DMARC enforcement goes smoothly. Go through your list of tools that send as @yourfirm.com: practice management, billing, e-signature, newsletters, scheduling, your website. In each tool's settings, look for "custom sending domain," "domain authentication" or "DKIM." The tool will give you records to add, usually a DKIM record and sometimes an SPF include.

The goal is that each tool signs with your domain, so it aligns for DMARC. If a tool can't do that, send its mail from a different address (such as a notifications address on the vendor's domain) or from a subdomain. Microsoft recommends using a subdomain such as news.yourfirm.com for bulk mail services you don't directly control. That way their reputation problems don't affect lawyers' everyday mail.

Don't forget your website. WordPress contact forms that send through the web server's built-in mail often fail SPF and DKIM. Route them through an authenticated SMTP service instead. Our law firm website security checklist covers this alongside other WordPress hardening.

Step 7: Publish DMARC in monitoring mode

Google advises waiting 48 hours after setting up SPF and DKIM before adding DMARC. Then add a TXT record with host _dmarc:

v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com

p=none means "take no action, just report." Your mail is delivered as normal. Receiving servers send daily aggregate reports to the rua address showing which servers sent mail as your domain and whether each passed.

Step 8: Check alignment in your reports

DMARC reports arrive as compressed XML files, which are hard to read by hand. A free or low-cost DMARC report viewer makes them much easier to work through. You're looking for:

  • Your provider: Google or Microsoft servers should show SPF and DKIM aligned and passing.
  • Known tools failing: a vendor you recognize that passes SPF for its own domain but fails alignment for yours. Go back to Step 6 for that tool.
  • Unknown sources: servers you don't recognize sending as your domain. These may be spoofing attempts, which is exactly what enforcement will block.

Step 9: Move to quarantine, then reject

Once your legitimate senders all pass, tighten the policy gradually. Google's recommended DMARC rollout is about a week of daily reports at p=none. Then move to p=quarantine with a small pct value (it suggests around 10% for a small organization) and raise it to 100% over time. Microsoft's guidance describes the same path, with p=reject as the end goal.

  1. v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com (monitor)
  2. v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; pct=10; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com (failing mail goes to spam for 10% of messages)
  3. v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; pct=100; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com
  4. v=DMARC1; p=reject; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com (failing mail is refused)

Keep reviewing reports after each change. Whenever you add a new tool that sends email, authenticate it before it starts sending.

Example DNS records (example.com)

Here is what a finished setup looks like. Replace example.com with your domain. Always copy tenant-specific values (Microsoft's MX and DKIM, Google's DKIM key) from your own admin console. Some DNS hosts add your domain to the host name automatically, so _dmarc becomes _dmarc.example.com.

If you use a third-party sender, its include goes into the same SPF record. For example: v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com include:spf.vendor.example ~all. Here spf.vendor.example is a placeholder; use the exact value from your vendor's documentation.

Do Google and Yahoo's bulk sender rules apply to your firm?

Google's email sender guidelines set requirements for anyone sending to personal Gmail accounts. All senders must set up SPF or DKIM, send over TLS, have valid forward and reverse DNS, and keep the spam rate reported in Postmaster Tools below 0.3%.

Senders of more than 5,000 messages a day to Gmail accounts have extra rules. They need SPF and DKIM, a DMARC record (p=none is allowed), alignment with the From domain, and one-click unsubscribe on marketing messages. According to Google's sender FAQ, mail from your main domain and its subdomains counts together toward that threshold, and bulk sender status doesn't expire. The same FAQ says Gmail has been ramping up enforcement, including rejecting messages that don't comply. Yahoo's sender requirements are similar and add that unsubscribe requests must be processed within 2 days.

Most small firms send nowhere near 5,000 emails a day. But a firm-wide newsletter to a large list can get there, and the all-sender rules apply to everyone anyway. Following the steps above puts you in line with both tiers.

Turn on two-factor authentication for every account

Authentication records protect your domain from being spoofed. They do nothing if someone steals a lawyer's password. Require two-factor authentication (2FA) for every mailbox:

  • Google Workspace: Google's 2-Step Verification guide recommends requiring it for anyone handling sensitive data. It rates security keys as the strongest option and discourages text-message codes.
  • Microsoft 365: Security defaults are free. They require every user to register for multifactor authentication and block older sign-in protocols that can bypass it. Microsoft turns them on for new tenants by default. Check that nobody has switched them off.

Also create a separate admin account with a strong password and 2FA. Don't use it as anyone's daily mailbox.

Email confidentiality and encryption basics

SPF, DKIM and DMARC prove who sent a message. They don't hide its contents. Confidentiality is a separate question, and the main national guidance is ABA Formal Opinion 477R (2017), "Securing Communication of Protected Client Information." In summary:

  • It applies Model Rule 1.6(c), which requires lawyers to make "reasonable efforts" to prevent unauthorized access to or disclosure of client information.
  • A lawyer may generally send client information over the internet, including by email, if they've made reasonable efforts to protect it.
  • What counts as reasonable is a fact-based judgment that weighs factors like how sensitive the information is and how likely disclosure is without extra safeguards.
  • The opinion declined to draw a bright line on encryption. It says special precautions, such as encryption, may be required when the information is highly sensitive or when the client or the law requires them.

In practice, that points to a few habits: keep 2FA on, train staff to spot phishing, and vet the vendors that handle your mail. Use your provider's encryption feature or a secure client portal for highly sensitive documents. Talk with clients about how they want to communicate, especially if they might use a shared or employer-owned email account. State rules and ethics opinions vary, so check your state bar's guidance too.

Email signatures and disclaimers

Set a consistent signature for everyone: name, title, firm name, office address, direct phone and website. Many providers let an admin apply a standard signature or footer to every user.

Many firms add a confidentiality notice to their footer. It's common practice, but it doesn't replace sending to the right person or using encryption where needed. Its legal effect varies, so don't rely on it alone. If your emails promote your services, your state's attorney advertising rules may also apply. The hands-on work takes an hour or two for a small firm. Waiting adds time: Google cites up to 72 hours for MX changes and up to 48 hours for SPF. Then allow 48 hours before DMARC and at least a week of monitoring before enforcing. Plan on two to four weeks to reach p=reject safely.

Will setting up DMARC block my own emails?

Not at p=none, which only reports. Problems happen when firms jump straight to quarantine or reject before their practice management, billing or newsletter tools are authenticated. That's why the monitoring step comes first.

Can I keep my old email while switching to Google Workspace for lawyers?

Yes. Existing mail stays with your old host until you migrate it. Create users first, migrate old messages with your new provider's import tool, then change MX records. New mail starts arriving at the new provider once DNS updates.

Yes. Google requires SPF or DKIM from every sender to personal Gmail accounts. And DMARC at enforcement is what stops criminals spoofing your domain to send fake wire instructions to clients, whatever your volume.

It separates email from your website, offers admin controls and 2FA enforcement, and makes host changes far less risky. Why should a law firm use domain email instead of Gmail or Yahoo?

An address like jane@smithlaw.com does more than look professional. It gives the firm control that a free personal account doesn’t:

  • The firm owns the mailbox. When someone leaves, an admin can suspend the account, forward it, or keep the mail. A personal Gmail account belongs to the person.
  • You can enforce security. Business plans let an admin require two-factor authentication for every user, which matters when the inbox holds client information.
  • You can authenticate your mail. SPF, DKIM and DMARC only work on a domain you control. That is what stops someone else sending fake invoices “from” your firm.
  • Clients can tell real messages from fakes. If every firm message comes from one domain, an email from smithlaw.attorney.mail@gmail.com stands out as suspicious.

  • intake@ or info@ for new inquiries and your website contact form.
  • billing@ for invoices and payment questions.
  • dmarc@ (or similar) to receive DMARC reports. Google and Microsoft both suggest a dedicated mailbox or group for these, because report volume can be high.

Each record does a different job. Together they let a receiving server decide whether a message claiming to be from your domain is real:

Step 1: Sign up and verify your domain

v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com

p=none means “take no action, just report.” Your mail is delivered as normal. Receiving servers send daily aggregate reports to the rua address showing which servers sent mail as your domain and whether each passed.

DMARC reports arrive as compressed XML files, which are hard to read by hand. A free or low-cost DMARC report viewer makes them much easier to work through. You’re looking for:

  • Your provider: Google or Microsoft servers should show SPF and DKIM aligned and passing.
