title.raw: .law vs .com vs .attorney: Which Domain Should Your Law Firm Use?
title.rendered: .law vs .com vs .attorney: Which Domain Should Your Law Firm Use?

content.raw:
Quick answer: If the .com version of your firm name is available at a reasonable price, register it and make it your main address. If it isn't, a .law domain is the strongest alternative, because only verified lawyers and law firms can hold one. Google ranks .law, .attorney and .lawyer the same as .com, so the choice comes down to trust, memorability and cost, not SEO.

This guide covers what each legal extension requires, what they cost as of November 2026, how to pick the name itself without running into bar rules or trademark problems, and how to register a domain and point it at your website.

.com, .law, .attorney, .lawyer and .esq at a glance

The letters after the dot are called the top-level domain, or TLD. .com is the original commercial TLD. The legal ones (.law, .attorney, .lawyer, .esq) are newer "generic" TLDs, or gTLDs, launched under ICANN's new gTLD program. They differ mainly in who is allowed to register them.

Prices are from the registrar pages listed in the cost section below. They change often and differ between registrars, so check before you buy.

Quick pick

Registering a domain? Search your firm’s domain on Namecheap →

We may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. It never changes our recommendations.

What does a .law domain require?

.law is the only legal extension with real eligibility verification. According to the .law registration FAQ, the registrant must be one of the following:

  • A qualified lawyer: currently licensed to practice. Lawyers with inactive or non-practicing status are not eligible.
  • A law firm formed by qualified lawyers.
  • A court, a law school, or a legal regulator such as a bar association.

Here is how verification works in practice:

  • Your name must match your licensing record. The registrant name on the domain has to match the name you use with your licensing body. An independent verification agency checks it against public records and may ask for documents if the records aren't enough.
  • No privacy service. You can't register with private registration or a placeholder name. GoDaddy's .law help page lists domain privacy as "not supported." (Personal data is still redacted from public lookups, per the FAQ.)
  • No separate verification fee. The FAQ says you will never be asked to pay separately for eligibility verification.
  • Eligibility is ongoing. GoDaddy describes verification as "an ongoing effort maintained by the .LAW registry." If you go inactive or leave practice, plan for the domain.
  • Don't let it lapse. The FAQ says an expired .law domain stops resolving, and after 75 days it becomes available to other qualified lawyers.

title.raw: How to Add a Secure Contact Form to Your Law Firm Website
title.rendered: How to Add a Secure Contact Form to Your Law Firm Website

content.raw:
Quick answer: A secure contact form for a law firm website runs over HTTPS. It asks for the minimum (name, contact details, opposing party, a short summary). It doesn't keep submissions on the web server longer than it has to, and it sends a notification instead of the whole message in plain-text email. Add spam protection, a short disclaimer, and a consent checkbox, then send leads into your intake CRM. On WordPress, a mainstream form plugin can do all of this once you turn on the right settings.

This guide explains why the form on your site carries real risk, what "secure" actually means in practice, and how to set it up step by step in WordPress. It also covers when an encrypted form service makes more sense, and how to test it before you go live.

Why is a contact form a risk for a law firm?

To a small business, a contact form is just a lead source. For a law firm it's also the first place a stranger tells you something confidential. People type in things like "my employer is about to fire me," "I was arrested last night," or "I want to divorce my husband, who works at X." That information can create obligations before you've agreed to anything.

Prospective-client duties (ABA Model Rule 1.18)

ABA Model Rule 1.18 covers duties to prospective clients: people who consult a lawyer about possibly hiring them. In general terms, the rule protects information learned in that consultation even if no representation follows. In some cases it can also prevent the lawyer from representing someone on the other side of the same matter.

Websites come up in the comments to the rule. As the Washington State Bar's discussion of RPC 1.18 explains, a consultation is more likely when a lawyer invites information through a website "without clear and reasonably understandable warnings and cautionary statements that limit the lawyer's obligations." A site that only describes the lawyer's experience and contact details is treated differently. The practical takeaway is that how you word and build your form affects your risk. States adopt their own versions of the rule, so check your state bar's rule and ethics opinions.

The data itself

Separately from the ethics rules, submissions have to live somewhere. Many WordPress form plugins save every entry in the site database, where anyone with an admin login can read it, and it stays there indefinitely by default. If the site is ever compromised, through an outdated plugin or a reused password, those stored enquiries are exposed. Plain-text email notifications put copies in more inboxes, phones and backups.

What does "secure" mean for a contact form?

No single plugin makes a form "secure." Security comes from a handful of decisions about where the data goes and how long it stays there:

  • HTTPS everywhere. The page and the form submission must use TLS (the padlock). This protects data on its way from the visitor's browser to your server, but not after it arrives. Any decent host includes free SSL; see our guide to hosting for law firm websites.
  • Minimal storage on the website. Either don't store entries in WordPress at all, or delete them automatically after a short period once they've reached your CRM or inbox.
  • No sensitive details in plain-text email. Send a notification that says "New enquiry from Jane Doe: log in to view." Don't paste the whole story into the email. Ordinary email is not end-to-end encrypted.
  • Authenticated email sending. By default, WordPress sends mail through PHP's mail function, and the WP Mail SMTP plugin page notes that without proper authentication those messages often land in spam or disappear. Send through an authenticated SMTP or API provider (your Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 account, or a transactional mail service). Pair it with correct SPF, DKIM and DMARC records, covered in our law firm email setup guide.
  • Spam and bot protection. A honeypot (a hidden field only bots fill in), a CAPTCHA, or Cloudflare Turnstile. Turnstile is designed to avoid visual puzzles and can be added to any site without routing traffic through Cloudflare. Its free plan allows up to 20 widgets per account.
  • Locked-down admin access. Strong unique passwords, two-factor authentication, and the fewest possible people with access to form entries. The rest of the hardening work is in our WordPress security checklist for law firms.

Which fields should a law firm intake form ask for?

Ask for less than you think. The first contact form should get enough to run a conflict check and call the person back, not the whole case. Detailed facts can wait until after the conflict check, ideally by phone or through a secure intake process.

  • Name (required)
  • Email and/or phone, plus preferred contact method
  • Practice area, as a dropdown (e.g. family, estate planning, personal injury)
  • Other parties involved, such as the opposing party, employer or spouse. This is the key field for a conflict check.
  • A short, optional summary with a character limit and a visible note such as "Please don't include confidential details yet."
  • How did you hear about us? (optional, for marketing)

Leave out file uploads, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, medical details and free-text boxes that invite long stories. Each extra field is more sensitive data to protect, and a longer form usually gets fewer submissions anyway.

Disclaimer, consent checkbox and privacy notice

Put a short, plain-English disclaimer directly above the submit button, not buried in the footer. A typical version says that submitting the form does not create an attorney-client relationship, that the firm can't represent the person until a conflict check is done and an engagement is agreed, and that they shouldn't send confidential information yet. Require a checkbox confirming they've read it. Link to a privacy notice that explains what you collect, where it goes (for example, your CRM), and how long you keep it.

Exact wording, and whether your state expects specific language, is something to confirm with your state bar's guidance or an ethics counsel. Don't copy another firm's disclaimer word for word.

Comparing form options for a law firm website

The three WordPress plugins below are widely used and can each be configured for a law firm. The fourth is a hosted encrypted-form service. Prices are from the vendors' pricing pages as of November 2026 and often change, so check before buying.

None of the three plugins' pricing pages advertise encryption of stored entries. If that's a requirement for you, plan to minimize storage instead, or use an encrypted service.

How to add a secure contact form in WordPress (step by step)

These steps work with any of the plugins above. Menu names differ slightly between plugins and versions.

  1. Confirm HTTPS. Load your contact page as https:// and check the padlock. Make sure http:// redirects to https://. If it doesn't, fix SSL with your host before going any further.
  2. Set up authenticated email first. Install an SMTP plugin (such as WP Mail SMTP) and connect it to your firm's email provider or a transactional mail service. Send a test email and confirm it arrives in the inbox, not spam.
  3. Install your form plugin. Choose from the table above. Keep the number of plugins small: every extra add-on is more code to update.
  4. Build the form with minimal fields. Use the field list above. Make the summary field optional, cap its length, and add the "no confidential details yet" helper text.
  5. Add the disclaimer and a required consent checkbox above the submit button, with a link to your privacy notice.
  6. Turn on spam protection. Enable the plugin's built-in anti-spam or honeypot. Then add Turnstile, hCaptcha or reCAPTCHA through the plugin's CAPTCHA settings. You'll need site and secret keys from the provider.
  7. Decide on entry storage. In WPForms, the form builder's Settings » General » Advanced section has an option to disable storing entry information in WordPress, per WPForms' own guide. In Gravity Forms, use the form's Personal Data settings to auto-delete entries after a set number of days and stop saving IP addresses. In Fluent Forms Pro, use auto-delete. If your CRM integration needs a stored entry to work, choose a short retention period instead of "forever."
  8. Write a minimal notification email. Edit the admin notification so it includes the name, contact method and practice area, but not the summary. Send it to a shared intake address rather than to every lawyer.
  9. Send a short confirmation to the visitor. Thank them, say when you'll respond, and repeat that no attorney-client relationship exists yet. Don't echo their message back to them by email.
  10. Connect your intake CRM (next section), then restrict access: only the people who handle intake should be able to view entries in WordPress.
  11. Embed the form on your contact page and practice-area pages, then run the testing checklist below.

When should you use an encrypted form service instead?

A well-configured plugin is enough for a general "contact us" form that collects little detail. Some practices really do need clients to send sensitive information early, though: immigration, family, criminal defense, or anything involving medical records. For those, a hosted encrypted-form service keeps the data off your web server and out of plain-text email altogether.

Hushmail for Law is one example built for firms. It combines encrypted email with encrypted web forms, and on some plans, e-signatures. Its legal page lists plans "for as little as $10.79 per month" as of November 2026. Its plans page shows secure web forms on the Law Essentials and Law Growth tiers but not Law Basic. Confirm current form limits and pricing with the vendor. Usually you'd link to or embed the hosted form from your site, so the design matches your site less closely than a native plugin form would.

Another option is to use your practice-management or intake software's own forms (see below). The data then goes straight into a system built for client information.

Sending leads to an intake CRM (Clio Grow, Lawmatics)

The safest place for an enquiry is your intake CRM, with two-factor authentication and proper access controls, not your WordPress database. There are three common patterns:

  • Vendor plugin. Clio publishes a Clio Grow Form plugin for WordPress that sends contact form submissions to the Clio Grow Inbox. It's intended only for Clio Grow customers. Check its "tested up to" version and recent updates before relying on it.
  • Hosted intake form. Intake CRMs such as Clio Grow and Lawmatics provide their own intake forms. Ask your vendor whether a form can be shared by link or embedded on your site, so submissions go straight to the CRM and never touch WordPress.
  • Plugin integration. Some form plugins connect to CRMs directly, or through tools like Zapier, but often only on higher tiers. For example, WPForms lists its named CRM integrations (Salesforce, HubSpot and others) on the Elite plan. Check that your CRM is supported before you buy.

Choosing between the two leading intake CRMs? Our Lawmatics vs Clio Grow comparison covers features and pricing in detail.

Testing checklist before you go live

  • The form page loads only over HTTPS, and http:// redirects.
  • A test submission arrives at the intake address within a minute and isn't in spam.
  • The notification email contains no case summary or other sensitive detail.
  • The visitor confirmation arrives and repeats the no-relationship statement.
  • The consent checkbox is required; the form won't submit without it.
  • The entry appears in your CRM with every field mapped correctly.
  • Entry storage in WordPress matches your decision: none, or auto-deleted on schedule. Check that the test entry is actually gone.
  • Spam protection works: the CAPTCHA or Turnstile widget loads, and the form still submits on mobile.
  • Validation errors are clear and labelled, and the form can be completed with a keyboard alone.
  • Only intake staff can view entries in WordPress, and everyone with access uses two-factor authentication.
  • Delete all test entries from WordPress and the CRM afterwards.

Re-test after plugin updates, theme changes or a host migration. Form email is often the first thing to break quietly. Regular checks like this belong in your website maintenance routine.

FAQ

Is a contact form with SSL/HTTPS secure enough for a law firm?

HTTPS is necessary but not sufficient. It protects the data in transit only. You also need to control where submissions are stored, keep sensitive details out of plain-text email, and lock down who can see entries.

Does a contact form submission create an attorney-client relationship?

Generally a form submission alone doesn't create a full attorney-client relationship. It can still create prospective-client duties under Rule 1.18 or your state's version, especially if your site invites confidential information without clear warnings. Use a visible disclaimer and check your state bar's guidance.

What is an encrypted contact form?

It's a form whose submissions are encrypted after they reach the server, as well as in transit. Typically they're delivered as encrypted messages that only authorized users can open. Standard WordPress form plugins protect data in transit via HTTPS, but they don't advertise encryption of stored entries on their pricing pages.

Should I use CAPTCHA or a honeypot?

Use both if you can. A honeypot is invisible and catches simple bots. A CAPTCHA-style check such as Cloudflare Turnstile stops more sophisticated ones while rarely asking real visitors to solve puzzles.

Can I use a free form plugin?

Yes. The free versions of WPForms and Fluent Forms include spam protection and email notifications. Paid tiers add features such as entry management, auto-deletion and CRM integrations. Choose based on the storage and integration settings you need, not the number of templates.

Conclusion and next steps

A secure law firm contact form is mostly a set of sensible defaults. Use HTTPS, ask for a few fields, add a clear disclaimer with a consent checkbox, keep storage minimal, send short notifications through authenticated email, use spam protection, and send leads to a proper intake system. Start by finding out where your current form stores submissions and what its notification emails contain. Then work through the steps and the testing checklist above. If your practice needs sensitive details at first contact, look at an encrypted form service or your CRM's hosted intake forms.

title.rendered: Squarespace vs WordPress vs Wix for Law Firms: Which Should You Use?

content.raw:
This guide contains affiliate links. If you buy through them, we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. It never changes our recommendations. Learn more.

Quick answer: If your firm wants to rank for many practice-area and city pages, keep full control of its SEO, and own a site it can move, self-hosted WordPress (WordPress.org) is usually the better long-term choice. If you are a solo lawyer who needs a clean, credible site this month and has no one to handle updates, Squarespace or Wix is often the smarter buy. Squarespace gives you a polished design with few settings to worry about. Wix gives you more SEO controls and built-in booking.

A disclosure first. ProSiteGuide is run by a WordPress developer who builds law firm sites for a living, so read this with that bias in mind. We have tried to be fair. Every price and feature below comes from the vendors' own pricing pages and help docs, checked in November 2026. We also say plainly where WordPress is the wrong tool.

First: WordPress.org or WordPress.com?

"WordPress" means two different things, and the difference matters for cost and control.

  • WordPress.org is the free, open-source software. It is licensed under the GPL, which gives you the right to run, change and move it. You pay a host to run it, and you (or someone you hire) look after it. When law firm marketers say "use WordPress," this is what they mean.
  • WordPress.com is a hosted service run by Automattic. It is closer to Squarespace: you pay a subscription and they handle the servers. According to its pricing page, paid plans let you install plugins. Plans run from Personal at $4/month to Business at $25/month, billed yearly (as of November 2026).

The rest of this article compares self-hosted WordPress.org with Squarespace and Wix, and mentions WordPress.com where it is a useful middle ground.

How much does each platform cost in 2026?

Squarespace and Wix charge one subscription that covers hosting, security patches and the builder. WordPress.org software is free, but you pay for hosting and any premium add-ons separately. Prices below are in USD, as of November 2026.

Sources: Squarespace pricing, Wix plans, WordPress.com pricing. Wix shows its prices for yearly subscriptions paid upfront. It also says prices vary by location and exclude tax, so check the figure at checkout.

What does self-hosted WordPress really cost?

"WordPress is free" is true of the software only. A typical small-firm WordPress.org site pays for:

  • Hosting: anything from budget shared hosting to managed hosting. Hostinger's WordPress plan starts at $1.99/month on a 48-month term and renews at $10.99/month. Kinsta's entry managed plans are $30/month billed yearly ($350/year). Our law firm hosting comparison covers the trade-offs.
  • Theme: many good themes are free. A premium theme bundle like GeneratePress One costs $99/year for one site.
  • Forms: free form plugins exist. A premium option like Gravity Forms Basic is $59/year.
  • SEO plugin: the free version of Yoast SEO covers sitemaps, canonical URLs and schema. Its redirect manager is a Premium feature.
  • Domain: a separate yearly fee wherever you register it. See our guide to .law vs .com domains.

Using the prices above, software and hosting come to roughly $130 to $510 a year before the domain. That is about the same as Squarespace Core ($348/year) or Wix Core. The bigger cost is labor: someone has to run updates, take backups and fix problems. If you pay someone for that, it will usually cost more than the software. Our maintenance cost guide explains what to budget, and the law firm website cost guide covers build prices.

Which platform gives you more SEO control?

All three can rank. Search engines don't penalize a site for being on Squarespace or Wix. The difference is how much you can adjust when you need to, such as consolidating duplicate pages, migrating old URLs, or adding schema markup (code that describes your firm to search engines). This is what each platform's own documentation says.

For a solo site of 10 to 15 pages, Squarespace's automatic approach is fine and saves you from mistakes. For a firm planning hundreds of pages, or migrating an old site with many URLs, the locked robots.txt, the redirect cap and the fixed schema are real limits. Wix sits in between: it exposes more controls than Squarespace, but you still work inside its system.

Which is easiest to use day to day?

Squarespace and Wix are easier for a non-technical lawyer. You edit what you see, and there are no plugins to update. Squarespace is more structured, so it is hard to make a page look bad. Wix gives more drag-and-drop freedom, which also makes it easier to create messy layouts. With WordPress's block editor, editing an existing page is straightforward once the site is built. Setting it up well, though, takes skill. That is why most firms on WordPress use a developer for the build.

Are there good law firm templates?

  • Squarespace has a law firm templates page. It says templates can be tailored to practice areas such as family law, criminal defense and estate planning, with attorney bios and contact forms. It doesn't say how many law-specific templates there are.
  • Wix has a law template category spread over several pages. The templates are named by practice area, such as Family Law Firm, Criminal Law Firm, IP Law Firm and Tax Lawyer.
  • WordPress has thousands of general themes and some law-specific ones. Quality varies widely, so choose for speed and accessibility rather than looks.

On any platform, a template is a starting point. Clear practice-area pages, attorney bios and the disclaimers your state requires matter more than the theme.

Forms, client intake and booking

Squarespace form blocks can send submissions to email, a Google Drive sheet, Mailchimp or Zapier. Each email contains every field the visitor filled in. For booking, Squarespace owns Acuity Scheduling. Acuity lists custom intake forms on all its plans, which run $16 to $55/month billed yearly, and it is a separate subscription. Only Acuity's top plan offers a signed BAA for HIPAA. Most law firms don't need that, but some health-law or injury intake workflows might.

Wix includes "scheduling and services" on its Core plan and above, according to its plans page. That makes it the simplest all-in-one route for a solo lawyer who wants to take booked consultations.

WordPress can connect to almost any form tool, scheduler or practice-management intake, including the tools compared in Lawmatics vs Clio Grow. Whatever platform you use, keep confidential details out of plain email forms. Our secure contact form guide covers how to do this.

What about accessibility?

The U.S. Department of Justice says the ADA's requirements for businesses open to the public apply to their online services. It points to WCAG as helpful guidance. No platform makes a site accessible on its own. Wix offers an Accessibility Wizard that scans for issues, but states that it cannot guarantee compliance and that site owners are responsible for their content. The same applies to Squarespace and WordPress. Accessibility depends on your template, colors, headings, alt text and forms. Ask your developer or your state bar about obligations specific to your firm.

Who is responsible for security and maintenance?

This is the strongest argument for Squarespace and Wix. They patch the platform, run the servers and provide SSL. You can't forget an update because there is nothing for you to update.

With WordPress.org, security is split between your host and you. Core, theme and plugin updates, backups, login protection and uptime checks are your job, or the job of whoever you hire. Done well, WordPress is very secure. A neglected WordPress site with old plugins is a common target. If no one at your firm will own this, either budget for a maintenance plan or choose a hosted platform. Our WordPress security checklist lists what needs doing.

Can you take your site with you if you leave?

  • Wix: no. Wix says a site "needs to be hosted and operated on Wix's servers". Leaving means rebuilding.
  • Squarespace: partial. It exports a WordPress-format XML file with layout pages, one blog, and text and image blocks. Most other page types, more than one blog, video and audio blocks, custom CSS and style settings don't export. Expect to rebuild the design.
  • WordPress.org: full. You own the files and database and can move them to any host. The built-in export tool also produces a portable XML file. Our guide to moving a law firm site to a new host walks through the process.
  • WordPress.com: content export is available, and full downloadable backups come with the Business and Commerce plans.

Whichever platform you choose, register your domain in the firm's own account, not a vendor's or a freelancer's. That keeps your most important asset portable.

Which scales better to many practice-area and location pages?

Growth-minded firms often build a page for each service in each city, such as "DUI defense in Dayton" or "estate planning in Springfield." That can mean 50 to 300 pages. WordPress handles this well. Custom post types and reusable templates keep pages consistent. An SEO plugin manages titles, schema and redirects in bulk, and there is no redirect cap. Squarespace and Wix can host that many pages, but you will mostly build and edit them one by one. On Squarespace, the fixed schema and roughly 2,500-line redirect limit matter more as the site grows. A firm that adds attorneys, offices or a second brand will usually feel these limits within a few years.

Squarespace vs WordPress vs Wix: side-by-side

Which should your firm choose? A decision guide

Choose Squarespace if…

  • You are a solo lawyer or a two-person firm, and most clients find you through referrals.
  • You want a professional site with about 5 to 15 pages and will rarely add more.
  • No one will handle updates or security, and you don't want a monthly maintenance bill.

Choose Wix if…

  • You want online consultation booking built in without a second subscription.
  • You want more SEO controls than Squarespace, such as an editable robots.txt, custom canonicals and bulk redirects, while staying hands-off on hosting.
  • You accept that leaving Wix later means rebuilding.

Choose WordPress.org if…

  • Organic search is a main source of new clients, and you plan many practice-area, location or blog pages.
  • You have several attorneys or offices, or plan to grow.
  • You want to own the site outright and be able to change hosts or developers.
  • You have a developer or maintenance plan, or will budget for one.

Consider WordPress.com if…

  • You want WordPress's flexibility and plugins but prefer a hosted service that handles servers, such as the Business plan at $25/month billed yearly.

FAQ

Is Squarespace or WordPress better for a law firm?

For a small firm that wants low effort, Squarespace is better. For a firm that competes on SEO and plans to grow, WordPress.org is better because it gives full control over redirects, schema, robots.txt and scale. The deciding question is whether someone will maintain a WordPress site.

Is Wix good for lawyers?

Yes, for many solo and small firms. It has law templates, built-in scheduling on Core and higher plans, and more SEO settings than many people expect. The main drawback is lock-in: Wix sites can't be exported to another host.

Can a Squarespace or Wix site rank on Google?

Yes. Content quality, local relevance, reviews and links matter far more than the platform. The platform affects how much technical tuning you can do, which matters more as a site gets bigger.

What is the best website builder for lawyers on a tight budget?

For lowest total effort, choose Squarespace Core ($29/month billed yearly as of November 2026) or Wix Core (check current pricing for your region). Self-hosted WordPress can cost less in software, but only if you can handle maintenance yourself.

Can I move from Squarespace or Wix to WordPress later?

From Squarespace, you can export some content to WordPress, but you will rebuild the design and some pages. From Wix, there is no export, so you rebuild everything. In both cases, map your old URLs to new ones with 301 redirects so you keep your search rankings.

Conclusion and next steps

No platform is right for every firm. Squarespace and Wix are honest, good choices for solo lawyers and small firms that value low effort over control. WordPress.org pays off when your website is a growth engine with many pages, strong SEO and a firm that expects to grow.

  1. Decide whether organic search is a main way you get clients, or mostly a credibility check.
  2. Count the pages you will need in two years, including practice areas, locations and attorneys.
  3. Decide who will maintain the site, and budget for it.
  4. Register your domain in the firm's own account and set up professional email on it.
  5. Pick the platform that matches those answers, not the one with the prettiest demo.

title.raw: How to Move Your Law Firm Website to a New Host Without Downtime
title.rendered: How to Move Your Law Firm Website to a New Host Without Downtime

content.raw:
Quick answer: To move your law firm website to a new host without downtime, build and test a full copy on the new host first, lower your DNS TTL a few days ahead, get SSL working on the new server, and only then point your domain at it. Keep the old host running until all traffic has moved over. The site stays online the whole time because visitors keep reaching the old copy until DNS sends them to the new one.

Generic migration guides stop there. A law firm has more to protect: the intake form that brings in new matters, email that must not bounce, client data sitting in form entries, and scheduling or portal widgets that quietly break. This guide covers the standard WordPress move plus those firm-specific checks, a rollback plan, and what to do in Search Console and Google Business Profile afterward.

Why is moving a law firm website different?

The technical move is the same as any WordPress site. The stakes are not. A few hours of broken forms can mean lost consultations you never hear about, because a failed form submission rarely tells the visitor anything useful. Watch for these risks in particular:

  • Intake and contact forms. Forms depend on email delivery, spam protection keys and sometimes a CRM connection. Any of these can fail silently on a new server.
  • Email. Your email often has nothing to do with your web host, but a careless DNS change can still break it.
  • Confidential form entries. If your form plugin stores submissions in the WordPress database, every backup and copy you make contains prospective client information.
  • Third-party embeds. Scheduling tools, chat widgets, payment links and client portal logins can be tied to your domain or to settings that do not copy cleanly.
  • Local search visibility. Your Google Business Profile links to your site. If the address changes or breaks, you lose calls from people who never see the problem.

What is DNS TTL, in plain English?

1. Take a full backup and store it safely

If your firm has a retention policy for web form entries, consider deleting entries you no longer need before you copy anything. 2. Set up the new hosting account

Create the site on the new host and match the PHP version your site currently runs. Do not cancel or notify the old host. You need it running until the end.

3. Copy the site with the host's tool, a plugin, or manually

Pick one method:

  • Host migration service: request it and let their team copy the site (see the table above).

4. Test the new copy before anyone else sees it

5. Lower the DNS TTL (ideally days ahead)

At your DNS provider, change the TTL on the records you will edit (usually the A record for the root domain and the www record) to a low value such as 300 seconds. Do this several days before the switch, or a week ahead as Google suggests, so the old long TTL has time to expire everywhere. If you will change nameservers rather than individual records, ask your provider how nameserver TTL is handled, because it can be set separately.

6. Get SSL working on the new host before the switch

If the new server has no valid certificate when DNS flips, visitors see a browser security warning on a law firm's website. That is worse than a few minutes of downtime.

During propagation some visitors still reach the old server, which is exactly why it must stay online.

Test intake and contact forms end to end

  4. The entry reaches your CRM or intake tool, if connected.
  5. Spam protection still works. reCAPTCHA and similar keys are often tied to a domain list.
  6. File uploads, if enabled, save and attach correctly.

  • URLs: a host change should not change any URLs. If you also changed structure (or moved from http to https or www to non-www), add 301 redirects. Google says 301 redirects don't cause a loss in PageRank and recommends pointing old URLs straight to their final destination.

  • Robots and noindex: make sure no test-time noindex setting or robots.txt block made it to the live site.
  • Google Business Profile: open your profile and confirm the website link loads the correct page over https. Google's Business Profile editing help asks for the full URL with the https prefix. Check appointment links too.
  • Analytics and tags: confirm tracking still fires so call and form conversions are recorded.

Once you are settled, run through our law firm website security checklist on the new host. Backups, logins and firewall settings rarely carry over exactly.

  2. Keep the old DNS values handy. The old A record IP (or old nameservers) from your pre-migration screenshot.

A host move with no URL changes is the simplest kind of site move in Google's documentation. Expect a short crawl-rate dip at most. Problems usually come from mistakes: a leftover noindex tag, a slow new server, or broken pages.

Plan the switch for an evening, test every form end to end, and keep the old host for a few days. content.raw:
Quick answer: A law firm website security checklist starts with the items that stop most break-ins: two-factor authentication on every admin account, prompt updates to WordPress and its plugins, and tested off-site backups. Next come HTTPS, a firewall with malware scanning, and contact forms that don't keep more client data than they need. The last pieces are monitoring and a written incident response plan, because ABA ethics opinions expect lawyers to make reasonable efforts to watch for breaches and to respond when one happens.

Below is the full checklist in priority order. Each item has a short "why" and a "how". After that you'll find who should own each task (host, firm or developer), a monthly and quarterly schedule, and what the main WordPress security plugins actually include.

Why does a law firm website need its own security checklist?

Most small firm websites don't hold case files. But they do hold admin logins, intake form submissions, and your firm's name and reputation. A hacked site can send spam, redirect visitors to scam pages, or leak what prospective clients typed into a form.

The ethics side matters too. In ABA Formal Opinion 483 (October 2018), the ABA's ethics committee concluded that lawyers "must employ reasonable efforts to monitor the technology and office resources connected to the internet, external data sources, and external vendors providing services relating to data." The opinion also says that when a breach happens, a lawyer must act "reasonably and promptly to stop the breach and mitigate damage," and it recommends having an incident response plan ready in advance. Its companion, Formal Opinion 477R (2017), says the right level of security depends on factors such as how sensitive the information is.

Both opinions apply a "reasonable efforts" standard, not a demand for perfect security. Your own state's rules and opinions control, so check with your state bar. Website security is one practical, written-down way to show you're making those efforts.

How to use this checklist

The items are grouped into three priority tiers:

  • Priority 1: do this week. Accounts and access, updates, backups. These close the most common ways in (weak logins, outdated code) and give you a way back.
  • Priority 2: do this month. Hosting and HTTPS, firewall and malware scanning, forms and data.
  • Priority 3: set up, then keep running. Monitoring and an incident response plan.

Priority 1: Accounts and access

Stolen or guessed passwords are the easiest way into a WordPress dashboard, so start here.

1. Give every person their own login. No shared "admin" account.

Why: With a shared login you can't tell who changed what, and you can't cut off one person without locking everyone out. How: Under Users, create a named account for each person who needs access. Then delete or downgrade any generic account, and reassign its content when WordPress asks.

2. Use long, unique passwords stored in a password manager

Why: WordPress's own Hardening WordPress guide warns against passwords built from your name, username, firm name or dictionary words. The FTC's small business guidance adds: never reuse passwords. How: Generate passwords in a password manager and use the WordPress strength meter whenever you change one.

3. Turn on two-factor authentication for every administrator

Why: Two-factor authentication (2FA) means a stolen password alone won't get anyone in. CISA's Cyber Guidance for Small Businesses says to enable multifactor authentication on all system administrator accounts and notes that "any form of MFA is better than no MFA." How: WordPress core doesn't ship with 2FA, so add it with a plugin (see the WordPress handbook page on two-step authentication). The free versions of Wordfence and Kadence Security (formerly Solid Security) both include 2FA. Do the same for your hosting account, domain registrar and firm email. Those logins can take over the website just as easily.

4. Give each person the lowest role that works

Why: Fewer administrators means fewer accounts that can install plugins or change settings. This is the "least privilege" idea CISA recommends for small business systems. How: Staff who only write blog posts should be Editors or Authors, not Administrators. When someone leaves the firm, remove their account the same day.

5. Limit login attempts

Why: Bots try thousands of password guesses against /wp-login.php. The FTC also recommends limiting failed login attempts. How: Turn on brute force protection in your security plugin (Wordfence and Kadence Security both include it free), or ask your host whether it already blocks these attacks at the server.

Priority 1: Updates

6. Keep WordPress core current, with automatic updates on

Why: The WordPress hardening guide notes that older versions stop getting security updates. CISA and the FTC both recommend turning on automatic updates where possible. How: Leave core auto-updates on and check the Dashboard for update notices. Download WordPress only from wordpress.org.

7. Update plugins and themes, and delete the ones you don't use

Why: Every plugin and theme is extra code that can contain a flaw. Deactivated plugins still sit on the server, and their code can still be attacked. How: Review updates at least weekly. Use per-plugin auto-updates for simple, well-maintained plugins. Test big updates (page builders, form plugins, anything tied to payments) on a staging copy first. Delete anything inactive, and never install "nulled" (pirated) premium plugins.

8. Patch known, actively exploited flaws first

Why: CISA advises prioritizing vulnerabilities in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, meaning flaws attackers are already using. How: If your security plugin or host flags a plugin vulnerability as actively exploited, update or remove that plugin the same day. Don't wait for your normal update window.

Priority 1: Backups

9. Back up both the files and the database, on a schedule

Why: A clean backup is often the fastest way back from a hack or a bad update. The WordPress backup guide points out that a file backup doesn't include the database, and a full restore needs both. How: The same guide suggests weekly backups for small sites, daily backups for busy ones, and a backup before every upgrade.

10. Keep copies somewhere your host can't lose

Why: If your only backups sit on the same server as the site, one incident can take out both. How: WordPress recommends keeping 3 to 5 recent backups in different places (for example, your host plus cloud storage). The hardening guide also suggests encrypting backups and keeping several dated copies, so you can roll back to a point before the compromise.

11. Test a restore

Why: CISA recommends testing both partial and full restores, and warns that restores can take much longer than expected. How: Once a quarter, restore a backup to a staging site and click through it. Write down how long the restore took.

Priority 2: Hosting and HTTPS

12. Serve the whole site over HTTPS

Why: The FTC advises using a web host that supports the latest version of TLS, so your address starts with https:// and data sent to the site is encrypted on the way. How: Most hosts include a free certificate. Confirm that every page, including form pages, redirects from http to https, and that the certificate renews automatically.

13. Choose a host that handles server-level security

Why: Some things only the host can do: patch the server, keep each site isolated from the others, offer current PHP versions, and run network-level protection. How: Ask hosts whether they include SFTP (the hardening guide prefers it over plain FTP), automatic daily backups, malware scanning and a firewall. If yours falls short, our guide to the best hosting for law firm websites compares options, and this walkthrough explains how to move a law firm website to a new host without downtime.

14. Harden wp-config.php and turn off the built-in file editor

Why: If someone gets into an admin account, the Dashboard's theme and plugin editor lets them change PHP code right away. How: Add define( 'DISALLOW_FILE_EDIT', true ); to wp-config.php. The hardening guide explains that this removes the edit-files capabilities from all users. It also notes the setting won't stop someone from uploading malicious files, so it's one layer, not a fix on its own. The same guide recommends restricting wp-config.php to 400 or 440 permissions, and 755 for folders and 644 for files across the install.

Priority 2: Firewall and malware scanning

15. Put a web application firewall in front of the site

Why: A web application firewall (WAF) filters malicious requests before they reach vulnerable code. How: There are two kinds. An endpoint firewall runs inside WordPress as a plugin (Wordfence works this way). A cloud firewall sits in front of your server and filters traffic before it arrives (Sucuri's firewall works this way). Many managed hosts also run their own. One well-configured firewall is enough. Stacking several often causes conflicts.

16. Scan for malware and file changes

Why: Some infections stay quiet. They add spam pages for search engines or redirect only mobile visitors, so you may never notice them yourself. How: Turn on scheduled scans and email alerts in your security plugin, or use your host's scanner. WordPress's hardening guide also recommends watching for added or modified files.

What do the main WordPress security plugins include?

This table lists features stated on each vendor's official page or WordPress.org listing, as of November 2026. It isn't a ranking. Pick one main tool, not all three.

The WordPress.org listing for Solid Security now carries the Kadence Security name, so you may see either name in your Plugins screen.

Priority 2: Forms and data

17. Map every place the site collects or sends data

Why: You can't protect data you don't know you're collecting. Contact forms, consultation booking, chat widgets, newsletter signups and analytics all collect something. How: List each one, what it collects, where it stores the data (the WordPress database, an email inbox, a CRM), and who can see it.

18. Keep only what you need, for as long as you need it

Why: Form plugins often keep every submission in the database forever. That's an unnecessary pile of prospective-client details if the site is ever breached. Opinion 477R ties the level of protection to how sensitive the information is. How: Ask only for what you need to run a conflict check and call back, add a "don't send confidential details" note, and set submissions to auto-delete. Field-by-field setup, spam protection and encryption options are covered in our guide on adding a secure contact form to a law firm website.

19. Protect the email that form notifications go to

Why: Form alerts usually land in an inbox. The FTC recommends SPF, DKIM and DMARC to make it harder for scammers to spoof your domain. How: Turn on MFA for the mailbox and set up email authentication. See law firm email setup: SPF, DKIM and DMARC.

Priority 3: Monitoring

20. Set up alerts that a person actually reads

Why: Opinion 483 treats monitoring as part of a lawyer's reasonable efforts. An alert nobody opens doesn't count for much. How: Send uptime, malware-scan and login alerts to a shared mailbox that someone checks. The WordPress hardening guide also recommends keeping server access and error logs, and filtering out noise so the real alerts stand out.

21. Watch for outside warning signs

Why: Sometimes the first sign of a hack is a browser warning, or strange pages showing up in Google results for your firm. How: Verify the site in Google Search Console so you get security notices, and search site:yourfirm.com now and then for pages you didn't create.

Priority 3: Incident response plan

Opinion 483 recommends deciding on a plan "before a lawyer is swept up in an actual breach." It says plans should name the team members and their backups, explain how to reach them, and set out the steps at each stage. CISA likewise recommends a written, approved and regularly reviewed plan, practiced with tabletop exercises (walking through a pretend incident around a table). For a small firm website, one page is enough:

  1. Contacts: who leads (usually a partner), plus phone numbers for your developer, host support, cyber insurer and IT provider.
  2. Contain: put the site in maintenance mode or take it offline, and change all admin, hosting and database passwords.
  3. Preserve: ask the host to save logs before anything gets cleaned up.
  4. Assess: work out what was accessed, especially form submissions or other client information.
  5. Clean and restore: remove the malware or restore a known-clean backup, then update everything.
  6. Notify: Opinion 483 says lawyers have a duty to notify clients when a breach involves, or has a substantial likelihood of involving, material client information. State breach-notification laws can add their own requirements. Talk to your state bar's ethics hotline and your insurer.
  7. Review: write down what happened and what you're changing so it doesn't happen again.

The FTC also suggests reporting incidents to the FBI's IC3 and to ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

Who does what: host, firm or developer?

Security gaps tend to show up where each party assumes someone else is handling it. Put the split in writing. Opinion 477R lists the vendor's security policies and the vendor agreement among the things to check when choosing technology vendors.

The firm's column never goes away. Even if you outsource the technical work, decisions about client information and notification remain with the lawyers.

Monthly, quarterly and yearly security cadence

If running this schedule in-house isn't realistic, it's the core of a maintenance plan. See law firm website maintenance: what it involves and costs.

WordPress can be run securely when core, plugins and themes are kept updated, admin accounts use 2FA, and the host is capable. Check your state bar's guidance for any local requirements.

title.rendered: Law Firm Website Maintenance: What It Involves and What It Costs

content.raw:
Quick answer: Law firm website maintenance means keeping the software updated, backing the site up, watching for downtime and malware, renewing the domain, SSL certificate and plugin licenses, and keeping attorney bios, practice pages and contact forms accurate. For a typical small-firm WordPress site, hard costs are hosting plus a few premium plugin licenses. Your choice is whether to spend your own time on the rest or pay for a care plan. Published care plans start at $39 to $199 a month at the providers listed below, as of November 2026.

This guide breaks the work into a weekly, monthly, quarterly and annual schedule. It also lists the real cost components, with prices taken from vendors' own pricing pages, so you can decide between DIY, a freelancer and an agency.

What does law firm website maintenance include?

Maintenance has two halves. The technical half keeps the site running and safe. The content half keeps it accurate. A law firm needs both, because a site that is up but lists a partner who left last year, or has a contact form that quietly stopped sending, still costs you clients.

1. Software updates (core, plugins, theme, PHP)

WordPress itself, every plugin and the theme all release updates, many of which fix security holes. Since version 3.7, WordPress applies minor and security releases automatically on most hosts, but major releases still need a click. The same official guide recommends backing up first, checking plugin and theme compatibility, and visiting the site afterward to confirm it still works. That "check afterward" step is the part people skip, and it is the part that matters on a site with intake forms and booking tools.

2. Backups you have actually tested

You need automatic daily backups, kept somewhere other than the server itself, with enough history to roll back past a problem you noticed late. Many managed hosts include them. For example, Kinsta's entry plan includes automatic daily backups with 14 days of retention (as of November 2026). A backup only counts if a restore works, so test one a few times a year.

3. Uptime monitoring and security scans

Uptime monitoring checks the site every few minutes and alerts you when it goes down, so you hear about an outage from a tool, not from a prospective client. Security scanning looks for malware, changed files and known-vulnerable plugins. The hardening side (logins, two-factor, firewalls, user roles) is covered step by step in our law firm website security checklist. Maintenance is what keeps that checklist true month after month.

4. Renewals: domain, SSL certificate and licenses

Renewals fail quietly, and when they fail the result is loud:

  • Domain. Under ICANN's Expired Registration Recovery Policy, registrars must send reminders about one month and one week before expiry. If the domain lapses, the registrar must interrupt its DNS for a period after expiry, which takes the website offline and can disrupt email on that domain. Turn on auto-renew and keep the registrar's contact email current. (Choosing a domain is covered in .law vs .com vs .attorney.)
  • SSL certificate. Certificate lifetimes are getting shorter. Under the CA/Browser Forum schedule, the maximum validity of public TLS certificates dropped to 200 days on March 15, 2026, and is set to fall to 47 days by 2029. Free Let's Encrypt certificates last 90 days and are meant to renew automatically. Manual renewal is no longer realistic. Confirm your host auto-renews, and monitor expiry anyway.
  • Premium plugin and theme licenses. Most are annual subscriptions. If one lapses, the plugin usually keeps running but stops getting updates, including security fixes.

5. Content accuracy: bios, practice pages, contact details

This half of the work is specific to law firms. Attorney bios need new admissions, awards and departures. Practice area pages need to match the work you actually take. Office addresses, phone numbers and hours must match your Google Business Profile. Lawyer advertising rules apply to your website too, so outdated claims, results or credentials can become an ethics issue as well as a marketing one. Check your state bar's advertising rules when you edit this kind of content.

6. Form and intake testing

Contact forms break silently after a plugin update, an email change or a host move. Submit a test through every form and confirm it reaches the right inbox or practice-management tool. Forms that handle sensitive details also need the setup described in our guide to a secure contact form for a law firm website.

7. Performance, broken links and accessibility

Sites slow down as images, plugins and scripts pile up. Check page speed periodically, remove plugins you no longer use, and fix broken links to removed pages or dead external sources. Accessibility deserves a recurring check too. The U.S. Department of Justice's guidance on web accessibility says it has consistently taken the position that the ADA applies to the web content of businesses open to the public, and it points to WCAG as helpful technical guidance. New content (PDFs, images without alt text, embedded videos) is where accessibility problems usually creep back in. Ask your state bar or counsel about your firm's specific obligations.

A law firm website maintenance schedule

Here is a practical cadence for a small firm's WordPress site. Automate whatever can be automated, and keep human attention for the things that need judgment: checking the site after updates, testing forms and reviewing content.

What does law firm website maintenance cost?

Most articles quote broad ranges with no source. A more useful approach is to add up the actual parts. Some costs you pay whoever does the work. Others depend on whether that's you or someone you hire.

Fixed costs: hosting, domain and licenses

The examples below are real list prices from official pages, as of November 2026. They are examples, not a market average, and your stack may need different tools. Prices change often, and several vendors run introductory discounts.

A small firm site using that exact stack would spend roughly $590 a year on hosting and those three licenses at regular prices, before the domain. Many sites need fewer premium plugins, and some need more. For how hosting choices compare, see our guide to the best hosting for law firm websites.

Labor: what WordPress care plans cost

A website care plan (also called a WordPress maintenance plan) is a monthly subscription where someone else handles updates, backups, monitoring and small edits. The published prices below come from each provider's pricing page, as of November 2026. They show how plans are structured. We have not tested them, and we are not endorsing them.

Two things stand out. First, "edits" mean very different things: an AI edit, a 30-minute human task and "unlimited" are not the same product. Second, whether updates are tested on a staging copy before going live is often reserved for higher tiers. For a site that brings in clients, that is the feature worth paying for. Also check whether hosting is included, because that changes the comparison a lot.

Maintenance is an ongoing cost, separate from the build. For the upfront side, see how much a law firm website costs in 2026.

DIY vs freelancer vs agency: which fits your firm?

A simple rule: if no one at the firm will reliably do the monthly and quarterly tasks, DIY isn't really free. It just postpones the cost until something breaks. On the other hand, if your site runs on a hosted builder, much of the technical work is done by the platform. Our Squarespace vs WordPress vs Wix comparison covers that trade-off.

What to ask a website maintenance provider

  1. Do you test updates on a staging copy first? And does a person check the live site afterward?
  2. Where are backups stored, how long are they kept, and when did you last test a restore?
  3. What counts as an "edit" and how many are included? Ask for an example, such as adding a new attorney bio.
  4. What's your response time for an outage, a hacked site and a routine request? Get it in writing.
  5. Is malware cleanup included, or billed separately?
  6. Do you test our contact and intake forms, including any integration with our practice-management software?
  7. Who owns the domain, hosting account and licenses? They should be in the firm's name, with the provider added as a user.
  8. What's the contract term and exit process? How do we get a full copy of the site if we leave?
  9. Who on your team can access our site, and do you use two-factor authentication and individual logins?
  10. What do the monthly reports show? Ask for a sample.

If you're switching hosts as part of the change, follow our guide to moving a law firm website without downtime.

Signs your law firm website is being neglected

  • The WordPress dashboard shows a long list of pending plugin updates, or plugins flagged as no longer maintained.
  • Browsers show a "Not secure" or certificate warning.
  • Nobody can say when the last backup was made, or where it is stored.
  • Attorney bios still list people who left, or miss recent hires.
  • The copyright year, office address or phone number is out of date.
  • Form submissions dropped off and no one checked whether the form still works.
  • Pages are noticeably slower than they used to be on a phone.
  • You don't have the logins for your own domain registrar or hosting account.
  • Google Search Console reports errors that have sat there for months.

Any two of these mean it's time to catch up, either with a one-time cleanup or by starting a regular plan.

FAQ

How much does lawyer website maintenance cost per month?

It depends on who does the work. If you handle it yourself, you pay only hosting and licenses. In the example stack above, that comes to roughly $49 a month averaged over the year. Published care plans from the providers we looked at start at $39, $89 and $199 a month (the last includes hosting), as of November 2026.

Doesn't my web host already do maintenance?

Partly. Good managed hosts handle server security, backups, SSL and uptime monitoring. They usually don't update your plugins with testing, check your forms or keep your content accurate. Read your plan's feature list to see where the host's job ends.

Can I just turn on automatic updates for everything?

Automatic security releases for WordPress core are sensible and on by default for most sites. Auto-updating every plugin is a trade-off. You get patches faster, but an update can break a page or form with nobody noticing. If you use auto-updates, pair them with uptime monitoring, daily backups and a regular form test.

How often should a law firm update website content?

Update immediately when something factual changes, such as a new attorney, a departure, a new office or a new phone number. Beyond that, a quarterly review of bios, practice pages and disclaimers is a reasonable minimum.

Do Squarespace or Wix sites need maintenance?

Less technical maintenance, because the platform handles software updates, hosting and SSL. You still own the content, form testing, accessibility of what you add, domain renewal and access control.

Next steps

  1. Make sure the firm owns, and can log into, the domain registrar, hosting account and every premium license.
  2. Turn on domain auto-renew and confirm your SSL certificate renews automatically.
  3. Confirm daily off-site backups exist, then test one restore.
  4. Put the schedule above on a calendar and assign each task to a named person, or price out a care plan with the questions above.
  5. Work through the security checklist once, then let maintenance keep it current.

Want hosting that handles more of this for you? Our Kinsta review for law firms explains what managed WordPress hosting takes off your plate.

Slow pages are a common sign of neglect; see our guide to speeding up a law firm website.

Your maintenance provider will usually pick one of the best WordPress security plugins for law firms.

To keep hosting and WordPress logins out of spreadsheets, see how to set up 1Password for a law firm.

If you want outside help with malware cleanup and monitoring, see our Sucuri review for law firms.
